title: Building a Docker + uv compute environment: review questions, tier 5 — Evaluate
text:
Date: 2026-11-24

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 5 of 5: Evaluate. Decide and justify your verdict before you read the answer; the criteria are the ones given in class.

1. Docker Desktop must be running
00:00:00–00:07:15

Q: A student plans to run docker build on a Mac or Windows machine without checking whether Docker Desktop is running, relying on Docker’s prompt to start it for them. Would you approve that plan?

A: No. The instructor warned that Docker Desktop must actually be running before a docker command is issued; otherwise the command will not reach the Docker daemon. Relying on Docker to prompt and start it is not the standard the class set. (00:07:04)




2. Prompting a coding agent for a Docker project
00:07:15–00:11:00

Q: A team asks a coding agent to “make a thing” for their container setup without naming the Dockerfile or the specific base image. Is that an acceptable way to set up the repository?

A: No. The instructor’s criterion is that the agent needs the actual tooling vocabulary, so the prompt should name the Dockerfile and the specific base image. A vague “go make a thing” prompt from someone who does not know the Docker words is the mistake he contrasted with the working demo. (00:08:38)




3. The default CMD in the R image (29.2.1 CMD or ENTRYPOINT?)
00:11:00–00:12:45

Q: A teammate argues that because the warm-up Dockerfile contains CMD ["R"], running docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker bash is not possible. Is that argument sound?

A: No, that is not a sound argument. CMD ["R"] only sets the default command for the 2026-11-24-docker image; the instructor said you can still pass another command, such as bash, when running the container. So CMD is not a hard lock on R. (00:12:19)




4. docker build and the required . (29 Customizing and building containers)
00:12:45–00:16:40

Q: A pull request changes docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker . to docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker, arguing that the tag is enough. Would you approve it?

A: No, I would not approve it. The trailing . is not punctuation; it is the required location argument telling docker build that the default Dockerfile is in the current directory. Since the build command needs an input location, omitting the dot leaves that input empty. (00:15:31)




5. Using --rm for risky experiments (28 Using and running containers)
00:16:40–00:20:05

Q: A student wants to test installing PyTorch directly on their own laptop because they are worried about breaking their environment. Is that the recommended approach?

A: No, not for a risky experiment. The class standard is to use a container run with --rm, because exiting removes the container and undoes the changes, like a Git reset. That makes a failed PyTorch test harmless: restart the container and nothing on the laptop is damaged. (00:19:58)




6. Choosing the base image for the Python/uv image (29.3 Choosing a base image for your Dockerfile)
00:20:05–00:27:40

Q: For the class’s Python/uv compute environment, one Dockerfile uses rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 and another uses ubuntu:24.04. Which would you approve, and why?

A: Approve the ubuntu:24.04 Dockerfile. The class switched from the R base to a Python-compatible base because the rocker/r-ver image carries unnecessary R software for this Python/uv project. The criterion was to keep the image smaller and be respectful of other people’s disk space, with Ubuntu as a good starting point. (00:23:55)




7. Pinning package versions in pyproject.toml (22 uv: pinning exact versions)
00:27:40–00:34:45

Q: A milestone project’s pyproject.toml declares cowsay>=6.1 and relies on uv.lock to keep version 6.1. Is that acceptable for a long-running analysis?

A: No, not for a long-running analysis. A >= lower bound can let a later major version, such as cowsay 7.0, be pulled during a rebuild, and a major version change is typically backwards incompatible. The class solution is to pin the packages that matter with == in pyproject.toml and set add-bounds = "exact" so uv add keeps writing exact pins. (00:31:06)




8. Copying the uv project files and enforcing the lockfile (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:35:00–00:39:25

Q: A Dockerfile copies pyproject.toml and uv.lock but omits .python-version, and the team says it is fine to use whatever latest Python is available. Is that acceptable?

A: No. The instructor said the Python version itself should be pinned because the Python version determines which package versions can be installed. He singled out PyTorch as almost never compatible with the latest Python, so relying on whatever latest Python is available does not meet the class standard. (00:35:59)

Q: A team removes --locked from RUN uv sync --locked to avoid build failures when pyproject.toml and uv.lock drift apart. Would you approve that change?

A: No. uv sync --locked is the check that pyproject.toml and uv.lock are in sync; if they are not, the build should error. Removing --locked would let the build quietly update the lockfile inside the image, so the image could stop matching the repository’s uv.lock. (00:39:14)




9. Dockerfile layer order and caching (29.1.3 Layer caching)
00:39:25–00:44:30

Q: A Dockerfile copies hello.py before RUN uv sync --locked. Would you approve that order for a project where scripts change often?

A: No, I would not approve that order for frequently changing code. Docker reuses cached layers, but a change to an earlier layer reruns that layer and everything below it. The class ordering puts the slow uv sync --locked environment install before the code copy, so editing hello.py does not force a long package install again. (00:43:10)




10. Not copying live analysis code into the image (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:49:36–00:52:15

Q: For a milestone with fast-changing EDA scripts, a teammate proposes COPY-ing all analysis scripts into the image and rebuilding after each edit. Is that acceptable?

A: No, that is not the scalable approach for active milestone work. COPY-ing all code into the image snapshots it at one moment and forces the team to track who copied what, plus commit, push, copy, and rebuild each time. The class goal was to separate compute from source code by keeping only the installed software in the image. (00:51:16)




11. Mounting the project folder instead of installing Git (28.1.2 Mounting volumes to containers)
00:52:15–00:59:35

Q: To get code into the container, a teammate proposes installing git inside the image and cloning the repository when the container starts. Would you recommend that for the course’s live-analysis workflow?

A: No, I would not recommend it as the preferred approach. Installing git in the container and cloning is valid only if the goal is to mimic a terminal, but the class preferred a mounted volume because it is a live shared drive. The mount avoids putting SSH keys or tokens in the container and avoids the problem of generating and updating a new key whenever the image is rebuilt. (00:55:24)




12. Keeping the container environment out of the mounted .venv (30.5 Why the packages go in /opt/venv)
00:59:35–01:07:00

Q: A team mounts the whole project folder, including the local .venv, over /workspace and lets the container use that .venv. Is that acceptable for a group project with different operating systems and CPU architectures?

A: No, that is not acceptable for a group project. A .venv contains the actual Python binary and packages for one operating system and CPU architecture, so it is not portable across the team’s different machines. The class standard is ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv, so the container keeps its Linux-built environment and ignores the mounted local .venv. (01:05:01)




13. Using a docker-compose.yml instead of a long docker run command (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
01:07:00–01:14:05

Q: A team records how to launch the container only as a long docker run command in a README, rather than in a docker-compose.yml. Would you recommend that?

A: No, I would recommend the docker-compose.yml instead. The class criterion is that a file records the build and run flags, can be version controlled, and makes changes trackable. A long copy-pasted docker run command is the fragile approach they contrasted with the compose file. (01:11:46)




14. The milestone Dockerfile standard
01:14:05–01:17:00

Q: A milestone submission builds a container but does not mount the project folder or render the report with uv run quarto render. Does it meet the standard the class set for this week?

A: No, it does not meet the standard. The class said the TA grades by taking the repository, building the container, and then running the analysis in that container. For this week, the container must be able to mount the needed folders and uv run quarto render must render the report inside it. (01:15:09)




15. Docker Compose as a general skill (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
01:17:00–01:20:10

Q: A teammate says Docker Compose is only for this class’s analysis environment and cannot be used to run open-source software like Actual Budget. Is that a fair judgment?

A: No, that judgment is not fair. The class showed that many open-source tools already ship a docker-compose.yml, and knowing Docker lets you start them with docker compose up. Compose was presented as a general skill for running applications, not only as a tool for this class’s analysis environment. (01:19:56)

title: Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose: review questions, tier 5 — Evaluate
text:
Date: 2026-11-24
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 5 of 5: Evaluate. Decide and justify your verdict before you read the answer; the criteria are the ones given in class.

1. Letting Claude Code build the repository
00:07:21–00:11:24

Q: A student who has never used Docker plans to skip the terminology and just ask a coding agent to “go make a container for my project.” Judge whether this is a sound plan.

A: It is not sound. The instructor’s point was that you need the vocabulary, such as Dockerfile, image and the exact image name, to put in the prompt. Those words are what steer the agent toward the correct answer. If you don’t know the words around what you are building, “that’s going to be a problem.” (00:08:06)

Q: Claude Code reports that it created the 2026-11-24-docker repository, built the image and tested it. Assess whether you can accept the result without looking at it.

A: You should not accept it unchecked. In class the agent created the folder under ~/temp instead of ~/git. It also added a README.md, a Makefile and a CMD ["R"] line that nobody asked for in the prompt. The instructor had to check where the folder went and what the Dockerfile contained before using it. (00:10:11)




2. Listing and building images (29 Customizing and building containers)
00:12:42–00:16:40

Q: A teammate’s README tells people to build with docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker, with no trailing ., arguing that Docker looks for a file called Dockerfile by default anyway. Would you approve this README?

A: No. docker build does look for a file named Dockerfile by default, but you still have to tell it where to look. It is like a function argument with no default, so you cannot leave it empty. The . means “here”, the current directory; it is not a full stop, and the class was warned not to forget it. (00:14:57)




3. Running a container, overriding CMD, and throwaway containers (28 Using and running containers)
00:16:40–00:20:07

Q: You want to try installing PyTorch but worry it might wreck your setup. One teammate says to install it on your laptop and uninstall it if things break. You propose trying it in docker run --rm -it <image> bash first. Which plan would you defend?

A: Trying it in the container is the better plan. With --rm, every change inside the container is undone when you exit, like a version of Git that automatically resets your changes. If the install goes wrong, you restart the container and nothing bad has happened to your computer. (00:19:58)




4. Choosing a base image for a Python project (29.3 Choosing a base image for your Dockerfile)
00:20:07–00:24:22

Q: A group’s project uses only Python, but their Dockerfile still says FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 because “it already builds.” A pull request changes it to FROM ubuntu:24.04. Would you approve the pull request?

A: Yes. The R image carries a lot of software installed for R that a Python project does not need. The instructor asked students to keep images small out of respect for other people’s disk space, which has become expensive. (00:23:55)

Q: A teammate argues that the group should use Alpine instead of ubuntu:24.04 because a smaller image is always better. Assess this argument.

A: It is not automatically better. Alpine is even smaller, but it may mean installing more software yourself, depending on what you need. The class treated Ubuntu as a pretty good starting point that balances size against convenience. (00:24:13)




5. Installing uv with COPY --from, and setting WORKDIR (30.2 A Dockerfile for a uv project)
00:24:22–00:27:42

Q: A Dockerfile has no WORKDIR line, so every container from it opens at /. Its author says that is fine because you can always cd yourself. Would you accept it?

A: It is better to add WORKDIR /workspace. Starting at / puts you among the operating system’s files. If you move a folder or mess something up there, everything can stop working. Setting the working directory lands everyone in a folder just for the project. (00:26:10)




6. Pinning exact versions in pyproject.toml (22 uv: pinning exact versions)
00:29:58–00:33:35

Q: A group’s pyproject.toml lists cowsay>=6.1 for a project that will run all term. A teammate says that is fine because it works today. Is it acceptable?

A: No. With >=, a rebuild next week could pull in cowsay 7.0. A change in the first version number usually breaks backwards compatibility, so behaviour you rely on in 6.x may not work in 7.x. Pin with cowsay==6.1, and set add-bounds = "exact" under [tool.uv] so that uv add writes == from now on. (00:31:06)

Q: To be safe, a teammate proposes listing every transitive dependency in pyproject.toml with ==. Critique the proposal.

A: It goes beyond what the class set out. pyproject.toml holds the explicit versions you care about, and the resolver picks compatible versions for everything else. You add a downstream package only when it actually causes trouble, as the instructor did when a dependency far below pandas updated and broke it. (00:33:16)




7. Copying the environment files and uv sync --locked (30.2 A Dockerfile for a uv project)
00:35:01–00:39:25

Q: A group whose analysis uses PyTorch deletes .python-version, arguing that requires-python = ">=3.14" in pyproject.toml already covers it. Would you approve this change?

A: No. The Python version decides which package versions can be installed. PyTorch is almost never compatible with the latest Python, so you usually have to pin an older version to get it installed. .python-version pins the interpreter the way uv.lock pins the packages, so uv doesn’t simply take the newest Python. (00:35:59)

Q: The build stops at RUN uv sync --locked because someone edited pyproject.toml by hand. A teammate proposes deleting --locked so the build goes through. Judge this fix.

A: Reject it. --locked exists to throw an error when pyproject.toml and uv.lock are out of sync. That is what you want: the build should fail loudly rather than produce something you didn’t expect. Bring the two files back in sync instead. (00:38:55)




8. Building the image and layer caching (29.1.3 Layer caching)
00:39:25–00:44:33

Q: A Dockerfile puts COPY hello.py ./ above RUN uv sync --locked. Would you approve it in a pull request?

A: No. Changing a layer reruns every step below it, so each edit to the script would rerun the slow uv sync. Put slow, rarely changing installs at the top and fast-changing code at the end. In class, appending COPY hello.py ./ as the last line rebuilt in under a second because uv sync stayed cached. (00:42:40)

Q: A reviewer rejects a beginner’s Dockerfile because it uses several separate lines instead of one combined command. Is that a fair reason to reject it?

A: No. Combining steps saves a bit of disk space and is more efficient, but it doesn’t affect the outcome. The instructor said there is nothing wrong with having more lines when you are starting out with Docker. (00:41:59)




9. Why not bake your code into the image
00:49:36–00:53:26

Q: For the milestone, a group adds COPY . . to its Dockerfile so the analysis code ships inside the image, and plans to rebuild whenever the code changes. Assess this plan.

A: It is a poor fit for work that is still changing. The code gets snapshotted into the image, so anyone opening the container has to ask when the code was copied, and by which teammate. Every change then needs a commit, a push and a rebuild, which doesn’t scale. The goal is to separate compute from source code: the image holds the software and packages, and the code stays outside it. (00:51:16)




10. Mounting the project folder with -v (28.1.2 Mounting volumes to containers)
00:53:26–00:59:33

Q: Instead of mounting, a teammate proposes installing Git in the image and cloning the repository from inside each new container. Judge this approach against mounting with -v "$(pwd):/workspace".

A: Cloning is valid with what you knew before this class, and the instructor has done it, but mounting is better. Git in the container needs its own SSH key or personal access token. Every rebuilt container makes a new key that you would have to register again. Mounting avoids that problem entirely, because you edit the same files your laptop already handles with Git. (00:54:52)

Q: A teammate wants the live shared folder set up inside the Dockerfile, so nobody has to type -v at docker run. Assess whether this can work.

A: It can’t. Mounting happens in the run process, not the build process. A build can only copy files, which gives you a snapshot rather than a folder shared with your computer. (00:56:06)




11. Keeping the image’s environment in /opt/venv (30.5 Why the packages go in /opt/venv)
00:59:33–01:06:53

Q: A teammate removes ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv from the Dockerfile because uv run hello.py still printed the cow in a mounted container on their Mac. Would you approve this change?

A: No. Without the line, the mount hands the Linux container the laptop’s .venv, which was built for one operating system and CPU architecture. Teammates may differ in both, and the instructor compared this to copying an Excel file from a Mac to Windows and hoping it runs. In class, uv deleted and rebuilt the mounted .venv, which changed the folder on the laptop itself. With the ENV line, the container uses its own Linux environment in /opt/venv. (01:02:40)

Q: A Dockerfile sets ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv on the line after RUN uv sync --locked. Is it correct?

A: No. The position of the line is flexible only as long as it comes before uv sync. Placed after it, uv sync has already installed the environment in the default .venv location. (01:03:56)




12. Docker Compose (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
01:06:53–01:14:06

Q: A team keeps its growing docker run --rm -it -v "$(pwd):/workspace" ... command in a chat message for everyone to paste. Someone proposes a docker-compose.yml instead, and another says Compose is overkill for one container. Decide which approach the team should adopt.

A: Adopt the docker-compose.yml. Pasted commands are hard to edit because you can’t click inside them. A file can be version controlled and its changes tracked, so the team relies on simple commands instead of copy and paste. The instructor granted that Compose is mainly for running several containers and may be a bit of overkill for one, but called it still very useful. (01:11:28)




13. This week’s milestone: a Dockerfile for your analysis
01:14:06–01:17:04

Q: A group checks its milestone only by running uv run quarto render on their own laptops, and the report renders. Judge whether that shows the milestone is done.

A: It does not. The TAs take your repository, build the container, and try to run the analysis inside it. The group has to confirm that, with the needed folders mounted, uv run quarto render renders the report inside the container. (01:15:01)

Q: A teammate adds a long list of extra RUN installs to the group’s image “just in case.” Assess this addition.

A: Extra tools are allowed, but this justification falls short. Adding a text editor, or system libraries that some packages need (for example for geospatial work), is fine. The instructor’s condition was that you know why you add each one. (01:16:03)

title: Docker Workflows with uv and Docker Compose: review questions, tier 4 — Analyze
text:
Date: 2026-11-24

Generated by qwen3.6-35b-a3b, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 4 of 5: Analyze. Take each one apart yourself before you read the answer; tiers 1 to 3 cover the facts, reasons and steps it relies on.

1. Docker and AI-Assisted Setup Review (28 Using and running containers)
00:00:00–00:13:56

Q: Trace the outcome of running docker run --rm -it <image> followed immediately by bash. How does this sequence override the container’s default behavior, and what does the resulting root prompt reveal about the container’s starting state?

A: The initial Dockerfile contained CMD ["R"], which automatically launches the R interpreter when the container starts. Appending bash to the docker run command replaces that default CMD, forcing the container to initialize a standard shell instead. The resulting root@...:/# prompt reveals that the container starts at the system root directory with no assigned user, showing it is a fresh, isolated Linux environment rather than a standard desktop session. (00:12:16)




2. Building a Python Container with uv (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:13:56–00:33:35

Q: Break down the Dockerfile steps used to install the Python project’s dependencies into the image. Which files are copied, what flag ensures reproducibility, and how does the build process react if those files conflict?

A: The image copies only pyproject.toml, uv.lock, and .python-version into the workspace, deliberately excluding the application code to separate environment setup from source files. It then runs uv sync --locked, which strictly compares the lockfile against the project metadata during the build phase. If the two files are out of sync, the --locked flag halts the build immediately with a clear error, preventing the creation of an image with mismatched or unverified dependencies. (00:38:26)




3. Layer Caching and Dockerfile Optimization (29.1.3 Layer caching)
00:33:35–00:51:21

Q: Examine how Docker’s layer caching affects build times when modifying a Dockerfile. How should you order instructions that install slow dependencies versus instructions that copy frequently changing code, and what is the structural consequence of changing an early instruction?

A: Docker saves each instruction as a read-only layer and only reruns a step if that step or anything above it has changed since the last build. Because installing packages and running uv sync takes significant time, these long, static setup steps should be placed at the top of the Dockerfile. Frequently changing code should be copied at the bottom so that editing a script only invalidates the final layer, allowing Docker to reuse all the cached installation layers and rebuild almost instantly. (00:42:33)




4. Volume Mounting and Cross-Platform Environments (28.1.2 Mounting volumes to containers)
00:51:21–01:06:55

Q: Differentiate between copying code into an image and mounting a local volume with docker run -v. How does volume mounting solve the problem of active development, and what cross-platform risk does it introduce regarding the .venv folder?

A: Copying code snapshots a static version into the image, requiring a full rebuild for every edit and complicating team collaboration on active scripts. Mounting a local volume with -v "$(pwd):/workspace" creates a live, bidirectional sync, allowing edits on the host to appear instantly inside the container without rebuilding. However, this introduces a cross-platform risk because the mounted local .venv folder contains macOS binaries that overwrite the container’s Linux environment, causing the container to crash or run incompatible executables. (00:59:52)




5. Docker Compose and Milestone Assignment (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
01:06:55–01:20:07

Q: Set up the components of docker-compose.yml side by side with a typical long docker run command. How does the compose file reorganize these parameters, and what specific YAML keys replace the --tag, -v, and interactive shell flags?

A: A standard docker run command bundles the image name, volume mounts, port mappings, and interactive flags into a single long string that is difficult to edit, read, or version control. The docker-compose.yml file separates these into a structured YAML layout using keys like build: (replacing --tag and pointing to the Dockerfile), volumes: (replacing -v to map host directories), and ports: (replacing -p). This structure allows developers to launch the container with a single command like docker compose up while keeping the configuration readable, auditable, and easily shared with teammates. (01:11:28)

title: Docker + uv compute environment: review questions, tier 3 — Apply
text:
Date: 2026-11-24

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 3 of 5: Apply. Work each situation through before you read the answer; tiers 1 (Remember) and 2 (Understand) cover the facts and reasons it relies on.

1. Warm-up setup and Docker Desktop
00:00:00–00:07:15

Q: You run docker images on a Windows or Mac laptop and the command does not reach the Docker engine. What check should you make before running more Docker commands?

A: Make sure Docker Desktop is actually running. If the Docker program is not started, Docker commands cannot communicate with the daemon. Start it deliberately rather than relying on a prompt to start the program. (00:07:04)

Q: You are starting a Windows or Mac computer, then locating the repository, then building the image. Put these three actions in the order required: start Docker Desktop, locate the folder containing the Dockerfile, and run docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker ..

A: Start Docker Desktop first, then locate the folder that contains the Dockerfile, and then run the build command from that folder. Docker commands need the running daemon before the build can use or pull the base image. The build uses the current directory, so the folder location must be correct before the trailing dot is interpreted. (00:07:00)

Q: You create the repository folder and run docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker ., but Docker cannot find an image definition. What file did you forget to create, and what line must it contain?

A: You forgot the Dockerfile, which must contain a base image line such as FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2. docker build . looks for that default file in the current directory. Adding the Dockerfile gives the build an image definition to use. (00:04:19)




2. Creating the repository with a coding agent
00:07:15–00:11:00

Q: You are writing a prompt for a coding agent to recreate the warm-up repository. What two specific details do you need to give it instead of saying “make a Docker thing”?

A: Tell it to create a Dockerfile and name the exact base image, such as rocker/r-ver:4.6.2. Those details let the agent create the intended file instead of guessing what Docker object you want. The demo prompt pointed toward the actual image for that reason. (00:08:06)

Q: The agent says it created the repository in a temporary folder and ran shell commands such as ls, mkdir, and docker. Before you run docker build, what do you inspect, and why?

A: Locate the folder it actually created and inspect the files, especially the Dockerfile, to confirm the base image and default command. The agent may also write extra files such as README.md and Makefile, so you need to confirm the contents before building. This keeps you from building from the wrong location or the wrong file. (00:09:26)

Q: The agent adds a Makefile and a README.md to the repository in addition to the Dockerfile. For the minimal warm-up requirement, which file must be present and what are the other files?

A: The Dockerfile is the essential file for the warm-up. The Makefile and README.md are optional extras generated from the usual templates. They do not satisfy the Docker image requirement by themselves. (00:11:34)




3. The CMD default in the warm-up R image (29.2.1 CMD or ENTRYPOINT?)
00:11:00–00:12:45

Q: You build the first-commit 2026-11-24-docker image and run docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker. What do you expect to start, and which instruction in the Dockerfile causes that behavior?

A: R starts because the warm-up Dockerfile contains CMD ["R"]. That instruction sets the default command used when no command follows the image name in docker run. It is the reason the container opens R automatically. (00:12:25)

Q: You want the warm-up image to start R automatically for a teammate, but you also want that default to be replaceable when debugging. Which instruction do you put in the Dockerfile, and what command later replaces it?

A: Use CMD ["R"] in the Dockerfile so R is the default startup command. Later, run docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker bash to replace the default with a shell. This works because a command after the image name overrides CMD. (00:17:45)

Q: You edit the warm-up Dockerfile so it has the base image but no default command. After rebuilding, what changes when you run the container with no extra command, and what do you do if you want a shell?

A: R no longer starts automatically from the project’s CMD ["R"] line. To get a shell, explicitly pass bash after the image name. The default startup is no longer controlled by that CMD line. (00:17:26)




4. Building the image with docker build and the current-directory dot (29 Customizing and building containers)
00:12:45–00:16:40

Q: You are in the root folder of the 2026-11-24-docker repository and need to rebuild the warm-up R image with the same tag. Complete the command and explain the trailing dot.

A: Run docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker .. The tag names the local image, and the trailing dot means the current directory. It tells Docker to look for the default Dockerfile in the folder where you are standing. (00:14:57)

Q: You are in a subfolder of the repository that contains hello.py but not a Dockerfile. You run docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker . there. What happens, and how do you fix it?

A: Docker looks for the default Dockerfile in that subfolder, so it does not use the repository’s Dockerfile. Move to the folder that contains the Dockerfile and run the build command there. The dot means the current location, not the project root. (00:14:57)

Q: You change FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 in the Dockerfile to an R version that is not already on your computer. What should you expect during docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker .?

A: Docker pulls the new base image before it runs the remaining build steps. That pull can take seconds or minutes depending on the connection speed. If the base image was already local, the build can finish much faster. (00:15:54)




5. Running the image with --rm, -it, and an overridden command (28 Using and running containers)
00:16:40–00:20:05

Q: You run docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker, see the R prompt, then exit. Predict whether a stopped container from that run remains available, and what happens to changes made inside.

A: --rm makes the container ephemeral, so exiting removes it. Any changes made inside are no longer available because the container was deleted. This is the reset-like behavior that makes it safe to discard the session. (00:19:29)

Q: You want to test a risky install, such as PyTorch, without harming your laptop. Which run pattern do you choose and why is it safe?

A: Start a disposable container with docker run --rm -it <image> bash, perform the install, then exit. --rm deletes the container on exit, so the install and any side effects are discarded. It is safe to start a new container if something goes wrong. (00:19:50)

Q: You type docker run --rm 2026-11-24-docker bash and expect to type commands interactively. What flag combination is missing, and what does it provide?

A: The command is missing -it. -it gives the container terminal access and passes your typed input into it. Without that flag, the run is not set up as an interactive shell. (00:16:53)




6. Choosing ubuntu:24.04 and installing uv (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:20:05–00:27:40

Q: You need to switch the warm-up R base to a Python-friendly base for the project. Which base image do you choose from the demo, and why did the demo prefer it over the R base?

A: Use FROM ubuntu:24.04. It is a smaller Linux base than the R image because it does not carry the R packages. The project can then install uv and let uv manage the Python version and packages. (00:23:46)

Q: You need uv inside the Ubuntu image, but you do not want to build it from source. Which Dockerfile instruction did the demo use, and what does --from specify?

A: Use COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/. --from names another published image as the source for the copy. This copies the uv and uvx programs into the new image while pinning the uv version by tag. (00:24:53)

Q: After writing WORKDIR /workspace in the Dockerfile, you build the image and start a container with bash. What starting directory do you expect, and what does WORKDIR do if the folder does not exist?

A: You should start in /workspace. WORKDIR sets the working directory for later build steps and for the running container. It creates the folder if it does not already exist, so you do not start at the filesystem root. (00:27:15)




7. Setting up the local uv project and exact pins (22 uv: pinning exact versions)
00:27:40–00:34:45

Q: You create a minimal uv project in the demo folder and need to add cowsay. In order, what commands do you run to create the project metadata, add the package, create the local environment, and run hello.py?

A: Run uv init --bare, then uv add cowsay, then uv sync, and finally uv run hello.py. uv add records the dependency and updates uv.lock; uv sync builds or updates .venv from the lock; uv run executes the script in that environment. This is the local workflow shown before building the image. (00:34:15)

Q: After uv add cowsay, you notice pyproject.toml declares cowsay>=6.1 instead of an exact version. For a long-running analysis project, what change should you make and why?

A: Change the dependency to cowsay==6.1 so the declared version matches the version the analysis was tested with. A >= lower bound can later pull a breaking major release, such as 7.0, when the project is rebuilt or relocked. Pinning the important package keeps the version from moving silently. (00:31:06)

Q: You want every future uv add in this project to write exact pins automatically. What setting do you add to pyproject.toml, and where does that setting belong?

A: Add a [tool.uv] table with add-bounds = "exact". This makes uv add write == versions for new dependencies instead of lower bounds. Because the setting is in pyproject.toml, all people working on the project get the same behavior. (00:32:02)




8. The uv Dockerfile: package-listing files and uv sync --locked (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:35:00–00:39:25

Q: You are writing the Dockerfile for the Python compute environment. Which three project files must be copied into the image before uv sync --locked, and why are analysis code files not required there?

A: Copy pyproject.toml, uv.lock, and .python-version into the image. These files list the packages, the locked dependency set, and the required Python version. The analysis code can be mounted later, so copying it into the image would create a stale snapshot. (00:37:44)

Q: You manually add a package line to pyproject.toml but forget to update uv.lock, then run docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker .. What do you expect at the RUN uv sync --locked step, and what command fixes it locally?

A: The build fails because --locked requires uv.lock to match pyproject.toml. Run uv lock locally to regenerate the lockfile, then rebuild the image. This makes the intended mismatch error out instead of silently updating the lockfile inside the image. (00:38:55)

Q: You need the image to use Python 3.14 rather than whatever Python a user’s computer might have. Which file controls that, and what does it contain in the demo?

A: Use .python-version, which in the demo contains 3.14. It tells uv which Python version to install or use for the project environment. Pinning the Python version matters because package compatibility can depend on the Python version. (00:36:38)




9. Layer caching and build order (29.1.3 Layer caching)
00:39:25–00:44:30

Q: You add COPY hello.py ./ after RUN uv sync --locked in the Dockerfile, then only edit hello.py and rebuild. What do you expect about the uv sync --locked step, and why?

A: The uv sync --locked layer should be cached because the package-listing files above it did not change. Docker only reruns the changed layer and the layers below it in the file, so copying the edited script is fast. This is why frequently changing code copies are placed after slow package installs. (00:43:49)

Q: You move COPY hello.py ./ above RUN uv sync --locked and then change hello.py often. What problem does that create during builds?

A: The COPY layer changes whenever the script changes, so Docker reruns uv sync --locked and every later layer for each small edit. That can make builds wait for package installation or environment setup that did not need to change. The better order is slow, stable steps first and changing code copies later. (00:42:33)

Q: You have finished building the 2026-11-24-docker image and want a teammate to skip building from the Dockerfile entirely. What are the two ways described for giving them the environment?

A: You can hand them the Dockerfile and have them run docker build, or you can publish the image to a registry and have them use docker pull to download it. The second way gives them the already built image without needing the build steps. This is the sharing goal after a successful build. (00:44:16)




10. Separating code from the compute environment (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:49:36–00:52:15

Q: Your group is doing EDA and edits scripts many times a day. If you keep a COPY instruction that puts all analysis code into the image, what maintenance problem do you predict?

A: The image snapshots the code at build time, so you must remember to rebuild after copying new code to match the repository. Teammates may then run an old copy of the analysis unless they know who copied what and when. That is not scalable for actively developed work. (00:50:47)

Q: You decide the container should hold only the installed software while your project folder supplies the source code. What change do you make to the Dockerfile that copied hello.py?

A: Remove the COPY hello.py ./ line so the image no longer embeds the analysis script. Keep the copies of pyproject.toml, uv.lock, and .python-version because those are needed to build the environment. The script can then be provided at run time through a mounted folder. (00:52:14)

Q: You considered installing git in the container and cloning the repository when the container starts, but you want the simpler approach for this project. Which approach separates compute from source more directly?

A: Use a volume mount for the live project folder instead of installing Git and cloning inside the container. The mount keeps the container focused on the installed software and avoids needing SSH keys or tokens inside the image. You can still run the mounted code with uv run in the container. (00:51:21)




11. Mounting the live project folder with -v (28.1.2 Mounting volumes to containers)
00:52:15–00:59:35

Q: You want the container to see the current directory of the demo repository as /workspace while you run an interactive shell. What docker run command do you use?

A: Use docker run --rm -it -v "$(pwd):/workspace" 2026-11-24-docker bash. $(pwd) expands to your current directory, and the -v flag mounts that folder at /workspace inside the container. This keeps the same command portable instead of hard-coding a local path. (00:57:13)

Q: You create my_secrets.txt in the mounted project folder on your computer, open the container, and edit the file there. What should you observe when you look at the file on your computer, and what does that show about -v?

A: The edit made inside the container appears on your computer because the mount is a live shared folder, not a one-time copy. It behaves like a shared drive between the container’s /workspace and your local project folder. This is how the mount was demonstrated with my_secrets.txt. (00:58:45)

Q: You are on Windows in Git Bash and need to mount the current directory at /workspace using the same volume idea. What path form does the textbook warn you to use, and why?

A: Use the doubled leading slash form, -v "/$(pwd):/workspace", in Git Bash. Git Bash can rewrite arguments that start with a single slash into Windows paths, so doubling the slash preserves the intended container path. The macOS/Linux form uses $(pwd) without the extra slash. (00:56:34)




12. Keeping the container’s Python environment in /opt/venv (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:59:35–01:07:00

Q: You mount your local project folder over /workspace, and your local folder contains a .venv built on your Mac. When you run uv run in the Linux container, what problem can the mount create?

A: The mount can hide or replace the image’s Linux .venv with your local .venv, which contains binaries for your machine’s operating system and architecture. uv may then complain that the existing virtual environment points to a nonexistent or incompatible Python interpreter and recreate .venv. This can leave your local environment broken if the container deletes or rewrites it. (01:02:40)

Q: You want the container to keep its Linux-built environment outside the mounted project folder. Which Dockerfile instruction do you add, and where must it be placed relative to uv sync?

A: Add ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv before RUN uv sync --locked. This tells uv to create the project environment in /opt/venv instead of .venv inside /workspace. The environment variable must be set before the sync step so the build installs packages in the intended location. (01:04:13)

Q: After rebuilding with that environment variable, you want to confirm the container is using /opt/venv rather than the mounted .venv. Which command do you run inside the container, and what output did the demo show?

A: Run uv run which python inside the mounted container. The output was /opt/venv/bin/python, showing that uv is resolving Python from the container’s /opt/venv environment. That confirms the mounted local .venv is being ignored. (01:06:20)




13. Docker Compose for build and run parameters (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
01:07:00–01:14:05

Q: Your docker run command now includes the image tag, a volume mount, and possibly a port. What file do you create to store those launch parameters, and what top-level key does it start with?

A: Create docker-compose.yml and start the service definition under services:. For the demo, the service is analysis-env with build: ., image: 2026-11-24-docker, and volumes: - .:/workspace. The file records the same parameters that would otherwise be typed as flags on docker run. (01:10:34)

Q: You have written the compose file for the demo project and want to build the image it describes. Which command do you run from the project folder, and what does it read?

A: Run docker compose build. It reads docker-compose.yml and builds the image from the build: . and image: settings. This replaces manually typing docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker . for that service. (01:11:09)

Q: You type docker compose up --detatch and Docker returns unknown flag: --detatch. What is the correct flag and what does it do?

A: The correct flag is --detach (or -d), so the command is docker compose up --detach or docker compose up -d. It starts the container in the background and returns your terminal prompt. The misspelled flag is not a valid Docker Compose option. (01:12:47)

Q: You run docker compose up for the demo, the container is created, and then docker compose exec analysis-env bash says the service is not running. What did the live output show, and what does that tell you to check?

A: The container analysis-env-1 exited immediately with code 0, so there was no running service to exec into. Check the container’s default command and whether it has a long-running process to keep the container alive. The compose demo was flagged as needing a fix. (01:13:50)




14. The milestone Dockerfile as a compute environment (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
01:14:05–01:17:00

Q: You are preparing the milestone Dockerfile for your analysis. What must the resulting container be able to do for the grader to run your analysis successfully?

A: The grader builds the container from your repository and runs the analysis inside it. Your Dockerfile must therefore create a reproducible compute environment with the needed Python packages installed. You should be able to mount the project folder and run the analysis in the container. (01:15:01)

Q: Your project is a Quarto report that already runs on your laptop. In the container, what command pattern do you use to render it with the uv-managed environment?

A: Mount the project folder at the container’s working directory and run uv run quarto render inside the container. uv run uses the environment that was built into the image, so the report renders with the locked packages. This is the specific goal stated for the milestone. (01:14:37)

Q: You discover the container lacks a text editor or a system tool your package needs. What kind of Dockerfile change is allowed, and what condition must you be able to satisfy?

A: Add extra RUN commands to install the missing editor or system tool, for example an editor or OS dependencies for a package. You must know why each extra item is needed for the analysis environment. The core requirement remains that the Dockerfile builds the compute environment and the report renders. (01:15:37)




15. Using other tools’ docker-compose.yml files (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
01:17:00–01:20:10

Q: You download an open-source application such as Actual Budget that ships with a docker-compose.yml defining a service with an image, ports, environment variables, and volumes. What command do you run to start it in the background, and what does it do?

A: Run docker compose up -d from the folder containing the compose file. Docker downloads any needed image, starts the service, and maps the configured port so you can reach the app in a browser. You do not need to learn that app’s normal installation steps. (01:18:29)

Q: You see a compose file with one service that exposes a web-app port. After docker compose up, where do you connect to the app?

A: You connect to the mapped port on your computer, just as you would for RStudio or JupyterLab. The compose file’s port mapping tells you which local port corresponds to the service inside its container. The app then appears in a browser on that local port. (01:19:21)

Q: You want to run one of the examples, such as Jellyfin or N8N, on an old laptop instead of your main computer. What does the compose-file approach require from that machine?

A: It needs a machine with Docker and enough resources to run the container, plus access to the compose file and image. Once Docker is available, the same docker compose up command starts the service and exposes its configured port. The choice of laptop versus cloud machine is separate from the Docker workflow. (01:19:34)

title: Python analysis images with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose: review questions, tier 3 — Apply
text:
Date: 2026-11-24
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 3 of 5: Apply. Work each situation through before you read the answer; tiers 1 (Remember) and 2 (Understand) cover the facts and reasons it relies on.

1. Listing and building images (29 Customizing and building containers)
00:12:42–00:16:40

Q: You are in ~/temp/2026-11-24-docker and type docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker, with nothing after the name. What is missing, and what do you add?

A: Add the trailing ., as in docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker .. docker build looks for a file named Dockerfile by default, but it still needs a location to look in, and you can’t leave that argument empty. The . means “here”, the current directory. It is not a full stop. (00:14:57)

Q: docker images already lists 2026-11-24-docker:latest, and you have edited the Dockerfile. Which command replaces that image, and what happens if you pass --tag pizza instead?

A: Run docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker .. Reusing the same name rebuilds that image and replaces it. The tag can be any name you like, so --tag pizza builds the same Dockerfile into an image called pizza. (00:14:13)

Q: Rebuilding the rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 image finishes in 0.2 seconds, and its FROM step says CACHED. You change FROM to an R version you have never downloaded. What do you expect from the next build?

A: The FROM step takes seconds or minutes, depending on your internet speed, because Docker has to download the new base image first. The first build was instant only because rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 was already on your computer. (00:16:15)




2. Running a container, overriding CMD, and throwaway containers (29.2.1 CMD or ENTRYPOINT?)
00:16:40–00:20:07

Q: Your Dockerfile is FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 followed by CMD ["R"]. What do you see after docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker?

A: An R session starts, with R’s startup banner, and you leave it with q(). With no command given after the image name, the container runs its default command, and CMD ["R"] sets that to R. (00:17:17)

Q: You want to start a container from 2026-11-24-docker, type into it, and have it deleted automatically when you exit. Which flags do you add to docker run?

A: Use docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker. --rm deletes the container when you exit, so it isn’t left running on your computer. -it gives you terminal access and passes what you type through to the container. (00:16:53)

Q: You want a shell in 2026-11-24-docker instead of R. What do you run, and where will pwd say you are?

A: Run docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker bash. The bash after the image name replaces the default R. pwd prints /, the root of the file system, so ls shows system folders such as bin, etc and usr. (00:18:12)

Q: You want to try installing PyTorch but worry it will wreck your setup. You do it inside a container started with --rm, then exit and start a new one. What state is the new container in?

A: It is back to the image exactly as built, because every change made in a --rm container is gone once you exit. That makes a container a safe place for risky experiments. If something goes wrong, restart the container and nothing bad has happened. (00:19:58)




3. Choosing a base image for a Python project (29.3 Choosing a base image for your Dockerfile)
00:20:07–00:24:22

Q: Your project is pure Python managed with uv, but your Dockerfile still starts FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2. What base do you switch to, and why?

A: Switch to FROM ubuntu:24.04. The R image carries a lot of R software that a Python project doesn’t need, and a smaller image is more respectful of other people’s disk space, which has become expensive. (00:23:46)

Q: You want an even smaller image and consider Alpine instead of ubuntu:24.04. What trade-off do you accept?

A: Alpine is smaller, but you may have to install more software yourself, depending on what your project needs. Ubuntu is a good starting point for most of that. (00:24:13)

Q: Your group’s analysis is in Python, but one teammate wants to make the figures with ggplot2 in R. Is a single-language image required?

A: No. One project that mixes languages is common and valid. The textbook’s example image has R and Python in the same container. (00:22:42)

Q: You work on Windows or macOS and start a shell in a container. Which operating system’s commands should you expect to use?

A: Linux, most likely some version of Ubuntu. Docker containers run on top of Linux whatever your laptop runs, so inside the container you are in the Linux world. (00:23:33)




4. Installing uv with COPY --from, and setting WORKDIR (30.2 A Dockerfile for a uv project)
00:24:22–00:27:42

Q: Your Dockerfile starts FROM ubuntu:24.04 and later runs uv sync, but the base image has no uv. Which line do you add, and where does it put uv?

A: Add COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/. It copies the uv and uvx programs out of uv’s published image into the container’s /usr/local/bin/. You are building a machine from scratch, so the copy of your setup that you hand out needs uv too. (00:25:14)

Q: You add WORKDIR /workspace, rebuild, and run docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker bash. Where does the prompt put you?

A: In /workspace. The prompt reads root@…:/workspace and pwd prints /workspace. WORKDIR changes the container’s working directory, so you no longer land in / among the system files. (00:40:54)

Q: ubuntu:24.04 has no /workspace folder. Does WORKDIR /workspace make the build fail?

A: No. WORKDIR creates the folder if it doesn’t exist and then makes it the working directory. (00:27:23)




5. Setting up the uv project locally (30.1 The project)
00:27:42–00:29:58

Q: In a folder that holds only a Dockerfile, you want a uv project that depends on cowsay. In order, what do you run?

A: First uv init --bare, which creates pyproject.toml. Then uv add cowsay, which installs cowsay==6.1 into a new .venv and records it in uv.lock. (00:29:45)

Q: Right after uv add cowsay installs cowsay==6.1, what line do you expect in the dependencies of pyproject.toml?

A: cowsay>=6.1. By default uv add writes a lower bound, even though exactly 6.1 was installed. (00:29:51)

Q: The pyproject.toml from uv init --bare only says requires-python = ">=3.14". If you need the image to use one particular Python version, is that line enough?

A: No. >=3.14 allows any newer Python, so you also need to set the Python version, which the project does with a .python-version file. (00:29:07)




6. Pinning exact versions in pyproject.toml (22 uv: pinning exact versions)
00:29:58–00:33:35

Q: Your pyproject.toml has cowsay>=6.1. cowsay 7.0 comes out next week, and you rebuild the image then. Which version do you get, and what is the risk?

A: You get 7.0, because >= allows anything newer. A change in the first number usually means a backwards-incompatible change, so behaviour you rely on in 6.x may stop working and your long-running project can break. (00:30:17)

Q: You want cowsay to stay at 6.1 no matter when the image is rebuilt. What do you change in pyproject.toml?

A: Change the dependency to cowsay==6.1. The double equals pins that exact version. (00:31:06)

Q: You want every future uv add in the project to write == instead of >=. What do you add to pyproject.toml?

A: Add a [tool.uv] table containing add-bounds = "exact". The [tool.uv] table holds the settings that control how uv behaves, so from then on uv add writes exact versions. (00:31:49)

Q: You pinned pandas with ==, but pandas still breaks after a rebuild because a package far downstream updated. How do you fix it?

A: Add that downstream package to pyproject.toml and pin it with == too. Rolling it back to the version that worked makes pandas work again. (00:32:47)

Q: Should you pin every package in the environment with == in pyproject.toml?

A: No. Pin the packages whose versions matter to you, and let the resolver choose compatible versions for everything else. uv.lock still records one exact version of each package. (00:33:16)




7. Running a script with the project environment (30.1 The project)
00:33:35–00:35:01

Q: Your project folder has pyproject.toml, uv.lock and hello.py. In order, what do you run to set up the environment and run the script?

A: Run uv sync, then uv run hello.py. uv run runs Python in the project’s environment, where cowsay is installed. (00:34:15)

Q: hello.py contains import cowsay and cowsay.cow("hello, moo."). What does uv run hello.py print?

A: An ASCII-art cow with a speech bubble that says “hello, moo.” (00:34:20)

Q: uv run hello.py works on your laptop, but your Dockerfile only installs uv. Can a classmate get your working environment from the image you build?

A: No. Every setup step must also be written into the Dockerfile. If a step isn’t in the Dockerfile, the image can’t be built with it, and if the image can’t be built you can’t share it. (00:34:45)




8. Copying the environment files and uv sync --locked (30.2 A Dockerfile for a uv project)
00:35:01–00:39:25

Q: After WORKDIR /workspace, you need the image to know your project’s Python version and packages. Which COPY line do you write, and where do the files land?

A: Write COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./. They land in /workspace, because ./ means the working directory set by WORKDIR. (00:35:09)

Q: Your project needs PyTorch, which is almost never compatible with the newest Python. How do you make sure the image installs a Python it supports?

A: Set the version in .python-version and copy that file into the image. uv installs the Python version that file names, and the Python version decides which package versions can be installed. (00:35:59)

Q: You maintain a package and want to check it against an upcoming Python release candidate before it comes out. Which file do you change?

A: .python-version. Point it at the release candidate to build an environment with the coming Python version, and check that your package still works when Python updates. (00:37:22)

Q: You edit pyproject.toml but uv.lock no longer matches it, and your Dockerfile ends with RUN uv sync --locked. What happens when you build, and is that what you want?

A: The build stops with an error at the uv sync --locked step. That is what you want. --locked requires pyproject.toml and uv.lock to be in sync, so a mismatch fails loudly instead of quietly building something you didn’t expect. (00:38:55)




9. Building the image and layer caching (29.1.3 Layer caching)
00:39:25–00:44:33

Q: You need to run docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker . again, a command you typed a few minutes ago. What is the quickest way?

A: Press the up arrow to bring back a command you have already typed, instead of retyping it. (00:39:29)

title: Docker Workflows with uv and Docker Compose: review questions, tier 2 — Understand
text:
Date: 2026-11-24

Generated by qwen3.6-35b-a3b, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 2 of 5: Understand. Explain each answer in your own words before you read it; tier 1 (Remember) covers the facts, tiers 3 to 5 put them to use.

1. Docker and AI-Assisted Setup Review (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:00:00–00:13:56

Q: Why did the instructor include the dot (.) at the end of the docker build command, rather than leaving it empty or omitting it?

A: The dot tells docker build where to look for the default Dockerfile and build context. Since Docker treats the command like a function that requires an input argument, you cannot leave it empty; you have to specify the current location (.) where the file resides. (00:14:46)

Q: Why does appending bash to the docker run command change the behavior of the container compared to just running the image name?

A: The CMD instruction in the Dockerfile sets the default command to run, such as starting the R interpreter. Appending bash to the run command overrides this default, replacing it with a standard shell prompt so you can interact with the container’s filesystem. (00:17:36)

Q: Why must students ensure that Docker Desktop is actually running before executing Docker commands in the terminal?

A: If Docker Desktop is not running, the Docker daemon is inactive, and any command you try to run will fail silently or return unhelpful errors. Keeping it running ensures that Docker can execute the commands you type without crashing or waiting indefinitely. (00:07:00)




2. Building a Python Container with uv (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:13:56–00:33:35

Q: Why did the instructor switch from using an R-specific image to ubuntu:24.04 as the base image for the Python container?

A: The R container comes preloaded with R-specific software and dependencies, making it unnecessarily large. Starting from ubuntu:24.04 provides a leaner, more generic Linux environment that is smaller in size and saves disk space while still allowing uv to install Python. (00:23:42)

Q: What is the difference between how uv handles package versions in pyproject.toml versus uv.lock, and why is it important to pin exact versions in pyproject.toml for a data analysis project?

A: uv.lock records the exact versions resolved, but pyproject.toml declares the ranges or versions. If pyproject.toml only uses lower bounds (e.g., >=3.1.1), a regenerated lockfile could install newer versions that break the analysis. Declaring exact versions (==) ensures that anyone reading the file or installing it elsewhere knows exactly what version the analysis was run with. (00:30:01)

Q: Why does the Dockerfile include the --locked flag in the RUN uv sync --locked command instead of just RUN uv sync?

A: The --locked flag ensures that the build fails if uv.lock does not perfectly match pyproject.toml. Without it, uv sync might quietly update the lockfile inside the container, causing the built image to no longer match the version-controlled uv.lock in the repository. (00:38:55)

Q: What role does the .python-version file play in the container build process, and why is it useful for package authors or long-term projects?

A: The file explicitly tells uv which Python version to install if it needs to set up the environment from scratch. It is useful for package authors who want to ensure their code works with upcoming or specific Python releases, rather than relying on whatever the latest version happens to be. (00:36:30)




3. Layer Caching and Dockerfile Optimization (29 Customizing and building containers)
00:33:35–00:51:21

Q: Why does Docker cache layers, and why is it recommended to place long-running setup steps at the top of a Dockerfile?

A: Docker caches each step’s result as a layer and reuses it if the command and its inputs have not changed since the last build. Placing long, static steps like installing software at the top means that if you only edit application code later, Docker will skip the slow installation steps and reuse the cached layers. (00:41:35)

Q: Why does changing a single instruction early in a Dockerfile force Docker to rebuild all the layers below it, and how does this affect development time?

A: Docker caches each instruction as a distinct layer. If you change an early step, the cache for that layer is invalidated, meaning Docker must re-execute that step and every subsequent step to construct the new image. This forces you to wait through slow installation steps again instead of just building the changed part. (00:42:23)

Q: Why is it counterproductive to copy your entire application code (like hello.py) into the Dockerfile during the build process for an actively developing project?

A: Copying code into the image snapshots a static version of the files at build time. If you edit the code on your host machine while working, the container still contains the old version, forcing you to rebuild the entire image to see your changes, which is inefficient for rapid iteration. (00:50:14)




4. Volume Mounting and Cross-Platform Environments (28 Using and running containers)
00:51:21–01:06:55

Q: Why did the instructor introduce the -v "$(pwd):/workspace" flag when running the container, instead of copying the code into the image?

A: The -v flag mounts the host’s current directory directly into the container, creating a live, bidirectional sync. This allows you to edit files on your computer and immediately see the changes reflected inside the container without needing to rebuild the image. (00:54:18)

Q: Why does mounting the local .venv folder into the container cause problems, and how does setting ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv solve this issue?

A: Mounting the local .venv overwrites the container’s packages with binaries compiled for the host operating system (e.g., macOS), which will fail inside the Linux container. Setting the environment variable forces uv to install the virtual environment in an isolated directory like /opt/venv, so the container ignores the mounted .venv and uses its own Linux-compiled packages. (01:00:45)

Q: Why might a team of developers working on the same project need to solve the cross-platform .venv problem, even if it works fine on one person’s laptop?

A: Team members often use different operating systems (macOS, Windows, Linux) and different CPU architectures (ARM, Intel/AMD). A virtual environment created on one system contains architecture-specific binaries that will not run on another system, breaking the environment if shared or mounted directly. (01:01:12)




5. Docker Compose and Milestone Assignment (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
01:06:55–01:20:07

Q: Why is it beneficial to replace long, manual docker run commands with a docker-compose.yml file?

A: docker-compose.yml consolidates all the parameters (like volumes, ports, and build contexts) into a readable, version-controlled YAML file. This prevents errors from typos, makes it easier to document and modify the setup, and allows anyone to run the exact same configuration using simple compose commands. (01:11:28)

Q: How does the structure of a docker-compose.yml file map to the docker build and docker run commands the instructor demonstrated manually?

A: The build: . line tells Compose to build the image from the current directory’s Dockerfile, equivalent to docker build. The volumes: section replaces the -v flag, mapping the local directory to a path inside the container. Together, they combine the setup and execution steps into one declarative file. (01:10:25)

Q: Why might a docker-compose.yml file be useful for deploying applications like personal finance or media servers in real-world settings?

A: In industry, complex applications often require multiple coordinated containers, such as a web app communicating with a database. A compose file allows you to define all these services, their ports, and their shared volumes in one place, making deployment and scaling much easier than managing individual commands. (01:08:35)

A: The hashes, locations, or package dependencies for the other operating systems. (01:01:22)

Q: What warning did the instructor give about a local .venv mounted over the container’s /workspace?

A: A local .venv is tied to your operating system and CPU architecture, so it is not portable across machines; the container should use the Linux environment it built instead. (01:02:40)




13. Docker Compose (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
01:07:00–01:14:05

Q: What file did the instructor introduce to hold the parameters for running the container?

A: docker-compose.yml, a YAML file. (01:08:10)

Q: What top-level key does the compose file begin with?

A: services:. (01:09:31)

Q: What service name did the class compose file use?

A: analysis-env. (01:09:40)

Q: What does build: . mean in the compose file?

A: Build the image from the current Dockerfile in the current location. (01:09:51)

Q: Which compose command did the instructor say builds the image?

A: docker compose build. (01:11:09)

Q: Which compose command did the instructor say starts the container in the background?

A: docker compose up --detach, or docker compose up -d. (01:11:59)

Q: What did docker compose up print before the container stopped?

A: It created the network 2026-11-24-docker_default and the container 2026-11-24-docker-analysis-env-1, then printed analysis-env-1 exited with code 0. (01:12:49)




14. The homework assignment: a Dockerfile as compute environment
01:14:05–01:17:00

Q: What did the instructor say this week’s homework assignment is?

A: Create the Dockerfile that will be the compute environment for your analysis. (01:14:10)

Q: What must the container run so your report renders?

A: uv run quarto render. (01:14:40)

Q: How did the instructor say the TA will grade the assignment?

A: The TA will take your repository, build the container, and run the analysis in the container. (01:15:01)

Q: What optional addition did the instructor mention if the container lacks a text editor?

A: You may add another RUN command to install a text editor, as long as you know why you are doing it. (01:15:41)




15. Docker Compose outside the class (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
01:17:00–01:20:10

Q: What did the instructor say many open-source tools already provide?

A: Docker Compose files. (01:17:23)

Q: What personal-finance app did the instructor use as an example?

A: Actual Budget. (01:17:36)

Q: What did the instructor say docker compose up -d does with those tools?

A: It downloads the image, runs the software, and lets you connect to the port. (01:18:29)

Q: Which other apps did the instructor list as examples that run on a port in a browser?

A: Jellyfin, N8N, and a recipe app. (01:19:03)
