title: Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose: review questions, tier 1 — Remember
text:
Date: 2026-11-24
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 1 of 5: Remember. Answer each question before you read its answer; tiers 2 to 5 build on these.

1. Warm-up exercise: a Dockerfile from a given image
00:00:00–00:04:30

Q: What did the first exercise of the day ask students to create?

A: A GitHub repository with a Dockerfile that uses a particular given image. It was review from the previous class. (00:00:00)

Q: According to the instructor, how much of a file did the warm-up solution need?

A: Essentially one line in one file, in a new repository. (00:04:19)

Q: What did the instructor do with the same warm-up task while students worked on it?

A: He gave it to a coding agent (Claude) to see what it would produce. (00:00:17)

Q: What base image did the warm-up Dockerfile in the demo repository 2026-11-24-docker build from?

A: rocker/r-ver:4.6.2, the same R version the class worked with last class. (00:15:45)

Q: What did the instructor say the warm-up exercise was for?

A: It was a way to set up the rest of the class, which builds on that repository. (00:04:25)




2. Course website updates and a Docker Desktop reminder
00:04:30–00:07:21

Q: Where can students now find the summary lecture notes?

A: On the course website. You no longer have to look in the GitHub UBC student repo for them. (00:04:58)

Q: What format does the other instructor of the course teach from, and where can you find it?

A: Slide decks. They are linked on the course website. (00:04:54)

Q: Which lecture materials stay on the private side, rather than the course website?

A: The transcript and the link. The site has only the summary. (00:05:11)

Q: What did the instructor say you can compare across the summary notes?

A: Summaries produced by different language models. (00:05:24)

Q: The lecture question-and-answer sets are written at different levels of which learning framework?

A: Bloom’s taxonomy. They range from basic factual questions to questions that need you to know what is going on under the hood. (00:05:48)

Q: Which page of the course site is for students who only want the commands that were run?

A: The command history page. (00:06:40)

Q: What must be running on your computer before any docker command will work?

A: Docker Desktop. Without it, any Docker command you run will fail. (00:07:00)




3. Letting Claude Code build the repository
00:07:21–00:11:24

Q: What name did the instructor give the new demo repository?

A: 2026-11-24-docker. (00:07:21)

Q: Which two programs did the coding agent check for on the instructor’s computer before it built anything?

A: docker and gh. (00:09:16)

Q: Which shell command did the coding agent run to make the repository’s folder?

A: mkdir. (00:09:26)

Q: In which folder did the coding agent create 2026-11-24-docker?

A: In the temp folder (~/temp/2026-11-24-docker), not in the Git folder the instructor wanted. (00:08:38)

Q: Besides the Dockerfile, which two files did the coding agent create without being asked in this prompt?

A: A README.md and a Makefile. The instructor usually asks for these, so the agent knew to make them. (00:11:24)

Q: What did the coding agent do after writing the Dockerfile?

A: It built the container and ran a script in it to test it. (00:10:37)

Q: How much did the coding agent’s run cost?

A: Fifty cents. (00:10:55)

Q: What did the instructor say you must already know before you can prompt a coding agent to build a Docker image well?

A: The tooling vocabulary and jargon, such as Dockerfile, image and the exact image name. Without it, you can’t steer the agent toward the correct answer. (00:08:06)




4. The default command: CMD ["R"] (29.2.1 CMD or ENTRYPOINT?)
00:11:24–00:12:41

Q: Which line did Claude add to the warm-up Dockerfile, beyond what the task required?

A: CMD ["R"]. (00:11:44)

Q: What does CMD ["R"] do when you run the container without any other inputs?

A: It starts R by default. (00:12:01)

Q: What analogy did the instructor use for an image’s default command?

A: If the image were a file and you double-clicked it, the default command decides what opens. Here, R opens. (00:12:28)

Q: Can you run something other than R in a container from an image whose default command is R?

A: Yes. You can always give it other parameters to turn on something other than R. (00:12:19)




5. Listing and building images (29 Customizing and building containers)
00:12:42–00:16:40

Q: Which command lists the images on your computer?

A: docker images. (00:13:03)

Q: Which tag did the image 2026-11-24-docker have when Claude built it?

A: latest, the tag Docker uses by default. (00:13:03)

Q: Which command did the instructor use to rebuild the 2026-11-24-docker image by hand?

A: docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker . (00:13:56)

Q: What is the short form of docker build’s --tag flag?

A: -t. (00:14:00)

Q: Does the name you give docker build --tag have to be anything in particular?

A: No. You can give it any name you want, even pizza. (00:14:13)

Q: Which file does docker build look for by default?

A: A file named Dockerfile, with a capital D. (00:14:46)

Q: What does the . at the end of docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker . stand for?

A: Your current location, “here”: that is where Docker should look for the Dockerfile. The instructor warned that it is not a period or full stop, and you can’t leave it out. (00:15:31)

Q: How long does the FROM step of a build take when you haven’t downloaded the base image yet?

A: A couple of seconds or minutes, depending on your internet speed, while Docker pulls it. (00:16:15)

Q: Which image did the instructor say you need some version of for this week’s milestone?

A: The R image from last class (rocker/r-ver), the image the warm-up Dockerfile pulls from. (00:15:45)




6. Running a container, overriding CMD, and throwaway containers (28.2 Docker command-line commands)
00:16:40–00:20:07

Q: What does the --rm flag of docker run do?

A: It deletes the container when you exit, so the container isn’t left running on your computer. (00:16:40)

Q: What does the -it flag of docker run do?

A: It gives you terminal access to the container and passes what you type through to that machine. (00:16:53)

Q: What started when the instructor ran docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker on the warm-up image?

A: R. The terminal printed R version 4.6.2 because of the CMD ["R"] line. (00:17:17)

Q: What did the instructor add after the image name to get a shell instead of R?

A: bash, as in docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker bash. It overrides the default command. (00:17:45)

Q: Where in the file system does a shell in the rocker/r-ver container start?

A: At the root of the computer: pwd printed /. (00:18:12)

Q: What did the instructor find in the container’s /home directory?

A: Nothing. No user is assigned in this image. (00:18:36)

Q: What happens to the changes you made inside a container started with --rm after you exit?

A: They are gone. When you go back in, any changes have undone themselves. (00:19:29)

Q: What did the instructor compare a throwaway container to?

A: A version of Git that automatically resets all of your changes. (00:19:29)

Q: What risky installation did the instructor suggest trying in a container first?

A: Installing PyTorch. If it goes wrong, you restart the container and nothing bad has happened. (00:19:50)




7. Choosing a base image for a Python project (29.3 Choosing a base image for your Dockerfile)
00:20:07–00:24:22

Q: How many students said they were working on an R project?

A: None. Everyone is on a Python project, so the demo focused on Python. (00:20:27)

Q: What did the instructor want someone to be able to do with the finished project image?

A: Pull the container and run it without setting anything up, apart from the bigger download, because everything is already installed. (00:21:18)

Q: Which languages does the Docker container in the textbook’s example have?

A: R and Python, at the same time. (00:22:26)

Q: Which R package did the instructor name as a reason he might mix languages in one project?

A: ggplot2. Projects that mix several languages are common and valid. (00:22:42)

Q: Which operating system do Docker containers run on, even on Mac and Windows computers?

A: Some version of Linux, most likely some version of Ubuntu. (00:23:16)

Q: Which base image did the new Python Dockerfile start from?

A: ubuntu:24.04. (00:23:42)

Q: Why did the instructor say not to keep using the R image as the base for a Python project?

A: It has a lot of R software installed, and he wanted a smaller image. Disk space is expensive because of the AI boom, so be respectful of other people’s. (00:23:55)

Q: Which base image did the instructor name as even smaller than Ubuntu?

A: Alpine. You might have to install more yourself, depending on what you need. (00:23:55)




8. Installing uv with COPY --from, and setting WORKDIR (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:24:22–00:27:42

Q: Which Dockerfile instruction, new this class, can copy files from one image into another?

A: COPY. (00:24:38)

Q: What line did the class use to install uv in the image?

A: COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/ (00:24:53)

Q: Which two programs does the COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 line copy, and to where?

A: uv and uvx, into the container’s /usr/local/bin folder. (00:24:53)

Q: Where did the COPY --from line for installing uv come from?

A: Straight out of the textbook and the uv documentation. (00:24:24)

Q: When did everyone in the class install uv on their own computer?

A: At orientation. (00:25:41)

Q: Which Dockerfile instruction changes the container’s working directory?

A: WORKDIR, for working directory. (00:26:42)

Q: Which working directory did the class set in the Python Dockerfile?

A: /workspace, a folder called workspace in the root directory. (00:27:15)

Q: What does WORKDIR /workspace do if the folder doesn’t exist?

A: It makes the folder. (00:27:23)




9. Setting up the uv project locally (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:27:42–00:29:58

Q: Which command created the demo project’s pyproject.toml?

A: uv init --bare. (00:28:32)

Q: Which file does uv sync create from pyproject.toml?

A: uv.lock, which is then used to install the packages. (00:28:03)

Q: What Python requirement did uv init --bare write into pyproject.toml?

A: Python 3.14 or newer (requires-python = ">=3.14"). (00:29:07)

Q: Besides typing a dependency into pyproject.toml by hand, which command adds cowsay to the project?

A: uv add cowsay. (00:29:38)

Q: Which version of cowsay did uv add cowsay install?

A: 6.1 (cowsay==6.1). (00:29:45)

Q: What did uv add cowsay write into pyproject.toml by default?

A: cowsay>=6.1, a “greater or equal” bound. (00:29:51)




10. Pinning exact versions in pyproject.toml (22 uv: pinning exact versions)
00:29:58–00:33:35

Q: With cowsay>=6.1 in pyproject.toml, what happens if cowsay 7.0 comes out next week and you rebuild the container then?

A: You get 7.0: the package updates. (00:30:17)

Q: What does a change in the first number of a package’s version typically mean?

A: A backwards-compatibility-breaking change: things in 6.x may no longer work in 7.x. (00:30:37)

Q: Which later MDS course did the instructor say covers version numbers in more depth?

A: DSCI 524. (00:30:32)

Q: What warning did the instructor give about >= bounds in a long-running project?

A: If you use “greater or equal” and the project runs a long time, there is a chance it will break when a new major version comes in. (00:30:51)

Q: Which operator pins a package to one exact version in pyproject.toml?

A: == (“double equal”), as in cowsay==6.1. (00:31:06)

Q: Which setting in the demo’s pyproject.toml makes uv add write == instead of >=?

A: add-bounds = "exact", in the [tool.uv] table. (00:31:31)

Q: How did the instructor describe pyproject.toml?

A: A general Python metadata file that other tools know how to read. Its [tool.uv] part controls how uv behaves. (00:31:37)

Q: What does uv.lock always record for each package, and which file is it created from?

A: One specific version. It is created from the pyproject.toml file. (00:32:26)

Q: What happened to the instructor even after he pinned pandas to a particular version?

A: Something far downstream updated and broke pandas, so he had to pin and roll back that package too. (00:32:47)




11. Running a script with the project environment (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:33:35–00:35:01

Q: What code is in the demo’s hello.py?

A: import cowsay, then cowsay.cow("hello, moo."). (00:33:49)

Q: Which two uv commands set up the environment and ran hello.py on the laptop?

A: uv sync, then uv run hello.py. (00:34:07)

Q: What did uv run hello.py print?

A: “hello, moo.” in a speech bubble from an ASCII cow picture. (00:34:20)

Q: What did the instructor say happens if a setup step isn’t in the Dockerfile?

A: He can’t build the image, and if he can’t build the image, he can’t give it to the class. (00:34:45)




12. Copying the environment files and uv sync --locked (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:35:01–00:39:25

Q: Which COPY line brings the project’s environment files into the image?

A: COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./ (00:35:09)

Q: Which folder does ./ refer to in COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./?

A: /workspace, because WORKDIR already changed to that directory. (00:35:09)

Q: What does the .python-version file tell uv?

A: Which version of Python to install. (00:36:38)

Q: What does the demo’s .python-version file contain?

A: 3.14. (00:36:30)

Q: Which package did the instructor name as almost never compatible with the latest version of Python?

A: PyTorch. You almost always have to pin an older Python to install it. (00:35:59)

Q: How can a package author use .python-version with upcoming Python releases?

A: To create an environment with an upcoming release candidate, to make sure the package works when Python updates. (00:37:05)

Q: Name the three environment files the Dockerfile copies, and what each one is for.

A: .python-version gives the Python version. uv.lock gives the packages and their versions. pyproject.toml is the human-readable file that controls them. (00:37:44)

Q: Which RUN instruction installs Python and the packages in the image?

A: RUN uv sync --locked. (00:38:03)

Q: What does the --locked flag of uv sync do?

A: It requires pyproject.toml and uv.lock to be in sync. If one is out of date, it throws an error. (00:38:55)




13. Building the image and layer caching (29.1.3 Layer caching)
00:39:25–00:44:33

Q: Which key recalls a command you’ve already typed in the terminal?

A: The up arrow. (00:39:29)

Q: At which step did the first build of the Python image pause?

A: The RUN uv sync --locked step. (00:40:07)

Q: Where did a shell in the new Python container start?

A: In /workspace, because of WORKDIR. (00:40:54)

Q: What did ls -a show in /workspace in the Python image?

A: .python-version, .venv, pyproject.toml and uv.lock. (00:41:03)

Q: What does Docker do with each instruction in a Dockerfile when it builds?

A: It saves each one as a layer and caches it. An unchanged layer reuses the cached version. (00:41:35)

Q: Is it wrong for a beginner’s Dockerfile to have more lines than it needs?

A: No. Fewer instructions only save a little space; they don’t change the outcome. (00:41:59)

Q: What happens to the later steps when you change one layer of a Dockerfile?

A: Docker has to rerun everything downstream of it. (00:42:33)

Q: Which R installation did the instructor say can take fifteen minutes?

A: The tidyverse, depending on how you install it. (00:43:10)

Q: Which line did the instructor add to the end of the Dockerfile to put the script in the image?

A: COPY hello.py ./ (00:43:33)

Q: Why was the rebuild after adding COPY hello.py ./ so fast?

A: It didn’t have to run uv sync again, and copying a file is very fast. (00:43:49)

Q: Which command will let someone get a published image without building it from the Dockerfile?

A: docker pull. (00:44:16)




14. Why not bake your code into the image
00:49:36–00:53:26

Q: What happens to your code if you copy all of it into the image?

A: It is snapshotted into the container. Anyone opening it has to worry about when the code was copied and which teammate copied it. (00:50:27)

Q: Which steps does every code change require if your code is copied into the image?

A: Git commit and push, then copying everything into the image and rebuilding it so it holds the right version of each file. (00:50:47)

Q: What other approach did the instructor call valid with what students knew before this class?

A: Installing Git in the container and cloning the repository from inside it. (00:51:21)

Q: What did the instructor name as the goal for separating the image from the project?

A: Separating compute from source code: the container holds only the installed software and packages. (00:52:14)

Q: Which line did the instructor remove from the Dockerfile, and which files did he keep copying?

A: He removed the line copying hello.py. He kept copying the environment files, because the container can’t be built without them. (00:52:21)

Q: What should you watch to know which machine you are typing commands into?

A: The terminal prompt. (00:52:53)

Q: Does deleting a line from a Dockerfile mean you have to rebuild the image?

A: Yes. Deleting something is a change to the container, so you must rebuild. (00:53:05)




15. Mounting the project folder with -v (28.1.2 Mounting volumes to containers)
00:53:26–00:59:33

Q: What does the -v flag of docker run stand for?

A: --volume. (00:53:48)

Q: What is the technical term for what -v does?

A: Mounting a volume: a folder from your computer appears in the container when it runs. (00:54:05)

Q: What did the instructor compare a mounted folder to?

A: A shared drive. It is not like a Google Drive sync: you are working on the same file. (00:55:34)

Q: Which Git credentials does mounting save you from setting up inside a container?

A: An SSH key or a personal access token. A key made in the container would be made new every time it rebuilds. (00:54:52)

Q: Does mounting a folder happen when you build an image or when you run a container?

A: When you run it. A build can only copy. (00:56:06)

Q: What does $ do in Bash, as in $(pwd)?

A: It pulls up a special variable or command. $(pwd) gives the current working directory. (00:56:50)

Q: What command did the instructor use to mount the project folder into the container?

A: docker run --rm -it -v "$(pwd):/workspace" 2026-11-24-docker bash (00:57:13)

Q: What might Windows users need to add to the mount path?

A: A slash. The textbook shows when you need it. (00:56:34)

Q: What file did the instructor create on the laptop to test the mount, and what did it say first?

A: my_secrets.txt, containing “i’m afraid of the dark.” (00:57:23)

Q: What happened when the instructor tried nano my_secrets.txt and vi my_secrets.txt in the container?

A: Both failed with command not found: the container has no text editor. (00:58:06)

Q: What happened in the container when the instructor added “i eat baby food.” to my_secrets.txt on the laptop?

A: cat in the container showed the new line straight away: the mount updates live. (00:58:53)

Q: Which editor did the instructor say sometimes misses that a file changed on disk?

A: Positron. You may have to tell it to refresh. (00:55:51)




16. Keeping the image’s environment in /opt/venv (30.5 Why the packages go in /opt/venv)
00:59:33–01:06:53

Q: What does the .venv folder contain?

A: The actual Python binary and the packages installed for the project. (00:59:52)

Q: What happened when the instructor ran plain python in the container?

A: bash: python: command not found. Python has to be run through uv, which knows where to look. (01:00:08)

Q: Which two CPU architectures did the instructor name?

A: AMD64 and ARM64. (01:00:45)

Q: How many combinations of operating system and CPU architecture did the instructor count for a team?

A: Four for Windows and Mac, and six if a teammate is on Linux. (01:01:08)

Q: Which file records packages for other operating systems, even though uv sync installs only for yours?

A: uv.lock. (01:01:22)

Q: Which kinds of packages did the instructor say are where cross-platform problems show up?

A: Compiled packages with C code, anything that “runs fast” in Python, such as pandas. (01:02:15)

Q: What did uv run hello.py print about .venv when the instructor ran it in the mounted container, before the fix?

A: That it ignored the existing virtual environment linked to a missing interpreter, then “Removed virtual environment at: .venv” and created a new one. It replaced the laptop’s .venv in the shared folder. (00:59:06)

Q: What warning did the instructor give about running the container with the laptop’s .venv mounted?

A: It amounts to copying the versions on your computer onto another operating system and hoping they work. Like opening a Mac file on Windows, that is not how things work. (01:02:40)

Q: Which environment variable tells uv where to put the project environment?

A: UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT. (01:04:01)

Q: What value did the class give UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT, and what is the default location it replaces?

A: /opt/venv, in place of the default .venv. (01:04:13)

Q: Where in the Dockerfile must the ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv line go?

A: The order doesn’t matter, as long as it comes before uv sync. (01:03:56)

Q: What did uv which python print in the container?

A: error: unrecognized subcommand 'which'. (01:06:00)

Q: What did uv run which python print in the mounted container after the fix?

A: /opt/venv/bin/python: it no longer looks in .venv. (01:06:20)




17. Docker Compose (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
01:06:53–01:14:06

Q: Which docker run flag might you need for JupyterLab or RStudio, making the command longer still?

A: -p, to forward a port. (01:07:09)

Q: What is the file name of a Docker Compose file, and what format is it in?

A: docker-compose.yml, a YAML file. (01:08:10)

Q: What is Docker Compose mainly for, beyond one container?

A: Running several containers at the same time, as with microservices, such as a dashboard and the database it reads from. (01:09:04)

Q: Which key does a compose file begin with?

A: services. (01:09:31)

Q: What name did the class’s docker-compose.yml give its one service?

A: analysis-env. You could call it pizza if you wanted. (01:09:43)

Q: What does build: . in the class’s docker-compose.yml tell Compose?

A: To build from the Dockerfile in the current location. (01:09:51)

Q: Which container port did the instructor give as the example for an RStudio container?

A: 8787. (01:10:15)

Q: Which entry of the class’s docker-compose.yml replaces -v?

A: volumes, which mounts the current working directory at /workspace. (01:10:25)

Q: Which command reads docker-compose.yml and builds the image?

A: docker compose build. (01:11:09)

Q: What advantages did the instructor give for keeping run options in a file instead of a pasted command?

A: Files can be version controlled, and changes can be tracked. (01:11:28)

Q: Which command starts a compose container in the background, and what does -d stand for?

A: docker compose up -d; -d stands for detach, and you get your prompt back. (01:11:59)

Q: What happened when the instructor ran docker compose up in class?

A: It created the network and container, then printed analysis-env-1 exited with code 0. A retry with --detatch failed with unknown flag. (01:12:32)

2. Creating the repository with a coding agent
00:07:15–00:11:00

The prompt and the result: the instructor asked Claude to create a repository named 2026-11-24-docker with a Dockerfile based on the image from last class. Claude created the folder (in a temp directory on his machine), wrote a Dockerfile, a README.md, and a Makefile, and committed the file (co-authored), for a cost of about fifty cents. Why the jargon matters: because he named the specific image and the term Dockerfile, the agent did the right thing. The instructor contrasted this with a vague “go make a thing” prompt from someone who has never heard of Docker, which would fail — knowing the tooling vocabulary lets you feed the agent the right information.
What the agent ran: the agent ran ordinary shell commands — ls, mkdir, docker — and checked whether docker and the gh command exist and what kind of machine it was on before writing files; the instructor walked through these as the shell commands the agent executes.
The default files: Claude wrote the Makefile and README.md on its own because the instructor’s templates usually ask for them. The Dockerfile itself only needed the base-image line to satisfy the exercise, and Claude added CMD ["R"] because it recognized an R container.
Templates: because the instructor’s machine is set up with defaults learned in DSCI 522, the agent reproduces those defaults; students with their own templates can start using them with a coding agent as well.

section: 3. Reviewing the Dockerfile: the CMD command (CMD or ENTRYPOINT?)
text:
3. Reviewing the Dockerfile: the CMD command (CMD or ENTRYPOINT?)
00:11:00–00:12:45

The minimal Dockerfile: to fulfil the warm-up, the Dockerfile only needs the base-image line; for the R image that is FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2.
CMD ["R"]: Claude added CMD ["R"], which sets the default command. The instructor’s analogy: it is like double-clicking a file and asking “what opens?” — here, R opens by default when you run the container with no other input.
Overriding the default: you can always pass a different command when you run the container, so CMD is a default, not a hard requirement.
The textbook distinction: this is the CMD vs ENTRYPOINT difference in the book — CMD holds the default that a command after the image name in docker run replaces.

title: Building a reproducible Docker + uv compute environment
section: 4. Building the image: docker build and the . (Customizing and building containers)
text:
4. Building the image: docker build and the . (Customizing and building containers)
00:12:45–00:16:40

docker build --tag <name> .: build the image by giving it a tag (--tag / -t) and the location of the Dockerfile. The tag here was 2026-11-24-docker; the tag can be anything (the instructor joked “you can call it pizza”).
The . means “here”: the trailing dot comes from DSCI 521 week 1, where . was “your current location.” docker build looks for a file called Dockerfile (capital D) by default; the dot tells it that default file is in the current directory. It is a required input, like a function argument — you cannot leave it empty.
What the build does: running it executes the steps in the Dockerfile. Because the R image was already pulled, the build was fast; if you pointed at a new R version you did not have, the pull step would take seconds to minutes depending on your connection.
You need this image for the milestone: the instructor noted the class needs some version of this R image for the week’s milestone.
Listing images: docker images shows the images on your machine; the book’s Introduction to containerization covers the image-vs-container distinction and container registries.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building a reproducible Docker + uv compute environment
section: 5. Running the image: docker run, --rm, -it, and overriding CMD (Using and running containers)
text:
5. Running the image: docker run, --rm, -it, and overriding CMD (Using and running containers)
00:16:40–00:20:05

docker run --rm -it <image>: --rm makes the container ephemeral — when you exit, it is deleted and any changes inside are undone. -it gives you an interactive terminal (Docker captures what you type and passes it to the container).
Default vs overridden command: with docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker, R started by default (because of CMD ["R"]). Adding bash after the image name overrides the default and gives you a normal shell.
Starting at the root: inside the container you start at the root of the filesystem and see the operating-system files; there is no dedicated user. For this class the container is a self-contained analysis setup, not a public service, so ownership is not a concern.
Ephemeral = safe to experiment: because --rm discards everything on exit, the instructor compared it to “another version of Git that automatically resets all of your changes” — a good place to try a risky install (he used “install PyTorch” as the example) and just restart the container if it goes wrong.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building a reproducible Docker + uv compute environment
section: 6. Choosing a base image: ubuntu:24.04 and installing uv (Python packages with uv in an image)
text:
6. Choosing a base image: ubuntu:24.04 and installing uv (Python packages with uv in an image)
00:20:05–00:27:40

Switching to a Python base: since no one was working on an R project, the goal was to swap the R base for a Python one and bundle the project’s packages so someone could pull the container and run it with everything already installed. The textbook also provides an image with both R and Python for mixed-language projects (the book’s Python and R in one image chapter); the class demoed the Python path only.
ubuntu:24.04 as the base: Docker containers run on some version of Linux; even on a Windows or Mac you are in the Linux world inside a container. ubuntu:24.04 was chosen over the R image mainly because it is smaller — the instructor urged being respectful of others’ disk space (“it is very expensive now because of the AI boom”), noting Alpine is even smaller but needs more manual installs, and that ubuntu is a good general starting point (see Choosing a base image for your Dockerfile).
Copying uv in: the COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/ line copies the uv and uvx programs out of the image uv publishes, taken from uv’s Docker guide, pinning uv’s version by tag the way a lockfile pins a package. The ghcr.io/... name is a registry path: think of it as a username, a repository, and a version number.
WORKDIR /workspace: this sets the container’s working directory (creating the folder if it does not exist). The working-directory idea comes from DSCI 521 and from R/Python file-loading — commands always need a starting point. After this, a container built from the image lands in /workspace instead of the root.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building a reproducible Docker + uv compute environment
section: 7. Setting up the uv project locally: pyproject.toml, pinning, and uv.lock (uv: pinning exact versions)
text:
7. Setting up the uv project locally: pyproject.toml, pinning, and uv.lock (uv: pinning exact versions)
00:27:40–00:34:45

Creating the project: uv init --bare creates a minimal pyproject.toml (a name, a version, and requires-python = ">=3.14"). uv add cowsay installs cowsay (6.1) and records it as a dependency; uv sync builds the .venv and installs from uv.lock.
What uv add writes by default: by default uv add writes a lower bound, cowsay>=6.1. The exact version is recorded only in uv.lock, so the project declares a range and locks one version.
Why pin with ==: the instructor flagged that a lower bound is a liability for a long-running project — if cowsay released 7.0 (a backwards-incompatible change), a rebuild could pull it and break the analysis. Pinning cowsay==6.1 keeps the declared and locked versions identical, and a version only moves when someone edits the pin (which then shows up in a diff).
add-bounds = "exact": adding a [tool.uv] table with add-bounds = "exact" makes every future uv add write == instead of >=; the setting lives in pyproject.toml, so the whole team gets the same behaviour.
pyproject.toml vs uv.lock: pyproject.toml holds the explicit versions you care about; uv.lock pins everything (including downstream dependencies) but is generated from the toml. The instructor noted that even with a package like pandas pinned, a far-downstream dependency can still update and break things, so you may pin extra packages; you do not have to specify everything, only what matters.
Running it locally: hello.py (import cowsay; cowsay.cow("hello, moo.")), then uv sync and uv run hello.py, which prints the ASCII cow.


[!WARNING]
A >= lower bound can silently break a long-running project: if the package’s major version bumps (e.g., 6.x to 7.0), that is usually a backwards-incompatible change and a rebuild can pull it. Pin the packages that matter with == in pyproject.toml.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building a reproducible Docker + uv compute environment
section: 8. The uv Dockerfile: the three files and uv sync --locked (Python packages with uv in an image)
text:
8. The uv Dockerfile: the three files and uv sync --locked (Python packages with uv in an image)
00:35:00–00:39:25

The three files: to install Python and its packages in the image you copy three files into it — pyproject.toml (which packages and which versions), uv.lock (the locked, exact set), and .python-version (which Python). These are “the files that list the packages,” not the code.
.python-version: this file tells uv which Python to install (the example holds 3.14). The instructor stressed pinning the Python version too: the Python version determines which package versions are installable, and PyTorch is “almost never compatible with the latest version of Python,” so you often must pin a Python version. It is also how a package author tests against an upcoming Python release.
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./: these land in /workspace because WORKDIR was already set.
RUN uv sync --locked: this installs Python and the packages at build time, exactly as you would run uv sync on your machine. The new --locked flag makes the step fail if uv.lock and pyproject.toml are out of sync — the instructor called these “little placeholders” so the build errors out when you want it to, instead of quietly updating the lockfile inside the image. The [tool.uv] block comes from the book’s docker-uv-renv example.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building a reproducible Docker + uv compute environment
section: 9. Building the image, layer caching, and publishing (Layer caching)
text:
9. Building the image, layer caching, and publishing (Layer caching)
00:39:25–00:44:30

Building and inspecting: docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker . now runs the COPY and RUN uv sync --locked steps; the build visibly stalled at the uv sync step because that is where it installs the environment. docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker bash lands in /workspace, and ls -a shows the copied files plus the .venv.
Layer caching: each step in the Dockerfile becomes a cached layer; if a layer and everything above it are unchanged, Docker reuses the cache. That is why people minimize steps (fewer layers, less disk), but nothing is wrong with having more lines.
Order matters: any change to a layer forces Docker to rerun that layer and everything below it. So the convention is to put the slow, rarely-changing steps (installing packages) near the top and the frequently-changing steps (copying code) near the bottom — the instructor’s example was that the tidyverse can take ~15 minutes to install, and you do not want to wait that out for a typo in a script. He demonstrated this by copying hello.py last, so a later rebuild was fast because uv sync was already cached.
Publishing: once built, you can either hand someone the Dockerfile to build, or publish the image and have them docker pull it so they skip the build entirely.
Break: a five-minute break here, then the session continued.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building a reproducible Docker + uv compute environment
section: 10. The problem with copying code into the image (Python packages with uv in an image)
text:
10. The problem with copying code into the image (Python packages with uv in an image)
00:49:36–00:52:15

The problem: for an actively developed project (milestones, fast-changing EDA files), copying all the code into the image and rebuilding snapshots the code at one moment. Then you have to worry about who copied what and when, and keep remembering to commit/push and re-copy and rebuild so the image matches.
Why it does not scale: the instructor called this “not a very scalable way of dealing with work that is actively being developed.”
A valid but inferior alternative: you could install git inside the container and clone the repository at startup; the instructor said that is totally valid and that he has done it (for example, to mimic a student’s terminal), but there is a better approach.
The goal — separate compute from source: keep the container holding only the installed software (the packages), and bring the code in some other way. So the COPY hello.py line is removed from the Dockerfile (you still keep the three package-listing files, because without them the image cannot build).
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building a reproducible Docker + uv compute environment
section: 11. Mounting volumes with -v (Mounting volumes to containers)
text:
11. Mounting volumes with -v (Mounting volumes to containers)
00:52:15–00:59:35

-v mounts a volume: -v (volume) tells Docker to “mount” a folder from your computer into the container when it runs, so the container sees your live files. -v "$(pwd):/workspace" takes the current directory ($(pwd) prints it) and places it at /workspace inside the container; using $(pwd) rather than a hard-coded path keeps the same command working on different machines.
It is a live shared drive: changes you make on your computer appear in the container and vice-versa; it is the same folder, not a synced copy like Google Drive. The instructor proved it by creating my_secrets.txt on his machine, seeing it in the container, editing it on the machine (“i eat baby food”), and watching the change appear live in the container.
Why not install git: with the mount, you do not need git (or an SSH key / personal access token) inside the container — a problem that would otherwise resurface every time the image is rebuilt with a new key. You are “just you working by yourself” on the same file, so there is no risk of clobbering a teammate’s work.
run vs build: you do the mounting in the run process, not the build process — at build time Docker can only COPY (a snapshot), but at run time it can mount a live folder.
Windows note: on Windows you may need an extra leading slash in the path (the textbook shows the per-OS forms); in Bash, the $ in $(pwd) pulls in the command’s output.
Editor note: the instructor tried nano and vi in the container and neither exists (command not found); Positron sometimes needs you to refresh to notice a file changed on disk.
The payoff: you can now verify code in the container (uv run hello.py, or uv run quarto render for your project) with the live files, so you have a test that it works locally and a test that it works in the container.


[!WARNING]
Pay attention to the terminal prompt so you know which machine you are typing on — the instructor was jumping between his local machine and the container, and mixing them up means editing the wrong environment.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building a reproducible Docker + uv compute environment
section: 12. The .venv problem across platforms and UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT (Why the packages go in /opt/venv)
text:
12. The .venv problem across platforms and UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT (Why the packages go in /opt/venv)
00:59:35–01:07:00

The .venv is not portable: the .venv folder holds the actual Python binary and the installed packages, all built for your machine’s operating system and CPU. A team spans different operating systems (Windows, Mac, Linux) and CPU architectures (amd64 vs arm64) — the instructor counted four to six “different computers” to think about. A .venv built on a Mac will not run on Windows (“you can’t just take my Excel file on my Mac, go to Windows, double click it, and expect it to run”). This is the Building images for several platforms idea: one image is built for one kind of processor.
What the mount broke: when the project folder (including its local .venv) was mounted over /workspace, it hid/overwrote the image’s Linux-built .venv; running uv run in the container then warned that the existing .venv was “linked to non-existent Python interpreter” (a macOS aarch64 Python), removed .venv, and recreated it.
The uv.lock already knows all platforms: uv.lock records the package locations/hashes for the other operating systems too — uv sync just did not install them for you locally because you do not need them on your machine. The image build, however, is on Linux and must install the Linux set.
The fix — ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv: set this environment variable in the build (it must be set before uv sync) to tell uv to put the project’s virtual environment in /opt/venv instead of .venv inside the project folder. Then the container ignores the mounted local .venv and uses the Linux environment it built, making the image portable across the team’s machines.
Verification: after rebuilding, uv run which python inside the container returns /opt/venv/bin/python, confirming the container uses /opt/venv and not the mounted .venv.


[!WARNING]
A local .venv is tied to one operating system and CPU architecture. Mounting your project folder over the image’s /workspace can make uv in the container discard your Mac/Windows .venv and build a Linux one in its place, which then no longer works on your machine. Keep the container’s environment in /opt/venv with UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building a reproducible Docker + uv compute environment
text:
13. Docker Compose (Containers: Docker Compose)
01:07:00–01:14:05

Why Compose: as the docker run command accumulates flags (-v, and -p for ports when using JupyterLab or RStudio on port 8787), it becomes long and painful to edit (you cannot click into the middle of a pasted command to fix it). A docker-compose.yml file records all of the run parameters, and a file is nicer than a command because it can be version controlled and tracked.
What the file holds: a docker-compose.yml is a YAML file (like pyproject.toml) that lists, under services:, each container and how to launch it — for this project one service, analysis-env, with build: . (build from the current Dockerfile), image: 2026-11-24-docker (the tag to build into), volumes: (.:/workspace), and optionally ports:.
Multiple containers: the instructor noted that one service is “a little bit overkill” here but still useful; compose is really for running several containers at once (microservices, for example a dashboard plus its database) where you want separation between the pieces.
The commands: docker compose build reads the file and builds the image; docker compose up starts the container (named after the folder and service, e.g., 2026-11-24-docker-analysis-env-1); docker compose up --detach (up -d) starts it in the background so the prompt returns.
It did not work live: in this session docker compose up created the container but it immediately exited with code 0, and the follow-on exec calls failed (“service not running”); the instructor said he would fix the demo next class. The point of the file is that it is reading all of those docker run flags and applying them.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building a reproducible Docker + uv compute environment
section: 14. The homework assignment: a Dockerfile as compute environment
text:
14. The homework assignment: a Dockerfile as compute environment
01:14:05–01:17:00

The task: this week’s homework is to create the Dockerfile that is the compute environment for your analysis — essentially a copy of the example built in class (see the demo repository). The container should replicate your compute environment, be able to mount the folders that need mounting, and run uv run quarto render so that your report renders inside the container.
What you already have: you already have the analysis running on your local machine and a pyproject.toml; the new part is making sure the container builds and the report renders in it.
How it is graded: the TA takes your repository, builds the container, and runs the analysis in it. The overarching goal is a reproducible compute environment: hand someone the Dockerfile (or an image) and the analysis is fully contained.
Optional extras: you may add other RUN commands for things the container lacks (the instructor noted it has no text editor, so you might add one to edit/inspect files), or the system tools some packages need (his example was geospatial analysis, which needs many system tools and the underlying libraries those Python packages are built on). The requirement is that you understand why you are installing each thing.
Main deliverable: the Dockerfile is the most important thing for this week; the instructor will get Compose working in a future class.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building a reproducible Docker + uv compute environment
section: 15. Docker Compose outside the class (Containers: Docker Compose)
text:
15. Docker Compose outside the class (Containers: Docker Compose)
01:17:00–01:20:10

Compose is a general skill: many open-source tools ship a docker-compose.yml, so if you know your way around Docker you can stand up whole applications with docker compose up — no need to learn each tool’s install steps.
Example — Actual Budget: a personal-finance app (similar to Firefly III) that you can run on your own computer or “a laptop in your closet.” Its compose file defines one service (actual-server), an image, ports, environment variables, volumes, and a health check; docker compose up -d downloads the image, runs the software, and exposes the port, giving you your own personal-finance app in a browser.
More examples: the instructor listed Jellyfin (serve movies/media), N8N (AI automation), and a recipe app, all of which “run like RStudio, just running on a port in a browser”; you just have to find a machine to run them on (an old laptop or a paid cloud machine).
Tie-back: the same compose-file skill used for the class’s compute environment is the skill used to deploy these apps; Docker is not only for reproducible analysis.

section: Building the uv image and mounting the project folder
text:
Building the uv image and mounting the project folder
docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker .                            # now runs uv sync --locked inside
docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker bash                       # lands in /workspace
docker run --rm -it -v "$(pwd):/workspace" 2026-11-24-docker bash # mount current dir at /workspace
# inside the container:
uv tree                  # show the dependency tree (cowsay v6.1)
uv run which python      # -> /opt/venv/bin/python (after ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv)
-v "$(pwd):/workspace" mounts your live project folder, and $(pwd) keeps the path portable across machines; the ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv line in the Dockerfile keeps the container’s Linux environment out of the mounted folder.

title: Building a reproducible Docker + uv compute environment
text:
Docker Compose
docker compose build               # build the image described in docker-compose.yml
docker compose up                  # create and start the container (exited immediately; see "what went wrong")
docker compose up --detach         # start in the background (the flag is --detach, not --detatch)
docker compose ps                  # list the project's running containers
docker compose exec analysis-env bash   # run a command in the running service

4. The default command: CMD ["R"] (29.2.1 CMD or ENTRYPOINT?)

section: 5. Listing and building images (27.7 Image vs container?)
text:
5. Listing and building images (27.7 Image vs container?)
00:12:42–00:16:40

docker images lists the images on your computer. Claude had already built 2026-11-24-docker:latest. latest is the tag Docker uses when you don’t give one.
Building by hand: docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker .. The --tag (-t) value is any name you like, even pizza. Reusing an existing name rebuilds and replaces that image.
The trailing .: docker build looks for a file named Dockerfile (capital D) by default, but you still have to tell it where to look. The . means “here”, in the current directory. This is the . from the first week of 521. Think of it as a function argument that has no default, so you must pass it.
Base images are pulled once: the rebuild finished almost instantly because rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 was already downloaded from last class. A base image you don’t have yet makes that FROM step take seconds or minutes, depending on your connection. You need some version of this image for this week’s milestone.


[!WARNING]
Don’t forget the . at the end of docker build --tag <name> .. It is not a full stop; it tells Docker where the Dockerfile is.

section: 6. Running a container, overriding CMD, and throwaway containers (28.2 Docker command-line commands)
text:
6. Running a container, overriding CMD, and throwaway containers (28.2 Docker command-line commands)
00:16:40–00:20:07

docker run --rm -it <image>:

--rm deletes the container when you exit, so it isn’t left running on your computer.
-it gives you terminal access and passes what you type through to the container.
The image name says which machine to start. Here it started R because of CMD ["R"].

Overriding the default: docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker bash replaces R with bash. You get a normal shell, like Git Bash or the macOS terminal, with full access to that Linux machine.
You start at the root of the file system: pwd printed /, and ls showed system folders (bin, etc, opt, usr, …). /home was empty because the image has no user. For this course everyone uses the container as a shared analysis setup, not a service for the public, so ownership and users don’t matter much.
Changes don’t survive: with --rm, everything you changed inside the container is gone after you exit. That makes containers a safe place to try risky things, such as installing PyTorch. If it goes wrong, restart the container and nothing bad has happened. The instructor compared it to a version of Git that automatically resets all your changes.

7. Choosing a base image for a Python project (29.3 Choosing a base image for your Dockerfile)
00:20:07–00:24:22

The goal: an image that already has the whole project environment installed. Anyone who pulls it can run your analysis without setting anything up, apart from the larger download.
Everyone in the class is on a Python project, so the demo swapped the R base image for a Python setup that uses uv. The textbook’s example image (Python and R in one image, repository docker-uv-renv) has both R and Python. Mixing languages in one project is common and valid, for example to use ggplot2 for plots.
Containers run Linux: even on a Mac or Windows laptop, inside a container you are in the Linux world, most likely some version of Ubuntu. The new Dockerfile starts FROM ubuntu:24.04.
Why not the R image: it carries a lot of R software you don’t need. Keep images small out of respect for other people’s disk space, which has become expensive. Smaller bases such as Alpine exist but may mean installing more yourself. Ubuntu is a good starting point.

text:
8. Installing uv with COPY --from, and setting WORKDIR (30.2 A Dockerfile for a uv project)
00:24:22–00:27:42

COPY from another image: COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/ copies the uv and uvx programs out of uv’s published image into the container’s /usr/local/bin/.

Read the image name like a GitHub path: registry/owner, repository, then the version tag.
This line comes straight from uv’s Docker guide and the textbook.

Why install uv at all: you are building a machine from scratch. Everyone installed uv at orientation, so the “copy of my machine” you hand out has to have it too.
WORKDIR /workspace: changes the container’s working directory. When it starts, you land in a project folder instead of /, where moving the wrong system folder could break everything. The folder is created if it doesn’t exist.
Working directories never go away: from 521 onward, every tool needs to know its starting point, whether it is called pwd, cd or WORKDIR.

section: 9. Setting up the uv project locally (30.1 The project)
text:
9. Setting up the uv project locally (30.1 The project)
00:27:42–00:29:58

What uv needs: a pyproject.toml. uv sync creates uv.lock, and the lockfile is what installs the packages.
uv init --bare created the pyproject.toml, with a name, a version (your milestone numbering doesn’t matter much) and requires-python = ">=3.14".
Adding a dependency: you can type it into dependencies by hand, or run uv add cowsay. Here it installed cowsay==6.1 and wrote cowsay>=6.1 into pyproject.toml.
The image only gets this far on its own: uv is now installed in the image. What remains is getting the project’s packages installed in the container, and that still has to work on your own machine first.

title: Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose
section: 10. Pinning exact versions in pyproject.toml (22 uv: pinning exact versions)
text:
10. Pinning exact versions in pyproject.toml (22 uv: pinning exact versions)
00:29:58–00:33:35

The >= problem: cowsay>=6.1 allows any newer version. If cowsay 7.0 comes out next week and you rebuild the lockfile and image next week, you get 7.0.
Major versions break things: a change in the first number usually means a backwards-incompatible change (more in 524). Something you rely on in 6.x may not work in 7.x.
Pin with ==: write cowsay==6.1. Make uv add do this from now on with a [tool.uv] table in pyproject.toml (see 22.3 Making uv add write exact versions):
[tool.uv]
# `uv add` writes an exact version (==)
add-bounds = "exact"
pyproject.toml is general Python metadata that many tools read. The [tool.uv] table holds the settings that control how uv itself behaves.
uv.lock vs pyproject.toml: the lockfile always records one exact version, but it is generated from pyproject.toml. List the packages you care about in pyproject.toml with ==, and let the resolver choose compatible versions for everything else.
Downstream dependencies can still move: the instructor has pinned pandas and still had something far downstream update and break it. The fix was to pin that package in pyproject.toml too.


[!WARNING]
A >= bound in a long-running project can silently pull in a new major version the next time the lockfile or image is rebuilt, and break your analysis. Pin the packages your results depend on with ==.

section: 11. Running a script with the project environment
text:
11. Running a script with the project environment
00:33:35–00:35:01

hello.py (in the demo repository):
import cowsay

cowsay.cow("hello, moo.")
Locally: uv sync sets up the environment, then uv run hello.py runs Python in that environment and prints an ASCII cow saying “hello, moo.”
Next step: everything works on the laptop. To hand it to the class it has to be in the Dockerfile, because if it isn’t in the Dockerfile the image can’t be built, and if it can’t be built it can’t be shared.
Same process inside the image: the container has to repeat exactly what you just did locally.

title: Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose
section: 12. Copying the environment files and uv sync --locked (30.7 When uv.lock does not match pyproject.toml)
text:
12. Copying the environment files and uv sync --locked (30.7 When uv.lock does not match pyproject.toml)
00:35:01–00:39:25

COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./ copies the three files into ./. Because of WORKDIR, that is /workspace.
.python-version (contents: 3.14) tells uv which Python to install. uv.lock only locks packages, and this file locks the interpreter. This matters because the Python version decides which package versions can be installed. For example, PyTorch is almost never compatible with the newest Python, so you usually have to pin an older one to get the neural-network stack installed.

Package authors (524) can also point this file at an upcoming Python release candidate, to check that their package will work when Python updates.

The three files:

.python-version gives the Python version.
uv.lock gives the exact packages and versions.
pyproject.toml is the human-readable file that controls them.

RUN uv sync --locked does what you would do on a fresh project, but --locked requires pyproject.toml and uv.lock to agree. If one is out of date, the build errors. You want it to fail loudly instead of building something you didn’t expect.

title: Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose
section: 13. Building the image and layer caching (29.1.3 Layer caching)
text:
13. Building the image and layer caching (29.1.3 Layer caching)
00:39:25–00:44:33

Rebuild with the same command: use the up arrow to recall a command instead of retyping it. The build paused on the RUN uv sync --locked step, which was installing Python and the packages exactly as you would on your own computer.
Inside the new container: pwd showed /workspace straight away. ls -a showed .python-version, .venv, pyproject.toml and uv.lock. Use -a, because some of those files are hidden.
Layers: each instruction becomes a cached layer. When a layer and everything above it are unchanged, Docker reuses the cache. That is why many Dockerfiles squeeze work into few instructions to save space (see 29.1.4 Guidelines for RUN commands). The outcome is the same either way, and more lines are fine when you are starting out.
Order by how often things change: changing a layer reruns everything below it. Put slow installs near the top and fast-changing files, like your code, near the bottom. Otherwise a typo fix in a script could trigger a 15-minute tidyverse reinstall.

Demo: adding COPY hello.py ./ as the last line rebuilt in under a second. Only that step ran, and uv run hello.py then worked inside the container.

Sharing: you can hand someone the Dockerfile to build, or (coming this week) publish the image so they can docker pull it, as with any other image (see 27.8 What is a container registry?).

title: Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose
section: 14. Why not bake your code into the image (30.4 Run the project in a container)
text:
14. Why not bake your code into the image (30.4 Run the project in a container)
00:49:36–00:53:26

The problem: during the milestones you change files constantly (EDA, analysis). COPYing code, or even COPYing everything, snapshots it into the image. Anyone opening the container then has to ask when the code was copied, and by which teammate.
It doesn’t scale: every change means commit, push, and rebuild the image so it holds the right version of each file.
Cloning inside the container: you could install Git in the image and clone the repository from inside the container. With what you knew before today that is valid, and the instructor has done it to mimic a student’s terminal. There is a better way.
The goal: separate compute from source code: the image holds the installed software and packages, and the code lives outside it. The COPY hello.py ./ line was removed and the image rebuilt. Removing a line is a change to the image too. The environment files still have to be copied, because the image can’t be built without them.
Watch your prompt: you will jump between the laptop and the container. The terminal prompt is how you know which machine you are typing into.

title: Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose
section: 15. Mounting the project folder with -v (28.1.2 Mounting volumes to containers)
text:
15. Mounting the project folder with -v (28.1.2 Mounting volumes to containers)
00:53:26–00:59:33

-v (--volume) mounts a folder: at run time it makes a folder from your computer appear inside the container, like a shared drive. Edits on either side are edits to the same file, not a sync.
The command: docker run --rm -it -v "$(pwd):/workspace" 2026-11-24-docker bash.

In Bash, $( ) runs a command and substitutes its output, so $(pwd) is your current folder.
The current folder appears at /workspace in the container.
Windows users may need a leading slash, /$(pwd). The textbook section shows each shell.

Demo: the instructor created my_secrets.txt on the laptop (“i’m afraid of the dark.”), and it appeared in the container. He then added a line on the laptop (“i eat baby food.” He says applesauce is great trail-running food), and cat in the container showed the new line immediately.
Why not Git in the container: it would need its own SSH key or personal access token. A rebuilt container would make a new key each time, so you’d re-register keys over and over. Mounting avoids that problem, which 521 solved on your laptop.
Run, not build: mounting happens at docker run. A build can only copy.
Testing in both places: you can still run uv run hello.py (for you, uv run quarto render ...) inside the container. That checks your work on your laptop and in the container.
Editor caveat: Positron sometimes doesn’t notice a file changed on disk, so you may need to refresh it.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose
section: 16. Keeping the image’s environment in /opt/venv (30.5 Why the packages go in /opt/venv)
text:
16. Keeping the image’s environment in /opt/venv (30.5 Why the packages go in /opt/venv)
00:59:33–01:06:53

.venv holds the actual Python binary and the project’s packages. Plain python doesn’t exist in the container (bash: python: command not found), and uv run knows to look in .venv.
The mount brings your laptop’s .venv with it: teammates’ computers differ in operating system (Windows, macOS, Linux) and CPU architecture (AMD64 vs ARM64), which gives up to six combinations. uv sync installs only for the system it runs on, although uv.lock records packages for every platform. The image was built under Linux, but the mount covered /workspace with the Mac’s .venv. Packages with compiled code (anything that “runs fast”, like pandas) are where this breaks. The textbook’s Building images for several platforms explains why an image is built for one kind of processor.
The fix, an environment variable set at build time: UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT tells uv where to put and find the project environment. Its position doesn’t matter as long as it comes before uv sync. The final Dockerfile:
FROM ubuntu:24.04

# how to install uv
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

WORKDIR /workspace

ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./
RUN uv sync --locked
Checking it: after rebuilding (uv sync reran because the steps below the change rerun), uv run which python inside the mounted container printed /opt/venv/bin/python. The container now ignores the mounted .venv and uses its own Linux environment, so the image works whoever’s laptop the project folder comes from.


[!WARNING]
Without UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT, a mounted project folder hands the container your laptop’s .venv. That is like copying a Mac program onto Windows and hoping it runs. In class, uv in the container deleted the mounted .venv and rebuilt it, which changes the folder on your own computer.

title: Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose
text:
17. Docker Compose (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
01:06:53–01:14:06

Why: docker run commands keep growing: --rm, -it, -v, and a -p port for tools like JupyterLab or RStudio. Pasted commands are hard to edit because you can’t click inside them. A file can be version controlled and its changes tracked.
docker-compose.yml is a YAML file listing how to build and run containers. Its main use is running several containers together (microservices, for example a dashboard and its database kept separate). With one container it is a little overkill, but still useful. The class’s file (docker-compose.yml):
services:
  analysis-env:
    build: .
    image: 2026-11-24-docker
    volumes:
      - .:/workspace

services: lists the containers. analysis-env is just a name (it could be pizza).
build: . builds from the Dockerfile in this folder.
image: names the image, like --tag.
ports: maps ports when needed, for example <host port>:8787 for an RStudio container. The class left ports out.
volumes: replaces -v, and can mount several folders. One more volume line in the template was deleted and left for Thursday, 2026-11-26.

Commands: docker compose build reads the file and builds. docker compose up --detach (-d) starts the container in the background and gives your prompt back.
Live demo didn’t work: the container exited straight away and couldn’t be reached. The instructor will fix the demo for next class. In principle Compose turns the file into the same flags as the docker run command used earlier.

text:
18. This week’s milestone: a Dockerfile for your analysis
01:14:06–01:17:04

Main task: write the Dockerfile that is the compute environment for your group’s analysis. It is almost copy-paste from today’s example.
What it must do: you should be able to mount the folders that need mounting and run uv run quarto render on your report inside the container, and have it render.
How it is graded: TAs take your repository, build the image, and try to run the analysis in the container. Your pyproject.toml and analysis should already exist, and this adds the container.

title: Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose
text:
19. Docker Compose outside the course
01:17:04–01:20:07

Ready-made Compose files: many open-source tools ship a docker-compose.yml, so you don’t need to know how to install them.
Example, Actual Budget (similar to Firefly III): personal finance software. Its Compose file defines one service, actual server, with an image, ports, environment variables, volumes and a health check. docker compose up -d downloads the image and starts it, and you connect in the browser on that port.
Other examples: Jellyfin (serving movies and media), n8n (AI automation), and a recipe manager. They are web apps running on a port, like RStudio.
Where to run them: any machine you like, from an old laptop in a closet to a paid cloud machine. Containers are a skill beyond compute environments.

title: Docker, uv, and Docker Compose for a Reproducible Analysis Environment
text:
2. Docker image and container review

Image vs container: An image is the buildable snapshot; a container is a running or stopped instance of that image. See the textbook’s 27.7 Image vs container?.
docker images: Lists local images and shows DISK USAGE and CONTENT SIZE. The live output included 2026-11-24-docker:latest, rocker/r-ver:4.6.2, ubuntu:24.04, and other images.
docker build: Builds an image from a Dockerfile.

docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker .
--tag names the local image.
The final . is the build context, usually the current directory. Daniel stressed that it is not punctuation; it means “look for the Dockerfile here.”

docker run:

--rm removes the container when it exits, so changes inside are not preserved.
-it gives interactive terminal access.
A command after the image name replaces the image’s default CMD.
Example:
docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker
docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker bash
The first command ran the default CMD ["R"]; the second replaced it with bash.

Default command analogy: Daniel compared CMD ["R"] to double-clicking a file: it says what opens by default when the container is run with no other command.
Container starting point: Running bash in the warm-up R container started at /, the root of the container’s Linux filesystem. The home directory was empty.
Ephemeral containers: Because --rm deletes the container on exit, changes inside the container are discarded. Daniel compared this to an automatic reset and recommended containers for testing risky installs.

title: Docker, uv, and Docker Compose for a Reproducible Analysis Environment
section: 3. uv project files and exact version pins
text:
3. uv project files and exact version pins

uv init --bare: Creates a minimal uv project, including pyproject.toml.
uv add cowsay: Adds a package and updates the project files. The live output showed:
Using CPython 3.14.3
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Resolved 2 packages in 126ms
Installed 1 package in 7ms
 + cowsay==6.1
pyproject.toml: Declares the project name, version, Python requirement, and dependencies. The class version pinned cowsay==6.1 and set:
[tool.uv]
# `uv add` writes an exact version (==)
add-bounds = "exact"
Exact pins vs lower bounds:

cowsay>=6.1 allows newer versions, including potentially breaking major-version changes.
cowsay==6.1 records the exact version the analysis was run with.
Daniel said data analysis projects should usually pin exact versions, while packages being published to other people should usually declare ranges.
uv add can write lower bounds by default; add-bounds = "exact" makes it write ==.
Existing lower bounds do not automatically convert; you may need to re-add a package with an exact version.

uv.lock: Records the locked dependency graph. It can contain information for multiple operating systems, but uv sync installs only what the current system needs.
.python-version: Tells uv which Python version to use for the project. The demo file contained:
3.14
Daniel emphasized that Python version matters because some packages, such as PyTorch, are not always compatible with the newest Python release.
uv run hello.py: Runs a Python script inside the project’s uv environment. The demo script used cowsay to print a short message.

title: Docker, uv, and Docker Compose for a Reproducible Analysis Environment
text:
4. Building a uv project image
The class built the following Dockerfile in the demo repository:
FROM ubuntu:24.04

# how to install uv
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

WORKDIR /workspace

ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./
RUN uv sync --locked

FROM ubuntu:24.04:

Starts from Ubuntu Linux.
Daniel said most Docker containers run some version of Linux even when the host is Windows or macOS.
Ubuntu was chosen as a reasonable starting point; smaller images such as Alpine exist but may require installing more system tools.

COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/:

Copies the uv and uvx programs from the official uv image.
The tag 0.13.7 pins the uv version, similar to how a lockfile pins a package.
This line follows uv’s Docker installation guide.

WORKDIR /workspace:

Sets the working directory for later build steps and for containers started from the image.
The project folder will be mounted at /workspace.

COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./:

Copies only the files needed to install the environment.
Does not copy the analysis code.
This supports layer caching: changing code files does not force package installation to rerun.

RUN uv sync --locked:

Installs Python and the packages from uv.lock into the image.
--locked makes the build fail if uv.lock is out of sync with pyproject.toml.
Daniel described this as a deliberate placeholder: if the files do not match, the build should stop.

Layer caching:

Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer.
If a layer and all layers above it are unchanged, Docker can reuse the cached layer.
Changing one layer reruns that layer and every layer below it.
Slow, rarely changing steps such as installing software should go near the top; frequently changing files should go near the end.
Daniel said starting with more Dockerfile lines is not wrong; layer order is an efficiency concern, not a correctness requirement.

Related textbook sections:

29 Customizing and building containers
29.1.3 Layer caching
30 Python packages with uv in an image
22 uv: pinning exact versions

title: Docker, uv, and Docker Compose for a Reproducible Analysis Environment
section: 5. Separating code from the installed environment
text:
5. Separating code from the installed environment

Problem with copying code into the image:

If the Dockerfile copies all analysis files into the image, every code change requires rebuilding the image.
The image becomes a snapshot of the code at build time.
This makes active EDA or group work harder because the container may contain stale code.

Mounting the project folder:

docker run -v "$(pwd):/workspace" ... mounts the current host folder into /workspace in the container.
The mount is live: files edited on the host are visible in the container, and files changed in the container can affect the host folder.
Daniel compared it to a shared drive, not a Google Drive sync: you are working on the same files.
The demo used my_secrets.txt to show that editing the file on the host changed what cat my_secrets.txt printed inside the container.

Why mount instead of installing Git in the container:

Installing Git inside the container raises SSH key and token problems.
The container would need credentials for git pull / git push.
A mounted volume avoids needing Git credentials inside the container for normal development.

Editor refresh:

Daniel warned that Positron may not immediately notice a file changed on disk.
You may need to refresh the file in the editor after external changes.

Build vs run:

COPY happens during docker build; it snapshots files into the image.
-v happens during docker run; it mounts a live host folder into the container.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Docker, uv, and Docker Compose for a Reproducible Analysis Environment
text:
6. Keeping the virtual environment in /opt/venv

The problem:

By default, uv uses a .venv folder inside the project.
If the project folder is mounted at /workspace, the host’s .venv can hide or replace the image’s environment.
The host .venv may contain Python binaries and packages for your host operating system, not for the container’s Linux environment.
Daniel compared this to copying a Mac .venv onto a Windows machine and expecting it to work.

Live warning from the terminal:

Before the ENV fix, uv run inside the mounted container reported that it was ignoring an existing virtual environment linked to a non-existent Python interpreter.
It then printed:
Removed virtual environment at: .venv
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
This is the dangerous behavior to avoid: the container can remove or overwrite the host-side .venv in the mounted project folder.

Fix:

Add:
ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv
before RUN uv sync --locked.
This tells uv to store the project virtual environment at /opt/venv, outside the mounted /workspace folder.
The image builds the Linux packages into /opt/venv.
When the project folder is mounted, uv should ignore the mounted .venv and use /opt/venv.

Checking the environment:

uv tree listed the project and cowsay v6.1.
uv which python failed because which is not a uv subcommand.
uv run which python printed:
/opt/venv/bin/python
That confirmed the container was using the image-built environment.

Portability:

Teams may have different operating systems and CPU architectures, for example AMD/Intel amd64 and Apple silicon arm64.
The container should contain a Linux-compatible environment.
Keeping the environment inside the image, rather than in the mounted project folder, makes the image more portable.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Docker, uv, and Docker Compose for a Reproducible Analysis Environment
text:
7. Docker Compose

Purpose:

Docker Compose stores container launch parameters in a YAML file.
It replaces long, repeated docker build and docker run commands.
The file can be version-controlled and shared.

File name: docker-compose.yml.
Class file:
services:
  analysis-env:
    build: .
    image: 2026-11-24-docker
    volumes:
      - .:/workspace

services: lists the containers to run.
analysis-env is the service name.
build: . builds from the Dockerfile in the current directory.
image: 2026-11-24-docker names the image.
volumes: - .:/workspace mounts the current folder into the container.

Common commands:

docker compose build: builds the image from the compose file.
docker compose up: starts the service.
docker compose up --detach: starts the service in the background.
docker compose ps: lists running compose containers.
docker compose exec <service> bash: runs a command inside a running container.

Live demo issue:

docker compose up created the container and printed:
Attaching to analysis-env-1
analysis-env-1 exited with code 0
The container did not stay running.
Daniel said he would fix the demo for next class.

Compose outside the course:

Many open-source applications ship their own compose files.
Examples mentioned included Actual Budget, Jellyfin, and n8n.
In those cases, docker compose up can start a complete software stack, not just an analysis environment.

Related textbook section: 33 Containers: Docker Compose

Goal: Create a Dockerfile that is the compute environment for your analysis.
Expected behavior:

The container should replicate the compute environment needed for your project.
You should be able to mount the necessary folders into the container.
You should be able to run the analysis, for example with uv run quarto render, and have the report render inside the container.

You may need extra tools inside the container, such as a text editor.
Some analyses may need system dependencies, for example geospatial tooling.
Extra RUN commands are acceptable if you understand why they are needed.
