text:
1. Warm-up: building with a coding agent, and why the jargon matters

The exercise: create a new repository with a Dockerfile that uses the given image. The solution is essentially one line: FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2.
Claude Code demo: the instructor asked Claude Code to create the repository 2026-11-24-docker.

What the agent ran: ls, checks that docker and gh exist, a Docker command to detect the machine type, and mkdir.
What it produced: it wrote the Dockerfile, then built and tested the image. It also committed the files with a co-author line.
Extra files: it added README.md and a Makefile, because the instructor’s setup asks for those by default. Templates and defaults are a strength of coding agents.
Cost: about 50 cents.
Wrong folder: it created the repository in ~/temp instead of ~/git, probably because Claude was started in a different folder.

Why learning the vocabulary matters: the prompt worked because it used the right terms (“Docker file”, the exact image name). Someone who has never heard of Docker cannot steer an agent to the correct answer.
The CMD ["R"] line the agent added: this sets the default command, so running the container without other inputs starts R. Think of it as “what opens when you double-click this file”. You can always pass a different command instead. (29.2.1 CMD or ENTRYPOINT?)
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

CMD ["R"]
Docker Desktop must be running. On macOS and Windows, Docker commands fail if Docker Desktop is not open. Recent versions tell you so.

title: Docker for a uv Project: Ubuntu Base Image, Volume Mounts, /opt/venv and Docker Compose
text:
2. Building and running an image (review)

docker build --tag <name> . builds an image from the Dockerfile and gives it a name. The tag can be anything (“you can call it pizza”). Without a version it gets the tag latest.
The . at the end is not punctuation. It means “here”, the current directory: the dot from week 1 of DSCI 521.

docker build looks for a file named Dockerfile (capital D) by default, but it still needs to be told where to look.
Treat it like a function argument that cannot be left empty.

Base images are downloaded once. If the base image is already on your machine, the FROM step is instant (CACHED). With a new version you have not pulled, that step takes seconds to minutes depending on your internet.
docker run --rm -it <image>:

--rm deletes the container when you exit, so it is not left running on your computer.
-it gives you interactive terminal access: your keystrokes are passed to the container.

Overriding the default command: docker run --rm -it <image> bash replaces CMD ["R"] with Bash. You then have an ordinary Linux terminal, like Git Bash or the macOS terminal.
You start at the root of the filesystem (/), and you see system folders such as bin, etc and usr.

/home is empty: no user is set up.
For a course analysis container this is fine, because everyone shares the same setup and it is not served to the public.

Containers are disposable. Any change made inside a --rm container is gone after you exit. That makes containers a safe place to try risky installs (for example PyTorch): if it goes wrong, just restart. “Like another version of Git that automatically resets all your changes.”
References: 28 Using and running containers, 28.2 Docker command-line commands.

3. Choosing a base image for a Python project

Containers run Linux. Even on a Windows or Mac laptop, inside a container you are in Linux, most likely some version of Ubuntu.
FROM ubuntu:24.04: no one in the class has an R project, so the R image was swapped for plain Ubuntu.

The R image carries a lot of R software you do not need.
Ubuntu has no Python, and uv installs it.

Keep images small. Be respectful of other people’s disk space, which is expensive now because of the AI boom.

Alpine is even smaller than Ubuntu, but you may have to install more yourself.
Ubuntu is a good starting point.

Mixed-language projects are valid. One project using both Python and R (for example ggplot2 for plots) is common. The textbook’s example image, docker-uv-renv, has both. The class demo used Python only.
References: 29.3 Choosing a base image for your Dockerfile, 32 Python and R in one image.

section: 4. Installing uv and setting a working directory
text:
4. Installing uv and setting a working directory

COPY copies files into the image. It can also copy from another image:
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

Read the image name like a GitHub address: registry, then owner, then repository, then version tag.
This takes the uv and uvx programs out of Astral’s image and puts them in /usr/local/bin/.
The line comes straight from uv’s Docker guide.

Why install uv at all? You are building a machine from scratch, so it is a virtual copy of your setup. Everyone installed uv in orientation, and the image needs it too.
WORKDIR /workspace sets the working directory for the rest of the build and for containers started from the image. It creates the folder if it does not exist.

You land in a project folder instead of /, where you could accidentally move or break system files.
The working-directory idea (pwd, cd, relative paths) never goes away: every command needs a starting point.

title: Docker for a uv Project: Ubuntu Base Image, Volume Mounts, /opt/venv and Docker Compose
section: 5. The three files that define a Python environment
text:
5. The three files that define a Python environment

uv init --bare creates a minimal pyproject.toml with a name, a version and requires-python. Version numbers do not matter much for a milestone project.
pyproject.toml is the human-readable list of the packages you care about. It is a general Python metadata file that other tools can read too.
uv.lock records exact versions of every package and dependency. It is generated from pyproject.toml.
.python-version says which Python version to install (here 3.14). This was new in this lecture.

The Python version affects which package versions resolve, because not every package supports the newest Python.
PyTorch is almost never compatible with the latest Python, so you often have to pin an older one.
Package authors (more in DSCI 524) can point it at an upcoming release candidate to test that their package still works when Python updates.

Summary: one file for the Python version, one for the exact package versions, and one human-readable file that controls it all. All three get copied into the image.
Reference: 30 Python packages with uv in an image.

title: Docker for a uv Project: Ubuntu Base Image, Volume Mounts, /opt/venv and Docker Compose
text:
6. Pinning exact versions (== vs >=)

By default uv add cowsay writes cowsay>=6.1, meaning “6.1 or anything newer”.

If cowsay releases 7.0 next week and you rebuild then, you can end up with 7.0.
Per the textbook, this happens whenever uv.lock gets regenerated.

Major version changes usually break backward compatibility. Code relying on 6.x behaviour may stop working in 7.x (more in DSCI 524). For a long-running project, >= is a real risk.
Pin exactly in pyproject.toml: change the dependency to "cowsay==6.1".
Make uv add pin exactly from now on by adding a [tool.uv] table. This section controls how uv itself behaves:
[project]
name = "2026-11-24-docker"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "cowsay==6.1",
]

[tool.uv]
# `uv add` writes an exact version (==)
add-bounds = "exact"
Downstream dependencies can still move.

uv.lock pins everything, but anything you did not name in pyproject.toml can change when the lock is regenerated.
The instructor has had pandas break because a dependency far downstream updated, even though pandas itself was pinned. The fix was to pin that dependency too.
Rule of thumb: pin explicitly the packages that matter, and let the resolver choose compatible versions for the rest.

Reference: 22 uv: pinning exact versions.

section: 7. Installing the packages at build time: uv sync --locked
text:
7. Installing the packages at build time: uv sync --locked

RUN uv sync --locked does in the image exactly what you do on your laptop when you get a new project or a homework repository.
--locked makes uv fail if pyproject.toml and uv.lock are out of sync. You want that error: it is a deliberate tripwire, so the image is built exactly the way you expect.
The build visibly pauses on this step, because it is downloading Python and installing packages.
After building, ls -a in /workspace shows the copied files plus a .venv. ls alone hides the dot-files.

title: Docker for a uv Project: Ubuntu Base Image, Volume Mounts, /opt/venv and Docker Compose
section: 8. Layer caching and the order of Dockerfile steps
text:
8. Layer caching and the order of Dockerfile steps

Each instruction is cached as a layer. If a layer and everything above it are unchanged, Docker reuses the cached version.
Changing a layer reruns every step below it, and deleting a line counts as a change.
Put slow, rarely-changing steps at the top (installing software and packages) and frequently-changing steps at the bottom (copying your code).

Installing the tidyverse can take about 15 minutes. You should not wait that long because you fixed a typo in a script.

In class, adding COPY hello.py ./ at the end made the rebuild take under a second: every earlier step said CACHED and only the copy ran.
Fewer, combined RUN lines save disk space. Many published Dockerfiles cram everything into a few steps. This does not change the outcome, and when you are starting out there is nothing wrong with more lines if it keeps things clear.
Reference: 29.1.3 Layer caching, 29.1.4 Guidelines for RUN commands.

section: 9. Separating compute from code: mounting a volume
text:
9. Separating compute from code: mounting a volume

Why not copy the code in? You could COPY everything and rebuild, but then the code is frozen in the image.

You have to remember to rebuild after every commit.
You have to worry about who copied which version.
It does not scale while you are actively doing EDA for a milestone.

Why not git clone inside the container? It is valid; the instructor has done it to mimic a student’s terminal. But the container then needs its own SSH key or personal access token. If it makes a new key on every build, you are re-registering keys constantly. Avoid it.
Goal: the image holds only the software and packages (compute). The source code stays on your computer.
-v / --volume mounts a folder at run time:
docker run --rm -it -v "$(pwd):/workspace" 2026-11-24-docker bash

$(pwd) runs pwd and substitutes your current directory. This is ordinary Bash, and it means teammates do not hard-code their own paths.
The folder is mounted at /workspace, matching WORKDIR.
On Windows (Git Bash) you may need an extra leading slash ("/$(pwd):/workspace"). The textbook has the per-OS versions.

It is a live shared folder, not a copy or a sync.

Edits on your laptop appear immediately in the container, and the other way round. You are working on the same file.
Positron sometimes does not notice that a file changed on disk, so you may need to refresh.

Mounting happens at docker run, not docker build. A build can only copy files.
Why this is useful: you can run the same code locally and in the container (for example uv run quarto render ...). That checks it works on your machine and in the reproducible environment.
Reference: 28.1.2 Mounting volumes to containers.

title: Docker for a uv Project: Ubuntu Base Image, Volume Mounts, /opt/venv and Docker Compose
text:
10. Cross-platform environments: UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv

.venv holds the actual Python binary and the installed packages. Inside the container, plain python does not exist; you go through uv, which knows to look in that folder.
Teammates have different machines.

Operating systems: Windows, macOS, Linux.
CPU architectures: amd64 and arm64.
That makes four to six different combinations to support.

uv sync installs only for the current system. uv.lock contains hashes for all platforms, but only your platform’s packages get installed. The image is Linux, so uv sync in the build installs Linux packages.
Mounting the project overlays the image’s /workspace, including its .venv. The container then sees your laptop’s .venv (built for macOS) instead.

That is like taking a program installed on a Mac and hoping it runs on Windows.
Problems are most likely with packages that “run fast”: compiled code or C extensions such as pandas, rather than cowsay.
Warning: in class, uv run in the container removed the host’s .venv and created a Linux one in its place. Because of the mount, that happened in the real project folder on the laptop (see What went wrong live).

The fix is an environment variable set before uv sync. The exact position does not matter as long as it comes before uv sync.
ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv

uv then puts the environment in /opt/venv, outside the mounted folder.
From then on it ignores the project’s .venv and uses the Linux environment built into the image.

Rebuild after the change. uv run which python in the container then prints /opt/venv/bin/python. Your laptop keeps its own .venv, and the container keeps its Linux one, so the image works on any host OS.
The finished Dockerfile from class (demo repo):
FROM ubuntu:24.04

# how to install uv
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

WORKDIR /workspace

ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./
RUN uv sync --locked
Reference: 30.5 Why the packages go in /opt/venv.

title: Docker for a uv Project: Ubuntu Base Image, Volume Mounts, /opt/venv and Docker Compose
text:
11. Docker Compose

The problem: docker run keeps growing (--rm, -it, -v, and -p port forwarding for JupyterLab or RStudio). Editing a long pasted command means arrow-keying through it.
docker-compose.yml is a YAML file that records how to build and run the container. Being a file, it can be version-controlled and its changes tracked.
Structure:

It starts with services:, listing one or more containers.
Each service has a name (analysis-env here; “you can call this pizza”).
build: . builds from the Dockerfile in this folder, and image: names the result.
Optional ports: uses the form "<host-port>:<container-port>", for example <host-port>:8787 for RStudio.
volumes: is the equivalent of -v, and you can mount several folders.
The instructor showed ports: and an extra volume, then deleted them for this demo. More on Thursday.

services:
  analysis-env:
    build: .
    image: 2026-11-24-docker
    volumes:
      - .:/workspace
Multiple containers (microservices): for example a dashboard container plus a separate database container, kept apart because some people only care about one. For one analysis container Compose is a bit of overkill, but still useful.
Commands:

docker compose build builds whatever the file describes.
docker compose up starts the service.
docker compose up --detach (-d) runs it in the background and gives you the prompt back.

Outside MDS: many self-hosted open-source apps ship a Compose file, so docker compose up -d downloads the image, starts the app, and you open it on a port in your browser.

Examples: Actual Budget and Firefly III (personal finance), Jellyfin (media server), n8n (AI automation), and a recipe manager.
The Actual Budget file shows the same parts plus environment variables and a health check.
You can run these on an old laptop “in your closet” or on a cloud machine.

Coming this week: publishing an image to a registry, so others can docker pull it instead of building from the Dockerfile.
Reference: 33 Containers: Docker Compose, demo docker-compose.yml.

text:
12. Extra software in your image (optional)

A bare Ubuntu image has no text editor: nano and vi are both missing. You may add RUN lines to install one, or other tools.
Some Python packages need system libraries. Geospatial analysis is the classic case, needing libraries installed from Ubuntu. What you need depends on your stack, so know why each install is there.

text:
What went wrong live

The agent put the repository in the wrong place. Claude Code created it under ~/temp rather than ~/git, likely because it was started from a different folder. The demo carried on in ~/temp/2026-11-24-docker.
No text editor in the container. The instructor tried to edit the mounted file inside the container:
bash: nano: command not found
bash: vi: command not found
He edited on the laptop instead and used cat in the container to show the change. If you want an editor inside, install one with a RUN line.
Mounting overwrote the laptop’s .venv. This happened before the ENV line existed. uv run hello.py inside the container found the host’s macOS .venv, deleted it, and made a Linux one in the shared folder:
warning: Ignoring existing virtual environment linked to non-existent Python interpreter: `.venv/bin/python` -> `/Users/dan/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.14-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.14`
Using CPython 3.14.10
Removed virtual environment at: .venv
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
This changes your real project folder, not a copy. The fix was ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv and a rebuild, after which uv run which python pointed at /opt/venv/bin/python. The same run also printed warning: Failed to hardlink files; falling back to full copy, which comes from installing across the mounted filesystem.
Two small typos.

ls 0alh failed (No such file or directory); it should be ls -alh.
python returned command not found, because Python exists only through uv (uv run ...).

uv which python is not a command. It failed with error: unrecognized subcommand 'which'; the fix was uv run which python.
docker compose up did not keep the container running. It printed analysis-env-1 exited with code 0 straight away.

docker compose up --detatch was a misspelling (unknown flag: --detatch); the flag is --detach (-d).
docker compose ps showed nothing, and docker compose exec analysis-env bash replied service "analysis-env" is not running.
The instructor ran out of time and will fix this demo next class (Thursday, 2026-11-26). Conceptually, Compose is meant to replace the long docker run command with flags read from the file.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 5 of 5: Evaluate. Decide and justify your verdict before you read the answer; the criteria are the ones given in class.

1. Project Advice and Course Logistics
00:00:14–00:05:43

Q: A teammate proposes spending the entire milestone building a complex neural network with hyperparameter tuning to boost their portfolio, arguing that the project grade is primarily about model performance. Judge this plan against the course’s explicit grading criteria and explain why it will fail.

A: Judge the plan as unacceptable. The instructor explicitly warned that the course is not a model fitting course and the grade focuses on technically correct data science practices and reproducible workflows, not model accuracy. Pursuing a complex model will cause a “very bad time” because it distracts from the core learning objectives and makes managing the workflow significantly harder. (00:02:03)




2. Git Branching and Pull Requests
00:06:05–00:25:29

Q: A team member creates a pull request description that only says “Updated README.” They do not link it to any existing issues or use any keywords to close them. Judge whether this PR description meets the class standard for project management and explain your reasoning.

A: Judge the description as inadequate. The class emphasized that the first comment in a PR or issue should be up-to-date and contain all necessary references because reviewers look there first and ignore the subsequent conversation. Failing to link to issues or use keywords like fixes #<number> or closes #<number> misses the opportunity to auto-close tasks and keeps the issue board cluttered, violating the class’s recommended project management workflow. (00:18:33)

Q: After merging a pull request, a team member deletes the branch on GitHub but leaves all local branch references untouched on their laptop, arguing it doesn’t matter because the work is merged. Judge whether this leaves the local repository in a healthy state and explain the potential consequence.

A: Judge the state as messy and prone to confusion. The class warned that leaving remote tracking references intact can lead to “weird Git states” where the local repository is cluttered with stale references, making it harder to see what is happening (e.g., too many colors in git log --graph). The class recommended running git fetch --prune to remove deleted remote references and git branch -d to clean up local branches. (00:24:05)




3. Introduction to Containers and Docker (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:25:33–00:46:44

Q: A student argues that using docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:latest is sufficient for a multi-week group project because it pulls the newest R version every time. Judge this approach against the class’s warning about software updates and explain the risk.

A: Judge the approach as risky and likely to fail. The class warned against relying on unversioned updates because an upstream package or tool update can break the build or analysis unexpectedly, causing hours of debugging instead of actual work. Pinning exact versions in the Dockerfile (e.g., rocker/r-ver:4.6.2) ensures the environment remains stable and reproducible over time, preventing silent breaks. (01:19:25)




4. Running Web Applications in Containers (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:46:47–01:03:00

Q: A teammate wants to run two separate RStudio containers simultaneously on their laptop to test different analyses. They plan to use -p 8787:8787 for both containers. Judge whether this command setup will work and explain why or why not.

A: Judge the setup as flawed. The class explained that -p maps a host port to a container port. If both containers try to map to port 8787 on the host machine, they will conflict. To run multiple containers simultaneously, each must be mapped to a different host port (e.g., -p 8788:8787 for the second container) so the browser can distinguish between the two running applications. (00:57:15)




5. Building Custom Containers with Dockerfile (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:03:00–01:20:39

Q: A student writes a Dockerfile that uses RUN Rscript -e "cowsay::say('Hello')" and expects the container to output the message every time it starts. They omit the CMD instruction. Judge whether this plan will achieve the desired default startup behavior and explain what actually happens.

A: Judge the plan as ineffective. RUN executes commands only during the image build process, not at runtime. Without a CMD instruction, the container will simply start and exit silently (or run the base image’s default command if not overridden). To run a command at startup, they must use CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello')"] to define the default behavior when the container instance launches. (01:13:36)

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment: review questions, tier 4 — Analyze
text:
Date: 2026-11-19

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 4 of 5: Analyze. Take each one apart yourself before you read the answer; tiers 1 to 3 cover the facts, reasons and steps it relies on.

1. Pre-lecture Docker setup (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:00:14–00:01:41

Q: Trace the setup the instructor asked students to finish before the Git exercise: what must be installed and running, what the three docker pull commands download, and how that prepared state changes what happens when docker run is later used?

A: The computer must have the Docker application installed and Docker Desktop open, because otherwise the commands can say that Docker cannot be found or is not running. The three pre-lecture commands pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, rocker/rstudio:4.4.2, and quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14 onto the local machine. docker pull downloads the images without running them, so the large downloads are mostly finished before class. Later, docker run can start a container from an already-present image instead of first waiting for a download, making the live examples faster. (00:00:33)




2. Git branch-and-pull-request workflow
00:06:05–00:09:50

Q: Trace the instructor’s README.md change in the 2026-11-19-docker repository from the working tree to pull request #3: which file, branch, commit, and remote artifact change at each step, and what would the branch workflow look like if git add were run before confirming the branch?

A: The change begins as an unstaged modification to README.md while git status still shows main. git switch -c today creates and moves to today, carrying the unstaged change with it, so git add README.md and git commit -m "today we are talking about containers" create commit 3c6d82a on today rather than main. git push origin today creates the remote today branch and GitHub offers pull request #3 for that branch. If the change had been staged or committed on main, the work would enter the mainline history and the later pull request would no longer be a clean branch-based change, so the branch would need to be moved or rebased. (00:09:44)




3. Issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: Set GitHub issues and pull requests in the demo repository side by side: what issue #1 and issue #2 track, how their numbering relates to pull request #3, and how an assignee or reviewer differs from the code change in a pull request.

A: Issue #1 tracks the broader question of today’s topic, while issue #2 tracks the concrete action of editing README.md. Issues and pull requests share one repository counter, so after issue #2 the next item can be pull request #3, and hash references such as #1 create two-way links between the items. A pull request carries the branch diff and merge decision, while issue assignment claims responsibility for a task and a pull-request reviewer asks someone to look at the change. This separation lets the project board record who owns what and why the work exists without relying on a separate document. (00:14:23)




4. Pull-request descriptions and auto-close keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: Take the description of pull request #3 apart: which part is a status checklist, which part creates the automatic link to issues #1 and #2, and why does the instructor keep the first comment current even if later comments discuss changes?

A: The checkbox lines - [x] item 1 and - [ ] item 2 show what is done and what remains without turning the pull request into a draft. The sentence ending with closes #1 fixes #2 is the GitHub keyword pattern that references those issues and makes them auto-close when pull request #3 merges. The first comment is the summary that future readers use to understand why the pull request exists, so the instructor edits it rather than relying on later conversation. This makes the merged record contain the decision context and the issue closure in one place. (00:18:50)




5. Merging and cleaning up the today branch
00:22:18–00:25:29

Q: Follow the today branch after pull request #3 merges: which commands remove which references, and what remains in git log --oneline --graph --all that still records the merge?

A: After merging, git switch main and git pull origin main bring the merge commit d25ddfa into local main. Deleting the branch on GitHub removes the remote today branch, and git fetch --prune then drops the local remote-tracking reference origin/today. git branch -d today deletes the local today branch, so the quick shortcut git switch today is gone. The commit 3c6d82a and the merge commit remain in the graph, so the history still shows that the today work was merged even though the branch names are no longer shown. (00:24:30)




6. Lock files versus containers (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:25:29–00:33:21

Q: Set a uv or renv lock file and a Docker container side by side: what each one pins, what a teammate on another operating system or CPU architecture still has to do, and how that changes the meaning of “this works on my machine.”

A: A lock file pins the versions of language packages, so a teammate can install the same R or Python packages if they already have the right language, system tools, and installer. A container pins a virtual computer that includes the language, packages, and system tools, so the teammate can run the same environment on a different Mac, Windows, Intel, or ARM machine without rebuilding the host system. The instructor’s point is that uv and renv solve package consistency on one machine, while Docker goes one level deeper by making the compute environment itself shareable. That changes “this works on my machine” from a private statement into a shared, reproducible environment that the whole team can run. (00:39:02)




7. Virtual machines versus containers (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:33:21–00:36:47

Q: Differentiate a virtual machine and a container as the instructor described them: what full operating-system parts each includes, how that affects disk, memory, and compute usage, and which one matches the class’s command-line habit?

A: A virtual machine installs a full operating system, such as Windows with its graphical interface, so the user can log in and click through the whole system. A container is a stripped-down environment containing only the tools installed for the task, typically accessed through a terminal rather than a graphical interface. The instructor contrasted a virtual machine as a 50–80 GB install with containers under about 1–2 GB, which use less disk, memory, and compute because there is less software to run. The container model therefore fits the DSCI 521 habit of typing commands, while the virtual machine keeps the “visual bits” that many data-science workflows do not need. (00:36:16)




8. Running the R container (28 Using and running containers)
00:36:47–00:45:01

Q: Break down docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 and the terminal result: which part selects the image, what --rm, -i, and -t each do, and which output lines prove that the container is running a different R than the host?

A: rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 names the R 4.3.2 image, and docker run starts a container from that image, downloading it first if it is not already local. --rm deletes the container when it stops, while -i keeps standard input open and -t attaches a TTY so the session behaves interactively. The container startup prints R version 4.3.2 on aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu, whereas the host R --version shows R 4.6.2 on the Mac. library(tidyverse) fails inside the bare container but works on the host, confirming that the two terminals are effectively two different machines. (00:44:09)




9. Browser-first web apps and containers (28 Using and running containers)
00:45:01–00:54:10

Q: Set the terminal-only R container and browser-first applications such as RStudio, JupyterLab, and VS Code side by side: where the user types in each case, what runs on the host versus in the container or remote machine, and why the browser interface matters for sharing a compute environment.

A: In the terminal-only R container, the user types R commands directly into the terminal that docker run opened. In browser-first applications, the interface appears in a browser, but the computational work can run in a container or on another machine, as with JupyterLab at localhost:8888 or the Code Space button in GitHub opening VS Code in a browser. The instructor explained that making the application browser-first lets the same interface connect to a machine with the required compute environment, rather than installing that whole environment on the user’s laptop. This is why a web app such as RStudio can be reached through a mapped port while the actual R session is running inside the container. (00:48:33)




10. Port mapping for RStudio (28 Using and running containers)
00:54:10–00:59:14

Q: Trace the RStudio web app from docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 to the browser: what the two sides of -p 8787:8787 mean, how the class could run two RStudio containers at once, and what credential or version difference shows that the browser is using the container?

A: In -p 8787:8787, the left 8787 is the port on the local computer and the right 8787 is the port where RStudio listens inside the container. Because only the container side is fixed by the image, a second RStudio container can be mapped to a different host port, such as 8788:8787, so both web apps can be open at the same time. The terminal prints the generated password for the first run, and the rstudio username is used to sign in at localhost:8787. The local RStudio on the host runs the host’s R, while the containerized RStudio runs the image’s R version, so the browser session is not the host application. (00:58:51)




11. Environment variables in the RStudio container (28 Using and running containers)
00:59:20–01:03:00

Q: Set the first RStudio run and the run with -e PASSWORD="apassword" side by side: what the terminal shows in each case, what the environment variable changes, and what the instructor checked about who can reach localhost:8787?

A: Without -e PASSWORD, the rocker/rstudio image prints a generated password in the terminal, such as the random string shown during the first run. With -e PASSWORD="apassword", the image receives the PASSWORD environment variable and uses that value as the RStudio login password instead of generating one. The instructor then checked that the exposed port is not a public service: if someone cannot log into the physical host machine, localhost:8787 is not available to them. This separates the container’s configuration, which comes from environment variables, from the host’s network access, which controls who can reach the mapped port. (01:00:28)




12. Testing the base image before writing the Dockerfile (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:03:00–01:08:46

Q: Break down the instructor’s interactive test of rocker/r-ver:4.6.2: why docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash starts a shell instead of R, what the cowsay install and call prove, and what happens when the container exits and is started again?

A: The rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 base image already contains R and enough Linux support to install packages, so it saves the manual compiler setup a fresh machine might need. Adding bash at the end overrides the image’s default R command and gives the instructor a shell where the installation command can be tried first. Running install.packages("cowsay") and then cowsay::say('hello') proves that the non-interactive install command works and that the package can be loaded. Because --rm deletes the container on exit and containers have no saved state, a new run of the same image does not still have cowsay installed. (01:07:10)




13. Writing the Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, and CMD (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:08:46–01:15:01

Q: Take the class’s Dockerfile apart: what FROM, RUN, and CMD each contribute to the hello-cowsay image, and how does the quoting in the RUN line match the command that was typed at the container shell?

A: FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 sets the base image, so the new image starts with R 4.6.2 already installed. RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" runs the install command during the image build, making cowsay part of the image instead of a temporary container. CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"] sets the default command that runs when a container starts from this image. The double quotes on the outside and single quotes on the inside mirror the shell command Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" that the instructor tested interactively. (01:13:12)




14. Building and running hello-cowsay (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:15:01–01:18:44

Q: Follow the hello-cowsay image from docker build --tag hello-cowsay . to the two docker run commands: what the . means, what docker images confirms, and what each run form shows about the CMD and the RUN step?

A: The final . in docker build --tag hello-cowsay . is the build context, the current directory where Docker reads the Dockerfile. docker images confirms that the local image hello-cowsay:latest exists and shows its disk usage. docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay executes the image’s CMD, so the container prints the cowsay greeting and exits. docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash overrides the CMD with a shell, and library(cowsay) succeeds there because the earlier RUN step installed the package into the image. (01:17:30)




15. Version pinning in the Dockerfile (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:18:44–01:20:39

Q: Trace the instructor’s warning about floating tool versions through the Dockerfile: where a pinned version would be written, what can update if that line is not pinned, and what happened in the instructor’s story when a container was restarted without hard pinning?

A: A pinned version is written in the Dockerfile install step, such as a RUN line that installs a specific Quarto or language tool version. That line becomes the control point: as long as it is not changed, the image should install the same tool version even when newer versions appear later. If the install line is not hard-pinned, a rebuild or restart can pick up an overnight update without the user asking for it. In the instructor’s example, a container was restarted after an unpinned update had appeared, and nothing worked, turning the project work into hours of fixing the broken update instead of doing the analysis. (01:19:55)

title: Git issues and pull requests, then Docker containers: review questions, tier 4 — Analyze
text:
Date: 2026-11-19
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 4 of 5: Analyze. Take each one apart yourself before you read the answer; tiers 1 to 3 cover the facts, reasons and steps it relies on.

1. Git review: working on a branch
00:06:16–00:09:50

Q: Break down the steps the instructor ran in the 2026-11-19-docker repository, from editing README.md to git push origin today. What did each step contribute, and which steps stayed on the laptop and which reached GitHub?

A: After the edit, git status showed he was still On branch main with README.md modified but not committed, and git pull origin main reported Already up to date. Because nothing was committed yet, git switch -c today could create the branch and carry the uncommitted edit onto it. git diff showed the added line “today we will talk about containers”. git add README.md and git commit -m "today we are talking about containers" then recorded commit 3c6d82a on today, and every one of these steps ran only on the laptop. Only git push origin today touched GitHub: it created the remote branch and printed the link to open a pull request. (00:08:57)

Q: Point out the two places in the branch workflow where the instructor said to stop and check something, and what each check protects later on.

A: The first check is right before git add, and definitely before git commit: look at which branch you are on. If you commit on main by mistake, you have to move those commits with the cheat-sheet commands from the textbook. In the demo, git status caught him on main before he had committed, so git switch -c today was enough to fix it. The second check comes before you start work: pull main, so you are not making changes to something out of date. This matters once several people work on several branches at the same time. (00:08:08)




2. GitHub issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: Relate issue #1, issue #2 and pull request #3 in the 2026-11-19-docker repository. What role did each play, why did the pull request get number 3, and how are the three linked?

A: Issue #1, “what are we doing today?”, worked like a meeting or planning note that asked for today’s topic. Issue #2, “edit the readme with today’s topic”, was an action item spawned from it, and its text points back with “meeting from #1”. Issues and pull requests share one counter, so the pull request opened after two issues became #3. Writing a # number in an issue or pull request creates a two-way reference: the item you name automatically shows a link back. That is how #3’s “this is the fix for #2” connects the pull request and the issue. (00:12:07)




3. Pull request descriptions, checkboxes and closing keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: Break down the description of pull request #3 into its parts. What does each part do on GitHub, and which part acts only when the pull request is merged?

A: The first line, “this is the fix for #2”, is a plain reference: it creates a two-way link but closes nothing. The checkboxes - [x] item 1 and - [ ] item 2 are Markdown tasks that track what is still to do. They show teammates the work isn’t finished, as an alternative to the draft button. The last line, closes #1 fixes #2, uses closing keywords: when the pull request is merged, GitHub closes those issues automatically. This is a GitHub feature, not a Git feature. In class the instructor wasn’t sure closes had worked, but the repository shows both #1 and #2 closed by #3. (00:19:30)

Q: Break down the issue-to-merge cycle the instructor uses for the textbook. What does each stage do to the issues tab, and how does one pull request handle several issues?

A: He files an issue for a piece of work, does the work, and writes “fixes” followed by the issue number in a comment or the pull request message. When that chapter update is merged, the issue closes at the same moment, so the issues tab shrinks. He then picks the next item from the list without clicking “close” anywhere. Keywords also work in commit messages, but they are harder to see there. A single pull request can name several issues: his refactor of the containers and virtual environment chapters fixed several separate issues at once. (00:20:28)




4. Cleaning up after a merge
00:22:18–00:25:19

Q: Separate the cleanup after merging pull request #3 into the steps done on GitHub and the steps done on the laptop. What does each step update?

A: On the laptop, git switch main and git pull origin main brought in the merge commit that GitHub created: the output shows Updating deb10c5..d25ddfa and Fast-forward. On GitHub, the branch is deleted with the button on the merged pull request, or with the trash can in the branches view, which listed today as pull request #3, merged. Deleting the branch on GitHub does not touch the laptop’s references. Two more local commands remove them: git fetch --prune for the remote-tracking reference and git branch -d for the local branch. Deleting branches is optional in this course, and teams differ in how they handle it. (00:24:30)

Q: Correlate the three git log --oneline --graph --all outputs with the commands run between them. What did each command remove, and what stayed in the history?

A: The first log shows commit 3c6d82a labelled (origin/today, today) under the merge commit d25ddfa. git fetch --prune printed [deleted] (none) -> origin/today, and the second log labels 3c6d82a only (today). git branch -d today printed Deleted branch today (was 3c6d82a), and the third log shows 3c6d82a with no label at all. The merge commit and 3c6d82a are still in the graph, so only the shortcut names are gone. That is why some people keep their branches: git switch today is easier than switching to a commit hash. (00:24:30)




5. Why data science workflows need stable environments (27.1 Documenting and loading dependencies)
00:25:29–00:30:13

Q: Break down the two stability goals the instructor set out for a project that lasts weeks or longer. What threatens each one?

A: The first goal is to keep your own environment stable over days, weeks, months or years. Packages update on different cycles, so an install-everything environment can become impossible to install, which is why the package list should be the bare minimum. The second goal is to make the same environment work on a teammate’s computer. That computer may run a different operating system or even have a different chip: Mac and Windows differ, and Windows now ships on both ARM and Intel, so things install differently. “It works on my machine” fails the second goal even when the first is met. (00:28:34)




6. What a container is (27.2 What is a container?)
00:30:13–00:34:28

Q: Set a uv.lock file and a container side by side. What does each hand a teammate, and what must the teammate already have or do?

A: A uv.lock file lets a teammate install the same Python packages. They still need uv on their own computer, which they might not use, and installing it might mess up other things their computer is set up for. A container hands over a whole computer instead: you build a virtual computer from scratch and give it to them. They then do all their work on that computer instead of directly on their own machine. Everyone effectively shares the same computer even on different physical machines, at the cost of a performance hit from the extra layer. (00:31:17)




7. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
00:34:31–00:36:40

Q: Set a virtual machine and a container side by side. Compare what each contains, the interface you get, the size, and when the instructor still reaches for a virtual machine.

A: A virtual machine installs a full operating system, such as all of Windows, with its graphical interface and buttons. A container is a stripped-down version that holds only the bare minimum you install and typically has no graphical interface. That is why DSCI 521 pushed typing commands in the terminal. A Windows virtual machine takes something like 50–80 GB. The containers used in class are under a couple of gigabytes, so they are lighter on disk, memory and compute. The instructor still uses a virtual machine to test the MDS install instructions as if he were on Windows. (00:35:33)




8. Pulling and running a container: R 4.3.2 beside local R (28.1.1 Launch and run containers)
00:36:40–00:45:01

Q: Break down docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 into its parts. What does each part contribute to what appeared on screen?

A: docker run says which computer to turn on, and it downloads the image first if it isn’t on your machine. --rm is a multi-letter flag, as its double dash shows: it deletes the container when it is turned off, instead of leaving you to delete it by hand. -it chains two single-letter flags: -i for interactive, and -t for a terminal (TTY) you can type in. rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 names the image: rocker is the organisation, r-ver is a machine with only R installed, and the tag 4.3.2 picks the R version. Together they opened an R 4.3.2 prompt. (00:41:48)

Q: Distinguish the laptop’s R from the container’s R using what the two terminals printed. Which details show that they are different machines?

A: R --version on the laptop reported R 4.6.2 “Diversified Portfolio” on aarch64-apple-darwin23. R in the container reported 4.3.2 “Eye Holes” on aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu, which is a Linux machine. In the container, library(tidyverse) failed with “there is no package called ‘tidyverse’”, because the image has only R. In the laptop’s terminal, tidyverse loaded. Two terminals on one laptop behave like two separate computers. (00:44:09)

Q: In the instructor’s clinical-trials example, separate what a lock file keeps stable from what the container adds.

A: A trial can run for years while R releases a new version every six months, and the regulator can ask for both the code and the compute environment. A lock file (renv or uv.lock) pins only the package versions. The container also pins the tools on the system, such as the version of R itself or of Git. The instructor’s example: hand people a container with an old Git, and they couldn’t run git switch. So you hand over the container that ran the full analysis, not your laptop. (00:39:02)




9. Know which machine you are typing on
00:45:01–00:46:44

Q: Point out the cues in the class’s terminal output that tell you which machine a command is running on: the laptop, a container, or a remote machine.

A: On the laptop, the prompt reads dan@Heartsbane 2026-11-19-docker %, and it came back after he quit the container. Inside a container started with bash, the prompt changes to something like root@95765251a970:/#: the user is root, then comes the container’s ID and the folder /. Inside R, the > prompt hides which machine you are on, so the R version banner is the clue. On the remote machine in his closet, the only cue was the hostname he had given it, and whoami reports the username as another check. The instructor warned that sometimes all you get is a blinking cursor, so read these cues before you type anything. (00:46:08)




10. Why so many data science tools run in a browser
00:46:44–00:49:11

Q: Relate Electron apps, Jupyter Lab and GitHub Codespaces to containers. What design do they share, and what does it let you separate?

A: All three are browser-first: Electron makes the browser itself the application, and VS Code is essentially a big browser app. Because the interface is a web page, the program can run in a container or on a remote machine while you view it in your local browser. Jupyter Lab opens at a localhost address because it was built to run on machines with more cores and memory than your laptop, while keeping the same interface. The Codespaces button gives you VS Code in a browser, running on a machine whose whole compute environment someone else has set up. (00:48:33)




11. Running RStudio in a container and mapping ports (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:54:10–00:58:59

Q: Break down docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 and trace how typing localhost:8787 in the browser reaches RStudio.

A: --rm shuts the machine down and removes it when you exit. The instructor warned that each running container uses RAM, and leaving “five computers” running grinds a laptop to a halt. In -p 8787:8787, the left number is the port on your machine and the right number is the port inside the container, where RStudio Server listens. The browser at localhost:8787 is therefore forwarded into the container. A second RStudio would need a different number on the left. Once connected, you sign in with the username rstudio and the password printed in the start-up output. (00:57:05)

Q: Relate the three R versions the class saw: in the laptop’s RStudio, in the rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 container, and in the rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 container. What does each one belong to?

A: The RStudio desktop app on the laptop runs the laptop’s own R 4.6.2. The RStudio in the browser runs R 4.4.2 inside the rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 container. The earlier rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 container ran R 4.3.2. Each is effectively a separate machine: the r-ver one is terminal-only, and the rstudio one is an application you reach through a browser. (00:58:51)




12. Passing environment variables into a container (27.2 What is a container?)
00:59:20–01:02:53

Q: Differentiate the start-up output of docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 from the run with -e PASSWORD="apassword" added. Which lines changed, and what does that show about how the image uses the variable?

A: Without -e, the 01_set_env step skipped only HOME and RSTUDIO_VERSION. The 02_userconf step then printed The password is set to ooph3Aef2Ohcahcu, with instructions for setting PASSWORD yourself. With -e PASSWORD="apassword", 01_set_env also lists PASSWORD, and 02_userconf prints no generated password: the container noticed the password had been set manually. Which variables a container reads depends on how its image was built, so not every container has PASSWORD. (01:00:39)

Q: Break down the dashboard hand-off the instructor described for DSCI 532. What does the person who builds the container do, and what does the person who uses it do?

A: The builder puts the dashboard code in a container and does all the installation inside it, such as setting up renv and the snapshot. The user only needs Docker. They type docker run with some flags and open the dashboard’s port in their browser. They skip the whole installation process, because they have been given a computer that was built from scratch. (01:02:20)




13. Starting from a base image and working inside it (28.1.4 Changing the containers default command)
01:03:00–01:08:19

Q: Differentiate docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 from docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash. Which part produces the difference in what starts, and why is the second form useful when you design a container?

A: The R version comes from the tag, but what starts comes from the word after the image name. Without anything after the image name, the container runs its default and you land at the R prompt. Adding bash replaces that default with a shell, so the prompt becomes the container’s own (root@...:/#), and you can still type R to start R. From that shell you can try install steps by hand. Once they work, you document them as the instructions for building the machine from scratch. (01:05:20)

Q: Trace the cowsay package across the three docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash sessions in the terminal log. Why did it appear and disappear?

A: In the first container (root@95765251a970), library(cowsay) failed until install.packages("cowsay") ran, and then cowsay::say('hello') drew the cow. In the second (root@97a536175dca), library(cowsay) failed again. After Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')", it loaded. In the third (root@a642984ec391), it failed once more. Each run is a new container, with a new ID, started from an unchanged image, so it resets to how the image was built: “there’s no save state of a container”. (01:07:10)




14. Running R from the command line with Rscript -e (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:08:19–01:10:18

Q: Break down Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')". How does it relate to typing install.packages("cowsay") at the R prompt, and to the line that later went into the Dockerfile?

A: Rscript runs R from the terminal, and -e says that what follows is an R expression. The quoting is double on the outside and single on the inside. It installs exactly what the interactive call did: the log shows crayon, rlang and cowsay installed both ways. The difference is that this is a shell command, and the instructor’s point was that saving a setup comes down to knowing the terminal command that makes it happen. That same line became the Dockerfile’s RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')". (01:09:27)




15. The Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, CMD (29.2 Dockerfile command summary)
01:10:18–01:15:01

Q: Break down the three lines of the class’s Dockerfile. When does each line take effect, and which step from the earlier hands-on work does it record?

A: FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 names the starting machine, which already has R 4.6.2: it records the image the class had been passing to docker run. RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" runs during the build, and it is the shell command tested by hand in the container. CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"] is written as a list rather than space-separated words. It is the default a container runs when it starts, and you can override it by giving a command such as bash. (01:13:52)

Q: Break down how the middle of the Dockerfile would change for a Python project, as the instructor sketched it. What does each piece contribute to the finished machine?

A: A RUN step would install uv. A copy command would bring the project’s lock files into the image. uv sync would then install all the packages, so the machine itself carries the compute environment. For next week’s project container, the image also needs the language and Quarto installed. Then the analysis runs both on your own computer and in the container. (01:14:15)




16. Building and running your own image (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:15:01–01:18:44

Q: Break down docker build --tag hello-cowsay . and relate its parts to the build output in the terminal log.

A: --tag hello-cowsay names the image, and the output ends with naming to docker.io/library/hello-cowsay:latest. The . tells Docker to look in the current directory for the file named exactly Dockerfile, which matches load build definition from Dockerfile. The two numbered steps come straight from the file: [1/2] FROM docker.io/rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 and [2/2] RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')". Afterwards, docker images lists hello-cowsay:latest alongside the images pulled earlier. (01:16:39)

Q: Trace library(cowsay) from failing in rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 to loading in hello-cowsay. Which steps caused the change, and what did each of the two docker run commands on the new image show?

A: The install was written into the Dockerfile as a RUN line, and docker build ran it once, saving the package into the hello-cowsay image instead of into a throwaway container. docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay ran the image’s CMD and printed the cow saying “Hello from my first image!”. docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash replaced that default with a shell, and there R loaded cowsay without any install. The instructor summed it up as three things: give the instructions in the Dockerfile, build the machine, then turn it on. (01:17:52)




17. Pinning versions, and what comes next
01:18:44–01:20:39

Q: Trace the failure in the instructor’s other class back to its cause. Then relate the lines of a project Dockerfile that prevent it.

A: He restarted a container whose versions weren’t hard-pinned, something had updated the day before, and nothing worked. On a real job that means hours spent fixing an update instead of doing the actual work. In a project Dockerfile, the FROM line pins the R version. A placeholder section holds the renv or uv setup that installs the packages. The tool install lines can name a specific version, even an older Quarto. A year later you are still on those versions, as long as you don’t change those lines, so nothing updates without you knowing. (01:19:55)

title: Git Workflow and Container Basics: review questions, tier 3 — Apply
text:
Date: 2026-11-19

Generated by qwen3.6-35b-a3b, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 3 of 5: Apply. Work each situation through before you read the answer; tiers 1 (Remember) and 2 (Understand) cover the facts and reasons it relies on.

1. Git Branching and Pull Requests
00:06:05–00:25:29

Q: You edit README.md but forget to create a new branch before staging the changes. git status shows the change on main. What commands do you run to safely move the change to a new branch named docker-topic without losing your work?

A: Run git switch -c docker-topic to create and switch to the new branch while keeping your unstaged modifications. Verify with git status that you are now on docker-topic before proceeding to stage and commit the changes. (00:08:08)

Q: You are creating a pull request to merge your docker-topic branch into main. You also opened Issue #5 earlier to track this task. What keyword and syntax should you add to the pull request description so that merging the pull request automatically closes Issue #5?

A: Add fixes #5 or closes #5 anywhere in the pull request description text. GitHub recognizes these keywords as special patterns and automatically closes the referenced issue once the pull request is successfully merged. (00:18:33)

Q: After your pull request for the docker-topic branch is merged and deleted on GitHub, you run git log --oneline --graph --all and still see a visual reference to the merged branch. What command removes the local remote-tracking reference for that deleted branch?

A: Run git fetch --prune to synchronize local tracking references with the remote repository and remove any stale references to deleted branches. This cleans up the graph output so only active branch history remains visible. (00:24:05)

Q: You want to completely remove the local docker-topic branch from your machine after cleaning up remote references. Which command deletes the local branch reference?

A: Run git branch -d docker-topic to delete the local branch. This removes the local shortcut reference to that commit history, though the merged commits remain safely stored in main. (00:24:30)




2. Running Web Applications in Containers (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:46:47–01:03:00

Q: You run docker run --rm -it rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 but realize the container starts an RStudio web app that you want to access from your local browser. What flag and syntax do you need to add to the command to map the container’s default port to your local machine’s port 8787?

A: Add -p 8787:8787 to the docker run command. This binds port 8787 on your local host to port 8787 inside the container, allowing you to access the RStudio Server web interface via localhost:8787 in your browser. (00:57:05)

Q: By default, the rocker/rstudio container generates a random password at startup. You want to set a custom password so you don’t have to look it up in the terminal logs every time. What environment variable flag and syntax do you use to set the password to mySecurePass123?

A: Use -e PASSWORD="mySecurePass123" in the docker run command. This passes the PASSWORD environment variable into the container, overriding the auto-generated credential during startup so you can log in with your chosen password. (01:00:05)

Q: You need to run two separate rocker/rstudio containers simultaneously for testing. The first uses the default port 8787 on the host. How do you configure the second container’s port mapping so it doesn’t conflict with the first one?

A: Map the second container to a different host port, such as -p 8788:8787. This binds port 8788 on your local machine to port 8787 inside the container, allowing both instances to run concurrently without network conflicts. (00:57:29)




3. Building Custom Containers with Dockerfile (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:03:00–01:20:39

Q: You interactively install an R package inside a running container, but when you exit and restart the container, the package is gone. You want to permanently include this package in a new image. Which Dockerfile instruction and command format do you use to execute the installation during the image build process?

A: Use the RUN instruction followed by a shell command, such as RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')". This executes the installation command during the image build phase, permanently baking the package into the image layers. (01:08:59)

Q: You have written a Dockerfile starting with FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 and adding RUN commands. You want the container to automatically run an R script that prints a message every time it starts, instead of opening the R interactive prompt. Which instruction and syntax do you add to the Dockerfile to set this default behavior?

A: Add CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"] to the Dockerfile. The CMD instruction defines the default executable that runs when a container starts from this image, replacing the base image’s default startup command. (01:13:39)

Q: After creating a Dockerfile in your project directory, you run the build command but forget to include the final argument that specifies the build context. What is the correct command to build the image and tag it as hello-cowsay using the Dockerfile in the current directory?

A: Run docker build --tag hello-cowsay .. The dot . specifies the current directory as the build context, telling Docker where to locate the Dockerfile and any other files required for the build process. (01:15:38)

Q: You want to override the default CMD in your custom hello-cowsay image and instead get an interactive Bash shell inside the newly built container. What command do you run to launch the container with this override?

A: Run docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash. Appending bash to the docker run command replaces the image’s default CMD, granting you direct interactive shell access to the container environment. (01:17:28)
