title: Introduction to containers: review questions, tier 2 — Understand
text:
Date: 2026-11-19

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 2 of 5: Understand. Explain each answer in your own words before you read it; tier 1 (Remember) covers the facts, tiers 3 to 5 put them to use.

1. Class setup: Docker Desktop and pre-lecture docker pull (Download the images before you start)
00:00:14–00:01:41

Q: Why run the three docker pull commands before the lecture?

A: The images take time to download, and the instructor says they should be done in about ten minutes if students run the commands right away. Doing the pulls before class is meant to have the images ready by the time the session finishes checking everything. (00:00:14)

Q: Why does the instructor say to make sure Docker Desktop is open before running Docker commands?

A: If Docker is not installed or is not running, Docker commands can produce an error such as “can’t find Docker.” Starting Docker Desktop makes the Docker commands available for the rest of the setup. (00:00:33)

Q: How does the pre-lecture Docker setup connect to the day’s Git practice?

A: While the Docker images download, students can start the exercise of making a branch, creating a pull request, and merging it. The instructor wants the downloads to be finished so the class can move through the practice without waiting on Docker. (00:00:43)




2. Project advice
00:01:41–00:06:05

Q: Why does the instructor tell students not to make the analysis difficult?

A: He says that if a simple model is enough, students should use the simple model because turning the project into something complicated can lead to “a very bad time in about two weeks.” The warning is about over-scoping the work in a course focused on workflows. (00:01:56)

Q: Why is DSCI 522 different from a model-fitting course?

A: The course is about data science workflows, so the instructor says almost no machine learning code appears in the lectures. The goal is to do the workflow correctly, not to maximize model performance. (00:02:16)

Q: Why does the instructor say a sixty percent accurate model is acceptable?

A: He says the model results do not matter, but the data science and machine learning techniques must be technically correct. For example, fitting logistic regression when the outcome is numeric would be wrong. (00:03:04)

Q: Why should a student do a portfolio project in parallel instead of inside this assignment?

A: There is a lot of workflow material in this class, and adding portfolio pressure to the assignment would create a more complicated report than the course needs right now. Doing a portfolio project separately keeps the course assignment focused on the required workflows. (00:03:27)




3. Git review: branch, commit, and push
00:06:05–00:09:50

Q: Why check git status before running git add and git commit?

A: In a branch workflow, you may be on the wrong branch, and commits can accidentally land on main. Checking before adding or committing helps prevent that, and the instructor mentions a textbook cheat sheet for moving commits if this happens. (00:08:08)

Q: Why pull main before starting work in a new branch?

A: In an actively collaborating environment, other people may have pushed changes to main. Pulling main first prevents you from making changes on top of something that is out of date. (00:08:27)

Q: Why can the instructor create the today branch after editing README.md but before committing?

A: He had only edited the file and had not yet committed anything, so the edit was still uncommitted. Creating the branch with git switch -c today lets him commit that edit on today instead of on main. (00:08:57)

Q: Why push the today branch to GitHub?

A: Pushing the branch creates the remote branch so GitHub can show the pull request button. That is how the local branch becomes a pull request that can be reviewed and merged. (00:09:50)




4. Issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: Why use GitHub issues as a project board?

A: Issues are a simple way to track what is happening in a project, including who is responsible for what. The instructor also says they can be used like meeting notes, with action items turned into separate issues after a meeting. (00:10:08)

Q: Why do issues and pull requests share the same numbering?

A: The shared counter lets one item refer to another by its hash number, such as “meeting from #1.” That makes it possible to link issues and pull requests together as parts of one project board. (00:11:54)

Q: What does a two-way reference between issues and pull requests mean?

A: When an item references a number, the referenced item gets a back-link automatically, so the items connect to each other. The instructor says this automatic linking is one reason GitHub became popular as a project management system. (00:13:34)

Q: Why is it okay for one pull request to deal with three issues?

A: The class requires three issues, but one pull request can fix all three if the work is related. Writing the pull request message with the relevant issue numbers gives students experience with the board without forcing one issue per branch. (00:14:23)

Q: Why can a team assign people to issues and pull requests?

A: Assigning an issue shows who is responsible for it, while assigning a reviewer on a pull request asks someone to look over the work. In larger projects, a reviewer can even block changes until they have approved the work. (00:14:47)




5. Pull-request descriptions, checkboxes, and auto-close keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: Why keep the first comment on an issue or pull request up to date?

A: People mainly read the first comment to understand what is happening and why the item exists, rather than reading the later conversation. The instructor edits the first comment so it holds the current references and explanation. (00:16:24)

Q: How do Markdown checkboxes help in a pull request?

A: They let the author mark items as done or not done inside the pull request. If the pull request is not a draft, teammates can see at a glance what is still unfinished. (00:17:37)

Q: What do closes #1 and fixes #2 do in a pull request description?

A: They reference issue numbers in a special GitHub pattern. When the pull request is merged, GitHub automatically closes the referenced issues. This is a GitHub service feature, not a Git version-control feature. (00:18:40)

Q: Why does the instructor say to write the pull request message strategically?

A: A message can reference multiple issues so that merging the pull request closes them all at once. This saves the author from going back and manually closing each issue later. (00:21:02)




6. Merging the pull request and cleaning up branches
00:22:18–00:25:29

Q: Why switch to main and pull after pull request #3 is merged?

A: The merged changes are on main, so switching and pulling brings the merge into the local main branch. That leaves the local repository current after the remote merge. (00:22:25)

Q: Why does the instructor say deleting the remote branch is not required in class?

A: Students may keep merged branches as a record, and different teams use different Git practices. The class is showing one valid cleanup path, not a universal rule. (00:23:16)

Q: What does git log --oneline --graph --all show after the today branch is deleted on GitHub?

A: It still shows the commit and the merge, so the history remains. Deleting the branch mainly removes the quick reference or shortcut to that commit, not the commit itself. (00:23:56)

Q: Why run git fetch --prune and then git branch -d today?

A: git fetch --prune removes the remote-tracking reference after the branch is deleted on GitHub, and git branch -d today removes the local branch reference. Together they clean up the old branch names while leaving the merged history visible. (00:24:30)




7. Why containers: a stable, shareable compute environment (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:25:29–00:33:21

Q: Why does the course move beyond the package files students received in earlier MDS courses?

A: Data science projects last longer, often involve teams, and each project can have its own package needs. Students need to manage a stable environment for their own project instead of relying on an instructor-supplied list. (00:25:52)

Q: Why are differences in operating system and CPU architecture a problem for sharing a data science project?

A: A teammate may be on a different machine, such as Windows versus Mac or Intel versus ARM, and software may install or run differently. A container gives everyone a shared virtual computer instead of depending on each person’s local setup. (00:28:53)

Q: What does it mean to say a container is a virtual computer?

A: The instructor builds a computer from scratch, installs what the analysis needs, and gives that virtual machine to others. Everyone then runs code inside that same environment even though they are on different physical machines. (00:31:49)

Q: Why is a container a useful sandbox even though there is a performance hit?

A: The extra layer has a cost, but if you break the sandbox you can restart it and get a fresh copy. That makes it a safe place to experiment with an operating system without damaging the real machine. (00:32:34)

Q: Why does the instructor advise keeping the package list to the bare minimum?

A: Installing packages that are not needed wastes disk space. It can also create problems later when packages with different update cycles are all updated together and may no longer be compatible. (00:28:04)




8. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
00:33:21–00:36:47

Q: What is the difference between a virtual machine and a container?

A: A virtual machine installs a full operating system, such as Windows, with the buttons and graphical interface you use to log in. A container is a stripped-down environment with only the bare minimum software and usually just a terminal. (00:34:48)

Q: Why are containers more performant than virtual machines?

A: They contain much less software, so they use less disk, memory, and compute. The instructor describes a container as a virtual machine without the full operating system and visual interface. (00:35:33)

Q: Why does the instructor still use virtual machines despite preferring containers?

A: He uses them when he needs to pretend to be on a different system, such as testing the MDS install on Windows. They are useful for that kind of full operating-system test, even though they are larger. (00:36:01)




9. Running the R container: docker pull and docker run (28.1.1 Launch and run containers)
00:36:47–00:45:01

Q: Why run docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 before running the container?

A: docker pull downloads or updates the image on the computer. The instructor already pulled it so that docker run would not need to wait for a long download during the lecture. (00:42:16)

Q: Why can the container run R 4.3.2 while the host has R 4.6.2?

A: The container is a separate machine with its own installed R version. Lock files track package versions, but a container can also pin system tools and the language version itself. (00:38:46)

Q: What does --rm do in docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2?

A: It tells Docker to delete the container when it stops. That avoids manually removing stopped containers later. (00:40:55)

Q: What do the -i and -t parts of -it mean?

A: -i keeps input interactive so the user can type commands, and -t attaches a TTY terminal for an interactive session. Together they let R run as an interactive terminal inside the container. (00:41:16)

Q: What does it mean when library(tidyverse) fails in the rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 container but works on the host?

A: It means the container and the host are different machines. The bare R container does not have tidyverse installed, while the host has that package available. (00:43:49)




10. Web-app containers: RStudio and browser-first tools (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:45:01–00:54:10

Q: Why are tools such as JupyterLab, VS Code, and RStudio built as browser-first applications?

A: If the application runs in a browser, the same interface can be used on a remote machine or inside a container. This lets the user connect to a machine that may have more cores and memory than the laptop. (00:47:15)

Q: Why is JupyterLab accessed through localhost in a browser instead of being treated only as a desktop app?

A: JupyterLab is built to run in a browser so it can also run on a remote container. The local browser then connects to the running Jupyter process through a port. (00:48:04)

Q: Why can RStudio be used from a browser when running in a container?

A: RStudio is an application that runs as a web app inside the container. Docker can expose it through a port so the browser can reach the running RStudio Server. (00:47:11)




11. Port mapping the RStudio container (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:54:10–00:59:14

Q: How does -p 8787:8787 make the RStudio container reachable from a browser?

A: It maps port 8787 on the user’s computer to port 8787 inside the container, where RStudio is running. The user can then open localhost:8787 in the browser to reach that container. (00:56:31)

Q: Why can you run more than one RStudio container at the same time?

A: The container’s internal RStudio port is fixed at 8787, but the host port can be mapped to a different local number. This lets several containers run simultaneously on different local ports. (00:57:05)

Q: Why does the instructor warn about running several containers at the same time?

A: Each running container uses RAM on the computer, so turning on several containers can make the machine sluggish. The instructor uses this to explain why containers should be stopped when they are no longer needed. (00:55:17)




12. Environment variables and running dashboards in containers (28 Using and running containers)
00:59:20–01:03:00

Q: How does -e PASSWORD="apassword" work when running the RStudio container?

A: It passes an environment variable into the container at run time. The rocker/rstudio image is set up to use the PASSWORD variable to choose the login password instead of generating a random one. (01:00:05)

Q: Why does the instructor say not every container has the same environment variables?

A: A container’s behavior depends on how its image was built, so only some images define variables that users can set. The PASSWORD variable works because that RStudio image was designed to read it. (00:59:34)

Q: Why does the instructor say the password is not exposed to people who cannot access the machine?

A: Access to the mapped port depends on access to the physical machine running Docker. If someone cannot log into that machine, they cannot use port 8787 on it. (01:00:16)

Q: Why put a dashboard in a container for DSCI 532?

A: A dashboard runs in the browser, so the container can include all the installation and dependencies. The end user only needs Docker and can run the application without installing the environment, Quarto, or packages themselves. (01:01:47)




13. Building interactively: base image and the cowsay package (29.1.1 Workflow for building a Dockerfile)
01:03:00–01:08:46

Q: Why start from the rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 base image?

A: That image already has R installed and probably includes system tools that a fresh Linux install would need. It lets the instructor skip some low-level setup steps while building a custom image. (01:04:00)

Q: Why run docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash instead of the image’s default R command?

A: Adding bash starts a terminal instead of R, so the instructor can type installation commands on the machine directly. This is useful for testing steps before writing them into a Dockerfile. (01:04:53)

Q: Why install and test cowsay interactively before putting the command in a Dockerfile?

A: The instructor wants to verify the terminal command actually works on that image. Only after the step works does it become a reliable instruction for building the machine from scratch. (01:05:43)

Q: Why is the cowsay package gone after the container is stopped and started again?

A: A container does not save changes made inside it after the image is created. When it restarts, it resets to the image unless the installation was saved in a Dockerfile. (01:06:49)




14. Writing the Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, and CMD (29.1 Building container images from Dockerfile’s)
01:08:46–01:15:01

Q: Why does the Dockerfile begin with FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2?

A: FROM sets the base image or starting machine for the build. In this case the new image starts from an image that already has R 4.6.2 installed. (01:11:10)

Q: What does RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" do during the build?

A: RUN executes a bash command while the image is being built. Here it uses Rscript -e to run the R expression that installs the cowsay package into the image. (01:12:44)

Q: What is the role of CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"]?

A: It sets the default command that runs when a container from this image starts. It replaces the base image’s default behavior, so the container prints the cowsay message unless the user runs a different command such as bash. (01:13:25)

Q: Why mention COPY and uv sync for a Python container?

A: A Python image can copy lock files into the image and then run uv sync during the build. That installs the required packages so the finished container has the project’s compute environment ready. (01:14:15)

Q: Why does the instructor say ENTRYPOINT is rarer than CMD?

A: ENTRYPOINT is used for very specific containers where a fixed command always runs, while CMD is the common default command that can be replaced by a command after the image name. (01:13:36)




15. Building and running the hello-cowsay image (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:15:01–01:18:44

Q: Why use docker build --tag hello-cowsay .?

A: --tag gives the new image the name hello-cowsay. The . tells Docker to use the current directory as the build context where it looks for the Dockerfile. (01:15:06)

Q: Why assume the build command is run from the repository root?

A: The . convention assumes the Dockerfile is in the current directory, which matches how milestone instructions are written. Running from the root means the command can be copy-pasted without changing directories. (01:16:11)

Q: What does docker images show after building hello-cowsay?

A: It lists the local images on the computer, including hello-cowsay:latest. That confirms the build produced a named image that can be run. (01:17:01)

Q: How do docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay and docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash prove the Dockerfile worked?

A: The first command runs the image’s CMD, which prints the cowsay message. The second opens a shell where library(cowsay) succeeds, showing the RUN step installed the package into the image. (01:17:14)




16. Version pinning and wrap-up (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:18:44–01:20:39

Q: Why pin tool versions in the Dockerfile?

A: Pinning tells Docker exactly which version of a tool to install, such as a specific Quarto version. As long as the install line is not changed, the environment stays on that version instead of silently updating. (01:19:25)

Q: What problem happened when the instructor did not hard-version-pin a container?

A: A restart picked up an overnight update, and then nothing worked. He spent hours fixing the update problem instead of doing the actual project work. (01:19:50)

Q: Why is the Dockerfile the control point for updates?

A: The Dockerfile says which version to install, and that version will not change until the author edits that line. This gives the team control over what gets updated and when. (01:20:27)

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers: review questions, tier 2 — Understand
text:
Date: 2026-11-19
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 2 of 5: Understand. Explain each answer in your own words before you read it; tier 1 (Remember) covers the facts, tiers 3 to 5 put them to use.

1. Project advice: keep the analysis simple
00:01:41–00:05:57

Q: Explain why the instructor urged students to keep the group project’s analysis simple, even if they could build something more ambitious.

A: An ambitious model, such as a neural net instead of a straight line, means “a very bad time in about two weeks.” This is a workflows course, not a model-fitting course, and there is almost no machine learning code in the lectures. The report is not the point of the class, and there is a lot more work to do around it. (00:02:16)

Q: Compare how the project treats a model’s performance with how it treats its correctness.

A: Performance doesn’t matter: a model that is sixty percent accurate is fine, and a simple linear or logistic regression is not penalised. The techniques must still be correct data science and correct machine learning. Fitting logistic regression to predict a numeric outcome, for example, “is just wrong.” (00:03:08)

Q: If the lectures show almost no machine learning code, why does the group project still need a machine learning analysis?

A: You need a machine learning project to start with. The project is the same analysis, built on over three or four weeks: Git this week, then containers next week. The analysis is what the workflow is applied to, even though class never teaches the modelling. (00:05:43)

Q: Explain why a student who wants a portfolio piece should build it in parallel rather than in this assignment.

A: A lot is happening in this class, and the instructor said you definitely don’t want to deal with a complicated report at the same time. If you want a portfolio version, do it separately, in parallel. (00:03:27)




2. Git review: working on a branch
00:06:16–00:09:50

Q: The instructor edited README.md in the 2026-11-19-docker repository while still on main. Why could he still move that work onto a new branch with git switch -c today?

A: He had only edited the file and had not committed anything yet. He could therefore create the branch at that point: git status then showed he was on branch today with the same modification. If you have already made commits on main, you need the textbook’s cheat sheet of commands to move them. (00:08:57)

Q: Why should you look at which branch you are on right before git add, and definitely before git commit?

A: The course assumes a branch workflow from now on, and the change is supposed to land on a branch, not on main. Checking git status before you stage and commit catches the mistake while it is still easy to fix. In the demo it showed the instructor was still on main. (00:08:08)

Q: When you are actively collaborating, why pull the main branch before starting new work?

A: Pulling brings everything up to date, so you aren’t working on and changing something that is out of date. With several people actively working on several branches, this is something you now have to pay attention to. (00:08:27)




3. GitHub issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: Explain why GitHub issues and pull requests share one numbering sequence. In the 2026-11-19-docker demo, what number did the pull request get, and why?

A: Issues and pull requests are counted together so that, inside any issue or pull request, you can refer to any other item by its number. In the demo there were two issues first, so the pull request became #3. (00:12:07)

Q: What does it mean that a # reference on GitHub is a “two-way reference”?

A: When you write something like “meeting from #1” in issue #2, it links to item 1, and item 1 also shows a link back. Everything links to everything else automatically. The instructor named this kind of issue and pull request tracking as one of the reasons GitHub, and not only Git, became so popular. (00:13:34)

Q: How can an issue board serve as a team’s meeting notes?

A: You can keep the meeting notes in one big issue, as MDS does in one of its internal repositories. After the meeting, any action items or to-dos for other people become separate issues spawned from that note. (00:10:49)

Q: Why does the instructor sometimes ask a coding agent to file an issue for a passing idea?

A: Opening a browser tab risks ending up on a site he doesn’t need to be on and losing track of what he was doing. Telling the agent to file the issue lets him throw the idea somewhere without breaking focus. Issues are a good place to dump ideas, such as a neural net someone would like to try later. (00:13:06)

Q: What is the difference between assigning someone to a pull request and adding them as a reviewer?

A: You usually assign yourself to your own pull request, which claims it as your responsibility. A reviewer is someone else, such as a teammate, whom you ask to look over your work. In larger projects there are sometimes ways to block changes until someone has actually reviewed them. (00:14:47)

Q: Why is it acceptable for one pull request to deal with all three issues the lab asks you to create?

A: One issue, one branch, one pull request is only one extreme; it isn’t always how the work splits up. The lab’s goal is for you to get experience with the project board system, not to match issues to pull requests one-for-one. (00:14:23)

Q: Compare tracking a team’s work in cross-referenced GitHub issues with keeping it in a shared Google Doc.

A: Issues and pull requests that reference each other keep all the notes and decisions connected to the work itself. You can see this in any large open-source project. The instructor called it a very good way to keep track of what is happening on your team without relying on a document of notes. (00:15:48)




4. Pull request descriptions, checkboxes and closing keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: Why should the first comment of an issue or pull request be edited to stay up to date?

A: People coming to it won’t read the whole conversation. They want to know what is happening and why the thing exists, and that should already be in the first comment. If a big decision is made later in the discussion, update the opening comment; project owners can usually edit others’ comments too. These comments are editable because they evolve over time. (00:16:56)

Q: How do Markdown checkboxes in a pull request description help you and your teammates?

A: They let you track for yourself what still needs doing as you fix things. They also tell teammates at a glance that the pull request isn’t done yet, because not every box is checked. That makes them an alternative to marking the pull request as a draft. (00:17:49)

Q: Explain how a closing keyword such as fixes #2 in a pull request description closes an issue.

A: A sentence containing a keyword like fixes #2 (or closes #1) declares that the pull request resolves that issue. When the pull request is merged, GitHub closes the referenced issue automatically. This is a GitHub feature, not a feature of Git, the version control system. The instructor wasn’t sure closes had worked in the demo and said he almost always uses fixes. (00:19:30)

Q: Closing keywords also work in commit messages. Why write them in the pull request description instead?

A: The instructor said you could put them in a commit message, but they are harder to see there. Writing the keyword in the pull request message makes it visible that this work deals with that issue. (00:19:55)

Q: Why do closing keywords make the issues tab more useful as a project management tool?

A: As work merges, the issues it fixes close themselves, so the issues tab gets smaller and you don’t have to think about those items again. You don’t have to click “close” on several issues by hand. You just look down the list for the next thing to work on, which is how the instructor works on the textbook. (00:20:12)

Q: Why is it fine to leave stretch-goal issues open at the end of the course?

A: The course does not grade you on closing all your issues. Creating issues for longer-term ideas or things you’d like to explore is good practice with the system, so open ones are fine. (00:21:50)




5. Cleaning up after a merge
00:22:18–00:25:19

Q: After the today branch was deleted on GitHub, why did the instructor still run git fetch --prune and git branch -d today locally?

A: Deleting the branch on GitHub doesn’t remove your local copies of the references, and git log --oneline --graph --all still showed them. git fetch --prune drops the reference to the branch that was deleted on GitHub (origin/today). git branch -d today deletes the local branch itself. (00:24:30)

Q: When you delete a merged branch, what do you lose and what stays?

A: The history stays: the commit and the merge are still in the graph, so you can tell something happened there. What you lose is the quick shortcut name pointing to that location. (00:24:30)

Q: Why do some people choose not to delete merged branches?

A: Deleting loses the reference. Keeping the branch name means you can type git switch today instead of git switch 3c6d82a. (00:25:05)

Q: Why does the instructor sometimes clean up branches anyway?

A: You can end up in very weird Git states where there are so many branch colours and labels on the screen that you can’t see what is happening anymore. Removing stale references makes the graph readable again. (00:24:05)

Q: Why does the course not require you to delete branches after merging?

A: Keeping branches as a record is perfectly fine. Teams and companies handle Git very differently, even groups within the same company. The class shows one way, and other workflows are modifications of it. (00:23:22)




6. Why data science workflows need stable environments (27.1 Documenting and loading dependencies)
00:25:29–00:30:13

Q: How does setting up a project’s environment differ from the homework you have done so far in MDS?

A: For homework you were given the package file. In a project, each group picks its own language and libraries (Python or R, and Altair, Plotly or Matplotlib), so the package requirements differ. You have to adapt the environment to your own project, just as every project at a company has different requirements. (00:27:06)

Q: Why keep a project’s package list to the bare minimum instead of installing everything?

A: Installing packages you don’t use wastes disk space. Packages also have different update cycles, so if you later try to update everything in one go, some may be incompatible and you can end up unable to install them all. (00:28:04)

Q: Explain why sharing a stable compute environment with a teammate is harder than keeping your own stable.

A: The teammate may have a different operating system, and even a different CPU chip: Macs and Windows machines differ, and Windows now ships on both ARM and Intel chips. Different architectures mean software gets installed in different ways. Your code has to run on a machine that isn’t set up like yours at all. (00:28:53)

Q: Why is “it works on my machine” not good enough for a data science project?

A: It doesn’t help a teammate who is trying to do the same analysis and can’t run your code. The goal of the course is a compute environment you can share, so everyone runs the code through that same environment. (00:29:39)

Q: Why do data science pipelines need to be modular?

A: Other people might need different parts of your analysis, not just the final report. (00:29:55)




7. What a container is (27.2 What is a container?)
00:30:13–00:34:28

Q: If you hand a teammate your uv.lock file, why might that still not be enough for them to run your analysis?

A: The lock file only lets them install the Python packages, and their computer may be set up differently from yours. They might not use uv at all. Installing it could mess up other things their computer is set up for. (00:31:17)

Q: Explain the idea behind a container as the instructor described it.

A: Instead of handing over your physical computer, you build a virtual computer from scratch and give that to everyone. Everyone then does their work on that virtual computer. You are all effectively sharing the same computer even though you are on different physical machines. (00:31:49)

Q: Why are containers useful when you prototype on your laptop but run the full analysis on a bigger machine?

A: The bigger machine has access to all the data, and the compute environment must be exactly the same on both. A container gives you that same environment on your laptop, on the other machine, and across multiple machines. (00:32:15)

Q: Containers carry a performance cost. Why use them anyway on remote machines?

A: The extra layer causes an unavoidable performance hit. But you often can’t install everything directly on a remote machine: other work may be running there, or the administrator doesn’t trust you to install what you think you need. A container gives you a sandbox to play in, and if you mess it up, it is restarted and you get a new sandbox. (00:32:34)

Q: How do containers relate to the “instances” offered by cloud providers?

A: Cloud providers such as Google typically don’t give you bare access to an actual machine. They give you a container on one of their servers, and you work inside it. Pretty much all cloud compute runs on some version of containers. (00:33:30)

Q: How does a container deal with the problem of software versions that cannot coexist on one computer?

A: A container is a little machine with everything it needs installed inside it. Two versions of the same software can live in separate containers even when they couldn’t both be installed together on one machine. (00:34:03)




8. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
00:34:31–00:36:40

Q: What is the main difference between a virtual machine and a container?

A: A virtual machine is a full-blown operating system, such as all of Windows, with its graphical interface and buttons. A container is a stripped-down version that typically has no graphical interface. It contains only the bare minimum that you install into it. (00:35:33)

Q: Explain why containers perform better than virtual machines.

A: A container has less in it and no visual parts, so it uses fewer resources. A Windows virtual machine can take 50 to 80 GB. The containers used in class are under two gigabytes, or even under one, yet still run a full computational stack, using less disk, memory and compute. (00:36:16)

Q: How does the container’s lack of a graphical interface explain why DSCI 521 pushed you to work by typing commands in the terminal?

A: There will be many times, inside a container or on a remote machine, when the terminal is the only interface you have. You can’t double-click through folders there. You have to type commands such as cd to get around. (00:35:00)

Q: If containers are lighter, why does the instructor still use virtual machines?

A: He uses them to test the MDS installation instructions, where he has to pretend he is on a Windows machine. That situation needs a full operating system. (00:36:01)




9. Pulling and running a container: R 4.3.2 beside local R (28.1.1 Launch and run containers)
00:36:40–00:45:01

Q: The instructor’s laptop has R 4.6.2. Why might someone need to run R 4.3.2 in a container?

A: Some work has to stay on one version of R for years. Clinical trials research at a pharmaceutical company can last several years, while R updates every six months, and you don’t want to redo or recheck your work each time. Regulators reviewing a drug submission want your code and the whole compute environment so they can reproduce it, so you give them the container that ran the analysis. (00:38:07)

Q: How does what a container pins differ from what the uv and renv lock files pin?

A: Lock files track only the package versions, not the tools installed on the system. A container goes one level deeper and fixes the tools themselves, such as R or Git. For example, a container with a 2019 version of Git would stop anyone from running git switch. (00:39:02)

Q: When the instructor ran docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 and the output said “Image is up to date,” what did that mean?

A: He already had that image downloaded, and it matched the current version. If a newer version had been published, the pull would have downloaded it. The hash in the output identifies the exact version. (00:39:51)

Q: Why is the command called docker pull, and what does the similarity to git pull tell you?

A: In both commands you are pulling something onto your computer. Tools in the data science and compute stack overlap and borrow words from one another, so a familiar word often hints at what a command does. (00:40:33)

Q: In docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, what does --rm do, and why does it have two dashes?

A: Two dashes mark a flag whose name is several letters long. --rm means that when you turn the container off, the machine itself is deleted automatically. Otherwise you would have to delete it manually. (00:40:55)

Q: Explain what -it means in docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, and why it is written as one flag.

A: Single-dash flags are single letters and can be chained, as in ls -alh, so -it is really two flags. -i is interactive: you will type into it. -t gives you an actual terminal (TTY) to interact with. (00:41:48)

Q: In class, library(tidyverse) failed inside the rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 container but loaded in a local R session. Why?

A: The container has only R installed, and nobody told it to install anything else. The local computer has tidyverse installed. The two terminals run on the same laptop, but the container is effectively a totally different machine. (00:43:54)

Q: How is working in a Docker container like working on a cloud machine?

A: In both cases you are connected to another machine through pretty much the same interface. The difference is that the Docker container happens to run on the same hardware you are typing on. (00:44:31)




10. Know which machine you are typing on
00:45:01–00:46:44

Q: Why is it important to read your terminal prompt when you work with containers or remote systems?

A: The prompt is often the only reference you have to which machine you are on. After quitting the container, the instructor’s laptop prompt returned, and that was the visual cue that he was back on his own computer. You should know where you are typing before you type. (00:45:04)

Q: The instructor opened a terminal on a computer in his closet at home. What did that example show?

A: It looks like any other terminal, but the commands run over there. The only visual cue that he was on a different machine was the hostname he had given it. Sometimes you really are given just a blinking cursor. (00:45:48)

Q: Explain why a command like whoami exists, in terms of knowing which machine you are on.

A: It reports the username on the computer you are using. That gives you another way to check you are on the machine you think you are working on. (00:46:08)




11. Why so many data science tools run in a browser
00:46:44–00:49:11

Q: Why are so many applications built on Electron, essentially as browsers?

A: A browser-first application can run inside a container and be opened in a browser. Making the browser the application is why so many tools you install are essentially browser applications. (00:47:39)

Q: Explain why you open Jupyter Lab at a localhost address in a browser instead of double-clicking an app.

A: Jupyter Lab was built to run on a remote container that can have many more cores and much more memory than your laptop, while giving you the same application interface. Because it runs in a browser, you just connect your browser to wherever it is running. (00:48:04)

Q: What is the point of GitHub’s Codespaces button giving you VS Code in a browser?

A: VS Code is effectively a big browser application, so it can run in a container. Codespaces gives you the same interface on a different machine. That machine’s entire compute environment has been set up for you, so you work on the same versions of all the software. (00:49:00)




12. Running RStudio in a container and mapping ports (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:54:10–00:58:59

Q: If you prefer a Jupyter notebook interface to Quarto, why does running RStudio in a container matter to you?

A: The project is written in Quarto, but some students are used to working in Jupyter notebooks. The same setup that runs RStudio from a container applies to running Jupyter from one. (00:54:23)

Q: Why keep the --rm flag when running rocker/rstudio:4.4.2?

A: --rm shuts down and deletes the machine when you exit; without it, the container keeps running. Each container takes up RAM. If you have started five containers while practising, your computer stops working because five computers are using its resources. (00:55:17)

Q: Explain what -p 8787:8787 does in docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2.

A: RStudio runs on port 8787 inside the container, and you must connect your browser to it, just as with Jupyter Lab’s port. -p connects a port on your local computer (the left number) to a port in the container (the right number). Here the container’s 8787 appears on the Mac’s 8787, so localhost:8787 reaches RStudio in the container. (00:57:05)

Q: How can you run two RStudio containers at the same time when both listen on port 8787?

A: Each container runs on 8787 internally, but you can redirect it to a different port on your own machine. Things running at the same time just use different host ports, which you specify in the left-hand number of -p. (00:56:38)

Q: Why does RStudio use port 8787, when Jupyter Lab uses a different number?

A: The numbers are very arbitrary. Each tool’s developers picked one, and that is the number they work with. Many tools happen to use numbers starting with eight. (00:56:19)

Q: In class, why did the RStudio in the browser and the RStudio desktop app show different versions of R?

A: They are effectively completely different machines. The browser RStudio runs inside the rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 container with that container’s R. The desktop RStudio uses the R installed on the laptop, 4.6.2. Both differ from the R 4.3.2 in the earlier r-ver container. (00:58:51)




13. Passing environment variables into a container
00:59:20–01:02:53

Q: What does -e PASSWORD="apassword" do in docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 -e PASSWORD="apassword" rocker/rstudio:4.4.2, and why use it?

A: -e passes an environment variable into the container as it runs. The RStudio container reads the variable PASSWORD and uses it as the login password. That replaces the hard-to-remember generated password that was printed at start-up. (01:00:05)

Q: Why can’t you assume that every container accepts a PASSWORD environment variable?

A: Containers behave differently depending on how whoever built them set them up. A container might use certain variables, but not every container has them. (01:01:08)

Q: The instructor typed his RStudio password in front of the class. Why wasn’t that a security problem?

A: The only way to reach that container is through his physical machine. Even though it is running on port 8787, if you can’t log into his machine, his 8787 is not available to you. (01:00:28)

Q: Why would you put a DSCI 532 dashboard into a container?

A: A dashboard runs in the browser, so someone can load your container, go to its port and see your dashboard. You have already done all the installation. The end user doesn’t have to go through the whole install process with renv, snapshots and so on. With Docker they just docker run with some flags, because you’ve given them a computer you built from scratch. (01:02:20)




14. Starting from a base image and working inside it (29.1.1 Workflow for building a Dockerfile)
01:03:00–01:08:19

Q: When building your own container, why start from an existing machine like rocker/r-ver:4.6.2?

A: Whoever designed that image has already installed R, and probably the other things a brand-new computer needs for R to work. Those are like the compiler tools you installed on your own laptop for R. Starting from it lets you skip a few steps. (01:04:00)

Q: How did adding bash to docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash change what happened compared with running the R container without it?

A: Without it, the container starts its default program, R, and drops you at the R prompt. With bash it skips that default and gives you a terminal on the container, and the prompt changes to show you are on that machine. You can still type R there to start R. (01:05:20)

Q: Why open a shell in the base image and try your install steps by hand before writing them down?

A: It lets you go through the steps first and see that they work. Only then do you document them, so you end up with working instructions for building the machine from scratch. (01:05:43)

Q: The instructor installed cowsay in a running rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 container. Why did library(cowsay) fail after he exited and started it again?

A: A container has no real save state. When you turn it back on, it resets to how it was set up, so anything installed by hand in the previous session is gone. The instructor called this a benefit “for better or for worse.” (01:07:10)

Q: Why is a container a good place to try the destructive commands that DSCI 521 warned you about?

A: Even a command that deletes the whole computer only deletes the container. When you turn it back on, it is as if you never ran the command. That makes containers a safe place to try new packages or learn Linux without messing up your actual computer. (01:07:37)

Q: Why is it a poor solution to make users follow README install steps every time they start your container?

A: It is extremely painful to repeat those instructions on every start. A tidyverse install on a poorly set up Linux machine can take 15 minutes. You would be spending 15 minutes to run a 30-second analysis. (01:08:19)




15. Running R from the command line with Rscript -e (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:08:19–01:10:18

Q: Why did the instructor switch from install.packages() typed inside R to Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"?

A: Saving the setup comes down to knowing the terminal command that makes it happen. He needed R to execute the install from the command line, not just to open R. Rscript is how R runs commands in the terminal. (01:08:59)

Q: Explain each part of Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')", including the quotes.

A: Rscript runs R from the terminal, and -e says “I’m going to give you an R expression.” The expression is the install command. Pay attention to the quotes: the expression is wrapped in double quotes, so the package name inside uses single quotes. (01:09:41)

Q: After Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" worked in the container, why was the problem still not solved?

A: It showed the terminal command was right, because library(cowsay) then loaded. But on exiting and re-entering the container, the package was gone again. The information had to be saved somewhere, which led to the Dockerfile. (01:10:13)




16. The Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, CMD (29.1 Building container images from Dockerfile’s)
01:10:18–01:15:01

Q: What is a Dockerfile for, and how does it explain why the rocker/rstudio image starts with RStudio ready?

A: A Dockerfile, named with a capital D, holds the instructions for installing and setting up a computer. The RStudio image has its own Dockerfile, which installs RStudio and opens the ports. That is why RStudio is there when you load the container. (01:10:45)

Q: Explain the role of the FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 line in the class’s Dockerfile.

A: FROM is normally the first line, and it states the starting-point machine. Here that is a machine that already has R 4.6.2 installed. Everything after it builds on top of that machine. (01:11:30)

Q: You could start from a bare-minimum Linux image and install everything yourself. Why is a beefier base image acceptable?

A: Disk space is cheaper than other resources, so starting from a bigger machine is fine if that’s what you want. The bare-minimum route means installing every single thing by hand. That is a good way to learn Linux on your own time, not a requirement. (01:12:02)

Q: What is the difference between RUN and CMD in a Dockerfile?

A: RUN holds the bash commands the container runs during the build, such as the Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" line. CMD sets what a container from the new image does by default when it starts, here printing “Hello from my first image!”. CMD is the last thing the machine runs, and you can override it. (01:14:05)

Q: How is CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"] written differently from a shell command, and when does it run?

A: It looks like a bash command, but it is written as a list instead of terms separated by spaces. It runs by default when the container starts, unless you give another command, such as bash, which overrides it. (01:14:05)

Q: How would the middle of a Dockerfile look for a Python project using uv?

A: The RUN lines would install uv. A copy command would bring in your lock files, and then you would run uv sync. All the packages would then be installed in the container, so the machine itself has your compute environment ready. (01:14:15)




17. Building and running your own image (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:15:01–01:18:44

Q: In docker build --tag hello-cowsay ., what does the final . mean?

A: It tells Docker where to look for the Dockerfile: right here, in the current directory. By default docker build looks for a file named exactly Dockerfile with a capital D. The instructor noted this is probably the first time a lone dot is something you have to type. (01:15:38)

Q: Why does the course assume commands like docker build --tag hello-cowsay . are run from the root of the repository?

A: You could give docker build a full path, but the course assumes every command is run from the project root. That lets commands be copied and pasted without changing directories in the middle of something. Milestone instructions are written on that assumption. (01:16:11)

Q: Why did library(cowsay) load inside hello-cowsay but not in a fresh rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 container?

A: The Dockerfile gave the instructions for installing cowsay, and the image was then built from them. Every container started from hello-cowsay therefore begins with the package installed. Nothing was installed by hand. (01:17:52)

Q: What is the difference between docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay and docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash, and why is the second useful?

A: Without bash, the container runs its default CMD and prints the cow saying hello. With bash, you get shell access inside the image instead. That lets you play inside the container directly, for example to work out why code runs on your machine but not in the container. (01:17:30)

Q: Why does writing a Dockerfile depend on knowing shell commands?

A: A Dockerfile usually has one starting point and a middle full of RUN and copy commands. Every one of those lines is a command you must give the machine to install what you need. If you don’t know the shell command, you can’t write the step. (01:18:07)




18. Pinning versions, and what comes next
01:18:44–01:20:39

Q: How does a container keep the version of Quarto stable for a project?

A: The install line in the container names a specific version, even an older one. As long as you don’t change that install command, a year later you are still on the same version of the tool. (01:19:35)

Q: What went wrong when the instructor restarted a container in another class a few weeks earlier, and why?

A: He had not hard-pinned the versions in the container. Something had updated the day before, and nothing worked. In a real job you would spend hours fixing the update instead of doing the actual work. (01:19:55)

Q: Explain why the instructor wants explicit control over when software updates, and how Docker gives it.

A: Things updating without you being explicit about it, and without you knowing an update happened, is very annoying. It can also break your work. A Dockerfile says “here’s the version I want,” and that version does not change until you edit that line. (01:20:27)

Generated by qwen3.6-35b-a3b, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 1 of 5: Remember. Answer each question before you read its answer; tiers 2 to 5 build on these.

1. Project Advice and Course Logistics
00:00:14–00:05:43

Q: What is the instructor’s primary tip regarding the complexity of the group project’s data analysis?

A: The instructor advises keeping the analysis very simple, such as fitting a straight line if appropriate, and explicitly warns against using complex models like neural networks. (00:02:03)

Q: According to the lecture, which aspect of the machine learning project is explicitly not graded or important for this course?

A: The accuracy or results of the model do not matter, as the course focuses entirely on technically correct data science practices and reproducible workflows. (00:03:04)

Q: What is the main focus of this week’s lab assignment compared to next week’s assignment?

A: This week focuses on setting up Git branching and pull requests, while next week introduces containers. (00:04:49)




2. Git Branching and Pull Requests
00:06:05–00:25:29

Q: What command did the instructor run to create and switch to a new branch named today?

A: The instructor ran git switch -c today. (00:09:05)

Q: Which keywords can be placed in a pull request description to automatically close linked issues upon merging?

A: The keywords fixes or closes followed by the issue number will automatically close the issue when the pull request is merged. (00:18:33)

Q: What command removes local tracking references for branches that have been deleted on the remote repository?

A: Running git fetch --prune removes the local tracking references to deleted remote branches. (00:24:30)




3. Introduction to Containers and Docker (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:25:33–00:46:44

Q: What does the --rm flag do when used with docker run?

A: The --rm flag tells Docker to automatically delete the container instance when it stops running. (00:40:50)

Q: What does the -it flag combination enable in a docker run command?

A: The -it flags enable an interactive session by keeping the container’s input open and connecting it to a terminal. (00:41:16)

Q: According to the instructor, what is the primary advantage of containers over virtual machines regarding size and resource usage?

A: Containers are much smaller and more performant because they strip away the visual interface and full operating system, consuming significantly fewer disk space and memory resources. (00:35:20)




4. Running Web Applications in Containers (28 Using and running containers)
00:46:47–01:03:00

Q: What flag is used to map a container’s internal port to a specific port on the host machine?

A: The -p flag is used to map ports, formatted as -p <host_port>:<container_port>. (00:56:35)

Q: Which environment variable can be passed to the rocker/rstudio container to set a custom login password?

A: The PASSWORD environment variable can be passed using the -e flag to set a custom password. (01:00:05)

Q: What URL address is used to access the RStudio Server web application running inside a Docker container on the local machine?

A: The application is accessed via localhost followed by the mapped port number (e.g., localhost:8787). (00:58:19)




5. Building Custom Containers with Dockerfile (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:03:00–01:20:39

Q: Which Dockerfile instruction specifies the base image to build upon?

A: The FROM instruction specifies the base image that the new Docker image will be built on top of. (01:11:15)

Q: What command was used to build the custom image named hello-cowsay from the current directory?

A: The command docker build --tag hello-cowsay . was used to build the image. (01:15:24)

Q: In a Dockerfile, which instruction is used to execute shell commands that permanently modify the image layers during the build process?

A: The RUN instruction is used to execute shell commands during the image build process. (01:12:45)

1. Project scope and data analysis

Keep the analysis simple and technically correct

This is not primarily a model-fitting course, so avoid unnecessary complexity. If a straight-line model fits the task, use one rather than adding a neural network just for complexity.
Simple linear or logistic regression is acceptable, but the method must match the outcome. For example, logistic regression is not appropriate for predicting a numeric outcome.
Model performance is not the main focus. A model that is 60% accurate is not automatically a problem if the data science and machine-learning techniques are technically correct.
Do not turn the assignment into a portfolio project. Students who want a portfolio project can work on one separately.

Complete the requested components without overbuilding

The work may include code to download data, data cleaning, exploratory data analysis (EDA), modeling, figures, tables, and a report. Keep these components straightforward and follow the assignment’s instructions for the requested report detail.
The project is developed over approximately three or four weeks. Students should begin with a machine-learning project even though the lectures contain relatively little machine-learning code.
The lecture described the week of November 19, 2026, as focused on getting everything on Git, and the following week, November 26, 2026, as focused on containers. Individual assignments provide short practice for the main assignment; a later assignment includes a very simple data analysis.

title: Summary
text:
2. Git and GitHub workflows

Use branches to make changes

The practical exercise is to create or use a repository, bring it onto the local computer, edit a file, and open a pull request. The example adds “Today we will talk about containers” to the README.
Check the active branch with git status before staging or committing, especially to avoid making changes directly on main. If work has already been committed on main, the textbook includes a cheat sheet with commands for moving it.
The demonstrated workflow is to create a branch with git switch -c today, check the branch and working tree with git status, review changes with git diff, stage the README with git add README.md, commit with a descriptive message, and push the today branch.
In an active collaboration, pull the latest main branch before beginning work so that changes are based on an up-to-date version.

Use GitHub issues to plan and track work

Issues can record tasks, ideas, plans, meeting notes, and responsibilities. Meeting action items can be recorded in notes and split into issues assigned to individuals.
Issues are also useful for longer-term ideas or stretch goals that are not part of the immediate assignment.
Students are expected to create three issues to practice using the project-board system. Not every issue needs to be closed by the end of class.

Connect issues and pull requests

Issues and pull requests share one numbering sequence. Referencing an item by number, such as #2, creates a link that can be navigated in both directions.
A pull request can address one or several issues; the relationship is not necessarily one issue, one branch, and one pull request.
GitHub recognizes closing keywords in pull-request text. For example, fixes #2 links a pull request to issue 2 and automatically closes the issue when the pull request is merged. The instructor also mentioned closes, while recommending fixes as the keyword they regularly use.
Issues may remain open for future exploration or stretch goals. The course does not require every issue to be closed.

Maintain useful pull-request information

Issues and pull requests can be assigned to people. Pull requests can also have reviewers, such as a teammate asked to inspect the work.
The main pull-request description should explain what the change does and include relevant issue references. Keep it current so readers can understand the work without reconstructing it from later discussion.
Markdown checkboxes can track remaining tasks. A draft pull request can indicate that work is not yet ready.

Update and optionally clean up branches after merging

After a pull request is merged, check the state with git status, switch to main using git switch main, and pull the latest changes.
GitHub offers an option to delete the remote branch after merging, or it can be deleted from the branches view. This cleanup is optional; teams may have different workflows, and retaining branches can provide convenient references to past work.
Deleting a remote branch does not automatically remove its local reference. Use git fetch --prune to remove references to remote branches that no longer exist, then optionally remove a local branch with git branch -d <branch-name>. This does not erase the merged history.
Keeping a local branch name can be more convenient than navigating to a commit hash. Cleanup may help when many branches make Git output difficult to follow.

title: Summary
text:
3. Why containers are useful

Projects need tailored, minimal environments

Projects may last weeks, months, or years and may use different languages and tools. Students can choose R or Python, and visualization tools might include Altair, Plotly, or Matplotlib.
Package lists should include only what the project needs. Unused packages waste disk space, and installing many packages can lead to compatibility problems as packages update on different schedules.
In real-world projects, users need to adapt the environment to the project rather than rely on one standard package set.

Reproducibility across people, computers, and time

A project that runs on one person’s machine may fail on another’s because collaborators use different operating systems, hardware, or processor architectures, such as ARM or Intel.
UV and “RM,” as referenced in the lecture, help keep required packages consistent. Lock files record package versions, but do not necessarily include all the instructions, tools, or system components needed to reproduce the environment on another computer.
Containers provide a broader, shareable environment. They can also support modular pipelines so collaborators can use different parts of an analysis, not just its final report.
Containers bridge local development and remote computing environments that may have more memory, processor cores, or access to project data.

Containers compared with virtual machines

A container is a stripped-down computing environment containing the software and tools needed for a task. It typically does not include a full graphical operating system.
A virtual machine typically runs a full operating system, such as Windows, with a graphical interface. Containers are generally lighter and more resource-efficient, though they still add a layer and can incur a performance cost.
The lecture contrasted virtual-machine installations that might use 50 or 80 GB with class containers that may be under 2 GB or even under 1 GB. Virtual machines remain useful for some purposes, such as testing an MDS installation in Windows.
Containers can act as sandboxes: if an environment is damaged, it can be restarted or replaced. They are also useful for experimenting with operating systems or command-line tools without changing the local computer.
Docker is the container tool used in class. LXC, LXD, and Podman were mentioned as alternatives. Cloud computing commonly uses containers or similar environments rather than providing unrestricted access to a physical machine.

Pinning tools and preserving long-running analyses

Docker can preserve specific tool versions, not just project package versions. For example, a Docker image can provide R 4.3.2 even if the host has a different version, allowing multiple R versions to be used without installing each directly on the computer.
The lecture also noted that system-tool versions affect available commands: a container with a 2019 version of Git, for example, would not support git switch.
Stable environments can be important for long-running or regulated research. A clinical-trial analysis may span several years while R updates about every six months. Repeatedly changing or revalidating the environment may be undesirable.
For a drug submission to the relevant Canadian regulator, described in the lecture as the Canadian equivalent of the FDA, submitted materials may need to include code and the computing environment so the work can be reproduced.
Lock files preserve package versions; containers can additionally preserve the tool itself and potentially system-level tools.

text:
4. Docker commands and running containers

Pulling and running images

docker pull <image> downloads a container image to the local computer. Image names resemble a username and repository, such as images provided by Docker for R. Docker may report that an image is already up to date and can identify a specific image version with a hash.
The word pull is similar to git pull: both retrieve something onto the computer.
docker run <image> starts a container. If the image is not available locally, Docker downloads it. Additional flags can determine how the container runs.
Docker Desktop must be open before running the class commands. If Docker cannot be found, install Docker; if it is installed but not running, the commands will prompt the user to start it.
The instructor directed students to find three Docker commands in Slack and run them; the setup was expected to take about ten minutes.

Flags, terminals, and host-versus-container behavior

Double-dash options introduce longer flags. In the example, --rm removes a container when it stops. Without it, the container may need to be removed manually.
Single-dash flags are typically single-letter options and can be combined. For example, ls -a -l -h shows all files, lists them, and uses human-readable sizes.
-i enables interactive input and -t allocates a TTY; they are often used together for an interactive terminal. docker run --rm -it <image> is a demonstrated pattern.
A container behaves like a separate computer on the same physical hardware. An R container with R 4.3.2 runs that version rather than the host’s version. Typing R in a separate host terminal starts the host’s version, if installed and available on its path. Windows may require different path handling.
The R container initially did not have tidyverse, so library(tidyverse) failed there even though it worked in the host’s R environment. This demonstrates that the host and container have separate software and packages.
Check the terminal prompt or other interface cues to determine which machine is active. Commands such as who am I? can help identify the current username. Confirm the active environment before running commands, especially on remote systems.
Running containers use memory and other resources. Shut down containers that are no longer needed; several running containers can make a computer unresponsive.

section: 5. Browser-based applications, ports, and environment variables
text:
5. Browser-based applications, ports, and environment variables

Accessing applications through a browser

Applications such as RStudio and Jupyter Lab can run inside containers and be accessed through a browser. The browser provides a familiar interface while computation runs in a separately configured environment, locally or remotely.
Jupyter Lab was described as commonly running at localhost:8 in the lecture. VS Code and GitHub Codespaces were also mentioned as examples of familiar interfaces connected to separate computing environments.
The instructor demonstrated rocker/rstudio:4.2, accessing its browser-based RStudio through localhost:8787. This was separate from RStudio installed on the host.

Mapping ports

Docker’s -p option maps a host port to a port inside the container. Mapping host port 8787 to container port 8787 allows a browser to connect through localhost:8787.
Port numbers are selected by the application and are not inherently special. RStudio and Jupyter Lab use different ports; other tools use others.
Multiple instances can run concurrently if they use different host ports. The lecture gave an alternate host-port example transcribed as 61.11; users must connect through whichever host port they map.

Passing environment variables and sharing applications

Docker’s -e option passes environment variables into a container. In the RStudio example, PASSWORD was set to a chosen password. The available variables and default username depend on how the image was configured and documented.
A containerized dashboard or other application can be shared through a port, allowing end users to run it without separately installing all its dependencies. Users still need Docker but can run the prepared application with the relevant docker run options.
The lecture noted that containerized browser-based applications may be useful when a graphical interface is desired, though students may not need to install Jupyter Lab independently for the current course.

title: Summary
text:
6. Building a customized container

Interactive changes are temporary

The instructor demonstrated installing the R package cowsay, which provides ASCII-art output, and loading it with library(cowsay).
Packages installed interactively are not retained when a container is stopped and restarted. A fresh start returns the container to its configured state unless the setup instructions preserve the changes.
This reset behavior is useful for experimentation, but manually reinstalling dependencies every time is inconvenient. The instructor contrasted a potentially 15-minute tidyverse installation on an improperly configured Linux machine with an analysis that may take only 30 seconds.

Dockerfile instructions

A Dockerfile (capital D) contains instructions for setting up an environment. Existing R and RStudio images already have their own setup instructions.
FROM specifies the base image and is typically the first Docker instruction. The example FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 starts from an image with R 4.6.2 installed.
Smaller, minimal Linux images are possible but require more components to be installed manually. A somewhat larger base image can be a reasonable choice.
RUN executes shell or Bash commands while the image is being built. Rscript -e can run an R expression from the terminal. The instructor demonstrated using it to install cowsay; the shell example used double quotes outside and single quotes inside.
CMD specifies the default behavior when the image runs without an overriding command. The example printed “hello from my first image.” ENTRYPOINT is another instruction, described as less common and suited to specific cases.
Dockerfiles can also use instructions such as COPY and multiple RUN steps. For a Python environment, for example, files such as lock files could be copied in and uv sync run to install packages. Depending on the image, port instructions may also be needed; port 8787 was given as an example.

Building and testing an image

docker build creates an image from a Dockerfile. The -t option assigns a name or tag. The example command was docker build -t hello-cowsay .; the final . tells Docker to look in the current directory for the file named Dockerfile.
A full path can be supplied, but commands are commonly run from the project root, consistent with course working-directory conventions.
docker images lists images available locally. docker run --rm hello-cowsay runs the image. Adding bash opens a terminal inside the container for testing or investigation.
The instructor also demonstrated docker run --rm -it with an R image intended to use R 4.6.2, opening a shell rather than launching R automatically. From the shell, users can test setup steps and start R by typing R.
The general workflow is to start from a base image, add the commands and files needed to configure it, and build the result. Testing setup steps interactively first can help before documenting them in the Dockerfile.

Version pinning and upcoming setup

Specifying versions in a Dockerfile keeps tools and packages consistent until the setup instructions are deliberately changed. The lecture gave a “Cordova” example: a project using version 1.11 could instead select version 1.10 and continue using it while the instruction remains unchanged.
Pinning helps prevent unexpected updates from breaking a project. The instructor described another project where a tool updated shortly before work, causing the project to stop working because versions had not been pinned.
In the next class, students will set up a container for the language they use (R or Python), install Quarto and project packages, and configure the environment so the analysis can run locally and inside the container. Copy-and-paste setup instructions will be provided. The lecture also mentioned an “RM setup” placeholder for installing, snapshotting, and loading packages.
Container material will continue in the next class, including connecting multiple containers. No container work is required for this week’s lab assignment.

2. Git Branching and Pull Requests (00:06:05–00:25:29)

Branch workflow: Always ensure you are on the intended branch before committing. Use git switch -c <branch-name> to create and switch to a new branch.
GitHub Issues as project management: Use issues to track tasks, meeting notes, and action items. Assign people to issues to clarify responsibility.

section: 3. Introduction to Containers and Docker (27 Introduction to containerization) (00:25:33–00:46:44)
text:
3. Introduction to Containers and Docker (27 Introduction to containerization) (00:25:33–00:46:44)

Why containers?: Virtual environments (uv, renv) manage packages but not the underlying OS or system dependencies. Containers isolate the entire operating system user space, solving compatibility issues across different machines and operating systems.
Containers vs. Virtual Machines: Virtual machines emulate full hardware and OS, making them heavy (gigabytes). Containers are stripped-down, share the host OS, and are lightweight (often <1 GB), making them faster to start and share.
Pulling and running images: docker pull <image> downloads an image. docker run --rm -it <image> starts an interactive session. --rm deletes the container when it exits, preventing clutter. -it enables interactive terminal mode.
Version isolation: Containers allow running specific software versions (e.g., R 4.3.2 inside a container while the host has R 4.6.2) without interfering with the host system.


[!WARNING]
Containers reset to their initial state when stopped. Any packages or changes installed interactively are lost upon exit unless explicitly saved via a Dockerfile or volume mount.

section: 4. Running Web Applications in Containers (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps) (00:46:47–01:03:00)
text:
4. Running Web Applications in Containers (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps) (00:46:47–01:03:00)

Browser-based apps: Tools like JupyterLab, RStudio Server, and VS Code run inside containers and are accessed via a web browser.
Port mapping: Use -p <host_port>:<container_port> to map a container’s port to your local machine. RStudio defaults to port 8787. You can run multiple containers by mapping them to different host ports (e.g., 8788:8787).
Environment variables: Pass configuration using -e VARIABLE_NAME="value". For RStudio, you can set a custom password with -e PASSWORD="yourpassword" to avoid the default generated one.
Security note: Port mapping only exposes the app to your local machine. External access depends on your network configuration, but locally it is restricted to localhost.

title: Introduction to Containers and Git Workflow Review
section: 5. Building Custom Containers with Dockerfile (29 Customizing and building containers) (01:03:00–01:20:39)
text:
5. Building Custom Containers with Dockerfile (29 Customizing and building containers) (01:03:00–01:20:39)

Dockerfile structure: A plain-text file (named Dockerfile) that defines the steps to build a container image. It always starts with a base image.
FROM: Specifies the starting base image (e.g., rocker/r-ver:4.6.2).
RUN: Executes shell commands during the image build process (e.g., RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')") to install software permanently into the image layers.
CMD: Sets the default command a container runs when started from this image. It replaces the base image’s default. Syntax uses JSON array format: CMD ["executable", "param1"].
Building and running: Use docker build --tag <image_name> . to build the image from the current directory. Run it with docker run <image_name>. You can override the default CMD by appending a command like bash to the run command.


[!WARNING]
Always pin software versions in your Dockerfile (e.g., FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2). Relying on latest can cause unexpected breaks if upstream packages update outside your control.

27.1 Documenting and loading dependencies
You’ve made some beautiful data analysis pipeline/project using Make, R, and/or Python. It runs on your machine, but how easily can you, or someone else, get it working on theirs? The answer usually is, it depends…
What does it depend on?
