title: Course materials: 2026-11-19 lecture
text:
27.2 What is a container?
Containers are another way to generate (and share!) isolated computational environments. They differ from virtual environments (which we discussed previously) in that they are even more isolated from the computer’s operating system, and they can be used to share many other types of software, applications, and operating system dependencies.
Before we can fully define containers, however, we need to define virtualization. Virtualization is a process that allows us to divide the elements of a single computer into several virtual elements. These elements can include computer hardware platforms, storage devices, computer network resources, and even operating system user spaces (e.g., graphical tools, utilities, and programming languages).
Containers virtualize operating system user spaces so that they can isolate the processes they contain, as well as control the processes’ access to computer resources (e.g., CPUs, memory, and disk space). What this means in practice is that an operating system user space can be carved up into multiple containers running the same or different processes in isolation. Below we show the schematic of a container whose virtual user space contains the:

R programming language, the Bioconductor package manager, and two Bioconductor packages
Galaxy workflow software and two toolboxes that can be used with it
Python programming language, IPython interpreter, and Jupyter notebook package


Schematic of a container for genomics research. Source: https://doi.org/10.1186/s13742-016-0135-4
Exercise
Running a simple container
To further illustrate what a container looks like, and feels like, we can use Docker (containerization software) to run one and explore. First we will run a Linux (Debian-flavored) container that has R installed. To run this, type:
Terminal
docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2
Here is what each part of the command does:

docker run starts a new container from an image. If the image is not on your computer yet, Docker first downloads (pulls) it from a container registry.
--rm deletes the container when it stops, so that stopped containers do not pile up on your computer.
-it is two flags written together. -i (--interactive) keeps the container’s input open, so that what you type reaches R. -t (--tty) connects R to a terminal, so that R runs as an interactive session. Without -t, R stops with Fatal error: you must specify '--save', '--no-save' or '--vanilla'.
rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 is the image to run, rocker/r-ver from Docker Hub with the tag 4.3.2, which picks R 4.3.2.

More information
R starts because the image’s Dockerfile sets CMD ["R"], the command a container runs when it starts. Building images explains CMD.
Running containers covers these flags in more detail, and Docker’s docker run reference lists them all.
When you successfully launch the container, R should have started. Check the version of R - is it the same as your computer’s version of R? Use getwd() and list.files() to explore the container’s filesystem from R. Does this look like your computer’s filesystem or something else?
Type q() to quit R and exit the container.
Compare this version of R that is running in the container to the version of R you have on your computer.
Exercise
Running a container with RStudio as a web app
Next, try to use Docker to run a container that has the RStudio Server web application installed:
Terminal
docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 -e PASSWORD="apassword" rocker/rstudio:4.4.2
Then open a web browser on your computer and type: http://localhost:8787
If it worked, then you should be at an RStudio Sign In page. To sign in, use the following credentials:

username: rstudio
password: apassword

The RStudio Server web app being run by the container should look something like this:

Type Ctrl + C in the terminal where you launched the container to quit R and RStudio and exit the container.
We can pass in multiple environment variables by using multiple -e flags. For example, we can set the password for the rstudio user with the PASSWORD environment variable, but we can also disable the login screen with the DISABLE_AUTH=true variable.
Terminal
docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 -e PASSWORD="apassword" -e DISABLE_AUTH=true rocker/rstudio:4.4.2
Each container will have its own set of environment variables to control its behavior. For the rocker/rstudio project, you can find the environment variable documentation here: https://rocker-project.org/images/versioned/rstudio.html#environment-variables.
Exercise
Running a container with Jupyter as a web app
Next, try to use Docker to run a container that has the Jupyter web application installed:
Terminal
docker run --rm -p 8888:8888 quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14
In the terminal, look for a URL that starts with http://127.0.0.1:8888/lab?token= (for an example, see the highlighted text in the terminal below). Copy and paste that URL into your browser.
Important
Do not forget to copy the token= portion of the URL. If you only go to localhost:8888 or http://127.0.0.1:8888, it will ask you for the password/token.

The Jupyter web application being run by the container should look something like this:

Type Ctrl + c in the terminal where you launched the container to quit Jupyter and exit the container.

text:
27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines
Virtual machines are another technology that can be used to generate (and share) isolated computational environments. Virtual machines emulate the functionality of an entire computer on another physical computer. With virtual machines, the virtualization occurs at the layer of software that sits between the computer’s hardware and the operating system(s). This software is called a hypervisor. For example, on a Mac laptop, you could install a program called Oracle VirtualBox to run a virtual machine whose operating system was Windows 8.1, as the screenshot below shows:

A screenshot of a macOS computer running a Windows virtual machine. Source: https://www.virtualbox.org/wiki/Screenshots
Below, we share an illustration that compares where virtualization happens in containers compared to virtual machines. This difference leads to containers being more lightweight and portable compared to virtual machines, and also less isolated.

Source: https://www.docker.com/resources/what-container
Key take-home: Containerization software shares the host’s operating system, whereas virtual machines have a completely separate, additional operating system. This can make containers lighter (smaller in terms of size) and more resource- and time-efficient than using a virtual machine.

text:
27.5 Virtualization strategy advantages and disadvantages for reproducibility
Let’s collaboratively generate a list of advantages and disadvantages of each virtualization strategy in the context of reproducibility:

27.5.1 Virtual environment
A virtual environment, such as a uv or renv project, isolates the packages for one programming language.

Advantages

Extremely small size
Porous (less isolated) - makes it easy to pair the virtualized computational environment with files on your computer
Specify these with a single text file



Disadvantages

Not always possible to capture and share operating system dependencies, and other software your analysis depends upon
Computational environment is not fully isolated, and so missed dependencies can go unnoticed




27.5.2 Containers
A container isolates an operating system user space, with its programming languages, packages and other software.

Advantages

Somewhat lightweight in size (manageable for easy sharing - there are tools and software to facilitate this)
Possible to capture and share operating system dependencies, and other software your analysis depends upon
Computational environment is fully isolated, and errors will occur if dependencies are missing
Specify these with a single text file
Can share volumes and ports (advantage compared to virtual machines)



Disadvantages

Possible security issues - running software on your computer that you may allow to be less isolated (i.e., mount volumes, expose ports)
Takes some effort to share volumes and ports (disadvantage compared to virtual environments)




27.5.3 Virtual machine
A virtual machine isolates a whole computer, including its operating system.

Advantages

High security, because these are much more isolated (filesystem, ports, etc.)
Can share an entirely different operating system (might not be so useful in the context of reproducibility however…)



Disadvantages

Very big in size, which can make it prohibitive to share them
Takes great effort to share volumes and ports - which makes it hard to give access to data on your computer

27.6 Container usage workflow
Below is a schematic of a typical container usage workflow from a blog post by Arnaud Mazin. The source code for container images is stored in a file called a Dockerfile. Like a pyproject.toml or an renv.lock file, you would typically version control this with Git and store this in your GitHub repository with your analysis code. From the source Dockerfile we can build a Docker container image. This image is a binary file, from which we can run one, or more, container instances. Container instances are the computational environment in which you would run your analysis. Containers are usually ephemeral - we create them from the image when we want to run the analysis and then stop and remove/delete them after it has run. Docker images can (and should) be versioned and shared via container registries (which are akin to remote code repositories).

section: 28.1 Launching containers using Docker at the command line
text:
28.1 Launching containers using Docker at the command line
Docker has many ways we can run containers (GUI, command line, Docker Compose configuration files). Here we will learn how to use the command-line interface for running container instances from container images. We will then build on this knowledge to move to using Docker Compose configuration files for increased efficiency. We are opting to use command-line and configuration file tools so that we can automate and scale the running of containers. It is also more reproducible.

28.1.1 Launch and run containers
Below we demonstrate how to launch and run containers using the ubuntu image as an example, which is Ubuntu Linux with almost nothing else installed. We will slowly walk through the 4 basic steps needed to run a container:

Step 1 - launch the Docker app (for OSX & Windows only)
On Mac and Windows, Docker runs in a virtual machine managed by the Docker Desktop app. To run a Docker container, you must have this running. To do this, use Launchpad/Finder/Start menu/etc. to find and launch Docker Desktop.

Note: Docker might already be running. If so, great, but if it’s not, the commands below will not work. So it is always good to check!



Step 2 - get container image from Docker Hub
To run a container instance, you need to have a container image locally. One way to get a container image locally is to pull (i.e., download) one from a container registry like Docker Hub. To do this we use the docker pull <CONTAINER> command. You will commonly see the container to pull written as: container_registry/container_user/container_image:container_image_version_tag.
If you only see container_user/container_image:container_image_version_tag, Docker will assume you are using Docker Hub as the container registry (this is the default). In the previous chapter, we ran the quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14 container from the quay.io registry, and rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 from Docker Hub.
Sometimes the container_image_version_tag is omitted. When this happens, the most recent container is pulled, and it has the version tag latest. In data analysis projects, we try to avoid using this strategy because Docker is lazy, and if you already have a latest image on your local host machine, docker run container_user/container_image will use it without checking whether there is a newer version of the container image on the remote container registry. Only docker pull checks the registry for a newer latest.
We will now pull the ubuntu Docker image, container image version 24.04, which is hosted on Docker Hub, by running the following in the terminal:
Terminal
docker pull ubuntu:24.04
We can verify that it successfully pulled by typing docker images ubuntu:24.04, or docker images to list all of your images. When you do that, you should see something like:
Terminal
docker images ubuntu:24.04
Output
IMAGE          ID             DISK USAGE   CONTENT SIZE   EXTRA
ubuntu:24.04   008173c23f95        141MB         30.9MB        
Note

You can skip this step and just go on to docker run ... as that command will pull the image if you do not have it locally.
If you ever need to delete a container image from your computer, you can run docker rmi <IMAGE_ID> to do so.



Step 3 - launch a container from the image and poke around!
We use docker run to launch a container instance from a container image. By default, the container instance will execute its programmed launch behavior and immediately stop. Thus, if we want to use the container in a more interactive way, we need to tell Docker that by adding the -it flag to our docker run command.
Terminal
docker run -it ubuntu:24.04
If it worked, then your command line prompt should now look something like this, which says that you are the user root in the container whose ID starts with 8f04536bf43d, in its folder /:
Output
root@8f04536bf43d:/#
You can use standard Bash shell commands like ls, cd, and pwd to explore the container:
Terminal
pwd
ls
Output
/
bin  boot  dev  etc  home  lib  media  mnt  opt  proc  root  run  sbin  srv  sys  tmp  usr  var
You can type exit to leave when you are done (your prompt will look normal again)!


Step 4 - clean up your container!
After you close a container, it still “hangs” around… It has stopped running, but the container instance still exists on your computer. You can view the containers on your computer, including the stopped ones, using docker ps -a. It may list other containers too:
Terminal
docker ps -a
Output
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE          COMMAND       CREATED          STATUS                     PORTS     NAMES
8f04536bf43d   ubuntu:24.04   "/bin/bash"   15 seconds ago   Exited (0) 3 seconds ago             ecstatic_hoover
You can remove the container by typing docker rm <container_id>:
Terminal
docker rm 8f04536bf43d
Output
8f04536bf43d
After you remove the container, you can prove to yourself that the container is no longer “hanging around” via docker ps -a, but that you still have the image installed (which you can see via docker images).

Note: to remove running containers, you will need to first stop them via docker stop <container_id>.



That’s a lot of work…
We walked through those steps slowly so that you understand how everything is working. However, it is not the most efficient way to work with Docker container instances when using docker run. What we typically do is tell Docker to delete the container upon exit using the --rm flag in the run command.
The command below runs a new container instance from the same image. This one command is equivalent to steps 2–4 above!
Terminal
docker run \
    --rm \
    -it \
    ubuntu:24.04
Note
We are using \ above to split a Bash command across lines to make it more readable. You will see that throughout this chapter.



28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps
Docker documentation on Container networking
If we want to use a graphical user interface (GUI) with our containers, for example to be able to use the computational environment in the container in an integrated development environment (IDE) such as RStudio or JupyterLab, then we need to map the correct port from the container to a port on our computer.
Note
In computer science, ports are points where network connections start and end. They can be physical (e.g., USB ports, Ethernet ports) or virtual. In the case of virtual ports, they are really a software-based addressing mechanism that identifies points to connect specific processes or types of network services. When we are discussing ports in the context of containerization, we are referring to virtual ports.
To do this, we use the -p flag with docker run, specifying the port in the host (your computer) on the left-hand side, and the port in the container on the right-hand side of :. For example, to run the rocker/rstudio container image we would type -p 8787:8787 to map the ports as shown in the docker run command below:
Terminal
docker run \
    --rm \
    -p 8787:8787 \
    -e PASSWORD="apassword" \
    rocker/rstudio:4.4.2
Then to access the web app, we need to navigate a browser URL to http://localhost:<HOST_PORT>. In this case, we would navigate to http://localhost:8787 to use the RStudio Server web app from the container.
Note that we can only map one port on our computer (the container/Docker host) to a container at any given time. However, our computer (the container/Docker host) has many ports we can choose from to map. So if we wanted to run a second rocker/rstudio container, then we could map it to a different port as shown below:
Terminal
docker run \
    --rm \
    -p 8788:8787 \
    -e PASSWORD="apassword" \
    rocker/rstudio:4.4.2
When we do this, to run the app in a browser on our computer, we need to go to http://localhost:8788 (instead of http://localhost:8787) to access this container as we mapped it to the 8788 port on our computer (and not 8787).
Another important note is that the container port is specific to the container, and the web app installed therein. So we cannot change that without changing the container image and/or the application installed therein. Where do you learn what port is exposed in a container image? The image documentation should specify this. For example, in the rocker/rstudio container image documentation it states:

Source: https://hub.docker.com/r/rocker/rstudio


28.1.4 Changing the containers default command
When we launch containers, they execute the command at runtime that was specified in their Dockerfile. For example, in the case of the Rocker and Jupyter images, this default behavior is to run a web app. Sometimes the default container behavior is not what we want to do. Instead, we want to do something different, like run the container as a Bash shell to test out some installation commands (common when we are building and customizing our own containers) or use the container to run a script non-interactively (like executing a data analysis pipeline from beginning to end).
To do this, we can append a new command to the end of our docker run commands. For example, to open the rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 image in an interactive Bash shell, we would run:
Terminal
docker run \
    --rm \
    -it \
    rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 \
    bash
Notice the command above does not specify the ports, nor does it set the password. This is because, in this instance, we are not using this container to run it as a web app; we are just running it as a Bash shell (which needs no ports or authentication).
The general form for running things non-interactively is this:
Terminal
docker run \
    --rm \
    -v PATH_ON_YOUR_COMPUTER:VOLUME_ON_CONTAINER DOCKER_IMAGE PROGRAM_TO_RUN \
    PROGRAM_ARGUMENTS

title: Course materials: 2026-11-19 lecture
text:
29.1 Building container images from Dockerfile’s

A Dockerfile is a plain-text file that contains commands primarily about what software to install in the Docker image. This is the more trusted and transparent way to build Docker images.
Once we have created a Dockerfile, we can build it into a Docker image.
Docker images are built in layers, and as such, Dockerfiles always start by specifying a base Docker image that the new image is to be built on top of.
Docker containers are all Linux containers and thus use Linux commands to install software. However, there are different flavors of Linux (e.g., Ubuntu, Debian, CentOS, Red Hat), and thus you need to use the right Linux install commands to match your flavor of container. For this course, we will focus on Ubuntu- or Debian-based images (and that means if we need to install software outside of R and Python packages, we will use apt-get as our installation program). However, most of what we’ll be doing for installation is R, Python, and their packages. For those, an image uses the same tools as your laptop, uv for Python and renv for R, which the next chapters put into an image.

apt or apt-get?
Ubuntu has two commands for its package manager. apt is designed for people typing at a terminal, and its behavior may change between versions. apt-get is the older command, which keeps working the same way, so Ubuntu’s apt manual page recommends apt-get for scripts. The RUN lines in a Dockerfile are a script, so this book uses apt-get in them. apt even prints a warning when a script runs it:
Output
WARNING: apt does not have a stable CLI interface. Use with caution in scripts.
At a container’s prompt either command works, but using apt-get there too means you can copy the command that worked straight into the Dockerfile.

29.1.1 Workflow for building a Dockerfile
It can take a LOOOOOOOONNNG time to troubleshoot the building of Docker images. Thus, to speed things up and be more efficient, we suggest the workflow below:

Choose a base image to build off (from https://hub.docker.com/).
Create a Dockerfile named Dockerfile and save it in an appropriate project repository. Open that file and type FROM <BASE_IMAGE> on the first line. Add any files that need to be accessed at build time via the COPY command.
In a terminal, type docker run --rm -it <BASE_IMAGE> bash and interactively try the install commands you think will work. Edit and try again until the install command works. The bash at the end starts a Bash shell in place of the image’s default command.
Write working install commands in the Dockerfile, preceding them with RUN, and save the Dockerfile.
After adding every 2–3 commands to your Dockerfile, try building the Docker image via docker build --tag <TEMP_IMAGE_NAME> <PATH_TO_DOCKERFILE_DIRECTORY>.
Once the entire Dockerfile works from beginning to end on your laptop, then you can finally move to building remotely (e.g., creating a trusted build on GitHub Actions).



29.1.2 Build your first image
Let’s follow the workflow to build a small image with R and the R package cowsay, which draws an animal saying whatever you give it.
For step 1, the base image is rocker/r-ver:4.6.2, Ubuntu Linux with R 4.6.2 installed. For step 2, make a folder for the project and move into it:
Terminal
mkdir hello-cowsay
cd hello-cowsay
In a text editor, create a file in that folder named Dockerfile, with no file extension, that has one line:
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2
For step 3, start a container from the base image with a Bash shell:
Terminal
docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash
Inside R, you would install the package with install.packages("cowsay"). At the container’s Bash prompt, Rscript -e runs a line of R code instead, which is the form a RUN line needs:
Terminal
Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"
Output
Installing package into ‘/usr/local/lib/R/site-library’
(as ‘lib’ is unspecified)
also installing the dependencies ‘crayon’, ‘rlang’

trying URL 'https://p3m.dev/cran/__linux__/resolute/latest/src/contrib/crayon_1.5.3.tar.gz'
trying URL 'https://p3m.dev/cran/__linux__/resolute/latest/src/contrib/rlang_1.3.0.tar.gz'
trying URL 'https://p3m.dev/cran/__linux__/resolute/latest/src/contrib/cowsay_1.2.2.tar.gz'
* installing *binary* package ‘crayon’ ...
* package ‘crayon’ successfully unpacked and SHA256 sums checked
* DONE (crayon)
* installing *binary* package ‘rlang’ ...
* package ‘rlang’ successfully unpacked and SHA256 sums checked
* DONE (rlang)
* installing *binary* package ‘cowsay’ ...
* package ‘cowsay’ successfully unpacked and SHA256 sums checked
* DONE (cowsay)

The downloaded source packages are in
    ‘/tmp/RtmpAypckK/downloaded_packages’
Then try it:
Terminal
Rscript -e "cowsay::say('Hello')"
Output
 _______ 
< Hello >
 ------- 
      \
       \

        ^__^ 
        (oo)\ ________ 
        (__)\         )\ /\ 
             ||------w|
             ||      ||
Type exit to leave the container.
For step 4, write the commands that worked into the Dockerfile:
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"

CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"]
RUN runs the install while the image is built. It is the same command you typed at the container’s Bash prompt, which is one reason this book works at the command line (see Introduction to the Bash Shell). CMD sets the command a container from this image runs when it starts. It replaces the base image’s own CMD ["R"] (see Introduction to containerization), so a container runs our line of R code instead of starting R.
A misspelled package does not stop the build
install.packages() only warns when it cannot find a package, and Rscript still finishes with exit status 0, which tells the shell that the command worked. echo $? prints the exit status of the last command:
Terminal
Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsya')"
echo $?
Output
Installing package into ‘/usr/local/lib/R/site-library’
(as ‘lib’ is unspecified)
Warning message:
package ‘cowsya’ is not available for this version of R

A version of this package for your version of R might be available elsewhere,
see the ideas at
https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-patched/R-admin.html#Installing-packages 
0
So a RUN line with a misspelled package builds without an error, into an image without the package. Adding library() after the install makes R stop with an error, which stops the build at that step:
Terminal
Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsya'); library(cowsya)"
echo $?
Output
Installing package into ‘/usr/local/lib/R/site-library’
(as ‘lib’ is unspecified)
Warning message:
package ‘cowsya’ is not available for this version of R

A version of this package for your version of R might be available elsewhere,
see the ideas at
https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-patched/R-admin.html#Installing-packages 
Error in library(cowsya) : there is no package called ‘cowsya’
Execution halted
1
For step 5, build the image from the folder that has the Dockerfile:
Terminal
docker build --tag hello-cowsay .

--tag hello-cowsay names the image. You can add a version after a colon, such as hello-cowsay:0.1; without one, Docker uses the tag latest.
. is the build context, the folder Docker reads the Dockerfile and any copied files from, here the current folder.

Output

Run a container from the new image. It needs no -it, because our R code prints its message and exits:

text:
29.2 Dockerfile command summary
The most common Dockerfile commands I use:







Command
Description




FROM
States which base image the new Docker image should be built on top of


RUN
Specifies that a command should be run in a shell


ENV
Sets environment variables


EXPOSE
Specifies the port the container should listen to at runtime


COPY or ADD
Adds files (or URLs in the case of ADD) to a container’s filesystem


CMD
Sets the default command a container runs when it starts; a command after the image name in docker run replaces it


ENTRYPOINT
Sets a command that always runs when a container starts; anything after the image name in docker run is passed to it as arguments


WORKDIR
Sets the working directory for any RUN, CMD, ENTRYPOINT, COPY and ADD instructions that follow it in the Dockerfile



And more here in the Dockerfile reference.

title: Course materials: 2026-11-19 lecture
text:
29.4 Dockerfile FAQ
These questions come up when you start writing your own Dockerfile.

29.4.1 1. Where does the Dockerfile live?
The Dockerfile should live in the root directory of your project.


29.4.2 2. How do I make an image from a Dockerfile?
There are 2 ways to do this! I use the first when developing my Dockerfile (to test quickly that it works), and then the second when I want a build that others can check, made from the Dockerfile in the repository.

Build a Docker image locally on your laptop
Build a Docker image on GitHub Actions (see Building images for several platforms)



29.4.3 3. How do I build an image locally on my laptop?
From the directory that contains your Dockerfile (usually your project root):
Terminal
docker build --tag IMAGE_NAME:VERSION .
Note
--tag lets you name and version the Docker image. You can call this anything you want. The version number/name comes after the colon.
After I build, I then try to docker run ... to test the image locally. If I don’t like it, or it doesn’t work, I delete the image with docker rmi {IMAGE_NAME}, edit my Dockerfile, and try to build and run it again.

title: Git Pull Request Review and Intro to Docker Containers
section: 1. Branch, issue, and pull-request workflow (Git review)
text:
1. Branch, issue, and pull-request workflow (Git review)

Before you commit, check your branch: run git status right before git add and definitely before git commit, and habitually git pull origin main first so you’re not branching from an out-of-date main. If you accidentally commit on main, the textbook has a set of recovery commands.
git switch -c <name>: create and switch to a new branch; uncommitted working-tree changes come along with you (the demo edited README.md on main, then created today before committing).
Pushing offers the PR: git push origin today prints a GitHub URL (.../pull/new/today) that opens the pull-request form.
Issues and pull requests share one numbering sequence: in the demo repo, issues #1 and #2 were followed by PR #3. You can reference any item by number (e.g. “meeting from #1”) and the reference is two-way — both items link to each other.
closes / fixes keywords: a sentence in the PR description that ends with closes #1 fixes #2 makes GitHub auto-close those issues when the PR is merged. This is a GitHub service feature, not a Git feature. One PR may deal with several issues (the lab task required three issues); referencing the same issue multiple times is fine.
Descriptions are editable and Markdown: keep the first comment of an issue or PR as the source of truth and edit it as decisions evolve; use checkboxes (- [ ] item 2) to track to-dos; assignees claim responsibility (“this is my responsibility, I’m claiming it”) while reviewers are requested separately — the instructor assigned Copilot as a reviewer.
Issues as meeting notes: record meeting notes on the issue board, then spawn action items out as separate issues. The instructor also files issues from an AI agent mid-work (“I just had this idea, can you file the issue?”) instead of tabbing away to a browser.
Cleanup after merging: delete the remote branch on GitHub (the “delete branch” button in the PR, or the trash can in the branches view), then git fetch --prune to drop the origin/today tracking ref and git branch -d today (lowercase -d) to drop the local ref. The merge commit remains visible in git log --oneline --graph --all. Deletion is not required in this class — keeping branches as a record is fine — and different teams use different Git conventions, so this is one valid workflow, not the only one.

title: Git Pull Request Review and Intro to Docker Containers
text:
2. Project scoping (the MDS group project)

Do not make your analysis difficult: this was the biggest tip of the session. If the model is a straight line, fit the straight line; do not say “it’s my time to shine” and build a neural net — “you’re going to have a very bad time in about two weeks.” This is not a model-fitting course; you will almost never see machine-learning code in the lectures.
Accuracy is not graded; correctness is: a 60%-accurate model is acceptable, but the technique must be right — “you shouldn’t be fitting logistic regression when you’re trying to predict a numeric outcome. That’s just wrong.”
Don’t turn it into a portfolio project: if you want a showcase project, do it in parallel, not inside this assignment.
Scope still includes: code that downloads the data, some cleaning, some EDA, modeling code, and figures/tables — just keep each part very simple. R or Python is fine, and per-project package choices (Altair, Plotly, Matplotlib, …) are expected; the instructor no longer provides one package list.
Milestone sequence: the same project is built on for three or four weeks. This week: getting everything on Git. Next week: containers. Follow the steps in the assignment in the student repository.

title: Git Pull Request Review and Intro to Docker Containers
text:
3. Why containers exist

The goal of the class: create a compute environment you can share with other people and run all of your code through — because “this works on my machine” doesn’t work when a teammate can’t run your code.
Lock files vs. containers: uv and renv lock files track package versions; containers go one level deeper and pin the tools themselves — the version of R, even the version of Git (joke: ship a 2019-era Git in the container and teammates can’t run git switch).
Real-world example: multi-year clinical-trial research needs a fixed R version even though R ships updates every six months; drug regulators ask for your code and your compute environment so they can reproduce the analysis. You hand over the container that ran the analysis, not your MacBook.
Hardware diversity: Mac vs Windows, ARM vs Intel chips — install paths differ, so a shared container is the same on all of them.
Containers vs. virtual machines: a VM installs a full OS (a Windows install is a 50–80 GB affair; the VM itself can take ~80 GB) with a GUI. A container is a stripped-down OS user-space with only what you install — the rocker images here are under 1–2 GB — so containers are lighter on disk, memory, and compute. They are less isolated than VMs, and there is a performance hit from the extra layer that there’s no way around.
Ephemeral by design: a running container has no save state; turn it off and it resets to the image. That’s a feature for experimenting: “if you blow it up, then you just restart it” — containers are a safe place to practice destructive commands and OS mucking-around. Remote machines also hand you containers as sandboxes when you can’t (or aren’t trusted to) install software directly.
Ecosystem: Docker is the tool in this course; LXC, LXD, podman, and cloud providers’ own options also exist. Cloud compute generally runs on containers — you get a container on a server, not bare access to a machine.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Git Pull Request Review and Intro to Docker Containers
text:
4. Pulling and running images

Docker Desktop must be open on macOS/Windows before any Docker command; a “can’t find Docker” error means the app isn’t running.
docker pull <registry>/<user>/<image>:<tag>: downloads an image from a registry without running it (Docker Hub by default; quay.io when the name says so). The rocker organization publishes images that only have R installed (rocker/r-ver), plus R+RStudio (rocker/rstudio).
The three class images (pulled from the commands posted in Slack; ~13 GB of disk space, ~3 GB to download in total): rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, rocker/rstudio:4.4.2, and quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14 (the largest, ~9 GB). Pulling them before class avoids waiting ~20 minutes mid-lecture; docker run will also pull a missing image on the fly.
docker run --rm -it <image>: --rm deletes the container when it stops, so stopped containers don’t pile up and eat RAM; -i (--interactive) passes your typing in, and -t (TTY) gives you a terminal to interact with — “you don’t have to know what that is, but you’ll see it everywhere.”
The image’s default command runs automatically: rocker/r-ver’s Dockerfile sets CMD ["R"], so the run command dropped straight into an R session — R 4.3.2 (2023-10-31) “Eye Holes” on Linux, versus the host’s R 4.6.2, proven by running R --version first.
Proof it’s a different machine: library(tidyverse) failed inside the fresh container with Error in library(tidyverse) : there is no package called 'tidyverse' while the same command works on the host. Pay attention to where you’re typing — the prompt changes when you’re inside a container or on a remote machine (the instructor’s “machine in the closet” example), and whoami-style commands from DSCI 521 help confirm which machine you’re on. q() quits R and exits the container.

title: Git Pull Request Review and Intro to Docker Containers
section: 5. Web apps in containers: ports and environment variables
text:
5. Web apps in containers: ports and environment variables

Browser-first applications: RStudio Server, JupyterLab, and VS Code are built as web apps so the same interface can run on a remote machine with more cores and memory — JupyterLab lives at localhost:8888 for the same reason, and GitHub’s Codespaces button is VS Code in a browser. Electron apps follow the same “the browser is the application” pattern.
Port mapping with -p: -p <host_port>:<container_port> forwards a port on your computer to the app’s port inside the container. RStudio listens on 8787 inside the image, so docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 puts it at http://localhost:8787. To run a second RStudio at the same time, map a different host port to the same container port. These port numbers are arbitrary conventions (Jupyter’s is 8888); the container-side port is documented per image.
Authentication: the first run prints a random password to the terminal (The password is set to ...). Set your own with an environment variable: -e PASSWORD="apassword" (multiple -e flags allowed). Sign in at http://localhost:8787 with username rstudio.
Stopping it: the web app runs in the foreground, so Ctrl+C in that terminal stops the container.
Security note confirmed in class: even with the port number known, the app is only reachable from the host machine — without access to the physical machine, port 8787 is not available to you.
DSCI 532 preview: a dashboard can be shipped as a container; the end user only needs Docker, not your whole install process.

title: Git Pull Request Review and Intro to Docker Containers
section: 6. Building your own image: the Dockerfile
text:
6. Building your own image: the Dockerfile

The problem it solves: packages installed in a running container disappear when it restarts (demonstrated live with cowsay), and teammates shouldn’t have to follow your README’s install steps every time — tidyverse on a bare Linux machine can be a 15-minute install for a 30-second script.
Rscript -e "<R expression>": runs R non-interactively from the shell — Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" — which is the form a RUN line needs. Mind the nested quotes: double on the outside, single on the inside.
Dockerfile (capital D, no extension, lives in the project root): the plain-text build recipe, version-controlled in Git alongside your analysis code.

FROM <base>: the starting machine. rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 already has R 4.6.2 plus the system packages R needs; you could start from a bare-minimum Linux image and install everything by hand.
RUN <bash command>: shell commands executed during the build.
CMD [...]: the default command a container runs when it starts (JSON-list form); it replaces the base image’s own CMD ["R"]. ENTRYPOINT exists but is “pretty rare”.
The file the class wrote, committed to main in the demo repository’s Dockerfile:
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"

CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"]

Recommended workflow: try the install commands interactively first — docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash gives you the container’s shell instead of R (a command after the image name replaces the default CMD) — verify they work, then write them into the Dockerfile; add every couple of lines and rebuild while you go.
docker build --tag hello-cowsay .: --tag names the image (no version given → latest); . means “the Dockerfile in the current directory” — the first time a dot is something you actually type. Docker by default looks for a file named exactly Dockerfile; you can also point it at a full path to another file. Assume all commands run from the project root — that’s what milestone-one instructions will say. The build prints each step, and unchanged steps show as CACHED (the class’s build reused the already-run install layer).
docker images: lists local images with their disk usage — hello-cowsay:latest came out at 1.45 GB on disk.
Running the result: docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay executed the CMD — the ASCII-art “Hello from my first image!” — while docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash opened a shell where library(cowsay) now works because the install is baked into the image.
Pin your versions (flagged as a real pain point): pin the base-image tag and any tool versions — Quarto is at 1.11; the instructor suggested building on 1.10 if you want to stay there. Anecdote: a container restarted without hard version pins picked up an upstream update the day before and “nothing worked” — hours spent fixing the update instead of doing the work.
Coming up: next week’s milestone builds an image that installs R or Python, Quarto, and your packages (materials sketch COPY-ing lock files plus uv sync / renv restore in the image); Docker Compose (chapter 33) is next class, not covered today.

section: 1. Project advice: keep the analysis simple
text:
1. Project advice: keep the analysis simple

The analysis is not the point of the course: the course is about workflows, not model fitting. You will see almost no machine learning code in lectures.
Still required: code that downloads the data, any cleaning, EDA, modelling code, figures and tables. Keep each part very simple.
Correctness still matters: the score of the model does not matter (60% accuracy is fine), but the methods must be correct. For example, do not fit logistic regression to predict a numeric outcome.
Warning: do not use this project as your portfolio piece. Choosing something complicated such as a neural net will give you “a very bad time in about two weeks”. Do a portfolio project in parallel if you want one.
Same project throughout: you build on the same project for three or four weeks. This week is getting everything on Git; next week is containers.
Language choice: R projects are allowed, but class demos will be in Python. Package choices such as Altair, Plotly or Matplotlib may differ between groups, so each project must define its own minimal package list.

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
text:
2. Branch workflow habits

Check your branch before git add, and definitely before git commit: branch-based work is assumed from now on. Run git status and read the “On branch …” line.
Pull main before starting work: with several people working on several branches, this avoids building on out-of-date code.
Edited files while on main? If you have not committed yet, git switch -c <branch> takes your uncommitted changes onto the new branch. If you already committed on main, the textbook has a cheat sheet of commands to move the commits.

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
text:
3. GitHub issues as project management

Issues track what is happening in a project: you can use them for:

assigning responsibility (who is doing what);
meeting notes, from which separate action-item issues are created;
parking ideas and stretch goals (for example, “it would be nice to try a neural net”);
asking a coding agent to file an issue for a passing thought, which the instructor does himself.

Shared numbering: issues and pull requests use one counter. In the demo, issues #1 and #2 were followed by pull request #3.
#N references are two-way: writing “meeting from #1” in issue #2 also shows a link back on #1. This automatic cross-linking is a GitHub feature, not a Git one, and is a big reason GitHub became popular.
Assignees and reviewers: you usually assign yourself to your own pull request. You can request a teammate (or Copilot, as in the demo) as a reviewer. Some projects block merging until someone has reviewed the work.
Keep the first comment up to date: readers look at the first comment to learn why an issue or pull request exists, not at the whole conversation. Edit it when decisions change. Project owners can edit other people’s comments.
Task lists: Markdown checkboxes (- [ ], - [x]) in issues and pull requests show what is still unfinished. A draft pull request is the other way to signal “not done yet”.
For this course: you must create at least three issues. One pull request may handle all three. You are not graded on closing every issue, so feel free to record longer-term ideas as issues.
Demo artefacts: Issue #1, Issue #2, Pull request #3.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
text:
4. Closing keywords in pull requests

fixes #N / closes #N: when a pull request containing these is merged, GitHub closes the referenced issues automatically.

The demo PR description was:
this is the fix for #2

- [x] item 1
- [ ] item 2

closes #1 fixes #2
In class the instructor briefly wondered whether closes worked, saying “fixes is the one I almost always use”. The demo repository shows both issue #1 and issue #2 were closed by PR #3, so both keywords work.

Write the message strategically: one pull request can close several issues, so you don’t have to close each one by hand. The keywords also work in commit messages, but they are harder to see there.
The instructor uses this for the textbook: he files issues, then lists fixes #… in the pull request, so his open-issues tab doubles as a to-do list.

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
text:
5. Cleaning up after a merge

Delete the remote branch on GitHub: use the “Delete branch” button on the merged pull request, or the trash-can icon on the repository’s Branches page.
Deleting branches is optional in this course: some people keep branches as a record. Teams and companies differ in how they use Git, so this is one workflow, not the only one.
git fetch --prune: removes local references to remote branches that no longer exist (here, origin/today).
git branch -d today: deletes the local branch label.
History is kept: the merge commit and the branch’s commit still show in git log --oneline --graph --all. Only the shortcut name disappears, so you would now need the hash (3c6d82a) instead of git switch today. Clean up when too many branch labels make the graph hard to read.

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
section: 6. Why containers? The problem a stable compute environment solves
text:
6. Why containers? The problem a stable compute environment solves
(Introduction to containerization)

Projects last a long time and involve other people: you need a stable environment for yourself over days, months or years, and one that also works for teammates.
Teammates’ machines differ: Mac vs Windows, and ARM vs Intel chips even among Windows machines. “It works on my machine” is not good enough when a teammate cannot run your code.
What virtual environments already cover: uv (Python) and renv (R), from 521, pin package versions through lock files.
What they don’t cover: the language version itself, and system tools.

Example: a container with a 2019 version of Git would not have git switch.
Lock files also assume the other person has uv installed. Installing it might disturb their setup.

A container is a virtual computer you build from scratch and hand to others: everyone runs code on “the same computer” even on different hardware.
Pharmaceutical example: clinical trial analyses can run for years, while R releases roughly every six months. Regulators reviewing a drug submission want the code and the full compute environment, so you give them the container that ran the analysis.
Other uses:

prototyping locally, then running the identical environment on a bigger machine that has the data;
giving someone a sandbox on a shared or remote machine without letting them install software directly on it.

Containers reset: if you break one, restart it and you get a fresh one. This makes them a safe place to learn Linux and the command line.
Cost: there is a performance hit from the extra layer, but this is often worth it.
Other container tools exist: LXC, LXD, Podman. Cloud compute mostly runs on containers, so you rarely get bare access to a machine.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
text:
7. Containers vs virtual machines

Virtual machine: a full operating system, typically with the full graphical interface. A Windows VM is roughly a 50–80 GB install. The instructor still uses VMs, for example to test the MDS install instructions as if on Windows.
Container: only the minimum set of things you install, usually with no GUI. That is one reason 521 pushed typing commands in the terminal. Many containers are under 1–2 GB yet run a full computational stack.
Result: containers use less disk, memory and compute than VMs.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
section: 8. Pulling and running other people’s images
text:
8. Pulling and running other people’s images
(Using and running containers)

Docker Desktop must be running before any docker command (on Mac and Windows). If you get a “can’t find Docker” error, Docker is not installed.
docker pull <image>: downloads an image, like git pull pulls code. Names look like a GitHub user and repository: rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 is the rocker organisation’s R-only image, with the tag 4.3.2 meaning R 4.3.2. If the image is already up to date, Docker says so and shows its digest (hash).
docker run: starts (turns on) a machine from an image. It also downloads the image first if you don’t have it.
--rm: a double-dash, multi-letter flag. It deletes the container when it stops; otherwise you have to delete it by hand.
-it: two single-letter flags chained together, the same way ls -alh chains -a, -l and -h.

-i: interactive, so what you type reaches the container.
-t: gives you a terminal (TTY) to interact with.

Demo result: rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 opened R 4.3.2, while R --version on the host showed R 4.6.2. Two versions of R ran side by side on one laptop.
Each container is a separate machine: library(tidyverse) failed in the container (“there is no package called ‘tidyverse’”) but worked on the host.
Know where you are typing: the prompt is often your only cue to whether you are on your laptop, in a container, or on a remote machine. Inside a container the prompt looks like root@<id>:/#. The instructor also showed a terminal on a machine at home, recognisable only by its hostname. Commands like whoami help confirm where you are.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
section: 9. Web applications in containers: ports and environment variables
text:
9. Web applications in containers: ports and environment variables

Browser-based apps: many tools (Electron apps, JupyterLab, VS Code, GitHub Codespaces) run as browser applications. That is why they can run in a container or on a remote machine with the same interface. It is also why JupyterLab opens at a localhost address.
-p <host port>:<container port>: maps a port inside the container to a port on your computer.

RStudio Server listens on 8787, so -p 8787:8787, then open localhost:8787.
JupyterLab uses 8888.
These numbers are arbitrary choices by each tool.
To run two copies of the same app, map the container’s 8787 to a different free port on your computer.

RStudio login: the username is rstudio. Without a password set, the container prints a random one at startup, which is hard to remember.
-e VAR=value: passes an environment variable into the container, for example -e PASSWORD="apassword". Which variables an image understands depends on how its authors built it, so check its documentation.
Is a visible password a problem here? The port is only reachable from the instructor’s own machine, so a simple demo password is acceptable in this context.
Warning: every running container uses RAM. Use --rm so containers are removed when they stop. Otherwise you will wonder why your computer is slow and find you have “five computers” running.
Looking ahead: in DSCI 532 you can put a dashboard in a container. Users then only need Docker and one docker run command, with no renv or uv setup of their own.

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
section: 10. Building your own image with a Dockerfile
text:
10. Building your own image with a Dockerfile
(Customizing and building containers)

Containers don’t keep changes: the instructor installed cowsay inside a running rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 container. After exiting and starting a new container, library(cowsay) failed again. Every new container starts fresh from its image.

Good: this makes containers a safe place for dangerous experiments, including the destructive “delete the computer” command warned about in 521.
Bad: users should not have to follow README install steps every time. A tidyverse install on Linux can take about 15 minutes for a 30-second analysis.

Recommended workflow:

Start the base image with bash instead of its default program.
Try the install commands interactively until they work.
Write the working commands into the Dockerfile.

Installing from the terminal: Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" runs an R expression from bash. Watch the quotes: double quotes outside, single quotes inside.
Dockerfile: a file with exactly that name, capital D and no extension, containing the build instructions for the machine. Published images such as RStudio have their own Dockerfile.
FROM: the starting-point machine. It is the first line, apart from optional metadata.

Starting from rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 skips steps such as installing compilers, which the image authors have already done.
Smaller, bare-bones Linux bases exist, but then you install everything yourself.

RUN: a shell command executed while the image is being built. Most Dockerfiles are mostly RUN and COPY lines, and sometimes port lines (for example, opening 8787).

Knowing the bash command for each install step is essential.
For Python, you would COPY in your lock files and run uv sync.

CMD: the default command when the container starts, written as a list (["Rscript", "-e", "..."]). Adding a command after the image name in docker run (for example bash) overrides it.
ENTRYPOINT: also exists, but the instructor called it pretty rare.
The class Dockerfile (in the demo repo):
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"

CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"]
docker build --tag hello-cowsay .: --tag names the image. The . is the current directory, where docker build looks for a file named Dockerfile.

This is “probably the first time a dot is actually something you have to type”.
Course instructions, including milestone 1, assume you run every command from the repository root, so commands can be copied and pasted without changing directories.

docker images: lists the images on your computer. The new hello-cowsay image appeared at 1.45 GB.
Pin versions: pin the language and tool versions (R, Python, Quarto) in the Dockerfile so nothing updates until you change that line.

Warning: in another class the instructor restarted a container with no pinned versions. Something had updated the day before and nothing worked. Fixing an unexpected update can take longer than the real work.

Next week: install your language, Quarto (copy-paste install steps will be provided) and your packages in a container, so the analysis runs both locally and in the container.

text:
Sync main after the merge and clean up
git status
git switch main
git pull origin main             # fast-forwards to the merge commit
git log --oneline --graph --all
git fetch --prune                # drop origin/today, already deleted on GitHub
git log --oneline --graph --all
git branch -d today              # drop the local branch label
git log --oneline --graph --all

*   d25ddfa (HEAD -> main, origin/main, origin/HEAD) Merge pull request #3 from chendaniely/today
|\

|/  
* deb10c5 Initial commit

| * 3c6d82a today we are talking about containers

title: Introduction to Containers with Docker (plus Issues and Pull Request Workflow Review)
text:
What went wrong live

Edited README.md while still on main: git status reported On branch main with README.md modified, but the exercise asked for a branch. Nothing had been committed yet, so git switch -c today moved the uncommitted change onto the new branch. If you have already committed on main, use the textbook’s cheat sheet instead.
Stopping the RStudio container took several Ctrl+C presses: the first ^C started the container’s shutdown scripts. It then sat at [s6-finish] waiting for services. until two more presses forced it: got 3 SIGTERM/SIGINTs, forcefully exiting. Because of --rm, the container was removed either way.
Installed packages vanished between runs: cowsay installed in one rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 container was missing (there is no package called ‘cowsay’) in the next one, twice. This was the intended lesson. The fix was to put the Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" line in a Dockerfile as a RUN step and build an image.

title: Git branches and pull requests: review questions, tier 5 — Evaluate
text:
Date: 2026-11-17

Generated by qwen3.6-35b-a3b, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 5 of 5: Evaluate. Decide and justify your verdict before you read the answer; the criteria are the ones given in class.

1. The problem with parallel work on main (Learning Objectives)
00:04:04–00:09:43

Q: Judge whether a teammate’s plan to commit a major feature locally and push it the next day is acceptable for the group project workflow.

A: This plan is not acceptable. The class explicitly established that code existing only on a local computer effectively does not exist for grading or project purposes until it is pushed to the remote repository. Until the work is synced to GitHub, it cannot be reviewed, integrated, or counted as part of the project deliverable. (00:10:48)




2. Creating and managing branches locally (Creating a branch using the command line)
00:09:43–00:25:12

Q: Decide if you would approve a peer’s proposal to use git checkout -b feature-name instead of git switch -c feature-name to create and move to a new branch.

A: You should not approve this shortcut. The class taught that git checkout is a legacy command that also handles file restoration and undo operations, which significantly increases the risk of accidentally losing work if flags are misremembered. The instructor specifically recommended using git switch for branch management to keep the commands specialized and safer. (00:26:59)




3. Pushing branches and initiating Pull Requests (Draft pull requests)
00:25:12–00:46:00

Q: Critique a pull request submission where the author provided a single-line description, added the script, and skipped reviewing the “Files Changed” tab for stray temporary files.

A: The submission fails to meet review standards and should be rejected. The class specified that reviewers must inspect the “Files Changed” tab to verify all intended work is present and to actively catch stray temporary or backup files like .ipynb_checkpoints or .DS_Store. Additionally, the instructor emphasized that the first comment of a pull request must comprehensively explain all changes rather than relying on a brief title. (00:39:16)




4. Merging, cleanup, and local synchronization (Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:52:17–01:03:51

Q: Assess the safety of a group member’s suggestion to run git branch -D old-feature on their local machine to clean up a merged branch, knowing another teammate might still need to reference the old code.

A: This action is unsafe and should be blocked. The class taught that lowercase -d must be used for branch deletion because it refuses to delete branches that have not been merged, protecting unmerged or experimental work from accidental loss. Using uppercase -D forces deletion and permanently destroys the commit history, directly violating the course’s principle of preserving project work. (01:02:46)




5. Resolving merge conflicts via rebase (Using rebase)
01:03:51–01:21:43

Q: Evaluate whether a student’s approach of fixing conflict markers in a Python script, saving the file, and pushing directly is sufficient.

A: This approach is insufficient and risky. The class emphasized that resolving conflict markers at a specific line does not guarantee the code will run, because variable names, imports, or logic dependencies may have shifted elsewhere in the file. The student must verify that the entire script executes correctly from top to bottom before marking the conflict as resolved and force-pushing the rewritten history. (01:11:21)

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts: review questions, tier 4 — Analyze
text:
Date: 2026-11-17

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 4 of 5: Analyze. Take each one apart yourself before you read the answer; tiers 1 to 3 cover the facts, reasons and steps it relies on.

1. Review Git basics in the demo repository (8 Git branches)
00:04:07–00:06:49

Q: Break down the first main workflow in 2026-11-17-git from a dirty README.md to a remote-visible commit: which command inspected the change, which staged it, which created the local commit, and which command made the remote branch move?

A: git status showed README.md modified and identified the local branch as main; git diff displayed the added Git-branches link. git add README.md staged that file, and git commit -m "intro and review" created local commit 145ff16. git push origin main then advanced origin/main from 1360d7f to 145ff16, making the work visible on GitHub. (00:11:18)




2. Why branches exist: escaping the “I have to pull before I push” friction (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: Differentiate the DSCI 521 shared slide-deck workflow from the branch-based workflow introduced for DSCI 522: which coordination steps disappear or change once a student owns a branch?

A: In the slide-deck exercise, two people pushing to the same shared target created friction: even without a content conflict, a student could need to pull before pushing because another had pushed. In the branch model, a student creates a private branch such as dan-b1 and works in “their own little world,” committing and pushing to that branch without waiting for teammates. The remote origin remains the coordination point, but the branch isolates the student’s commits from main until a review step is ready. This turns constant pull-before-push friction into parallel streams that can be reviewed later. (00:08:46)




3. Local repository versus remote origin (8 Git branches)
00:09:46–00:11:11

Q: Point out which parts of the demo repository existed only on Daniel Chen’s computer after the first commit, which parts existed on origin, and what that meant for work that had not been pushed.

A: After cloning and committing on main, the local commit existed on the computer and moved local main ahead of origin/main. The origin reference was the local computer’s record of what GitHub had, so it did not include the new commit until git push sent it upward. This made the remote the shared state that teammates and grading could actually use, because work sitting only on a laptop was not available to them. The warning from class was that local-only work “effectively doesn’t really exist” for project or grading purposes. (00:10:48)




4. main, origin/main, HEAD, and what a branch is (8 Git branches)
00:11:11–00:16:05

Q: Examine the git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all state after git switch -c dan-b1 and after the commit on dan-b1: which ref moved when the branch was created, which ref moved when the commit was made, and which refs stayed where they were?

A: Before the commit, dan-b1 was created at the same commit as main and origin/main, and HEAD moved from main to dan-b1. The commit 4a14a64 moved only HEAD -> dan-b1; main and origin/main remained at 145ff16. The local main ref stayed behind because no commit was written to it. This shows that a branch is a movable name attached to the history that HEAD advances, while origin/main only changes when the remote is pushed or pulled. (00:23:21)




5. Branches are useful even when working alone (8 Git branches)
00:16:05–00:17:54

Q: Correlate Daniel Chen’s solo textbook workflow with the group-project branch workflow: what did a branch isolate in each case, and what did the instructor gain by reviewing and testing on a branch before merging?

A: In the solo textbook example, a branch isolated a sequence of changes so the main textbook did not move around during a teaching day. In the group project, a branch isolates one student’s exploratory or unfinished work from main and from other teammates’ work. In both cases, the branch lets the author test, review, and confirm the work before it becomes part of the stable shared branch. If the branch turns out to be a bad idea, abandoning or deleting the branch is easier than untangling commits already written on main. (00:16:51)




6. Creating a branch with git switch -c (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:23:46

Q: Break down the pre-branch check Daniel Chen performed before creating dan-b1: what git status confirmed, what git pull origin main contributed, and what git switch -c dan-b1 changed without creating a commit?

A: git status confirmed the starting branch was main and that the working tree was clean before new branch work. git pull origin main synchronized local main with origin/main, so the new branch would start from the current shared state rather than an old local commit. git switch -c dan-b1 then created dan-b1 at that commit and moved HEAD to it, as shown by On branch dan-b1. No new commit was created yet, so git log still showed the existing commits, only with HEAD -> dan-b1 attached to the new branch. (00:18:55)




7. Switching between branches and seeing the repository state (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:23:46–00:28:26

Q: Set git switch -c dan-b1, git switch main, and the older git checkout -b side by side: what does each command do to HEAD, which one creates a new branch, and why did Daniel Chen recommend switch when working in a shared repository?

A: git switch -c dan-b1 creates dan-b1 and moves HEAD to it in one step. git switch main does not create anything; it moves HEAD back to the existing main branch and returns the working files to the state stored at main. The older git checkout -b <branch> was the pre-2020 equivalent of creating and switching to a new branch, while plain checkout also handled restore-like behaviors that newer commands split out. Daniel Chen used switch in teaching and suggested asking tools to use switch when a student is not comfortable with checkout. (00:27:48)




8. Pushing a branch to origin and viewing it on GitHub (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: Trace the branch dan-b1 from the local repository to GitHub: what was different about git push while on main, what did git push origin dan-b1 add locally, and how could a teammate inspect dan-b1 without merging it?

A: While on main, git push had nothing new to push for main, so it reported everything up to date even though dan-b1 had a local commit. Running git switch dan-b1 and then git push origin dan-b1 pushed only the branch work to origin/dan-b1, leaving main and origin/main unchanged. After the push, git log --all showed the new origin/dan-b1 reference, meaning the local computer now knew GitHub had that branch. On GitHub, the branch dropdown allowed anyone to view the dan-b1 files and changes before the pull request was merged. (00:30:44)




9. Opening a pull request and reviewing the changed files (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:39:56

Q: Break down the pull-request setup for dan-b1 into its review parts: what GitHub’s “Compare and Pull Request” step did, what Daniel Chen said to check at the top of the pull request, and what the Files Changed tab was used to verify before merging?

A: The green “Compare and Pull Request” step started a review object for the pushed branch, and the pull request could be started early even while work was still in progress. At the top, the reviewer had to check the source branch and target branch, usually main in this course, so the changes would merge into the right place. The title and first description comment defined the whole set of changes and could be edited later instead of appending disconnected notes. In Files Changed, the reviewer separated the intended README.md changes from files that did not belong, such as .ipynb_checkpoints, .DS_Store, or backup files, because unwanted repository files can cost points. (00:38:44)




10. Pull request conversation, code review, and updating the same branch (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:39:56–00:45:41

Q: Trace how the second commit on dan-b1 reached pull request #1 Learning about branches and PRs: which local commands updated the branch, which pull-request surface showed the new diff, and what role did the first pull-request comment play?

A: Daniel Chen edited README.md on dan-b1, staged it with git add README.md, committed it as b90e441 with the message “show you the long git log command,” and pushed it with git push origin dan-b1. Because pull request #1 was tied to the dan-b1 branch, that push updated the same open pull request without closing and reopening it. The Files Changed tab then showed the new diff, which is the surface where inline review comments are attached to specific added or removed lines. The first comment remained important because it was the main explanation of the pull request; later changes should update that first comment rather than leaving the description fragmentary. (00:44:55)




11. Draft pull requests, merging, and deleting the remote branch (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:58:51

Q: Differentiate an open pull request and a draft pull request for dan-b1: what visual cue changed, what happened to the merge button, and what was that state communicating to teammates or agents?

A: An open pull request had the green review/merge styling, while converting it to a draft changed the visual bar to gray. The draft state also grayed out the merge button so no one could accidentally merge work that was explicitly not ready. This signaled that the branch could still be viewed, but the person working on it had not marked it ready for final review. When the work was ready, “Ready for review” converted the draft back into an open pull request and re-enabled the normal merge buttons. (00:54:48)

Q: Examine the post-merge state of pull request #1 after dan-b1 was merged: what happened to the pull-request counter, the branch dropdown, main’s commit history, and the commits from dan-b1?

A: Merging closed pull request #1, so the open pull-request counter went down by one. Deleting the remote dan-b1 branch removed the branch marker from the GitHub branch dropdown, keeping the list from growing with finished branches. The commits from dan-b1 were not lost; they were now reachable from main through the merge commit “Merge pull request #1 from chendaniely/dan-b1.” The history therefore kept the feature work and the merge event even after the branch name itself was deleted. (00:58:19)




12. Local cleanup after a merge: git pull, git branch -a, git fetch --prune, and git branch -d (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:58:53–01:03:51

Q: Separate the local cleanup workflow after dan-b1 was merged on GitHub: what git pull origin main updated, what git branch -a displayed, what git fetch --prune removed, and what git branch -d dan-b1 removed?

A: git pull origin main brought the merged pull-request commits into local main, so the local working copy matched the remote shared state. git branch -a listed both local branches and remote-tracking references, with a star marking the branch where HEAD currently was. git fetch --prune synchronized the local view of origin and removed the stale origin/dan-b1 reference after the branch had been deleted on GitHub. git branch -d dan-b1 then deleted the merged local branch, while a capital -D could force-delete unmerged work and is the dangerous shortcut Daniel Chen warned about. (01:03:21)




13. Creating a merge-conflict scenario with two branches (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:03:51–01:10:51

Q: Correlate pull requests #2 define fetch –prune and #3 branch -d and -D with the merge-conflict state that appeared after one of them was merged: what did the two branches share, what did the two pull requests look like side by side, and what happened when main moved forward?

A: Both dan-fetch and dan-delete were created from the same main state and changed overlapping lines in README.md. Looking at the two pull requests side by side showed separate diffs against their original base, but it did not obviously reveal that both would touch the same later region. When pull request #2 was merged, main advanced to include dan-fetch, so GitHub rechecked the remaining open pull requests against the new main. Pull request #3 then could no longer be cleanly merged because its commit now conflicted with the new main state. (01:10:31)




14. Resolving the conflict locally with git rebase main and git push --force-with-lease (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:10:51–01:20:42

Q: Differentiate resolving a simple conflict in GitHub’s web editor from resolving it locally with git rebase main: what each approach changes, where the conflict appears, and what push was required afterward?

A: The web editor can resolve a simple text conflict by editing the conflict markers directly on GitHub, which is enough for small documentation-style changes. The local path used by Daniel Chen started by syncing main with git pull origin main, then switched to dan-delete and ran git rebase main to replay that branch’s commit onto the updated main. The conflict appeared locally in README.md, where Daniel Chen edited the file, staged it with git add README.md, and finished with git rebase --continue. Because rebase rewrote the history of the already-pushed dan-delete branch, a normal push was not enough; git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete updated pull request #3 with the rebased commit. (01:19:34)

Q: Point out what “fixing” the merge conflict meant beyond removing the <<<<<<< markers in README.md: what could still go wrong later in the file or code, and what did that mean for the person responsible for the pull request?

A: The visible conflict markers only marked one overlapping line or region in README.md; removing them does not automatically prove the rest of the document or code is consistent. Daniel Chen said that if resolving line thirteen changed a variable or concept used later, the student could still have broken something around line fifty. The responsibility for that downstream effect stayed with the pull-request author, not the reviewer who pointed out the problem. In this course, “fixed” therefore meant the whole report or script worked top to bottom again, not just that the conflict markers were gone. (01:12:08)
