title: Git branches, pull requests and rebasing to fix conflicts: review questions, tier 4 — Analyze
text:
Date: 2026-11-17
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 4 of 5: Analyze. Take each one apart yourself before you read the answer; tiers 1 to 3 cover the facts, reasons and steps it relies on.

1. Why branches: escaping the 521 push/pull friction (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: Break down a group project’s timeline as the class described it, from the 521 shared slide-deck exercise to a Friday review. Which phase brings back the “pull before you can push” friction, and how do branches change the Tuesday-to-Friday stretch?

A: Early in a project everyone is blocked on one or two people getting the basics in place. In that phase, work on the shared main brings back the 521 friction: you can’t push because someone else pushed first, so you have to pull, whether or not there is a conflict. Later each person owns a self-contained part and works on their own branch. On that branch they can push and pull freely without caring what teammates are doing. Coordination moves to a single review point, for example a Friday review where the group goes over everyone’s work and merges it. (00:08:46)




2. Review: the local–remote picture
00:09:46–00:11:47

Q: Separate the commands in the 521 review cycle (clone, add/commit, push, pull) into those that act only on your computer and those that move commits between your laptop and GitHub. Then point out which side counts for grading, and why.

A: git add and git commit record work only on your computer. clone is a one-time command that brings the repository down from GitHub. push sends your commits up, and pull brings down commits that teammates pushed. The remote is what gets graded and published. Work that exists only on your laptop “effectively doesn’t really exist” for grading or project purposes, like an unshipped product. (00:11:33)




3. What a branch is: main, HEAD and origin/main (8 Git branches)
00:12:03–00:17:54

Q: Examine the labels in the log line 145ff16 (HEAD -> main, origin/main, origin/HEAD) intro and review from the demo repository 2026-11-17-git. What does each of HEAD, main and origin/main mark, what moves each one, and how does a branch change which label your commits drag along?

A: HEAD marks where you are; HEAD -> main means you’re on main. Each git commit therefore moves main forward. origin/main is what your computer thinks the state of main on GitHub is. It moves only when you sync, so committing without pushing puts local main ahead of origin/main. A branch is a name you choose: with HEAD attached to it, your commits move that name instead of main, and the git add/git commit workflow itself doesn’t change. (00:13:30)




4. Creating and switching branches (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:26:29

Q: Trace the git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all output through three steps: git switch -c dan-b1, then git commit -m "define swtich -c", then git switch main. Which labels moved at each step, and which stayed put?

A: After git switch -c dan-b1, the log showed 145ff16 (HEAD -> dan-b1, origin/main, origin/HEAD, main). No commit was made; only HEAD moved onto a new name at the same commit. After the commit, 4a14a64 (HEAD -> dan-b1) sat one commit ahead, while main and origin/main stayed at 145ff16. After git switch main, HEAD -> main was back at 145ff16, and README.md returned to main’s version. dan-b1 stayed at 4a14a64, because the branch you leave never moves. (00:25:25)




5. git checkout and git branch versus git switch (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:26:40–00:28:26

Q: Distinguish git switch -c <name>, git checkout -b <name> and git branch <name>. For each, say whether it creates a branch, whether it moves HEAD to it, and what else the command can do. Then relate this to the failed git switch -b dan-delete in the demo.

A: git switch -c creates a branch and moves HEAD to it. git checkout -b is the older, pre-2019/2020 equivalent. checkout also does much of what restore and revert now do, which is why the class advised asking an AI for the switch version when you don’t know what a checkout command will do. git branch <name> only creates the branch, so you still need switch or checkout to move onto it. Mixing the two flags caused the demo error: git switch -b dan-delete failed with unknown switch `b', because -b belongs to checkout, and git switch -c dan-delete worked. (00:28:13)




6. Pushing a branch and viewing it on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: Trace how the commit 4a14a64 got from the laptop to GitHub. Point out why a bare git push run on main printed Everything up-to-date, and which references changed, locally and on GitHub, after git push origin dan-b1.

A: The new commit lived on dan-b1, so pushing from main had nothing new to send. After git switch dan-b1 and git push origin dan-b1, GitHub reported a [new branch] and printed a link to create a pull request. The log then showed 4a14a64 (HEAD -> dan-b1, origin/dan-b1), while origin/main stayed at 145ff16. On GitHub, the repository’s main view still showed only the first change. The pushed work was visible only through the branch dropdown at the top left. (00:31:19)




7. Opening a pull request (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:41:16

Q: Break down the “open a pull request” page for dan-b1 into the parts you should check before clicking “Create pull request”, and say what problem each part catches.

A: The line at the top should name your branch and its target, main in this course. This catches sending code to the wrong branch, which matters in DSCI 524 and with forks. The title and first comment are the report of what changed. Edit that first comment as the pull request grows, because it is what people read. The changed-files list at the bottom is your second line of defence after reviewing locally. A missing file usually means you forgot to add, commit or push, and junk such as .ipynb_checkpoints, .DS_Store or Word backup files will lose you points even when the instructions don’t mention them, so your .gitignore still matters. (00:38:44)




8. Code review and updating a pull request (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:41:16–00:45:41

Q: Separate the reviewer’s job from the author’s job in a GitHub code review. Then trace how the author’s follow-up change reached pull request #1 without anyone opening a new pull request.

A: The reviewer reads the diff in the Files changed tab and adds comments with the + beside a line. Those comments also appear in the Conversation tab. The author’s job is to fix the code. Here the author went back to dan-b1 locally, ran git add README.md and git commit -m "show you the long git log command", then git push origin dan-b1 (4a14a64..b90e441). The pull request is tied to the branch, so the second commit appeared in #1, sometimes only after a refresh. A comment on a line that changed may then collapse as outdated. (00:43:15)




9. AI reviewers and draft pull requests (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:55:41

Q: Set a draft pull request and an open pull request side by side. How does each look, what can be done with its merge button, what does it tell the team, and how do you move between the two?

A: “Convert to Draft” at the top right turns an open pull request into a draft. The draft shows a grey bar instead of a green one, which tells everyone “you can look, but it’s not ready.” Its merge button is greyed out, so nobody can merge it by accident. Daniel believes this also stops an agent from merging everything that’s green. “Ready for review” at the bottom (“this pull request is a work in progress”) turns it back into an open pull request with green merge buttons. (00:54:30)




10. Merging and deleting the branch on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:55:41–00:59:07

Q: After pull request #1 was merged and “Delete branch” was clicked, separate what disappeared from what remained, on GitHub and in the history.

A: The open pull request count went down by one, and the branch count went from two to one, so the branch dropdown doesn’t grow into a giant list. The commits were not deleted. main’s history shows the branch’s two commits (4a14a64, b90e441) plus a merge commit, “Merge pull request #1 from chendaniely/dan-b1” (3851b00). Because those commits remain, a feature can still be found and undone later. The laptop still held origin/dan-b1 and dan-b1 until they were cleaned up locally. (00:58:19)




11. Syncing and cleaning up locally after a merge (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:59:07–01:03:51

Q: Break down the local cleanup after #1 was merged: git pull origin main, git branch -a, git fetch --prune and git branch -d dan-b1. Which of these changed files on disk, and which changed only branch references?

A: git pull origin main fast-forwarded main from 145ff16 to 3851b00 and added 6 lines to README.md, so it was the only step that changed files. git branch -a changed nothing; it showed dan-b1, * main and the stale remotes/origin/dan-b1. git fetch --prune synced history without touching files and printed [deleted] (none) -> origin/dan-b1. That is the difference from git pull, which is a fetch followed by a merge. git branch -d dan-b1 printed Deleted branch dan-b1 (was b90e441), and the log then showed b90e441 with no label, so the commit stayed in history. (01:02:22)

Q: Distinguish git branch -d from git branch -D: what does each check before deleting? Then point out where in a branch workflow a pasted -D does damage, and what it destroys.

A: Lowercase -d deletes a local branch only if it has been merged. It worked on dan-b1 because #1 was already in main. Capital -D force-deletes even an unmerged branch. That bites on a branch you’re still working on, or one you abandoned before merging: its commits were never in main, so the work is lost. The class warned that this is a one-character difference, and that ChatGPT may hand you -D when you copy commands. (01:03:21)




12. Setting up two conflicting pull requests (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:04:00–01:10:00

Q: Examine the log in which cb810d5 (dan-delete) and 157c3cd (dan-fetch) both leave 3851b00. Deduce which setup steps made pull requests #2 and #3 conflict, and why neither pull request warned of it on its own.

A: Both branches were created from the same main commit, 3851b00. dan-fetch was pushed as #2 but deliberately not merged, which is what lets you practise a conflict on your own. Switching back to main before git switch -c dan-delete meant the fetch line wasn’t in that branch’s README.md. Both commits then added text at the same spot in README.md, around line 13, which is the condition for a conflict. Each pull request is compared only against the current main, so both looked mergeable until one of them changed main. (01:09:28)




13. When a merge creates the conflict: resolving on GitHub (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:10:00–01:12:44

Q: Trace how merging #2 turned #3 into a conflict. Then distinguish what “fixed” means for the report’s prose and for code, and point out where a fix that only removes the markers fails.

A: Merging #2 changed main, and GitHub rechecks every pull request targeting main, so #3 landed on the conflict page. There you can resolve it in the web editor by finding the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers. For prose, “fixed” means the remaining text is English that makes sense. For code, it means the code runs from top to bottom again. A change made at line 13, such as renaming a variable, can break line 50, and the class warned that this is still your problem even though Git only flagged line 13. (01:11:39)




14. Resolving the conflict locally with rebase (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:12:44–01:20:42

Q: Follow dan-delete’s commit through the rebase by its hashes: what was its parent before and after, what did origin/dan-delete point to at each stage, and why did the final push need --force-with-lease?

A: Before, cb810d5 sat on 3851b00. git pull origin main brought local main to 3167d10, the merge of #2 that contains 157c3cd. git rebase main replayed the commit on top of 3167d10, and after the conflict was fixed it became the new commit 0e16503. origin/dan-delete still pointed at the old cb810d5. Because the branch’s history had changed, a plain push could not update it, and git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete printed + cb810d5...0e16503 dan-delete -> dan-delete (forced update). GitHub records that force push (“you’ve mangled history”), which matters in compliance settings. (01:19:47)

Q: Break down the stop-and-continue sequence of git rebase main on dan-delete, step by step, as git status guided it. Relate it to how the same conflict was triggered in 521.

A: git rebase main stopped with CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in README.md. git status then reported a rebase in progress onto 3167d10, listed README.md as both modified, and offered --continue, --skip and --abort; --abort is the escape hatch if something goes wrong. After the markers were fixed in the editor, keeping both definitions, git add README.md marked the file resolved, and git status said “all conflicts fixed: run git rebase –continue”. git rebase --continue confirmed the commit message and finished. Fixing the markers is the same skill as week 3 of 521; only the trigger differs: there it was git pull origin main, here it is replaying commits onto another branch. (01:18:20)

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, and Conflict Resolution: review questions, tier 3 — Apply
text:
Date: 2026-11-17

Generated by qwen3.6-35b-a3b, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 3 of 5: Apply. Work each situation through before you read the answer; tiers 1 (Remember) and 2 (Understand) cover the facts and reasons it relies on.

1. Creating and managing branches locally (Creating a branch using the command line)
00:09:43–00:25:12

Q: You are starting a new feature in a shared project. Sequence the two commands you should run first to ensure your local environment is synchronized and your new branch is created safely.

A: Run git pull origin main to fetch the latest coordinated updates, then run git switch -c <branch_name> to create the branch and move the HEAD pointer to it. This sequence guarantees you are building on the most recent stable state, preventing base mismatch errors. (00:18:03)

Q: You need to switch your working directory back to the default branch to review existing documentation, without creating a new branch. Choose the correct command to complete this task.

A: Run git switch main. This command moves the HEAD pointer to the existing main branch, allowing you to inspect the stable codebase while preserving all your previous commits on the feature branch. (00:25:22)

Q: You want to apply the recommended naming convention for a collaborative repository to clearly indicate ownership. Modify your branch creation workflow to sequence the proper prefix and command.

A: Prefix the branch name with your username (e.g., dan-b1) so teammates can immediately identify the responsible developer, then run git switch -c <name>. This convention organizes the commit history and makes it easier for collaborators to track active development streams. (00:20:48)




2. Pushing branches and initiating Pull Requests (Creating a pull request)
00:25:12–00:46:00

Q: You have finished writing code on your feature branch and want to sequence the workflow to share it for peer review. Predict the exact command to run, and demonstrate what to do if the GitHub banner prompting a pull request disappears.

A: Run git push origin <branch_name> to upload the branch to the remote. If the banner disappears, navigate to the branches tab, click the expansion menu next to your branch, and select “new pull request” to initiate the review process. (00:30:44, 00:35:00)

Q: Your feature will take several days to complete, but you want to share your progress and prevent teammates from accidentally merging unfinished work. Choose the correct UI option when opening the pull request and predict the visual and functional changes it introduces.

A: Select “Convert to Draft” when creating the pull request. This changes the interface bar from green to gray, disables the merge button to prevent accidental integrations, and clearly signals to the team that the branch is still a work in progress. (00:53:52, 00:54:04)

Q: A reviewer comments on your pull request’s “Files Changed” tab suggesting you remove a temporary debugging print statement. You modify the file locally, commit, and push the update. Predict how the pull request interface reflects this new commit and what happens to the original comment.

A: The pull request automatically updates to show the new diff when you push the updated branch. The original comment may auto-collapse with an “outdated” tag if it refers to an edited line, but it remains in the conversation history for context. (00:44:43, 00:45:20)




3. Merging, cleanup, and local synchronization (Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:52:17–01:03:51

Q: Your pull request has been merged into main on GitHub and the remote branch was deleted. Sequence the commands you must run locally to update your history and remove the stale tracking reference that still appears in git branch -a.

A: Run git pull origin main to fast-forward your local main branch to include the merge commit, then run git fetch --prune to remove local tracking references for branches deleted on GitHub. This synchronizes your local repository with the remote’s current state without modifying working files. (01:00:08, 01:01:30, 01:02:07)

Q: You need to complete the local cleanup of a feature branch that has already been successfully merged into main. Choose the correct deletion command and explain why the specific flag is important for data safety.

A: Run git branch -d <branch_name>. The lowercase -d flag acts as a safety guard that prevents you from accidentally deleting a branch containing unmerged work, thereby protecting your commits from permanent loss. (01:02:46, 01:03:02)

Q: Your team enforces strict compliance rules that require keeping all historical branches, but your local repository is accumulating a long list of inactive remote branches. Apply the command that updates your local reference list without triggering a merge or changing any files on your disk.

A: Run git fetch --prune. This command synchronizes your local repository’s history with the remote, refreshing your view of active branches while cleaning up tracking references for deleted ones, leaving all working files and local commits completely untouched. (01:01:52, 01:02:07)




4. Resolving merge conflicts via rebase (Using rebase)
01:03:51–01:21:43

Q: A teammate merged a pull request that modified the same lines of a file that you are editing locally. Sequence the commands you should run to replay your commits on top of the updated main branch, and demonstrate how to finish the process after fixing the conflict markers in your editor.

A: Ensure main is updated locally, switch to your branch, and run git rebase main to replay your commits. After editing the file to remove the <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> markers, run git add <file> to mark the resolution, then run git rebase --continue to apply the commit. (01:16:33, 01:18:44)

Q: After successfully rebasing and fixing a conflict, you attempt to push the branch to GitHub but receive an error because the remote history no longer matches your locally rewritten history. Complete the push using the safest command to update the remote, and explain why the specific flag is required.

A: Run git push --force-with-lease origin <branch_name>. This flag is required because rebasing rewrites commit history, and it safely updates the remote only if no new, untracked commits were added by others in the meantime, preventing accidental overwrites of collaborative work. (01:19:34, 01:20:02)

Q: You are resolving a merge conflict in a Python script. After removing the conflict markers and keeping the correct variable names, you notice that a function call later in the file references the old variable name. Apply the recommended workflow principle to determine your responsibility beyond fixing the conflict markers.

A: You must ensure the entire file or script runs correctly from top to bottom, as resolving one conflict marker does not guarantee the rest of the code is consistent. You are responsible for catching and fixing any downstream breakages or mismatched dependencies that resulted from the merge. (01:11:39, 01:12:13)

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts: review questions, tier 2 — Understand
text:
Date: 2026-11-17

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 2 of 5: Understand. Explain each answer in your own words before you read it; tier 1 (Remember) covers the facts, tiers 3 to 5 put them to use.

1. Course logistics: lab groups, GitHub usernames, lab attendance, and interview week
00:00:01–00:04:04

Q: Why did the instructor collect students’ GitHub usernames, even though asking for them seemed annoying?

A: The usernames fill a column in the lab-sections repository. They’re used as metadata “everywhere else under the hood” in the program, which is why he said they’re super important. (00:02:01)

Q: Why is lab attendance mandatory in DSCI 522?

A: Lab attendance is mandatory because it is a group project. During lab the TAs go around and talk to every single group, so you should be there when a TA is with your group. (00:02:19)

Q: Why does the interview-week conversation cover a student’s actual group codebase, not just Git?

A: It’s because you should know the code base you’re working in, especially in the world of AI, where anything in the codebase is fair game to be asked about. The conversation is really testing how well you know what you’re doing, like at work. (00:03:15)




2. Why branches exist: escaping the “pull before I push” friction (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: In DSCI 521’s shared slide-deck exercise, why did students often have to pull before they could push even when there was no actual conflict?

A: Someone else had also pushed to the shared deck, so Git required you to pull their work down before you could push your own. That “I have to pull first” step happened whether or not the edits actually conflicted. (00:07:06)

Q: Why does the instructor want each person to reach a part of the project they own and put on a branch?

A: When two people work on the same thing at the same time, you keep hitting the friction of “I want to add something, but I can’t.” A branch gives you your own little world where you can push and pull until your work is ready for your teammates’ review. (00:08:19)

Q: Why can’t a group project simply start with everyone doing four parallel pieces of work at once?

A: Not every project can start with four parallel pieces of work at once. There’s always going to be a part where you’re bound or stuck by one or two people, so the parallel-streams phase comes sooner or later as you each take ownership of your part. (00:07:40)




3. Local repository versus remote origin
00:09:46–00:11:11

Q: Why did the instructor say work that exists only on your local computer “effectively doesn’t really exist” for the project?

A: The remote (origin) is the thing that matters — it’s what gets graded and what gets published. If your code is only on your local machine, it’s not anywhere to be shipped, so for grading or project purposes it’s as if it doesn’t exist. (00:10:48)

Q: How do a local repository and the remote origin stay coordinated in this workflow?

A: git clone is a one-time command that brings the repository down. After that, local commits are sent up with git push, and work your teammates commit is brought down with git pull, so each person coordinates their computer with the shared remote. (00:11:18)

Q: Why is there “a lot of coordination work” when several teammates use one repository?

A: You have to coordinate your own computer with the GitHub remote, and each of your other teammates also has to coordinate with that same remote. That’s why multiple local repositories all depend on the one shared remote state. (00:10:20)




4. main, origin/main, and what a branch is (8 Git branches)
00:11:11–00:16:05

Q: What does the origin/main reference in git log mean, and why can your local main run ahead of it?

A: origin/main is the remote reference — what your computer thinks the state of main on GitHub is at. It’s separate from your local main, so if you keep committing on main without pushing, your local main moves further ahead than origin/main. (00:13:30)

Q: How does a branch differ from main in what moves when you commit?

A: A branch is just another name you give. When you write a commit, instead of incrementing where main is, you increment that other name, so main (and origin/main) stay where they are while your branch moves. (00:13:55)

Q: Why did the instructor describe main as like “production” that should stay stable and working?

A: In coordinated projects you want the moving pieces to move at a steady rate. You don’t want to try something that stops working on your computer and then on all your teammates’ computers, so main holds the stable, working state while risky or unfinished work stays off it. (00:14:50)

Q: Why did the instructor say the only thing that belongs in main in this course is the already-cleaned dataset?

A: Exploratory analysis and plots are not ready yet, because you’re still exploring the dataset. So main should only hold the stable piece everyone is based on, and you do your individual bits of work off on branches. (00:15:10)




5. Branches are useful even when working alone (8 Git branches)
00:16:05–00:17:54

Q: Why does the instructor use branches even when working alone on a repository such as the course textbook?

A: He uses branches to section off work and test a whole bunch of stuff without changing main until he’s reviewed and confirmed everything works. For the textbook he did it that way because a class was being taught and he didn’t want the book moving around mid-teaching-day, then merged after lectures. (00:16:37)

Q: Why is it easier to abandon a bad idea on a branch than to undo commits made directly on main?

A: If a branch was a bad idea, you can just delete it and come back to main. But if you wrote one big commit on main that did many things, undoing a portion of it means digging through the Git history copying and pasting the relevant bits, which is much harder. (00:16:51)

Q: How do branches compare to git reset and git revert as undo mechanisms?

A: You could have reset and reverted everything as an undo without branches. But branches make it a little bit easier by isolating the work so you can discard it all at once rather than untangling commits on main. (00:17:22)




6. Creating a branch with git switch -c (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:23:46

Q: Why should you run git pull origin main (or otherwise sync) before creating a branch when you’re building on coordinated project work?

A: You want your starting point to be up to date before you branch. The instructor gave the example of creating a branch while he’d already done half the work on another laptop, which he could have avoided by syncing first, so you don’t start from a stale local state. (00:18:09)

Q: What does git switch -c <branch> do that a plain git switch <branch> does not?

A: git switch moves HEAD to an existing branch. Adding -c also creates the new branch and then moves HEAD onto it, so after git switch -c dan-b1 the only thing that changed in git status is that it now says you’re on that new branch. (00:20:09)

Q: Why does the instructor sometimes start a branch name with a teammate’s name in group repositories?

A: It signals ownership. If something is going on around that branch and looks weird, other people know who to talk to because the branch name carries their name. (00:20:31)

Q: After you commit on a branch such as dan-b1, why does main not move?

A: The commit brings along the branch you’re on, not main. The same git add/git commit process runs, but instead of dragging along main it drags along your branch name, so main and origin/main stay where they were. (00:22:58)




7. Switching between branches and seeing the repository state (8.1.1 Switching to branches that already exist)
00:23:46–00:28:26

Q: Why does the instructor say you need the --all flag when running git log --oneline --graph --decorate to see your other branch names?

A: Without --all, the log doesn’t show the other branch names. Adding --all includes every branch so you can see dan-b1 alongside main in the same graph. (00:25:34)

Q: How is the older git checkout command different from git switch?

A: checkout is the older command that did what switch does (moving HEAD) but also did a lot of what revert and restore now do. The instructor uses switch when teaching and suggests that if you’re not comfortable with checkout you should ask tools to do it with switch instead. (00:26:59)

Q: Why doesn’t git branch <name> on its own get you onto the new branch?

A: git branch only creates the branch; it does not move HEAD. So you still have to switch (or checkout) to it afterward to actually be on it. (00:28:13)

Q: Why does the VS Code / Positron Git graph view help when learning branches?

A: That graph is essentially the same as what the terminal log shows — local main, origin/main, and your branch’s commits. So it’s a visual cue for what git switch and your commits are doing to HEAD and the branches. (00:24:09)




8. Pushing a branch to origin and viewing it on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: Why does pushing a new branch to GitHub not require any Git command beyond git push?

A: push is the only command that links your local computer to the remote. You point it at the branch with git push origin dan-b1, and afterward git log shows an origin/dan-b1 reference meaning GitHub now has the branch in the same place as your local one, while main hasn’t changed. (00:29:22)

Q: Why did a plain git push while on main report that everything was up to date instead of pushing the new branch?

A: A plain git push only pushes the branch you’re currently on, and you were on main. You have to say where and what you’re pushing, so the command is git push origin dan-b1 — you change the last word from main to the branch you’re pushing. (00:29:34)

Q: Why is it useful that you can view the dan-b1 branch in the GitHub branch dropdown even before it’s merged into main?

A: It lets you check that your work exists on GitHub. In a group, a teammate can also look at your code or a figure without running it or merging it, even though it isn’t combined into main yet. (00:32:36)




9. Opening a pull request and reviewing the changed files (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:39:56

Q: Why did the instructor say to start the pull request right away, even before the work is finished?

A: Starting the pull request right away means the review process exists from the start and updates as you keep pushing commits to the branch. It also lets you confirm the setup is working, and the “Compare and pull request” pop-up can disappear after a day or so, so starting early avoids losing it. (00:35:15)

Q: Why is it important to check which branch a pull request is merging into before creating it?

A: In this course main is usually the target branch. But in 524 it’s not always main, and with forks or large open-source projects you have to make sure you’re sending your code to the right repository and branch. (00:35:38)

Q: Why does the instructor tell you to scan a pull request’s changed files for things like .ipynb_checkpoints and .DS_Store?

A: Those are temporary or hidden backup files that don’t belong in the repository. In this course, if such unwanted files show up in a repository you’ll lose points, so the scan is a second line of defense that your .gitignore is still doing its job. (00:38:44)

Q: Why should you confirm in the “Files changed” view that all the code you intended to change is actually present?

A: If your intended code isn’t in the “Files changed” view, you probably typed something wrong or forgot to git add, commit, and push. So the check confirms the pull request actually represents your real work. (00:39:37)




10. Pull request conversation, code review, and updating the same branch (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:39:56–00:45:41

Q: Why did the instructor say to edit the very first pull-request comment instead of just adding new ones as you make more changes?

A: The first message is what people are going to read, so all of your changes should be defined and explained in that first comment. You can edit it (or any comment) to keep it accurate as the work evolves. (00:40:48)

Q: What does the “Files changed” tab in a pull request show, and why is that what code review looks at?

A: It shows the diff between the original file and the new file. That’s what reviewers look at when doing code review — you can hover over a line and use the plus button to add a line-specific comment, which gets tracked in the conversation. (00:41:16)

Q: Why is it the pull-request author’s job, rather than the reviewer’s, to fix the issues found in review?

A: The rule of thumb is that if it’s your pull request, it’s your job to fix it all. The reviewer’s job is to say “rewrite this” or “this doesn’t look right,” not to fix the code for you. (00:42:17)

Q: Why don’t you need to close and recreate a pull request when you need to make a change to address review?

A: You can just go back to the branch the pull request was working from, git add, commit, and push to that same branch. The pull request is tied to the branch, so it updates automatically (sometimes after a refresh). (00:43:09)

Q: Why might GitHub collapse an earlier review comment as “outdated”?

A: If you edited or made a change to the line the comment was on, that original comment probably doesn’t exist or is relevant anymore. So GitHub collapses it so you don’t end up looking at too much stale stuff. (00:45:00)




11. Draft pull requests, merging, and deleting the remote branch (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:58:51

Q: Why did the instructor convert the pull request to a draft instead of just leaving it open while still working?

A: A draft signals to you and the team that the work isn’t ready yet — it shows a gray bar instead of a green one and the merge button is grayed out. That means nobody can accidentally merge something that’s explicitly not ready, and he sometimes keeps drafts going for months as a “still working on this” signal. (00:53:59)

Q: Why did the instructor say a draft pull request also helps against automated AI reviewers?

A: He believes the draft status forces an agent not to just merge everything that’s green. So the “not ready” signal protects against an automatic merge. (00:55:03)

Q: Why did the instructor recommend deleting the remote branch after merging it into main?

A: Otherwise the branch dropdown slowly grows into a giant list of finished branches. Deleting the merged branch keeps things clean, and it doesn’t lose the commits, which stay in the history along with the separate merge commit. (00:56:08)

Q: If you request an AI (Copilot) review of your pull request, why aren’t all of its comments something you must accept?

A: Having more eyes on something is a good thing, but it doesn’t mean every comment the LLM makes is one you have to keep. You can push back, reject, or accept each one. (00:52:30)




12. Local cleanup after a merge: git pull, git fetch --prune, and git branch -d (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:58:53–01:03:51

Q: Why did the instructor say individual assignment 1 has you review merge conflicts again, even though the group project uses branches?

A: Even when you work in branches, conflicts can still happen — agents or teammates can’t help but fix a typo in the part you’re working on. So you still need to know how to get yourself out of a merge conflict. (00:59:07)

Q: Why didn’t your local main automatically reflect the pull request that was just merged on GitHub?

A: The merge happened on the remote, not on your machine. To update your local copy you have to switch to main and run git pull origin main, which is the synchronization step that brings the remote main down to your machine. (01:00:14)

Q: What does git fetch --prune do that a plain git fetch does not, and why run it?

A: git fetch coordinates the history with the remote without changing the files on your computer. Adding --prune also removes the local references to any branches that were deleted on GitHub, so after deleting dan-b1 on GitHub, fetch --prune drops the origin/dan-b1 marker from your local log. (01:01:30)

Q: Why is it safer to delete a local branch with lowercase git branch -d than with a capital -D?

A: Lowercase -d will only delete a branch that has been merged, which protects you from losing unmerged work. A capital -D force-deletes even unmerged work, so if you copy a -D from a tool you could permanently delete commits you were still working on. (01:02:38)

Q: How does git pull relate to git fetch and git merge?

A: When you run git pull, it’s doing two commands — fetch and then merge on top. But if you don’t want the files on your computer to change, you only run fetch, which just coordinates the history. (01:01:52)




13. Creating a merge-conflict scenario with two branches (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:03:51–01:10:51

Q: How does the instructor set up a merge conflict using the dan-fetch and dan-delete branches?

A: He creates two branches from the same main state and makes conflicting changes to the same region of README.md on each. Then he pushes both and opens a pull request for each; the key is to not merge the first one immediately, so the second branch is still based on the old main. (01:04:00)

Q: What does the “split” you see in git log --graph mean when two branches come out of the same main commit?

A: It means two parallel pieces of work are happening — one branch on each side (here dan-fetch and dan-delete). Both are based on the same main starting point, which is the setup that lets them later conflict when merged. (01:08:18)

Q: Why didn’t the two open pull requests, viewed side by side, show that they would conflict?

A: The conflict isn’t visible until one of them is merged and main changes. Then GitHub rechecks every open pull request that merges into main to see if it can still be merged, and the one that can’t now shows a conflict even though it looked green before. (01:09:28)




14. Resolving the conflict locally with git rebase main and a force-with-lease push (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:10:51–01:20:42

Q: Why did the instructor say “fixing” a conflict means more than just removing the conflict markers?

A: In this course “fixed” means the report or code works from top to bottom again. A conflict on one line doesn’t mean that’s the only place affected — for example, changing a variable name there might break line 50, so it’s still your responsibility to make the whole thing work. (01:11:09)

Q: Why did the instructor use git rebase main to resolve the conflict instead of just merging?

A: Rebase replays the commits on dan-delete on top of the updated main, turning the forked state into a linear one. That’s where the conflict gets triggered on his local computer, where he can fix it; it’s his preferred way, though he acknowledged people have opinions and there are many ways. (01:14:04)

Q: How is the conflict triggered in this branch workflow different from how it was triggered in DSCI 521?

A: In 521 you triggered a conflict by running git pull origin main. Here you trigger it by replaying your commits over another branch with git rebase main, since your branch is based on the old main and needs to be re-applied on top of the new one. (01:17:56)

Q: Why did the instructor have to use git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete instead of a normal push after the rebase?

A: The rebase rewrote the history of a commit that had already been pushed — its previous commit changed from the old main to the new merge commit. So a simple push is no longer enough; you have to force-update the branch, and he noted you can’t get around it because you’ve mangled the history. (01:19:34)

title: Git branches, pull requests and rebasing: review questions, tier 2 — Understand
text:
Date: 2026-11-17
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 2 of 5: Understand. Explain each answer in your own words before you read it; tier 1 (Remember) covers the facts, tiers 3 to 5 put them to use.

1. Course logistics: lab groups, attendance and interview week
00:00:01–00:04:04

Q: Explain why the instructor insisted that everyone submit their GitHub username correctly.

A: The usernames build a main list of everyone’s GitHub accounts. That list is the source of the username column in the lab sections repository, and it is “a piece of metadata that is used everywhere else under the hood” in the rest of the program. That is why getting it right is super important. (00:01:50)

Q: Why is lab attendance mandatory in DSCI 522?

A: The course is built around a group project. During lab the TAs go around and talk to every single group, and you should be there when a TA comes to your group. (00:02:19)

Q: Why can anything in your group’s code base come up in your interview-week conversation?

A: You are expected to know the code base you work in, as you would at work. This matters “especially in the world of AI”: if something is in your code base, it is fair game to be talked about. (00:03:15)

Q: How should you approach the seven-minute interview, given how it is graded?

A: Treat it like a technical interview about your Git work and your project. It’s okay not to know things, because the course is trying the format out. You will get a grade, but it won’t affect your mark. (00:02:55)




2. Why branches: escaping the 521 push/pull friction (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: Explain the friction from the 521 shared slide-deck exercise that branches are meant to remove.

A: Even when there was no conflict, you often couldn’t push your finished part, because someone else had already pushed. There was always the annoying step in the middle of pulling first before you could push again. (00:07:06)

Q: Why will some of that push/pull friction exist in every project, even when the team uses branches?

A: Not every project can start with four parallel pieces of work. Early on, the group has to get the basics down first, and everyone is bound or stuck by one or two people. (00:07:40)

Q: Why do you want to reach the phase of a project where each part is one person’s responsibility?

A: If two people work on the same thing at the same time, they keep running into the friction of “I want to add something, but I can’t”, conflict or not. Separate responsibilities let the team work in parallel streams instead. (00:08:19)

Q: How do parallel streams on branches change how a week of group work can run?

A: Each person is “in your own little world” on their own branch and can push and pull until they’re done, without caring what others are doing. For example, you could work on your part from Tuesday to Friday, and then on Friday the group reviews and coordinates everyone’s work. (00:08:46)




3. Review: the local–remote picture
00:09:46–00:11:47

Q: Why is the GitHub remote “the thing that matters” rather than your local repository?

A: The remote is what gets graded and what gets published. Work that exists only on your local computer effectively doesn’t exist for grading or project purposes. At work, it would be like a product that isn’t shipped, because the code isn’t anywhere it could be shipped from. (00:10:53)

Q: Compare clone with push and pull in the local–remote diagram.

A: clone is a one-time command that brings the repository down to your computer. push sends the commits you made locally up to GitHub. pull brings down commits that others, such as teammates, have pushed. (00:11:25)

Q: Why does working with teammates add so much coordination work?

A: You don’t only have to coordinate your computer with the GitHub remote. Each of your teammates also has to coordinate their own computer with that same remote. (00:10:35)




4. What a branch is: main, HEAD and origin/main (8 Git branches)
00:12:03–00:17:54

Q: Explain how HEAD and main relate when you make a commit on the main branch.

A: When you’re on the main branch, HEAD is attached to main. Every time you run git add and git commit, main increments to the new commit. (00:13:17)

Q: What does origin/main in the Git log represent, and why can your local main be ahead of it?

A: origin/main is what your computer thinks the state of GitHub is. If you write commits on main without pushing, your local main moves forward while origin/main stays put, so the local branch is further ahead. (00:13:30)

Q: How does committing on a branch differ from committing on main?

A: The process is the same: git add, git commit, and so on. The only difference is which name moves. Instead of incrementing main, each commit moves a branch name you chose yourself, such as b1. (00:14:06)

Q: Why should you treat main as the production version of the project?

A: main is the stable part, where at least the code works even if the project isn’t finished. You don’t want one person’s experiment to break things so that the project “no longer works on all of my teammates’ computers”. (00:15:10)

Q: Give the class’s example of what belongs on main and what stays on a branch.

A: The cleaned dataset goes on main, and everyone bases their work on that clean part. Exploratory data analysis, with all its plots, isn’t ready yet while you’re still exploring the data, so it stays on your own branch. (00:15:24)

Q: Why use branches even when you are the only person working in a repository?

A: Branches section off work, so you can test and build things without main changing until you’ve reviewed everything. The instructor made textbook edits in a sequence of branches while another instructor was teaching from it, so pages wouldn’t move around mid-lecture. He merged them after reviewing and testing. (00:16:37)

Q: Why is it easier to throw away a failed idea on a branch than to undo it from a commit history?

A: If the idea didn’t work, you just come back to main, or delete the branch, and you’re back at your starting point. Undoing part of a commit that did twenty different things means going through the history and copying out the relevant bits. git reset and git revert from 521 could do the same job, but branches make it easier. (00:16:51)




5. Creating and switching branches (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:26:29

Q: Why run git pull origin main before creating a branch for coordinated work?

A: Pulling makes sure your starting point includes everything everyone has already pushed. The instructor has created branches on one computer and then realised he had already done half the work on another laptop. Syncing first would have saved him that time. (00:18:09)

Q: Explain what git switch does to the repository, and how the log shows which branch you’re on.

A: git switch moves HEAD around the repository. You can tell you’re on main because HEAD points to main in the log, and git switch -c <name> creates a new branch and moves HEAD to it. (00:19:46)

Q: Why does the instructor start his branch names with his own name in shared repositories?

A: It tells other people who to talk to: if something weird is going on in that branch, they know which person is responsible for it. (00:20:31)

Q: Interpret the log line 145ff16 (HEAD -> dan-b1, origin/main, origin/HEAD, main) intro and review, shown right after git switch -c dan-b1.

A: No new commit was made. All that happened is that a new branch, dan-b1, was created on the same commit as main and the remote references, and HEAD moved to it. “Nothing really different other than a word has changed.” (00:21:13)

Q: After committing “define swtich -c” on dan-b1, the log shows dan-b1 one commit ahead of main and origin/main. Explain why.

A: Whatever branch HEAD is on gets dragged along when you commit, so this time dan-b1 moved instead of main. origin/main stays behind because nothing has been pushed or synced with GitHub. (00:22:58)

Q: Why is it worth knowing these commands and how to draw them, even if you use VS Code or Positron?

A: The graph view in the Git tab of VS Code and Positron shows the same thing as the terminal log: origin/main, the local main, and the commit on dan-b1. Knowing the commands and the diagram lets you read what that view is showing. (00:23:51)

Q: What happens to README.md on disk after git switch main, and why is that useful?

A: The file goes back to its state at the commit where main is, and the branch you left doesn’t move. Because you can move between parallel states of the project, you can try a new feature on a branch, or look at a teammate’s work, without disturbing main. (00:25:46)

Q: Why does the instructor type git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all rather than leave off --all?

A: Without the --all flag, the log may not show your other branch names. That’s why he always types it out in full. (00:25:38)




6. git checkout and git branch versus git switch (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:26:40–00:28:26

Q: Explain why git switch exists when git checkout already moved HEAD around.

A: checkout did what switch does, moving HEAD, but it also did much of what restore and revert do. The newer commands were carved out of checkout around 2019–2020. checkout still has all those behaviours, which is why it is fine to use but harder to predict. (00:27:09)

Q: Why should you ask an AI assistant for the switch version when it tells you to run checkout?

A: checkout can do many things. If you don’t know what a particular checkout command will do and you’re worried about losing work, think about the commands you’re typing. Asking for the switch version gives you a command whose effect you understand. (00:27:34)

Q: Compare git branch <name> with git switch -c <name> and git checkout -b <name>.

A: git switch -c and the older git checkout -b both create the branch and move you onto it. git branch only creates the branch and doesn’t move you, so you still have to checkout or switch afterwards. (00:28:13)




7. Pushing a branch and viewing it on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: Why did the instructor get dan-b1 into main through GitHub rather than merging on his own computer?

A: He called going through a review process the easiest way. Instead of merging locally, you push the branch and merge it through a pull request, also called a merge request. (00:28:58)

Q: Running a bare git push while on main printed Everything up-to-date and did not send the new commit. Explain why.

A: The new commit was on dan-b1, not main, so there was nothing new on main to push. Once you work with branches, where you push and what you push start to matter, so you first need to be on the branch you want to push. (00:29:34)

Q: Explain what each of the last two words does in git push origin dan-b1.

A: origin says where you are pushing: the GitHub remote. dan-b1 says what you are pushing: the branch, in place of the main you’ve typed for ten weeks. Otherwise the behaviour is exactly the same: your local work goes up to GitHub. (00:30:36)

Q: Interpret the log after git push origin dan-b1: origin/dan-b1 sits beside dan-b1, while origin/main is still one commit back.

A: GitHub now has a branch called dan-b1 at the same commit as your local dan-b1. Pushing a branch doesn’t change main, either locally or on GitHub. (00:31:19)

Q: Why did the pushed work not appear on the repository’s GitHub front page, and how can you see it?

A: The front page shows main, and the work was only on dan-b1. The dropdown in the top-left corner, labelled main, lets you view other branches, such as dan-b1 and its changes. (00:32:21)

Q: Why is it useful to view a teammate’s branch on GitHub before it is merged?

A: You can look at their code, for example to see how they made a figure, without running it, while it is still not combined into main. It is also how you check that your own local work actually reached GitHub. (00:32:36)




8. Opening a pull request (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:41:16

Q: Why does the instructor open a pull request right away, even after one small commit?

A: The “Compare and Pull Request” pop-up seems to disappear after a day or so. Starting the pull request immediately means he doesn’t risk losing it, and the pull request can stay “in process” while he works. If the pop-up does vanish, you can reach the same page from the Branches tab with “New pull request”. (00:34:32)

Q: Why check the line at the top of a new pull request that names the two branches?

A: It says which branch you are merging and which branch it goes into, and you want to make sure your code is sent to the right place. In this course the target is probably main, but in DSCI 524 it won’t always be. With forks of open-source projects, this matters too. (00:36:20)

Q: Explain how a pull request lets you review your own work, including work an AI produced.

A: Your first line of review is on your own computer. The pull request page is a second one: it lists every changed file and its diff relative to main, so you can check your work, or an AI’s work, before anyone merges it. (00:38:15)

Q: If a file you worked on is missing from the pull request’s changes, what does that most likely mean?

A: You probably typed something wrong or forgot to add, commit and push it. The pull request shows only what reached the branch on GitHub. (00:39:37)

Q: Why must you check the pull request’s file list for files that don’t belong there?

A: Files such as .ipynb_checkpoints, macOS .DS_Store or hidden Word backup files shouldn’t be in the repository. If they’re in the repository, points are taken off even if the instructions don’t explicitly say so. This check is your second line of defence, and your .gitignore file still matters. (00:38:44)

Q: Why edit the pull request’s first comment instead of adding “now I’m also doing…” comments?

A: The very first message is what people read. As the pull request changes, all your changes should be defined and explained in that first comment, which is why GitHub lets you edit it. (00:40:48)




9. Code review and updating a pull request (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:41:16–00:45:41

Q: Explain what “code review” means on GitHub’s Files changed tab.

A: You look at the diff between the original code and the code someone is adding or removing. Hovering over a line shows a + button, which lets you comment on that line, for example “why are you using switch and not checkout?” Those comments are also tracked in the main conversation tab. (00:41:34)

Q: Compare the jobs of a pull request’s author and its reviewer.

A: The reviewer’s job is to point out problems: “rewrite this” or “this doesn’t look right”. It is the author’s job to actually fix their pull request. (00:42:17)

Q: How do you update an open pull request such as #1 after a reviewer asks for a change?

A: You don’t close it and open a new one. Go back to the branch the pull request was made from (here dan-b1), then add, commit and push to that same branch. The pull request is tied to the branch, so it updates, although sometimes you have to refresh the page. (00:43:15)

Q: Why might GitHub collapse a reviewer’s comment and mark it outdated?

A: You changed the line the comment was made on, so that original comment probably isn’t relevant anymore. GitHub collapses it so you don’t end up looking at too much stuff. (00:45:02)




10. AI reviewers and draft pull requests (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:55:41

Q: How should you treat comments from a Copilot review on your pull request?

A: Requesting one isn’t a bad thing, because having more eyes on something is never really a bad idea. You don’t have to keep every comment the LLM makes: you can push back on a comment, reject it or accept it. (00:52:30)

Q: Why does the instructor convert a pull request he opened early to a draft?

A: He opens the pull request first and keeps pushing to it, so it needs to say “this isn’t ready yet”. A draft shows a grey bar instead of a green one, which signals to him and the team that they can look but the work isn’t ready. He has kept drafts open for three or four months on long work. (00:54:12)

Q: How does a draft pull request prevent accidental merges?

A: The merge button is greyed out, so no one can accidentally merge work that is explicitly marked as not ready. The instructor believes this also stops an agent from merging everything that’s green. (00:54:30)

Q: How do you turn a draft back into a pull request that can be merged?

A: At the bottom of the pull request, where it says the pull request is a work in progress, click “Ready for review”. It becomes an open pull request again, with green merge buttons. (00:55:28)




11. Merging and deleting the branch on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:55:41–00:59:07

Q: Why does the instructor delete a branch on GitHub after its pull request is merged?

A: A project has many features, branches and pull requests over its lifetime. Without cleanup, the branch dropdown grows into a giant list, and the merged branch name no longer needs tracking. (00:56:08)

Q: Explain why deleting dan-b1 after merging #1 did not lose any work.

A: Deleting the branch only removes the branch marker. main’s history still has the branch’s two commits, plus a separate commit saying the pull request was merged. You can still find the commits for a pull request and undo a feature, so “nothing’s really lost”. (00:58:10)

Q: When should you not delete merged branches?

A: If a law or compliance rule says you can’t delete things, don’t. Otherwise your team’s workflow decides, but at least clean up your own work. (00:57:00)




12. Syncing and cleaning up locally after a merge (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:59:07–01:03:51

Q: Why do merge conflicts still happen when every teammate works on their own branch?

A: Even when people agree who works on which part, other people or agents sometimes can’t help fixing a typo in your part. If you fix the same typo, there’s still a merge conflict. That’s why individual assignment 1 has you practise merge conflicts again. (00:59:39)

Q: Why did local main need git pull origin main after #1 was merged on GitHub?

A: Local main doesn’t update itself when something is merged on GitHub; you need a synchronization step. The pull fast-forwarded main and added the new lines from the merged pull request to README.md. (01:00:17)

Q: Interpret the output of git branch -a.

A: It lists all the branches your computer knows about. The branches you created locally appear by name, with a star next to the one you’re on, and the remote ones appear as entries such as remotes/origin/dan-b1. (01:01:06)

Q: Compare git fetch with git pull.

A: git pull does two things: it runs a fetch and then a merge on top. git fetch only synchronizes the history with origin. You run fetch alone when you don’t want the files on your computer to change. (01:01:52)

Q: Explain what --prune added, and why origin/dan-b1 disappeared from the log after git fetch --prune.

A: When a branch has been deleted on the remote, the fetch also removes that branch’s marker on your computer. The output showed [deleted] (none) -> origin/dan-b1, and the log no longer showed that reference. (01:02:22)

Q: Why use lowercase git branch -d rather than capital -D to delete a local branch?

A: Lowercase -d only deletes a branch that has been merged: deleting an unmerged branch could lose work, so Git makes it harder. Capital -D force-deletes even unmerged work. It’s a one-character difference, so be very careful when copying commands from ChatGPT: it might hand you -D, and you could delete the commits you’re working on. (01:03:21)




13. Setting up two conflicting pull requests (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:04:00–01:10:00

Q: Explain what kind of change produces a merge conflict between two branches.

A: Two different changes to the same line of the same file. The instructor set up dan-fetch and dan-delete to edit the same spot in README.md. (01:04:00)

Q: Why did the instructor not merge the dan-fetch pull request (#2) right away?

A: Leaving #2 unmerged is the key to practising conflicts on your own. It stands in for two people opening pull requests where one has conflicting changes. Merging it first would have been just another review, not a conflict. (01:06:07)

Q: Why was the fetch line missing from README.md on dan-delete?

A: He switched back to main before creating dan-delete, and the fetch line existed only on dan-fetch. Both branches were based on main. (01:07:20)

Q: Interpret the log graph where cb810d5 (dan-delete) and 157c3cd (dan-fetch) both come out of 3851b00.

A: There is literally a split: from the same main commit, two lines come out, one per branch. That means two parallel pieces of work are happening. (01:08:53)

Q: Why didn’t GitHub warn that #2 and #3 would conflict?

A: Each pull request is judged on its own against main, and it isn’t obvious they share a starting point. Each one looked fine to merge into main, even though both changed line 13. (01:09:48)




14. When a merge creates the conflict: resolving on GitHub (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:10:00–01:12:44

Q: Explain how #3 went from mergeable to conflicting once #2 was merged.

A: Merging one pull request changes main. Every other pull request that merges into main is then rechecked. #3 could no longer be merged cleanly, so it landed on the “you have a conflict” page. (01:10:08)

Q: Compare what “fixing” a conflict means for report text and for code.

A: For report writing, whatever is left must be English that makes sense. For code, removing the conflict markers isn’t enough: the code has to work from top to bottom again. (01:11:21)

Q: Why might code still be broken after the conflict markers on line 13 are cleaned up?

A: Git only tells you that line 13 has conflicting changes; your fix can affect code elsewhere. If resolving it renames a variable used on line 50, that is still your problem. Resolving a conflict means the code runs as you expect, not just that the markers are gone. (01:11:39)

Q: When does the instructor resolve a conflict in GitHub’s web editor, and when on his own computer?

A: For simple conflicts like this one, the web editor is fine. Resolving on your own computer is a little more involved because it takes more commands, and he showed it for that reason. (01:12:19)

01:12:44–01:20:42

Q: Explain what git rebase main does to the dan-delete branch.

A: It replays the branch’s commits on top of the updated main, so that dan-delete’s parent is no longer 3851b00 but the merge that contains 157c3cd. The replay is where the conflict comes up on your own computer, so you can fix it there. (01:14:31)

Q: Why do you sync main before running git rebase main on your branch?

A: The conflicting commit was already merged into main on GitHub, and your local main doesn’t have it yet. Step one is to get that commit onto your computer with git switch main and git pull origin main, so you have something to rebase onto. (01:13:42)

Q: Compare how a conflict was triggered in week 3 of 521 with how it is triggered with branches.

A: Fixing the markers is the same skill as in 521. In 521, git pull origin main triggered the conflict. Here the trigger is replaying your branch’s commits over another branch with git rebase main. (01:17:56)

Q: How does git status guide you through a rebase that has stopped on a conflict?

A: After you fix the markers, it tells you to use git add to mark the resolution. It then tells you to run git rebase --continue, which asks for the commit message. If you’re scared that something got messed up, you can abort the rebase. (01:18:20)

A: The branch is now at the top of the history, after main, with the conflict fixed. Its commit has a new hash because it has a new parent. GitHub’s copy of the branch is still the old commit on the old base, so local and remote now disagree. (01:19:14)

Q: Why could the rebased dan-delete branch not be pushed normally?

A: The rebase changed the branch’s history: the commit’s parent is now a different commit. A simple push no longer works, so you have to force push to update the branch, here with git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete. You can’t get around force pushing after a rebase. (01:19:47)

Q: Why is a force push after a rebase something to take seriously?

A: You’ve “mangled history”, which can be a compliance concern, and GitHub records that a force push happened. Once it’s done, the pull request shows the green merge button again. (01:20:21)

title: Summary
text:
2. Git fundamentals and branches

Local and remote repositories

Work takes place on a student’s computer and in the shared remote repository. Cloning brings the repository to a computer; commits record local changes; pushing sends commits to the remote; and pulling brings down work that teammates have committed and pushed.
The shared GitHub remote is the authoritative version for grading and publication. Code that exists only on a local computer is unavailable for grading or delivery.
In the course 521 shared-slide-deck exercise, students sometimes had to pull teammates’ changes before pushing their own. Similar friction can occur when people work on the same project area. Separating work into self-contained streams helps reduce these coordination issues.

Basic repository workflow

The reviewed workflow includes creating a GitHub repository, bringing it to a computer, editing the README, checking the repository with git status, reviewing changes, staging files with git add, and committing them. The demonstration also added a link to the Git branches chapter.
A repository could be initialized with a README, a Python-related option, and a license. The demonstrated commit message was “Intro and review.”
These steps recap material practiced in course 521 over approximately the preceding ten weeks.

What branches are for

main is the default branch and represents the stable, production-like version of a project. Its contents should work or be finished, although course work does not necessarily have to be fully finished to appear there.
Branches let people develop, test, or explore work separately from the shared main line. For example, cleaned data could remain in main as a common starting point while exploratory analysis and plots are developed on a separate branch.
Branches make it easier to set aside or abandon unsuccessful work without disentangling changes from the main project history. The instructor contrasted this with using reset or revert, which were covered in course 521.
Branches also support peer review: work can be developed separately, reviewed and tested, and then merged into the shared project. The instructor’s textbook example used branches for changes made during a class, avoiding disruptive updates while teaching was underway.

Branch references and HEAD

HEAD points to the currently checked-out branch. When working on main, commits advance the local main reference; when working on another branch, commits advance that branch instead.
origin/main represents the remote state of main on GitHub as understood by the local computer. If commits are made locally on main but not pushed, local main moves ahead of origin/main.
Creating and switching to a branch does not create a commit or change project files. It changes the branch that HEAD points to. The existing main branch and remote references remain in place.
A local branch is not automatically synchronized with GitHub. The lecture example remained one commit behind the remote because nothing had been pushed, fetched, or synchronized.

title: Summary
text:
3. Creating, using, and switching branches

Create a branch and switch to it

Use git switch -c <branch-name> to create a branch and move HEAD to it. The -c option means create. Examples included B1 and the local branch Dan-B1.
In group repositories, the instructor sometimes begins branch names with their own name so teammates know whom to contact about the work.
After switching, git status reports the new branch. Before creating a branch, check that you are on main and start from an up-to-date base when the work depends on coordinated project changes. Starting from outdated work can cause duplicated effort.

Continue the usual edit-and-commit workflow

Branching does not change the normal workflow: edit a file, use git status to see what changed, and use git diff to review the changes.
If satisfied, stage the file—for example, with git add README.md—and commit it with a message. One example commit message was define switch -c.
The branch that is checked out is the one that advances when a commit is made.

Inspect branches and move between them

Use git switch <branch-name> to move to an existing branch, such as main. Switching away does not move the branch being left; the working files change to match the branch that is now checked out.
A log view can show where main, remote references, and local branches point. The instructor noted that the --all option is needed to show branch names that might otherwise be absent. The demonstrated one-line log command was git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all.
VS Code and Positron display branch and commit relationships in a graph, corresponding to the relationships shown in the terminal. The example showed three commits, origin/main, local main at the same point, and a later commit on Dan-B1.
Branches are inexpensive to create and can be left in place if an experiment is unsuccessful. Switch back to main to continue other work, or create another branch. Successful work can later be merged into the main line.

Related Git commands

git checkout was commonly used to switch branches before the newer git switch command. The instructor placed the transition to newer commands around 2019–2020, while noting uncertainty about the exact year.
The older branch-creation command is git checkout -b <branch-name>, equivalent to git switch -c <branch-name>. checkout also covered behaviors now associated with revert and restore, which remain available through checkout.
Tools such as GitHub Copilot or ChatGPT may suggest checkout commands. Understand a suggested command before running it, especially when work could be at risk; if unsure, ask for an equivalent using switch.
git branch <branch-name> creates a branch without switching to it. Use git switch <branch-name> or git checkout <branch-name> afterward to begin working on it.

title: Summary
section: 4. Pushing branches and using pull requests
text:
4. Pushing branches and using pull requests

Push the branch containing your work

Check which branch is active and switch to the branch you intend to share, for example, with git switch dan-b1. Switching changes the working files to the state committed on that branch.
Push the feature branch rather than main. The example was git push origin dan-b1: origin is the remote, and the branch name specifies what is being pushed.
After pushing, the log can show an origin reference for the feature branch at the same commit as the local branch, while main remains unchanged. On GitHub, use the branch selector to view the branch and confirm it is available for teammates to inspect. A branch being visible does not mean it has been reviewed or approved.
Branch lists can grow as projects add contributors, features, and projects. Branches can be deleted when they are no longer needed.

Create and configure a PR

After pushing a branch, GitHub may show a Compare and Pull Request button. If the prompt disappears, find the branch under the repository’s branches tab and select New pull request.
The instructor recommends opening a PR early, even while work is in progress, so review can happen as changes are made. The initial prompt may disappear after roughly a day, but the branch menu remains another route.
Verify the base branch that will receive the changes and the source branch being compared. In this class, the destination is generally main; other courses or projects may differ. For forks or large open-source projects, confirm the intended repository and branch.
Write a clear title and description that briefly report what the branch changes. One example title was “Learning about branches and PRs,” with a description about git switch and creating PRs. Keep the original description current by editing it as the work changes, rather than adding disconnected updates that reviewers may miss.

Review changes and collaborate through the PR

The PR displays changes between the feature branch and the base branch, including affected files, code, and commits. Check that all intended work is present; missing changes may not have been added, committed, or pushed.
Check for unnecessary files, such as temporary checkpoint files, Microsoft Word backup or fallback files, Jupyter Notebook .ipynb_checkpoints, and macOS .DS_Store files. Keep .gitignore appropriate; unwanted repository files can cost points in the class.
People with repository access can review the PR and discuss it in the conversation. The Files Changed tab shows a diff, and reviewers can comment on specific lines. Code review means examining that diff and commenting on the changes.
The PR author is responsible for making requested code changes; the reviewer identifies concerns or suggests changes. Review can happen locally or on GitHub. GitHub Copilot can also be asked to review work, but its suggestions can be considered, challenged, rejected, or acted on.
To address feedback or add work, return to the PR’s source branch, make changes, then add, commit, and push to that same branch. The existing PR updates with the new commits; there is no need to close it or create another one.
The example added a line about viewing Git history with git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all, staged the README with git add README, committed it, and pushed it. The instructor recommended pushing regularly, even about every 10 minutes, so work remains available for review. Refresh the PR page to see updates. If a changed line had a review comment, GitHub may collapse the comment and mark it outdated.

Use draft PRs for unfinished work

An open PR can be converted to a draft with Convert to Draft. A draft displays a gray status bar rather than a green one, signals that the work is not ready to merge, and disables the merge control.
Drafts can remain open for extended work; the instructor mentioned drafts lasting three or four months. Draft status communicates the work’s state to the team and may discourage an agent from merging work automatically.

title: Summary
section: 5. Merging pull requests and cleaning up branches
text:
5. Merging pull requests and cleaning up branches

Review and merge completed work

Change a draft PR to Ready for review when it is ready. Once the PR has been reviewed and its checks are green, merge it into the target branch, such as main.
The intended workflow is to develop work on a feature branch, review it through a PR, and merge approved commits into main. A merged PR is closed. The changes should then be present on main, and the commit history can confirm the branch commits and, depending on the merge method, a separate merge commit.

Synchronize local work after a merge

Switching to local main does not automatically update it with changes merged on GitHub. Switch to main and run git pull origin main to bring the remote changes onto the local computer.
git branch -a lists branches known locally, including remote-tracking branches; an asterisk marks the current branch.
git fetch --prune updates the local view of remote history and removes remote-tracking references for branches deleted on GitHub. Use git fetch alone when you want to update your knowledge of remote history without changing local files.
git pull combines fetching with merging fetched changes into the current branch.

Delete branches carefully

Deleting a branch after its work is merged can keep a long-running project’s branch list manageable. Deleting the branch marker does not delete the commits or remove the work from history; relevant commits remain available if the feature later needs to be undone.
Branch deletion depends on the team’s workflow and any compliance or record-retention requirements. Do not delete work that must be retained.
After pruning, use git branch -d <branch-name> to delete a merged local branch. Lowercase -d refuses to delete a branch Git believes contains unmerged work.
Uppercase -D force-deletes a branch even if it has not been merged. Use it cautiously, since it can remove a branch containing work you still need.
A branch can also be deleted on GitHub after merging, removing it from the remote branch list.
