title: Summary
section: 6. Merge conflicts and local rebase workflow
text:
6. Merge conflicts and local rebase workflow

Understand how conflicts arise

A merge conflict can occur when two branches based on the same starting point make different changes to the same line in the same file. The demonstration used two branches and PRs with conflicting edits around lines 12–14, including line 13.
When one PR is merged, main changes. GitHub then checks whether other open PRs can still be merged. A later PR may conflict even if it initially appeared mergeable and had green checks.
Conflicts can still occur when work is divided among contributors; another person or an agent might make a small edit in the same area, such as correcting a typo.
Resolve conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>>) by choosing the correct final content and removing the markers. For report writing, the result should read as sensible English; for code, it must work from top to bottom. A conflict can have implications elsewhere in the file, such as a variable name used on another line, so check the broader result.

Resolve simple conflicts on GitHub or locally

Simple conflicts can be resolved in GitHub’s web editor. More complex conflicts can be handled locally.
In the local rebase demonstration, one PR had already been merged into main, while another branch, named DanDelete in the example, remained open.
Update local main first with git switch main and git pull origin main. Then switch to the still-open branch, for example with git switch dan-delete, and run git rebase main. Rebase replays the branch’s commits on top of the updated main, bringing the conflict into the local working files.
Open the conflicted file, remove the markers, choose the correct content, and check the result. The example retained both definitions and cleaned up whitespace.
Use git status to inspect the repository state and Git’s suggested next steps. Stage the resolved file, for example with git add README.md, and run git rebase --continue. Git also provides an abort option if the rebase needs to be abandoned.
After the rebase completes, the branch’s commit appears at the top of the updated history with the conflict resolved.

Force-push a rebased branch

Rebasing rewrites branch history by replaying commits onto a different base, so a normal push is not sufficient to update the remote branch.
Use a force push, such as git push --force origin dan-delete, to update the remote branch and its PR. GitHub indicates that a force push occurred.
Once updated, the PR can be merged if its checks and review allow it. Then synchronize and clean up branches as appropriate, while observing team and compliance requirements.

3. Creating and managing branches locally (8 Git branches) (00:09:43–00:25:12)

Before starting new work, run git pull origin main to sync your local repository with the remote, ensuring you branch off the most up-to-date coordinated code.
Use git switch -c <branch_name> to create a new branch and immediately move the HEAD pointer to it, detaching it from origin/main.
git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all provides a visual map of the commit history, clearly showing how the HEAD advances on the new branch while origin/main remains static.

text:
4. Pushing branches and initiating Pull Requests (9 Pull requests) (00:25:12–00:46:00)

Push a new branch to the remote using git push origin <branch_name>. GitHub typically prompts you to create a Pull Request immediately after the push.
A Pull Request initiates the code review workflow, presenting a diff of all changes in the “Files Changed” tab for peers to inspect and comment on.
Reviewers should verify that all intended work is present, check for stray temporary files (like .DS_Store or .ipynb_checkpoints), and ensure the .gitignore is functioning.
You can update a PR dynamically by making new commits and pushing them to the same branch; the GitHub interface automatically reflects the new state.
Use the “Convert to Draft” option to open a Pull Request as work-in-progress. Draft PRs display a gray bar, disable the merge button, and signal to the team that the code is not yet ready for review.

text:
5. Merging, cleanup, and local synchronization (8 Git branches) (00:52:17–01:03:51)

Once a Pull Request is approved, click “Merge Pull Request” to integrate the branch’s commits into main. This automatically closes the PR on GitHub.
After merging, delete the branch on GitHub via the UI dropdown menu to prevent the repository from accumulating a cluttered list of inactive branches.
Switch back to your local main branch and run git pull origin main to fetch and fast-forward the local history to include the newly merged commits.
Run git fetch --prune to remove local tracking references for remote branches that were deleted on GitHub, then use git branch -d <branch_name> to delete the local branch.
Use lowercase -d for safe deletion (it refuses to delete unmerged work to prevent data loss); uppercase -D forces deletion but carries a high risk of losing commits.


[!WARNING]
Blindly copying force-deletion commands from AI tools can permanently destroy unmerged work. Always verify the branch state before using -D.

title: Branches, Pull Requests, and Conflict Resolution
section: 6. Resolving merge conflicts via rebase (8 Git branches) (01:03:51–01:21:43)
text:
6. Resolving merge conflicts via rebase (8 Git branches) (01:03:51–01:21:43)

Merge conflicts occur when two branches independently modify the same lines of the same file. The conflict becomes apparent when a second PR attempts to merge after the first has already updated main.
To resolve conflicts locally, switch to the affected branch and run git rebase main. This replays your branch’s commits sequentially on top of the updated main branch, triggering the conflict resolution process locally.
Git halts at the conflicting commit and inserts markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) into the file. Edit the file to keep the correct content, run git add <file> to mark the resolution, and finish with git rebase --continue.
Because rebasing rewrites commit history, a standard push will fail. You must force-push the updated branch using git push --force-with-lease origin <branch_name>, which safely updates the remote only if no new, untracked commits were added by others.


[!WARNING]
Fixing a conflict marker at a specific line does not guarantee the code will run. You must verify that the entire file functions correctly after the merge, as variable names, imports, or logic dependencies may have shifted elsewhere.

text:
Learning Objectives

Describe what branches are in Git and explain why they are useful for collaboration.
Use Git to create new branches, switch between branches, and merge branches locally.
Bring a branch that has fallen behind the default branch up to date, using merge or rebase.

Branches allow you to have a playground for developing and testing new additions to your code, as well as fixes. This playground lets your explore, experiment and test in a safe place - away from others that might be using or depending on the current version of your code. This is perhaps more obviously useful if your project is deployed and has users (e.g., a data visualization dashboard, an R or Python package, a phone app, etc), but this can also be useful for code that make up a data analyses. As, in addition to the reasons stated above for branching, branching also lets you organize units of work into smaller, more manageable chunks that are easier for collaborators to check over and review.
Once the new code additions or fixes have been finalized in their branch playground, they can be merged back to the main code-base. Several branch playgrounds can co-exist, one for each new code addition or fix being worked on. This allows for parallelization of work!
We can use a construction of a house as a metaphor for this kind of development. First, you need to build the foundation. Since everything depends on the foundation being built, this would be developed on the main branch. When the foundation is finished, the construction of other parts of the house that don’t depend on each other could take place in parallel, e.g. some contributors might start working on the walls and others on the floor. When either of these features is finished, it can be added back to the house (merged into main). When depicted graphically, this process would look something like this (each dot is a commit).

section: 8.1 Creating a branch using the command line
text:
8.1 Creating a branch using the command line
In the terminal, and in the working directory of the project in which you wish to create a branch, use git switch with the -c flag and specify the branch name. This create a new branch and immediately switch to it. For example, to create a branch named patch-docs (a good branch name if we were planning on working on a fix in the project’s documentation), we would type:
git switch -c patch-docs
To ask Git what branches now exist and to see where we are, we can use the branch command with the -v flag (for “verbose”, meaning tell us everything!):
git branch -v
And we should see something like the output shown below, which lists the branch names in the first column, the SHA of the last commit on each branch in the second column, and the commit message associated with the last commit in the third column:
  main       f756bbb initial
* patch-docs f756bbb initial
As you work here on this new branch, you can commit your changes to version control locally, and even push your changes to the remote repository. All the changes however will live only on that branch until you do something to move them to another branch. When you want to start discussing your changes with your collaborators to start the process of bringing these changes into the main branch (main code-base) you typically create what is called a pull request. A pull request is a like an asking your collaborators “is it OK to merge my code?” Usually there will be some discussion and a few more revisions to the code, but eventually they will give you the thumbs up when everything looks good and the code can then be merged. We will discuss this more in Pull requests.

8.1.1 Switching to branches that already exist
After you have been working on your new brain for some time, you will eventually want to get back to the project’s default branch, or some other branch. To do this, we use git switch <branch_name>. Note that we do not use the -c flag this time, as we are not creating a new branch.


8.1.2 Getting remote branches you did not create locally
If your collaborator creates a branch that you want to run or test locally, but it only exists on the remote repository you have to tell Git to fetch (go get it) for you first, before you can switch to it. You can specify which branch you specifically want to grab, but for simplicity it is often easy to ask Git to fetch all of them for you, using the fetch command with the --all flag:
git fetch --all


8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands
Below is a table of the most commonly used Git commands for branching. This table includes the commands we presented above as well as the a few other useful ones.







Description
Command




list all local branches
git branch -v


create a new branch & immediately switch to it
git switch -c <branch_name> or git checkout -b <branch_name>


switch to a branch
git switch <branch_name> or git checkout <branch_name>


fetches all changes to all branches
git fetch --all


retrieve a branch you don’t have locally on your laptop from GitHub
git checkout --track origin/<branch_name


merge changes from another branch
git merge <branch_name>


delete a local branch
git branch -d <branch_name>


push changes to a remote branch
git push origin <branch_name>



Exercise

Make your own copy of this GitHub repository by clicking the green “Use this template” button. And then clone your copy of the repository to your computer.
Create a new branch named better_error_msg in the local repository using Git.
On that branch, fix the sqrt.py so that if you run this script with a negative number as an argument you do not get an difficult to understand error, but instead throw a helpful exception informing the user that the number should be positive. Fix to add to sqrt.py:

if number < 0:
  raise Exception("n should not a positive number")

Add and commit those changes.
Switch back to the main branch and look at the sqrt.py file - do you see the change there?
Switch back to the better_error_msg branch - do you see the change there?
Push your change to the remote GitHub repository, and see where you can find it there!

Note
Note: if you use the Git command line tool and get an error message like the one shown below, this is because you did not state the remote (usually it is origin). Try pushing again using git push origin <branch_name>
fatal: The current branch better_error_msg has no upstream branch.
To push the current branch and set the remote as upstream, use
    git push --set-upstream origin better_error_msg
To have this happen automatically for branches without a tracking
upstream, see 'push.autoSetupRemote' in 'git help config'.

8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?
There are a few ways you can fix this problem.

8.3.1 Using merge

How to catch up a branch that has fallen behind the main branch using the command line:

run git pull origin main to pull any changes from the remote version of main that we might not have
run git switch <branch> to make sure we are on the branch we want to catch up
run git merge main to merge the changes
run git push origin <branch> to push our updated branch to the remote




8.3.2 Using rebase

Make sure everything is committed in your new branch
Move to the main branch: git switch main
Make sure the main branch is up to date: git pull origin main
Move back over to your branch: git switch <branch>
Update the changes from main: git rebase main

text:
9.1 Creating a pull request
To create a pull request, you first need to ensure all the local changes you made on the new branch are also available on the remote repository (i.e., you need to push them). Once that has happened you need to go to the remote GitHub repository, as pull requests are created from there.
GitHub often tries to be helpful when a change is pushed to a new branch that doesn’t yet exist on the default branch by showing you a yellow banner listing any recently pushed branches.

To create a pull request, you click the green button “Compare & pull request”. In the new page, add a message to describe the changes you have made, scroll down to review the changed files, and the click the green button that reads “Create pull request”. If you are working together in a team, you could also designate certain team members to review your work and assign relevant labels, via the right hand side panel.
The next step is for a collaborator to review your work and merge it in if they approve it (see Code review on GitHub).

text:
9.2 Draft pull requests
Sometimes you want to open a pull request before the work is finished, to show your teammates where you are heading, to ask for early feedback, or to see whether your changes pass the project’s automated checks. Instead of adding “WIP” (work in progress) to the title, open the pull request as a draft. On the page where you write the pull request’s description, use the drop-down arrow beside the green “Create pull request” button, select “Create draft pull request”, and then click “Draft pull request”.
A draft pull request cannot be merged, and it tells your teammates that it is not ready for review yet. When the work is ready, click “Ready for review” in the merge box at the bottom of the pull request’s “Conversation” tab. If you need to go back to working on it, click “Convert to draft” under “Reviewers” in the right-hand sidebar.

text:
Learning Objectives

Use GitHub’s pull requests tool to perform code reviews, with in-line comments and suggested changes.
Accept suggested changes from a code review and merge the pull request.

We very often need to have a conversation to get pull requests into good shape before merging the changes into the main branch. GitHub has a very nice tool we can utilize to do this: GitHub code reviews. This tool allows us to add inline comments to proposed changes, as well as inline suggested changes that can be accepted with a click of a button. These features increase review efficiency and effectiveness!

In the project, you are expected to read and review each other’s code BEFORE accepting a pull request.
Do not expect all (or even most) pull requests to be perfect in their first submission.
Pull requests are opened, reviewed and merged by people. You may use AI tools to help check the code in a pull request, but a person reviews it and decides whether to merge it. Write down how your project uses AI tools in its AI policy.


Exercise
Demo: do a code review
I am going to demo a code review of a pull request. I have set-up a template GitHub repository for you so that you can easily generate a pull request for you to review if you want to try this later.
Steps:

Click the green “Use this template” button in this repository to obtain a copy of it for yourself (do not fork it).
Go to Repository Settings > Actions > General and change two settings:

Under “Actions permissions”, select “Allow all actions and reusable workflows”.
Under “Workflow permissions”, select “Read and write permissions”, and tick “Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests”. A repository made from a template does not keep this box ticked, so you need to tick it yourself.

Click the “Save” button under each section you change. When you are done, the page should look like this:



GitHub’s Settings, Actions, General page for a repository. Under Actions permissions, Allow all actions and reusable workflows is selected. Under Workflow permissions, Read and write permissions is selected and Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests is ticked.


Here are the two “Workflow permissions” settings up close:



The Workflow permissions section, with red arrows pointing to the selected Read and write permissions option and the ticked Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests checkbox.


If you skip this step, the workflow in the next step fails with an error like remote: Permission to <user>/<repo>.git denied to github-actions[bot] and The requested URL returned error: 403. Changing these settings fixes it.
Click on the Actions tab, and then click on the workflow .github/workflows/pr.yml. You then should see a “Run workflow” button with a drop down menu, from that menu select “Run workflow”.
Click on the Pull Requests tab of your copy of the repository, click on the pull request titled “Report most accomplished pilots”, and then click on “Files Changed”. Next click on the star-wars.Rmd file. Review the file and observe the following problems with the R Markdown report that was submitted via the pull request:

Reasoning of the sentence on line 15
Incompatibility with the sentence on line 15 with the code in the code chunk named table-of-most-accomplished-pilots
Incorrect code in code chunk named table-of-most-accomplished-pilots (unnested film instead of starships) leads to naming the wrong pilot as the most accomplished pilot on line 19
Incorrect code in code chunk named table-of-most-accomplished-pilots (unnested film instead of starships) leads to the use of the wrong character’s picture in the image that is sourced in the code chunk named top-pilot (it should be a picture of Obi-Wan Kenobi, you could use this URL for example: https://hips.hearstapps.com/hmg-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/images/ewan-mcgregor-obi-wan-1570898048.jpg).

Add comments and suggested changes using the + sign beside the line numbers (the first time you do this will trigger the start of your code review. Need help? See GitHub’s how to on reviewing proposed changes in a pull request.
After you have made all the comments and suggested changes, then add a general comment for the code review, select “Request Changes” and submit your code review.

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, and Conflict Resolution
text:
1. Git Branches and HEAD

Branch: A movable pointer to a commit. Creating a branch allows you to work in an isolated environment so that commits on main remain stable and ready for review.
HEAD: The reference that points to your current working directory and active branch. Moving branches is fundamentally about moving the HEAD pointer.
main vs origin/main: main tracks your local default branch. origin/main tracks what your local computer believes the remote GitHub repository’s state is. They only stay synchronized when you push and pull.
Diagram reference: ![Git local vs remote and branch structure](git1.png) (Illustrates clone, origin, main, and branch b1 with local laptop on the left and remote cloud on the right).
crumbs: Nov 17 · Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, and Conflict Resolution
text:
2. Creating and Switching Branches

git switch -c <branch_name>: Creates a new branch and immediately switches HEAD to it. This is the modern, purpose-built replacement for older checkout workflows.
Branch naming conventions: In group projects, it is standard to prefix branch names with your GitHub username (e.g., dan-b1) so teammates can identify ownership and know who to contact if issues arise.
Legacy commands: git checkout historically handled branch switching but also performed revert/restore actions, which caused significant confusion. Modern Git splits these responsibilities into git switch and git restore. If AI tools or tutorials suggest checkout for branching, prompt them to use switch instead.
crumbs: Nov 17 · Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, and Conflict Resolution
text:
3. Pushing Branches and Pull Requests

git push origin <branch_name>: Sends your local branch commits to the remote repository. GitHub typically displays a yellow banner prompting you to compare and create a pull request.
Draft Pull Requests: Use the dropdown next to “Create pull request” to open a draft. This grays out the merge button, signaling to the team that the work is incomplete or in progress, and prevents accidental merges.
Code Review: The “Files changed” tab shows the diff between the target branch and your branch. Reviewers add inline comments using the + button. The author is responsible for fixing flagged issues by pushing new commits to the same branch, which automatically updates the pull request without needing to close or recreate it.
crumbs: Nov 17 · Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, and Conflict Resolution
text:
4. Merging, Cleanup, and Local Sync

Merging: When a PR is approved, clicking “Merge pull request” integrates the commits into main on GitHub and adds a merge commit to the history. The original branch commits remain in history and can be referenced later.
Remote cleanup: Delete merged branches on GitHub via the repository’s branches dropdown to prevent clutter.
git fetch --prune: Synchronizes local tracking references with the remote. The --prune flag removes local references to branches that have been deleted on GitHub.
git branch -d <branch_name>: Deletes a local branch that has already been merged. Git protects against accidental data loss by refusing to delete unmerged branches with lowercase d. Use uppercase D (-D) only when you are certain you want to permanently discard unmerged work.
crumbs: Nov 17 · Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, and Conflict Resolution
text:
5. Resolving Merge Conflicts with Rebase

Merge conflicts: Occur when two branches modify the same lines in the same file. In a group project, even if you work on separate files, someone might edit a shared configuration or typo, causing conflicts when merging.
git rebase main: Replays your local branch commits on top of the updated main branch. If conflicts arise, Git pauses and requires you to manually resolve them in your text editor.
Resolving workflow: Open the conflicted file, remove conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>), keep the necessary code, run git add <file>, then execute git rebase --continue to proceed. The author must ensure the entire file works end-to-end after resolution, not just the conflicted lines.
Force pushing: After a rebase, the commit history has been rewritten. You cannot use a standard git push; you must use git push --force-with-lease to update the remote branch. Be extremely careful with force pushes, as they overwrite remote history and can delete teammates’ work if misused.
Diagram reference: ![Rebase workflow showing conflict resolution](git2.png) (Illustrates parallel branches, pull requests, and how rebase replays commits onto an updated main branch).

# build on top of template of minimal notebook
FROM quay.io/jupyter/minimal-notebook:afe30f0c9ad8

# copy all conda environment dependencies
COPY conda-linux-64.lock /tmp/conda-linux-64.lock

# conda install all the other packages
RUN mamba update --quiet --file /tmp/conda-linux-64.lock \
    && mamba clean --all -y -f \
    && fix-permissions "${CONDA_DIR}" \
    && fix-permissions "/home/${NB_USER}"

section: 💡 What are the benefits of using scripts?
text:
💡 What are the benefits of using scripts?


Abstraction: Hide the complexity of the code from the user
Reusability: The script can be reused by others

e.g., I moved the update_environment_yml.py script out from my original repository and shared it with you

Efficiency: Jupyter Notebook runs in linear fashion, while the script can be run in parallel
Automation: Scripts can be used with other tools (e.g., GNU Make) to automate the entire workflow
Ease of use: The script can be run with a single command
Ease of debugging: Modular code is easier to debug

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 5
text:
🦦 Greet otters using click!

"""Otter Greeting Generator

This script allows you to greet otters with different levels of enthusiasm.
"""

import click

@click.command()
@click.option('--count', default=1, help='Number of otter greetings.')
@click.option('--name', prompt='Your name', help='The person to greet.')
@click.option('--enthusiasm', type=click.Choice(['low', 'medium', 'high']), 
              default='medium', help='How enthusiastic should the otters be?')
def greet_otters(count, name, enthusiasm):
    """ Otter greeting generator
    
    Simple program that has adorable otters greet NAME for COUNT times. 🦦
    
    Parameters
    ----------
    count : int
        Number of otter greetings to display. Must be a positive integer.
        Default is 1.
    name : str
        The name of the person to greet. Will be prompted if not provided
        via command line.
    enthusiasm : {'low', 'medium', 'high'}
        The enthusiasm level of the otter greetings:
        - 'low': Simple, calm greeting
        - 'medium': Friendly greeting with some emojis
        - 'high': Very excited greeting with lots of emojis and caps
        Default is 'medium'.
    
    Returns
    -------
    None
        Outputs greetings directly to the console using click.echo().
    
    Examples
    --------
    Run from command line:
    
    >>> python otter_greeting.py --name "Oyster" --count 3 --enthusiasm high
    
    This will display 3 highly enthusiastic otter greetings for Oyster.
    """
    # Different enthusiasm levels
    emojis = {
        'low': '🦦',
        'medium': '🦦✨',
        'high': '🦦🎉🌊'
    }
    
    messages = {
        'low': f"hello {name}.",
        'medium': f"Hello {name}! 🌊",
        'high': f"HELLO {name.upper()}!!! Who is that lovely, amazing, genius friend over there?? The otters are SO excited to see you! 🎊"
    }
    
    click.echo(f"\n{emojis[enthusiasm]} Otter Greetings Incoming! {emojis[enthusiasm]}\n")
    
    for i in range(count):
        click.echo(f"  Otter #{i+1}: {messages[enthusiasm]}")
    
    click.echo(f"\n🦦 You've been greeted by {count} friendly otter(s)! 🦦\n")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    greet_otters()

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 5
text:
Tips for python scripts






Note



if __name__ == "__main__": lets you source the other functions in the script without running the main function.
click commands need to be placed right above the main function.





Example:
# import libraries/packages
import click

# parse/define command line arguments below
# define main function
@click.command()
@click.argument('num1', type=int)
@click.argument('num2', type=int)
def main(num1, num2):
    """Simple program that adds two numbers."""
    result = num1 + num2
    click.echo(f"The sum of {num1} and {num2} is {result}")

# call main function
if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 5
section: Command line for R: docopt package
text:
Command line for R: docopt package

Example:
"This script greets you with adorable otters! 🦦

Usage: greet_otters.R --name=<name> [--count=<count>]

Options:
--name=<name>      Your name (the person to greet)
--count=<count>    Number of otter greetings [default: 1]
" -> doc

library(docopt)

opt <- docopt(doc)

main <- function(name, count) {
  # Convert count to numeric (docopt returns strings)
  count <- as.numeric(count)
  
  # Generate otter greetings
  cat("\n🦦 Otter Greetings Incoming! 🦦\n\n")
  
  for (i in 1:count) {
    cat(paste0("  Otter #", i, ": Hello ", name, "! 🌊\n"))
  }
  
  cat(paste0("\n🦦 You've been greeted by ", count, " friendly otter(s)! 🦦\n\n"))
}

main(opt$name, opt$count)

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 4
text:
🙋‍♀️ What is && \ in Dockerfile?

FROM python:3.14-slim

# install command-line tools in one layer, then delete the download cache
RUN apt-get update \
    && apt-get install --yes --no-install-recommends make git \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# copy uv from its official image
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

# install the Python packages from uv.lock into /opt/venv
WORKDIR /home/project
ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./
RUN uv sync --locked
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"


\ at the end of a line: the command continues on the next line. &&: run the next command only if the previous one worked.
Why chain them into one RUN? Every RUN makes a new layer of the image. If rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* were its own RUN, the download cache would already be saved in the layer before it, and the image would not get smaller.
The uv part is the same as the lecture 3 Dockerfile. Tested: builds with Docker 29.7.2, and make, git and pandas all work inside the container.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
section: A shopping list and a receipt
text:
A shopping list and a receipt

pyproject.toml is the shopping list: what you asked for (e.g., “pandas”)
uv.lock is the receipt: the exact models, charger and cable included, with a plug for every country (pandas 3.1.1, numpy 2.5.5, …)
.python-version says which Python to use (3.14)
.venv/ is the box bought in Vancouver, it only has one Canadian plug that only works here!


MDS should send you the list, the receipt and the Python version.
Never ship the box (.venv/)!


If MDS sends only the shopping list (“a laptop”), the Zurich office buys an Apple laptop in iOS system and the Jakarta office buys a Lenovo laptop in Windows system. Everyone teaches with a different setup.
With the receipt, every office buys exactly the same models. The receipt also lists what came in the box that nobody asked for, like the charger and the cable: I asked for pandas and also got numpy.
The receipt names each model with the plug for every country. That is really what uv.lock does: it records the right files for macOS, Windows and Linux, so one lock file works for everyone.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
text:
Demo: create a uv project
Live demo in the terminal: create the environment, add a package, look inside the files.

DSCI 521 notes: Virtual environments with uv
Textbook: Python + uv projects, sharing a uv environment


Terminal, step by step:

mkdir -p ~/Desktop/uv_demo
cd ~/Desktop/uv_demo
uv init --bare → creates only pyproject.toml. (Without --bare uv also makes a main.py, a README.md and a Git repo, which we do not need.)
cat pyproject.toml → point at dependencies = []: the shopping list is empty.
uv python pin 3.14 → creates .python-version
cat .python-version → one line: 3.14
uv add pandas → watch the output: “Creating virtual environment at: .venv”, “Resolved 5 packages”, “+ numpy, + pandas, + python-dateutil, + tzdata”. I asked for one package and got four.
cat pyproject.toml → "pandas>=3.1.1" appeared in dependencies.
ls -a → .python-version, .venv, pyproject.toml, uv.lock
cat .venv/.gitignore → just *: uv tells Git to ignore the whole folder.
uv run python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)" → prints 3.1.1. uv run runs the command inside the environment, no need to activate it.
Open uv.lock in VS Code (code uv.lock) and scroll to the pandas block. Then go to the next slides.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
text:
What you asked for


.python-version
3.14

pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "uv-demo"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "pandas>=3.1.1",
]


Only the packages you asked for. Short enough to read and edit by hand.


>=3.1.1 means “pandas 3.1.1 or newer”. So the shopping list alone does not say which pandas you will get. That is the job of the lock file.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
text:
What you got: uv.lock

[[package]]
name = "pandas"
version = "3.1.1"
source = { registry = "https://pypi.org/simple" }
dependencies = [
    { name = "numpy" },
    { name = "python-dateutil" },
    { name = "tzdata", marker = "... or sys_platform == 'win32'" },
]
sdist = { url = ".../pandas-3.1.1.tar.gz", hash = "sha256:05fed3e3..." }
wheels = [
    { url = ".../pandas-3.1.1-...-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl", hash = "sha256:862f6fbe..." },
    { url = ".../pandas-3.1.1-...-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl", hash = "sha256:326459d8..." },
    { url = ".../pandas-3.1.1-...-win_amd64.whl", hash = "sha256:fdd87cf4..." },
]

This is a shortened version of the real uv.lock file, which lists 32 pandas wheels, one per operating system and chip.


Exact version: 3.1.1, not “3.1.1 or newer”.
What pandas itself needs: numpy and python-dateutil. Each of those has its own [[package]] block further down.
The marker: tzdata is only installed on Windows (and in the browser). One lock file covers every operating system. This is why we no longer need one lock file per OS like we did with conda-lock.
Download links and hashes, one per OS and chip. The hash is a fingerprint of the file: if anyone tampers with the download, the fingerprint no longer matches and uv refuses to install it.

Never edit uv.lock by hand. uv writes it, Git tracks it.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
section: How many packages did you actually get?

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
section: Make uv add write exact versions
text:
Make uv add write exact versions
By default uv add writes “this version or newer” into the shopping list:
dependencies = [
    "pandas>=3.1.1",
]

Add these two lines to pyproject.toml
[tool.uv]
add-bounds = "exact"
Every uv add from now on will write the exact version using ==:
dependencies = [
    "pandas>=3.1.1",       # added before the setting
    "requests==2.34.2",    # added after the setting
]







Tip


Your milestone 1 should use exact versions too!




Why bother if uv.lock already pins everything? Because the lock file gets rebuilt sometimes: someone deletes it, or runs uv lock --upgrade. With >= the versions can then jump. With == the shopping list itself says exactly which version the analysis was written with.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
text:
Your teammate’s side: uv sync

Your teammate clones the repository: they get the list, the receipt and the Python version, but no .venv/
uv sync builds .venv/ from uv.lock, exactly as on your computer
uv run ... runs any command inside that environment


Demo, in the same uv_demo folder, pretend I am my teammate, or the Sydney office:

rm -rf .venv → no box, only the shopping list and the receipt arrived.
ls -a → only the three text files left.
uv sync → rebuilt in under a second, because uv keeps a cache of everything it downloaded before.
uv tree → shows what pulls in what: pandas → numpy, python-dateutil.
uv run python -c "import pandas; print(pandas.__version__)" → 3.1.1 again.

Say: add packages with uv add, never uv pip install. uv sync removes anything that is not in uv.lock, so a package installed with pip disappears at the next sync.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
section: iClicker: What can still go wrong?
text:
iClicker: What can still go wrong?
Your teammate cloned your project and ran uv sync. The report still does not render on their laptop. What could still be different?

(A) The Python packages
(B) The operating system and its system libraries
(C) Other software, like Quarto or make
(D) Both B and C


Answer: (D).

is covered: uv.lock pins every Python package, and .python-version pins Python.

But a data analysis needs more than Python packages. Some examples students may have hit already:

Quarto is not installed, or is a different version, so the report renders differently.
A package needs a system library (for example geopandas needs GDAL) that uv cannot install.
The analysis runs on Linux on the server, but was written on a Mac.

Meanwhile, in Shanghai
A fourth student goes to Shanghai…

Bad news: Google, ChatGPT and Claude do not open, many shops do not take Visa, and people pay with Alipay or WeChat Pay. The electronics are fine. Everything is different.
our project is the same. uv got the packages right, but the computer around them can still be different.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
section: What uv.lock covers, and what it does not
text:
What uv.lock covers, and what it does not
The breast cancer predictor needs:




Pinned by uv?




Python 3.14
✅


pandas, scikit-learn, altair, …
✅


Quarto, to render the report
❌


make, to run the whole pipeline (lecture 7)
❌


The operating system and its system libraries
❌




We need to ship the whole computer setup, not just the Python packages.


the electronics are the Python packages. Quarto, make and the operating system’s libraries are the apps and services around them, like the payment apps in Shanghai. uv never sets those up.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
section: A container is a shipping container for software
text:
A container is a shipping container for software


before shipping containers, every cargo (sacks of coffee, barrels, cars) was loaded differently, by hand. The standard box made it possible to move anything with the same cranes and trucks.
MDS turns a shipping container into a classroom: laptop, kettle, projector, its own wall sockets, and every app already installed and set up. Every city just needs a crane and one standard power cable to the outside.
Map it: the room inside is Linux, so the same sockets everywhere. The one standard cable is Docker Desktop: on a Mac or Windows laptop it runs a small Linux behind the scenes, so the container always finds the same “country” inside. That is why the same image runs the same way on every laptop.
Docker is the most common software to build and run containers. Its logo is a whale carrying containers.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
section: Demo: run a container and look around
text:
Demo: run a container and look around
Textbook: Using and running containers

Before typing anything: open Docker Desktop (Launchpad on Mac, Start menu on Windows). Show the whale icon in the menu bar. No docker command works without it.
Terminal, step by step:

docker pull python:3.14-slim → already pulled before class, so it says “Image is up to date”.
docker images → the image is on my laptop.
python3 --version → my laptop’s Python (3.9.6 on my Mac).
docker run -it python:3.14-slim → a Python prompt opens INSIDE the container. -it = interactive, so I can type into it.
In that Python prompt: import sys, then sys.version → 3.14. Different from my laptop.
exit() → back on my laptop.
docker ps -a → the stopped container is still hanging around. Copy its CONTAINER ID.
docker rm <container_id> → paste the ID. Then docker ps -a again → gone. The image is still there (docker images).
docker run --rm -it python:3.14-slim bash → --rm deletes the container when I leave. bash at the end replaces the default command (Python) with a shell.
In the container shell: cat /etc/os-release → Debian Linux, on my Mac!
ls / and ls /home → this is the container’s file system, not my laptop’s. My Desktop files are not here.
exit → back on my laptop. docker ps -a → nothing left behind, thanks to --rm.

important: exit is switching off the lights and locking the classroom. docker rm is demolishing the room, though the blueprint (the image) is still there

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
section: Commands we ran in class: run a container
text:
Commands we ran in class: run a container
# 0. Mac and Windows: open Docker Desktop first

# 1. download an image from Docker Hub, then list the images on your computer
docker pull python:3.14-slim
docker images

# 2. Python on your laptop vs Python in the container
# (in the container's Python: import sys, then sys.version; leave with exit())
python3 --version
docker run -it python:3.14-slim

# 3. a stopped container still hangs around: find it and remove it
docker ps -a
docker rm <container_id>

# 4. --rm deletes the container when you leave, bash opens a shell instead of Python
docker run --rm -it python:3.14-slim bash
cat /etc/os-release    # Debian Linux, even on a Mac
ls /
exit

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
section: How does the container see my files?
text:
How does the container see my files?
It cannot, unless you mount a folder with -v:
docker run --rm \
    -v "/$(pwd)":/home/project \
    python:3.14-slim \
    python /home/project/hello.py

-v "/$(pwd)":/home/project: this folder on your laptop shows up as /home/project inside the container


Terminal, step by step:

mkdir -p ~/Desktop/docker_demo
cd ~/Desktop/docker_demo
nano hello.py, paste the three lines from the next slide, Ctrl + X, Y, Enter to save.
cat hello.py
python3 hello.py → on my laptop it says Darwin (macOS).
docker run --rm -v "/$(pwd)":/home/project python:3.14-slim python /home/project/hello.py → “Hello from Linux running Python 3.14”. The same file, run by the container’s Python.

Point out the order: docker run, the flags, the image, then the command to run instead of the default.
Why "/$(pwd)" and not just $(pwd): the extra / makes the same command work in Git Bash on Windows, and the quotes protect folder names with spaces.

The cliffhanger: docker run --rm python:3.14-slim python -c "import pandas" → ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'. This image has Python but none of our packages. Next lecture we build our own image with our uv.lock inside.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
section: Commands we ran in class: mount a folder
text:
Commands we ran in class: mount a folder
# 1. make a folder for the demo and move into it
mkdir -p ~/Desktop/docker_demo
cd ~/Desktop/docker_demo

# 2. write a tiny script (paste the 3 lines below, then Ctrl + X, Y, Enter)
nano hello.py

# 3. run it on your laptop, then inside the container
python3 hello.py
docker run --rm \
    -v "/$(pwd)":/home/project \
    python:3.14-slim \
    python /home/project/hello.py

# 4. the image has Python, but not our packages
docker run --rm python:3.14-slim python -c "import pandas"
import sys
import platform
print("Hello from", platform.system(), "running Python", sys.version.split()[0])

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
section: Start the model server in the background
text:
Start the model server in the background
docker run -d --rm --name llm \
    -p 11434:11434 \
    -v "/$(pwd)/models":/root/.ollama \
    ollama/ollama:0.40.16


-d (detach): run in the background, give me my terminal back
--name llm: a name we choose, so we do not need the container ID
-v "/$(pwd)/models":/root/.ollama: downloaded models are saved in models/ on your laptop



A server inside a container. How does your laptop talk to it?


Terminal, step by step:

cd ~/Desktop/llm_demo (made before class, the model is already in models/).
ls models → there is already something in there. Do not explain yet.
docker run -d --rm --name llm -p 11434:11434 -v "/$(pwd)/models":/root/.ollama ollama/ollama:0.40.16 → prints a long container ID and gives me my terminal back.
docker ps → llm is running, PORTS column shows 0.0.0.0:11434->11434/tcp.

Leave the -p explanation for the next slide.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
section: Talk to the container through a port
text:
Talk to the container through a port
-p 11434:11434: http://localhost:11434 on your laptop goes to port 11434 in the container

curl http://localhost:11434
Ollama is running


Chat with the model inside the container (-it, like the Python prompt earlier):
docker exec -it llm ollama run qwen2.5-coder:1.5b


A port is like a door number on your computer: each server listens behind its own door. Ollama listens behind door 11434 inside the container. Without -p, that door is closed to the outside. The image’s page on Docker Hub tells you which door.
Step by step:

curl http://localhost:11434 → “Ollama is running”. My laptop just talked to the container.
Browser: open http://localhost:11434 → the same “Ollama is running” text.
docker exec -it llm ollama run qwen2.5-coder:1.5b → docker exec runs a new command in a container that is already running. A >>> prompt appears.
Ask it: “Write a Python function that loads a CSV with pandas and returns the number of rows.” It is a coding model, so code questions show it best. Then ask a class member for a question.
Type /bye to leave the chat. The container keeps running (docker ps).

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
text:
Same question, same answer?
curl http://localhost:11434/api/generate -d '{
  "model": "qwen2.5-coder:1.5b",
  "prompt": "Give a name for a pet otter. Reply with the name only.",
  "stream": false
}'

Run it three times: Otterly, Smokey, Puddle… NOT reproducible!


Fix the random seed, turn off the randomness:
  "options": {"seed": 522, "temperature": 0}
Otterly, Otterly, Otterly ✅


This is the judge comic from lecture 1: same case, same evidence, different verdict.
Step by step:

Paste the first curl command (from the commands slide) and run it 3 times (arrow up, Enter). Point at "response":"..." near the start of the output: a different name each time.
Ask: “how would we make this reproducible?” Someone may say “set a seed”, like np.random.seed or random_state in scikit-learn.
Run the second curl command (with "options") 3 times: the same name every time.

Say: the container pins the software, the seed pins the randomness. Reproducibility needs both. (Same idea as random_state in scikit-learn.)
The names on the slide came from my test run; the class may see different ones, the point is only that they change.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
text:
Where is the model?

The model was downloaded before class, by a container that no longer exists
-v saved it in models/ on my laptop, so every new container finds it again


-e: set an environment variable inside the container. By default Ollama unloads the model after 5 minutes of quiet, and the next answer is slow again:
docker run -d --rm --name llm \
    -p 11434:11434 \
    -v "/$(pwd)/models":/root/.ollama \
    -e OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=1h \
    ollama/ollama:0.40.16


Step by step:

docker exec llm ollama ps → qwen2.5-coder:1.5b is loaded, UNTIL “4 minutes from now”.
du -sh models → about 1 GB on my laptop.
docker stop llm → stops it, and --rm deletes it.
docker ps -a → nothing left.
Start it again, this time with -e OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=1h (command on the slide).
docker exec llm ollama list → qwen2.5-coder:1.5b is still there, no download. That is the mount.
docker exec -it llm ollama run qwen2.5-coder:1.5b, ask one question, /bye.
docker exec llm ollama ps → UNTIL “59 minutes from now”. That is the environment variable.
docker stop llm when done.

What would happen without -v? The model lives inside the container, and --rm deletes it with the container: we would download 1 GB again every time.

title: DSCI 522 Lecture 2
section: Commands we ran in class: run a local LLM (1/3)
text:
Commands we ran in class: run a local LLM (1/3)

cd ~/Desktop/llm_demo

    -v "/$(pwd)/models":/root/.ollama \

docker run \

Flag
What it does




-d
run in the background (detach)


--rm
delete the container when it stops


--name
give the container a name


-it
interactive: let me type into it (not needed for servers)


-p laptop:container
connect a port


-v laptop:container
mount a folder


-e NAME=value
set an environment variable





Click through the highlights line by line and say what each one does.
Order matters: flags go between docker run and the image name. Anything after the image name is the command to run inside the container (like bash or python hello.py).
docker exec is the partner of -d: it runs a command in a container that is already running.
⚠️ The command line is very sensitive to spaces and quotes. A space after \ breaks the line continuation.

section: (Bonus) Which port is free on my laptop?
text:
(Bonus) Which port is free on my laptop?
Only one program can listen behind each door. List the doors that are taken:
# every port a program is listening on (macOS, Linux)
# lsof: "list open files" (a network door counts as a file)
# -iTCP: TCP doors only, -sTCP:LISTEN: only programs waiting at their door
# -n, -P: print raw IP and port numbers, skip the slow name lookup
lsof -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN -n -P

# one port: no output means it is free
lsof -i :11434

# Windows: -a all doors, -n numbers, -o process ID; findstr keeps matching lines
netstat -ano | findstr :11434

If the port is taken, Docker says port is already allocated. Change only the laptop side: -p 11435:11434, then curl http://localhost:11435
⚠️ On macOS, avoid 5000 and 7000: AirPlay Receiver uses them

title: Lecture Overview
text:
Title


Description






1. Introduction to Reproducible and Trustworthy Data Science Workflow


See what goes wrong when analyses are untested or cannot be reproduced. Learn what makes an analysis reproducible, auditable and trustworthy.




2. uv Lock Files, Containerization, and Docker


Recap uv: what pyproject.toml, uv.lock and .python-version each hold and how uv sync rebuilds an environment. Then meet Docker: what a container is, how it differs from a virtual machine, and how to run one with ports, volumes and environment variables.




3. Customizing and Building Containers


Recap virtual environments and lock files, launch containers with a docker-compose.yml file, and write a Dockerfile to build your own image from the command line.




4. Data Validation with Pandera


Automate building and pushing a Docker image to Docker Hub with GitHub Actions, organize the complete workflow, then walk through the data validation checklist and check a dataset with Pandera.




5. Non-interactive scripts coming soon


Wrap up Docker, then compare interactive (REPL) work with scripts. Organize a Python script, write docstrings, parse command line arguments with click, and save model objects.




6. Reproducible reports coming soon


Recap the Python main guard, see why reports written in WYSIWYG editors are hard to reproduce, and learn about syntax of writing beautiful Quarto report.




7. Data Analysis Pipeline and GNU Make coming soon


Learn what a data analysis pipeline is, run one with a shell script, see where shell scripts fall short, and use a Makefile to rebuild only what changed.




8. Testing Code & Conclusion coming soon


Modularize scripts into functions, plan test cases, create simple test data, and write tests in Python and R. Then a look back at everything in the course.

title: Quarto Cheatsheet
text:
2.1 Create a new repository

Use this github repository as a template, and create a new repository under your own GitHub account.

Click on “Use this template” button, and then click “create a new repository” button to create a public repository using default settings under your own GitHub account.


Clone the repository and cd into the repository.

git clone <repository_url>
cd <repository_name>

Launch the Docker container using the following command:

docker compose up

Copy and open the URL that starts with http://127.0.0.1:8888/lab?token= in your browser, to launch jupyter lab docker container.
Run the python script in the terminal to generate the plots and tables in the results folder.

python scripts/generate_figures.py --input_dir="data/00030067-eng.csv" \
    --out_dir="results"
You will see the results folder now has new plots and csv files saved.

title: Quarto Cheatsheet
text:
2.2 Update .qmd file

2.2.1 Header formatting & table of contents

TODO: Add header formatting to sections (e.g., “Aim”, “Data”, “Methods”, “Results”, “References”) and Quarto configuration so that a table of contents that is automatically generated from the document headers will be created when the document is rendered

We will update the yml header to add table of contents. We will add table of content (toc) with depth 3 for both html and pdf formats. Your yml header at the begining of the file (i.e., qmd_example.qmd) should be updated to look like this:
title: "DSCI 310: Historical Horse Population in Canada"
author: "Tiffany Timbers & Jordan Bourak"
editor: source
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
  pdf:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
Delete the template’s old format: html line: a setting can only appear once in the YAML header.
You will format header sections using #, ##, ###, etc. For example, I’ve added the following header sections to the qmd_example.qmd file:
# Aim
...
# Data
...
# Methods
...
# Results
...
# References


2.2.2 References

TODO: Add correctly formatted inline BibTeX references so that a nicely formatted reference list will be present at the end of the document.

You already have a references.bib file in the repository under the reports folder. We will point bibliography to look for references in this file in the yml header as follows:
title: "DSCI 310: Historical Horse Population in Canada"
author: "Tiffany Timbers & Jordan Bourak"
editor: source
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
  pdf:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
bibliography: references.bib






NoteHigh bug zone: indentation & missing colon:




Quarto’s yaml uses 2 whitespaces to indent the yaml fields (not 4 whitespaces!! not tab!!).
Please use : to separate the field name and the field value.



Let’s render what we have so far to see the result. In your terminal, please run the following commands:
# go to the reports directory if you are in the root directory
cd reports

# render the html file
quarto render qmd_example.qmd






NoteNo references listed in the rendered report??



You will notice that no references are listed in the rendered pdf or html file. This is because we have not added in-text citations to the .qmd file. You can list as many BibTex references as you want in your references.bib file. However, only the references that are cited in the .qmd file will be listed in the rendered pdf or html file under “References” section.


Let’s add in-text citations to the .qmd file. We will use the [@reference_key] syntax (or [@reference_key1; @reference_key2] when you have more than 1 reference) to cite references. Please note the reference_key is the first phrase after { in the BibTex entry. For example, for this entry in the references.bib file:
@Manual{click,
    title           = {Click Python Package},
    author          = {Pallets Team},
    year            = {2020},
    url             = {https://click.palletsprojects.com/},
}
The reference_key is click. We will use [@click] to cite this reference in the .qmd file.
For example, I’ve added the following in-text citations to the .qmd file. Please complete all other in-text citations yourself:
Horse population data were sourced from the 
[Government of Canada's Open Data website](http://open.canada.ca/en/open-data) [@horses1; @horses2]...


2.2.3 Figure formatting

TODO: Edit the figure formatting so that Quarto:

automatically numbers them
has a label for easy cross referencing
controls the figure sizes so the figures are not too big (in particular the second figure in the report should be only 60-70% of the default width)


We use the syntax ![description](relative/path/to/figure.png){#fig-label width=60%} to format the figure. For example, I’ve added the following figure to the .qmd file, and I use @fig-label to refer to it in the text. This will be rendered as Figure 1 in the rendered pdf or html file. You will do so for both Figure 1 + 2.
# Results

![Horse populations for all provinces in Canada from 1906 - 1972.](../results/horse_pops_plot.png){#fig-horse-pop width=60%}

We can see from @fig-horse-pop that Ontario, Saskatchewan and Alberta 






NoteHigh bug zone: Pay attention to using fig-label




You have to name your figure with starting with a fig prefix (sorry for my mistakes in class!).
You have to use - instead of _ in the figure label.
Example: fig-horse-pop instead of horse_pop.





2.2.4 Table formatting

TODO: add a table description argument so that they are automatically numbered by Quarto and use cross referencing to link to the table if/when it is discussed in the text

We use the syntax below inside of python code block to format the table:
#| label: tbl-label
#| tbl-cap: Table description
For example, I’ve added the following table to the .qmd file. @tbl-horse-sd will be rendered as Table 1 in the rendered pdf or html file.
We present the standard deviations in @tbl-horse-sd.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-horse-sd
#| tbl-cap: Standard deviation of historical (1906-1972) horse populations for each Canadian province.

horses_sd_table = pd.read_csv("../results/horses_sd.csv")
largest_sd = horses_sd_table['Province'].values[0]
Markdown(horses_sd_table.to_markdown(index = False))
```






NoteHigh bug zone: Pay attention to using tbl-label




You have to name your table with starting with a tbl prefix (sorry for my mistakes in class!).
You have to use - instead of _ in the table label.
Example: tbl-horse-sd instead of horse_sd.





2.2.5 Cross-referencing

TODO: Edit the narrative so it uses cross-referencing to refer to the figures and tables instead of having their reference hardcode the figure and table numbers.

In the steps above, we have already used cross-referencing to refer to the figures and tables (e.g., @fig-horse-pop and @tbl-horse-sd).


2.2.6 Inline Quarto code

TODO: replace the ??? in the Quarto report narrative text with inline Quarto code, so that the text will be automatically updated with the correct value

We use the syntax below to do inline Quarto code. It will execute the python / R code inside of the code block and resulting value will be displayed in the text.
`{python} <python_code>`
For example, I’ve added the following inline Quarto code (i.e., {python} largest_sd) to the .qmd file:
```{python}
#| label: tbl-horse-sd
#| tbl-cap: Standard deviation of historical (1906-1972) horse populations for each Canadian province.


horses_sd_table = pd.read_csv("../results/horses_sd.csv")
largest_sd = horses_sd_table['Province'].values[0]
Markdown(horses_sd_table.to_markdown(index = False))
```

...

In @fig-horse-largest we zoom in and look at the province of `{python} largest_sd`, which had the largest spread of values in terms of standard deviation.


2.2.7 No code chunk visible

TODO: change the code chunk options so that no code is viewable in the rendered report, just the code outputs where needed (e.g., figures and tables)

We will set echo: false in the yml header to hide the code chunk in the rendered report.
title: "DSCI 310: Historical Horse Population in Canada"
author: "Tiffany Timbers & Jordan Bourak"
editor: source
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
  pdf:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 3
bibliography: references.bib
execute:
  echo: false


2.2.8 GitHub Pages

TODO: (optional/bonus) Turn on GitHub pages so that it serves up the docs directory so that the report is viewable on the web.

At the root directoy of your repository, please create a new file called _quarto.yml and add the following content:
project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs
This file will tell Quarto to output the rendered report to the docs folder, as a website.
Also create an empty file called .nojekyll at the root directory of your repository:
touch .nojekyll
Quarto copies it into the docs folder every time you render, and it tells GitHub Pages to serve your files exactly as they are (see Turning off Jekyll with .nojekyll in the DSCI 521 notes).
Then, at the root directoy of your repository, please run the following command to render the report in the terminal:
quarto render
You will see that the rendered report is now all in the docs folder. There is a index.html file in the docs folder, you can open it in your browser to view the report.
Confirm that .nojekyll is in docs, the folder GitHub Pages publishes from. ls hides files whose names start with a dot, so add -a:
ls -a docs
You should see .nojekyll in the list.






NoteNo image showing in Jupyter lab??



It is normal to not see figures being rendered inside of Jupyter lab. You will need to go to local folder, and double click on the index.html file to view the report in a browser.

title: Git Cheatsheet
text: Run all of these commands in your terminal, from inside your project folder (except git clone, which creates the folder for you). For the full explanations, see the textbook chapters on Git basics, Git history, Git branches, and merge conflicts.

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
1 The Everyday Workflow







Task
Command




Clone a remote version control repository from GitHub.com to your local computer
git clone <URL>


Check the status of the local version control repository
git status


Add a file to the staging area
git add <FILENAME>


Commit staged files to the version control history
git commit -m "Some relevant message about the changes"


Push changes from the local repository to the remote repository on GitHub.com
git push


Pull changes from the remote repository on GitHub.com to the local repository
git pull


View the version control history
git log



The usual loop is: git pull → edit files → git status → git add → git commit → git push.

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
2 Getting a Repository

git clone <URL> — Copy a remote repository from GitHub.com to your computer

Example: git clone https://github.com/UBC-MDS/DSCI_522_dsci-workflows_students.git

This creates a new folder named after the repository. Use cd <folder_name> to go into it.

Do not clone a repository inside another repository.

git init — Turn the current folder into a new, empty Git repository

Only needed when you start a project locally. If you start on GitHub.com and then git clone, you do not need it.

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
3 Checking the Status

git status — Show which files are modified, staged, or not tracked yet

Run it often, especially before git add and git commit.

git diff — Show the changes you made that are not staged yet

git diff --staged — Show the changes that are staged and will go into the next commit

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
4 Staging and Committing

git add <FILENAME> — Add a file to the staging area

git add <FILE1> <FILE2> — Add several files at once

git add <FOLDER>/ — Add everything in a folder

git add . — Add all changes in the current folder (check git status first so you only stage what you mean to)

git commit -m "Some relevant message about the changes" — Commit the staged files to the version control history

Write a short, specific message that says what changed and why.
Only staged files are committed.

git restore --staged <FILENAME> — Unstage a file (your edits to the file are kept)
git restore <FILENAME> — Discard your unstaged edits to a file and go back to the last commit

⚠️ This cannot be undone.

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
5 Syncing with GitHub

git push — Send your local commits to the remote repository on GitHub.com

First push of a new branch: git push -u origin <BRANCH_NAME> (-u stands for --set-upstream). See the branches section below for the difference between this and git push origin <BRANCH_NAME>.

git pull — Get changes from the remote repository on GitHub.com and merge them into your local repository

Pull before you start working, and before you push, to avoid conflicts.

git fetch — Download the latest changes from GitHub.com without merging them into your files
git remote -v — Show the URL of the remote repository your local repository is connected to

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
6 Viewing the History

git log — View the version control history

Press q to exit the log. Use the arrow keys, b, or the space bar to scroll.

Press / + a search term + Enter to search the log; n / N jump to the next / previous match.

git log -n 3 — Show only the last 3 commits

git log <FILENAME> — Show only the commits that changed this file

git show <COMMIT_ID> — Show the changes made in one commit

The commit ID (also called the commit hash, or SHA) is the long string of letters and numbers after commit in git log. It is a hash of the commit’s contents, so each commit has a unique one.

The first 7 characters (the short SHA) are usually enough: git show 238dbcb








TipJust want a look at the past?



On GitHub.com, click the commits link on the repository’s main page to see the history and commit messages. Click the <> button next to a commit to view the state of the whole repository at that point in time.

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
7 Going Back in Time
Use these in your local repository when you want to run or explore files from the past, or bring a past version of a file into the present.

git checkout <COMMIT_ID> . — Move the whole project (all files and directories) back to the state of that commit

The last . is really important, so don’t forget it!

Example: git checkout 9b4af1d .

The files now look like they did at that commit, so you can explore and run them.

git checkout HEAD . — Go back to the future: return to the most recent commit

HEAD is the nickname for the most recent commit.

Run git log afterwards to check you returned safely.

git checkout <COMMIT_ID> <FILENAME> — Bring back the version of a single file from a past commit

Example: git checkout 5837143 doc/count_report.Rmd

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
8 Branches

git branch — List the local branches (the current one is marked with *)

git branch -v — Also show the SHA and message of the last commit on each branch (-v stands for --verbose)
git branch -a — Also list the branches on the remote

git switch -c <BRANCH_NAME> — Create a new branch and switch to it

Same as git checkout -b <BRANCH_NAME>

Use a descriptive name, e.g. patch-docs for a fix to the documentation.

git switch <BRANCH_NAME> — Switch to an existing branch (no -c, since we are not creating one)

Same as git checkout <BRANCH_NAME>

git fetch --all — Download all changes to all branches from the remote, so you can switch to a branch a collaborator created
git push origin <BRANCH_NAME> — Push the changes on a branch to the remote repository (usually named origin)

This pushes once. Git does not remember the connection, so a plain git push on that branch fails with fatal: The current branch <BRANCH_NAME> has no upstream branch, and you have to type git push origin <BRANCH_NAME> every time.

git push -u origin <BRANCH_NAME> — Push and link your local branch to the remote branch of the same name (-u stands for --set-upstream). After this, plain git push and git pull work on that branch, and git status tells you whether you are ahead of or behind the remote.

You only need -u the first time you push a new branch.

git merge <BRANCH_NAME> — Merge the branch <BRANCH_NAME> into the branch you are currently on

If the same lines were changed in both branches, Git stops with a merge conflict. Open the files with <<<<<<< markers, choose what to keep, then git add and git commit.

git branch -d <BRANCH_NAME> — Delete a local branch that has been merged







TipTypical branch workflow




git switch main and git pull — start from the latest main
git switch -c my-new-feature — create a branch
Edit, git add, git commit (repeat as needed)
git push -u origin my-new-feature — push the branch
Open a pull request on GitHub.com, get it reviewed, and merge it there
git switch main and git pull — bring the merged work back to your computer

title: Git Cheatsheet
text:
9 Ignoring Files
.gitignore — A text file in the root of the repository listing files and folders that Git should not track
- One pattern per line, e.g. .venv/, *.log, .DS_Store
- Prepend **/ to a file or folder name (e.g. **/.venv/, **/.DS_Store) to also ignore it in subdirectories anywhere within the repository

Message or situation

rejected ... failed to push some refs
The remote has commits you do not have. Run git pull, fix any conflicts, then git push again.

Open the file, resolve the <<<<<<< / ======= / >>>>>>> sections, then git add <file> and git commit.

title: Milestone 4
text:
NoteThe end-of-course project goal





Your team answers a predictive question with a public data set, in R and/or Python, with a focus on reproducible and trustworthy workflows. By the end of the course, your single Quarto document will have become a project with:

well-documented, modular scripts in R and/or Python
a pipeline automated with GNU Make
a reproducible Quarto report
a Docker container for the computational environment
a GitHub repository for collaboration and sharing

title: Milestone 4
text:
Milestone 4 summary
This milestone ties your project together: one command runs the whole analysis, your code is tested, your report reads like a finished paper, and you fix what reviewers pointed out.

Write a Makefile so make all runs every script, renders the report and publishes it
Move some code into functions (at least one per team member) and write tests for them
Polish your report: no visible code, numbered and cross-referenced figures and tables, citations
Address feedback from the TAs and from the peer review







ImportantSee what a finished Milestone 4 looks like



An example Milestone 4 that corresponds to our expectations is here: Breast Cancer Predictor 3.0.0. Look at its Makefile, src/ and tests/ folders. It uses conda for its environment: ignore that part and keep the uv/renv setup from Milestone 2.








TipReadings for this milestone






Data analysis pipelines with GNU Make and the Makefile cheatsheet
Testing, then pytest (Python) or testthat (R)
Reproducible reports with Quarto and the Quarto cheatsheet (you practised these in Individual Assignment 3)





1. Write a Makefile that runs everything
Put a file named Makefile in the root of your repository, as you did in Individual Assignment 4. It needs:

an all target: runs the whole analysis from top to bottom, including publish
a clean target: deletes everything the pipeline made, so make all can start fresh
a publish target: copies the rendered report to docs/index.html, replacing the steps you did by hand in Milestone 2
real file targets for the other steps, with their dependencies (the data and the script), so Make only reruns what changed. Only all, clean, publish and similar group names may be phony.
comments that explain each rule, and a README section that says how to run it

Your scripts run in the container, so the commands in the rules start with uv run (Python), for example uv run python scripts/download_data.py ... and uv run quarto render .... Run the pipeline with docker compose run --rm analysis-env make all.






TipExample: the publish target





Change the report’s path to your own:


Makefile

publish: docs/index.html

docs/index.html: reports/<your-report>.html
    mkdir -p docs
    cp reports/<your-report>.html docs/index.html
    touch docs/.nojekyll

Because docs/index.html depends on your rendered report, make publish copies it only when the report has changed. Commit and push docs/ after it runs.





2. Write functions and test them
Look for code that repeats (cleaning several columns the same way, many similar plots, tuning several models) or that you would reuse in another project.

Write at least one function per team member, following the textbook’s workflow for writing functions and tests: write the documentation first, then the tests, then the function body.
Put them in their own files: src/*.py (Python) or R/*.R (R). One function per file, or all in one file, both are fine.
Use them in your scripts with import (Python) or source() (R).
Write tests in tests/ with pytest (Python) or testthat (R). Add the test package to your environment, and say in your README how to run the tests in the container.







TipHow your functions are marked






Quality: each function does one thing, and returns a value unless it is meant to write a file or plot.
Usability and readability: clear names and arguments; black (Python) or tidyverse (R) style.
Documentation: a docstring (Python) or roxygen comment (R) saying what it does, its arguments and what it returns.
Tests: they cover expected cases, edge cases and errors.

More functions than the minimum are welcome, but each one is held to these standards.





3. Polish your report
A reader who is not a data scientist should not be able to tell that code made the report. Render it to HTML (that is the version on GitHub Pages); a PDF as well is optional.

A table of contents
Citations from a BibTeX file, with a reference list at the end
Figures with a label and a caption, so Quarto numbers them, at a sensible size
Tables with a label and a caption, so Quarto numbers them
The text refers to figures and tables with cross-references (@fig-..., @tbl-...), never typed numbers
Values in the text (accuracy, sample size…) come from inline code, not typed in by hand
No code shows in the rendered report, only its output



4. Address feedback

From the TAs
Fix what the TAs pointed out in earlier milestones. Then submit a regrade request on Gradescope for that question, with links to the pull requests or commits that show the change. If the TA confirms the fix, you get back 50% of the points you lost on that question. Keep the request easy to follow, or we can’t give points back.


From the peer review
Address at least one peer review item per team member (a team of 4 fixes at least 4). List them in a CHANGELOG.md in the root of your repository: for each item, the feedback, what you changed, and a link to the evidence (an issue, pull request, commit or lines of code). Feedback that the TAs also gave can go in too. See keepachangelog.com for an example.



5. Update your README
Your README must take someone from a fresh clone to the rendered report: pull the image, run make all in the container, and how to run the tests. Also say how to run make clean.






Important5 all-or-nothing points for your README instructions



If someone can’t run your whole pipeline by following your instructions exactly as written, you lose all 5 points. Test them on both Windows and Mac. If your team doesn’t have both, ask another team to test them.

text:
Submission instructions

Just before you submit, create a GitHub release named exactly 3.0.0 (how to create a release).
On Gradescope, enter these three URLs (there is no PDF to make):

TipCheck yourself before submitting






From a fresh clone, make all in the container runs everything and updates docs/index.html
Running make all a second time does nothing; make clean removes everything the pipeline made
At least one tested function per team member, in src/ or R/, used by your scripts
All tests pass in the container
The rendered report shows no code and every item in the polish list above is done
CHANGELOG.md lists at least one peer review item per team member, with links
Someone on Windows and someone on Mac followed your README steps exactly
Your report on GitHub Pages matches your release
You created the 3.0.0 release










TipTeamwork expectations (these are marked)






Everyone contributes equally to code, writing and project management, shown by a roughly equal number of commits, pull request reviews and GitHub issue comments.
Use the GitHub flow: a branch for each feature or fix, reviewed by at least one teammate before the pull request is merged.
Commit and push every time you work on the project, with meaningful commit messages (one or two less meaningful ones are OK).
Talk to your teammates in GitHub issues, not email or Slack: at least 3 issues per person on average in this milestone.
Your question, analysis and visualization should make sense. They don’t have to be complicated.
Your analysis should be correct and run reproducibly from your README instructions.
Follow the black style guide (Python) or the tidyverse style guide (R).
Don’t commit generated files, except docs/, which GitHub Pages needs.
Write your README in full sentences with proper grammar. Keep point form under 10% of it.
