title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts
section: 13. Syncing and cleaning up locally after a merge (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
text:
13. Syncing and cleaning up locally after a merge (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:59:07–01:03:51

Conflicts still happen with branches: even when people split the work, someone, or an agent, may fix a typo in your part. That is why individual assignment 1 has you practise merge conflicts again.
Local main doesn’t update itself: after git switch main, run git pull origin main. In class this fast-forwarded main and added 6 lines to README.md, which were the merged pull request’s changes.
git branch -a: lists the local branches (with * on the current one) and the remote-tracking branches such as remotes/origin/dan-b1.
git fetch --prune: syncs history with origin without changing your files. It also removes local references to branches deleted on GitHub; the output showed [deleted] (none) -> origin/dan-b1.

git pull is git fetch followed by a merge. Run fetch alone when you don’t want your working files to change.

git branch -d <branch>: lowercase -d deletes a local branch only if it has been merged. Git makes it harder to lose unmerged work.
git branch -D <branch>: capital -D force-deletes the branch even if it has not been merged.


[!WARNING]
Use lowercase git branch -d. Capital -D force-deletes a branch even if it was never merged, which can throw away commits you’re still working on. It’s a one-character difference — be very careful when copying commands from ChatGPT, which may hand you -D.
crumbs: Nov 17 · Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts
section: 14. Setting up two conflicting pull requests (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
text:
14. Setting up two conflicting pull requests (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:04:00–01:10:00

What causes a conflict: two changes to the same line of the same file. Daniel created two branches from main that both added text at the same spot in README.md.
First branch, dan-fetch: he documented git fetch --prune, committed with git commit -m "define fetch --prune", pushed, and opened #2. He did not merge it straight away; that is the key to practising conflicts on your own.
Second branch, dan-delete: he switched back to main, created dan-delete, and documented git branch -d and -D. Because he branched from main, the fetch line was not in this version of the file. He committed with git commit -m "branch -d and -D" and opened #3.
The split is visible: git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate shows two lines leaving the same main commit, which means two parallel pieces of work.
GitHub hides it at first: each pull request on its own looks fine and mergeable into main. Nothing warns you that both edit the same line.
crumbs: Nov 17 · Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts
section: 15. When a merge creates the conflict: resolving on GitHub
text:
15. When a merge creates the conflict: resolving on GitHub
01:10:00–01:12:44

How it appears: when one pull request merges, main changes, and GitHub rechecks every other pull request that targets main. Once #2 was merged, #3 showed a conflict.
Web editor: simple conflicts can be resolved in GitHub’s web editor. Find the conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) and fix them.
What “fixed” means for prose: the remaining report text must be English that makes sense.
What “fixed” means for code: the code must run from top to bottom again. A conflict on line 13 can break line 50, for example if a variable was renamed, and that is still your problem.


[!WARNING]
Resolving a conflict doesn’t just mean deleting the conflict markers. Your code has to work again from top to bottom — a change made at the conflicting line can break code elsewhere in the file.
crumbs: Nov 17 · Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts

title: Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts
section: 16. Resolving the conflict locally with rebase (8.3.2 Using rebase)
text:
16. Resolving the conflict locally with rebase (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:12:44–01:20:42

Many valid ways: Daniel uses rebase and noted that people who know Git well will have opinions about it.
The idea: replay your branch’s commits on top of the updated main. The conflict then surfaces on your own computer, where you can fix it.

In the demo, dan-delete’s parent was 3851b00. It needed to sit on top of the merge that contains 157c3cd (the fetch commit).

Step 1, sync main: git switch main, then git pull origin main.
Step 2, rebase your branch: git switch dan-delete, then git rebase main. Git stops on the conflict.
Step 3, fix the file: open README.md in your editor and resolve the markers. Here he kept both definitions and tidied the whitespace. This is the same skill as week 3 of 521; only the trigger differs (git rebase main instead of git pull origin main).
Step 4, let git status guide you: it tells you to git add the file to mark it resolved, and then to run git rebase --continue, which asks you to confirm the commit message. If you are scared, git rebase --abort gets you back to where you started.
Step 5, force-push: the rebased commit has a new parent, so the branch’s history has changed and a normal push is rejected. Daniel used git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete. GitHub then records that a force push happened, and the pull request shows a green merge button again.
Finish up: merge, delete the branch on GitHub, and clean up locally with git fetch --prune and git branch -d.


[!WARNING]
Rebasing rewrites your branch’s history, so you can’t avoid a force push afterwards — and it shows up on GitHub as a force push (“you’ve mangled history”, which matters in compliance settings). Only do this to your own branch.

Rebase the conflicting branch onto main and force-push
git switch main
git pull origin main                      # brings in the merge of PR #2
git switch dan-delete
git rebase main                           # stops on the conflict
git status                                # explains the next steps
# fix the conflict markers in README.md in your editor
git add README.md                         # mark the conflict as resolved
git status
git rebase --continue
git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate
git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete   # history changed, so force-push

Auto-merging README.md
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in README.md
error: could not apply cb810d5... branch -d and -D

Plain git push from main did nothing: it printed Everything up-to-date because the new commit was on dan-b1. The fix was git switch dan-b1 followed by git push origin dan-b1.

text:
3. Why branches exist: escaping the “I have to pull before I push” friction (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

DSCI 521 shared slide deck: In week 3 of 521, students collaborated on a shared slide deck and often had to pull before they could push, even when there was no actual conflict.
Collaboration friction: If two people are editing the same thing, there is constant friction around coordinating updates; this problem exists in every project.
Parallel streams: The goal is to reach a part of the project where a student owns a self-contained piece of work and can work on it without constantly waiting for others.

section: 4. Local repository versus remote origin (8 Git branches)
text:
4. Local repository versus remote origin (8 Git branches)
00:09:46–00:11:11

Two places work happens: Git work happens locally on a computer and remotely on the cloud/remote, called origin in this session.
Coordination: With teammates, everyone coordinates through the remote; the remote is the shared source of truth.
One-time clone: git clone is a one-time command that brings the repository down to the computer.
Push and pull: Local commits are sent upward with git push; work created by others is brought down with git pull.


[!WARNING]
Daniel Chen stressed that if your work exists only on your local computer, it “effectively doesn’t really exist” for grading or project purposes. The remote repository is what matters.

section: 5. main, origin/main, HEAD, and what a branch is (8 Git branches)
text:
5. main, origin/main, HEAD, and what a branch is (8 Git branches)
00:11:11–00:16:05

main: main is the default branch and the place that often represents the stable, final, or production state of the project.
origin/main: origin/main is the local computer’s record of what the remote main branch is at.
HEAD: HEAD is the current pointer into the Git history; when it points to main, you are on the main branch.
Branch as a name: A branch is essentially another name that moves forward when you commit, instead of moving main.
Stable main: In larger projects, main should be stable and working; exploratory work, unfinished analysis, or plots that are still being tested should live on a branch until ready.

section: 6. Branches are useful even when working alone (8 Git branches)
text:
6. Branches are useful even when working alone (8 Git branches)
00:16:05–00:17:54

Solo branching: Branches are not only for collaboration; many single-person Git repositories also use branches.
Section off work: A branch lets you test a large set of changes without changing main until you have reviewed and confirmed that everything works.
Easy abandonment: If a branch was a bad idea, it is much easier to abandon or delete the branch than to undo a tangled set of commits on main.
Textbook example: Daniel Chen described working on the course textbook by making a sequence of branch-based changes and merging them after lectures and testing.

section: 7. Creating a branch with git switch -c (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
text:
7. Creating a branch with git switch -c (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:23:46

Check starting state: Before creating a branch, run git status and confirm you are on main.
Sync before coordinated work: If you are building on shared project work, first synchronize with the remote, for example with git pull origin main, so you do not start from an old local state.
Create and move: git switch -c dan-b1 creates a new branch named dan-b1 and immediately moves HEAD to it.
Visible state: After switching, git status says On branch dan-b1, and git log --all shows the new branch at the same commit as main before any new branch-specific commits exist.
Branch naming: In group repositories, Daniel Chen sometimes prefixes branch names with the owner’s name so teammates know who to talk to when something looks odd.
Commit moves the branch: After committing on dan-b1, the branch moves forward while main and origin/main remain where they were.

section: 8. Switching between branches and seeing the repository state (8.1.1 Switching to branches that already exist)
text:
8. Switching between branches and seeing the repository state (8.1.1 Switching to branches that already exist)
00:23:46–00:28:26

Editor Git view: In VS Code or Positron, the Git graph shows local main, origin/main, and branch-specific commits; this graph corresponds to the terminal log.
Switch back to main: git switch main moves HEAD back to main, and the working files return to the state stored at main.
Seeing all branches: If branch names do not appear in git log --oneline --graph --decorate, use the --all flag.
switch vs switch -c: git switch <branch> switches to an existing branch; git switch -c <branch> creates and switches to a new branch.
Older checkout command: git checkout is the older equivalent. git checkout -b <branch> created a branch; git branch <branch> creates a branch without moving to it. Daniel Chen uses switch in teaching and suggests that, if you are unsure about checkout, ask tools to use switch instead.

text:
9. Pushing a branch to origin and viewing it on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Remote review process: Instead of merging locally, the class workflow is to push the branch and use a GitHub review process.
Check the current branch: Before pushing, confirm which branch you are on; a plain git push while on main may simply report that everything is up to date.
Push the branch: From dan-b1, the command is git push origin dan-b1; this is the same push behavior as before, but the final branch name changes from main to the branch being pushed.
Remote branch appears: After the push, git log --all shows origin/dan-b1, meaning the local computer now knows that GitHub has that branch.
GitHub branch dropdown: On the GitHub repository page, the branch selector can be used to view another branch without merging it into main.
Pre-merge inspection: Teammates can inspect pushed branch code on GitHub even before a pull request is merged.

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 10. Opening a pull request and reviewing the changed files (9.1 Creating a pull request)
text:
10. Opening a pull request and reviewing the changed files (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:39:56

Compare and pull request: When GitHub recognizes a newly pushed branch, it often shows a “Compare and Pull Request” button or popup.
If the popup disappears: Daniel Chen said the popup can disappear after a day or so; to start the same process later, go to the branches tab, find the branch, and choose the option to create a new pull request.
Open the pull request early: He recommended opening the pull request right away, even while work is in progress, so the process exists and updates as commits are pushed.
Check the base branch: In DSCI 522, the target is usually main, but in 524 the target may not always be main; forks and large open-source projects also require checking that the pull request goes to the right repository and branch.
Title and description: The first pull-request comment should explain the whole set of changes; later edits should update that first comment rather than just appending new notes.
Review the Files Changed tab: Confirm that all intended files are present and that no unwanted files are included.


[!WARNING]
Check the pull request’s changed files for things that do not belong in the repository, such as .ipynb_checkpoints, .DS_Store, Word backup files, or other hidden/temporary files. Daniel Chen said that, in this course, visible unwanted files in a repository can cost points.

The demo pull request created from branch dan-b1 was #1 Learning about branches and PRs.

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 11. Pull request conversation, code review, and updating the same branch (10 Code review on GitHub)
text:
11. Pull request conversation, code review, and updating the same branch (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:39:56–00:45:41

Pull requests tab: Once created, the pull request appears under the repository’s Pull Requests tab and can be revisited later.
Conversation tab: The conversation area is where people discuss the pull request; the original post can be edited, and Daniel Chen recommended keeping the first comment as the definitive explanation.
Files Changed tab: This is where code review happens: GitHub shows the diff between the original file and the proposed new file.
Inline comments: Hovering over diff lines gives a plus button that allows line-specific review comments, which are tracked in the conversation.
Author fixes the code: If it is your pull request, it is your job to fix the issues; reviewers point out problems, but the author updates the codebase.
Push to the same branch: To address review comments, go back to the branch, make the change, commit, and push to the same branch; the pull request updates automatically, though the page may need refreshing.
Outdated comments: If you edit a line that has a comment, GitHub may collapse the comment as outdated.

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 12. Draft pull requests, merging, and deleting the remote branch (9.2 Draft pull requests)
text:
12. Draft pull requests, merging, and deleting the remote branch (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:58:51

Draft workflow: For work that may take more than a day, open the pull request early and then use “Convert to Draft” to signal that it is not ready for merge.
Visual cue: A draft pull request shows a gray bar instead of a green one, and the merge button is disabled so nobody accidentally merges it.
Ready for review: When the work is ready, use “Ready for review” to turn the draft back into an open pull request.
AI review: Daniel Chen mentioned that you can request AI/Copilot review, but AI comments are not automatically mandatory; a person still reviews and decides whether to accept or reject them.
Merging: After merging, the pull request counter decreases because the pull request is closed.
Remote branch cleanup: He recommended deleting the remote branch after merging so the branch dropdown does not become a long list of finished branches.
Commits remain: Deleting the branch does not delete the commits; they remain in history, including the separate merge commit created by the pull-request merge.
crumbs: Nov 17 · Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 13. Local cleanup after a merge: git pull, git branch -a, git fetch --prune, and git branch -d (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
text:
13. Local cleanup after a merge: git pull, git branch -a, git fetch --prune, and git branch -d (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:58:53–01:03:51

Group-project warning: Even when teams use branches, merge conflicts can still happen because agents or teammates may edit the same line, file, or typo.
Individual assignment 1: Daniel Chen noted that individual assignment 1 has students review merge conflicts again, because they still need to know how to recover from them.
Local main is not automatic: After a branch is merged on GitHub, local main does not update by itself; run git switch main and then git pull origin main.
List branches: git branch -a shows local branches and remote-tracking branches; the current branch has a star.
git fetch --prune: This fetches remote state and removes local references to branches that were deleted on GitHub, such as origin/dan-b1.
Safe local branch deletion: git branch -d dan-b1 deletes a local branch only if it has been merged; lowercase -d protects you from deleting unmerged work.
Force local branch deletion: git branch -D <branch> force-deletes a local branch even if it has not been merged.


[!WARNING]
Use lowercase git branch -d <branch> for normal cleanup. A capital -D can permanently delete unmerged work. Daniel Chen specifically warned that copied-and-pasted AI advice might say to use -D, and that can delete commits you were still working on.
crumbs: Nov 17 · Git Branches, Pull Requests, Code Review and Rebasing to Fix Conflicts

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 14. Creating a merge-conflict scenario with two branches (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
text:
14. Creating a merge-conflict scenario with two branches (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:03:51–01:10:51

Two competing branches: Daniel Chen created two branches from the same main state: dan-fetch and dan-delete.
Conflicting edits: Both branches made changes to the same region of README.md, so they would conflict if both were merged.
Two pull requests: The two branches produced two open pull requests: #2 define fetch –prune from dan-fetch and #3 branch -d and -D from dan-delete.
First merge changes main: When one pull request is merged, main moves forward.
Other pull requests are rechecked: GitHub rechecks open pull requests against the new main; a pull request that looked mergeable before can become conflicted afterward.
Conflict is not always obvious side by side: Looking at the two pull requests separately did not clearly show that they would conflict; the conflict appears after one branch is merged.

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts
section: 15. Resolving the conflict locally with git rebase main and git push --force-with-lease (8.3.2 Using rebase)
text:
15. Resolving the conflict locally with git rebase main and git push --force-with-lease (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:10:51–01:20:42

Local versus web resolution: Simple conflicts can be resolved in GitHub’s web editor, but Daniel Chen showed local resolution because the command-line process is more general.
What “fix the conflict” means: Fixing the conflict markers is not enough. In this course, “fixed” means the resulting report or code works from top to bottom again.
Sync main first: Switch to main and run git pull origin main so the local main includes the already-merged pull request.
Rebase the conflicting branch: Switch to dan-delete and run git rebase main; this replays the branch’s commit on top of the updated main.
Resolve and continue: When Git stops with a conflict, edit the file, run git add README.md, check git status, and then run git rebase --continue.
Force-with-lease push: Because rebase rewrites the commit history of a branch that was already pushed, a normal push is no longer enough; the session used git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete.
Merge and cleanup: After the force push, the pull request could be merged, and the usual branch cleanup could be done.




Several branches, pull requests, a conflict, and a rebase



[!WARNING]
Resolving the visible conflict markers does not mean the work is done. Daniel Chen stressed that, if changing the conflict affects later code, the student is still responsible for making the whole thing work. Also, after rebase has changed pushed history, use git push --force-with-lease origin <branch>, not a plain push.

title: Git branches, pull requests and rebasing to fix conflicts: review questions, tier 1 — Remember
text:
Date: 2026-11-17
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 1 of 5: Remember. Answer each question before you read its answer; tiers 2 to 5 build on these.

1. Course logistics: lab groups, attendance and interview week
00:00:01–00:04:04

Q: Where do you look up your DSCI 522 group, and which column tells you who is in it?

A: In the lab sections repository on UBC’s GitHub. Find your lab section, then the group number column: everyone with the same number is your group. (00:01:24)

Q: State what the GitHub usernames collected from students are used to build.

A: A main list of every student’s GitHub username, a piece of metadata used everywhere else in the program. (00:02:01)

Q: State the rule for attending lab this year, and what the TAs do during lab.

A: Lab attendance is mandatory, because this is a group project. The TAs go around and talk to every group, and you should be there when a TA comes to yours. (00:02:19)

Q: How long is the interview week conversation, and what is it modelled on?

A: About seven minutes, run like a technical interview. (00:02:50)

Q: Name the two things the interview week conversation covers.

A: How much you know about what you are doing with Git, and your group’s actual code base. Anything in your code base is fair game, “especially in the world of AI”. (00:03:15)

Q: Does the interview week conversation affect your grade?

A: No. You get a grade, but it does not affect your course grade. (00:03:02)

Q: What happens if the TAs don’t reach everyone in their scheduled interview week?

A: It moves by plus or minus a week. You might be called and you might not, and some students need the full seven minutes while others don’t. (00:03:29)

Q: What did the instructor say this interview format might become next year?

A: It “might actually be the exam next year.” (00:03:48)




2. Git recap: setting up the demo repository
00:04:07–00:06:49

Q: Name the demo repository created and cloned in class.

A: chendaniely/2026-11-17-git, named for the day. It was cloned with git clone git@github.com:chendaniely/2026-11-17-git.git. (00:05:18)

Q: What did the instructor initialise the demo repository 2026-11-17-git with, instead of leaving it empty?

A: A README. He noted you could also add a Python option and a license if you want. (00:05:06)

Q: What change did the instructor make to README.md in 2026-11-17-git before the first commit?

A: He added a line saying the class will review 521 Git basics and then go into branches, plus a link to the textbook’s Git branches chapter. (00:05:57)

Q: What did git status report after the first edit to README.md in 2026-11-17-git?

A: That README.md was modified, with Changes not staged for commit. (00:06:13)

Q: What was the commit message of the first commit in the demo repository 2026-11-17-git?

A: intro and review. (00:06:32)




3. Why branches: escaping the 521 push/pull friction (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: Which DSCI 521 exercise, and in which week, did the instructor recall to illustrate push/pull friction?

A: The shared slide deck exercise in week 3 of 521. (00:06:54)

Q: State the annoyance from the 521 slide-deck exercise that happened even when there was no conflict.

A: You couldn’t push because someone else had pushed first, so you had to pull before you could push again. (00:07:06)

Q: What kind of work did the instructor say you want to reach in a group project, once the basics are in place?

A: Parallel streams: a part of the project that is just your responsibility, worked on in your own branch. (00:08:41)

Q: Recall the example schedule the instructor gave for working on branches and then reviewing.

A: You work on your own part from Tuesday to Friday, and on Friday the group reviews and coordinates all the work. (00:08:46)




4. Review: the local–remote picture
00:09:46–00:11:47

Q: Name the two places where you do work in Git.

A: Your computer (local) and the cloud (the GitHub remote). (00:10:09)

Q: Which copy of the project did the instructor say is the one that matters, the one graded and published?

A: The copy on GitHub, the remote. Work that exists only on your local computer “effectively doesn’t really exist” for grading or project purposes. (00:10:53)

Q: How often do you run git clone on a repository?

A: Once: clone is a one-time command. (00:11:25)

Q: Name the command that sends commits to GitHub and the one that brings down commits your teammates pushed.

A: push sends code up; pull brings other people’s commits down. (00:11:33)




5. What a branch is: main, HEAD and origin/main (8 Git branches)
00:12:03–00:17:54

Q: What is the main branch?

A: The default branch that you are working on. (00:12:38)

Q: What happens to main each time you commit while HEAD is attached to it?

A: It increments: it moves forward with each commit. (00:13:17)

Q: What does origin/main represent in the Git log?

A: What your computer thinks the state of main on GitHub (the remote) is. (00:13:30)

Q: Define a branch, as the instructor put it.

A: A name you give yourself that your commits move forward instead of main. You use the same git add and git commit process as before. (00:14:06)

Q: What was the branch called in the instructor’s hand-drawn diagram?

A: B1 (labelled b1 in the drawing). (00:14:06)

Q: What did the instructor say you can think of the main branch as?

A: The production, final, stable version, where everything should be in working order, or at least the code works. (00:15:10)

Q: Recall the example the instructor gave of using branches while working alone.

A: He did all his edits to the course textbook in a sequence of branches, so the textbook wouldn’t move around in the middle of a teaching day. He merged them after lectures were over and he had reviewed and tested everything. (00:16:37)

Q: Which two 521 commands did the instructor name as another way to undo work, besides branches?

A: git reset and git revert. (00:17:22)




6. Creating and switching branches (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:26:29

Q: Which command did the instructor run first to confirm he was on main before creating a branch?

A: git status, which showed On branch main. (00:18:03)

Q: Which command did the instructor run to sync up before branching, when the work builds on coordinated work?

A: git pull origin main. (00:18:39)

Q: What does git switch do?

A: It moves HEAD around the Git repository, switching between branches. (00:19:46)

Q: What does the -c in git switch -c stand for?

A: Create. (00:20:09)

Q: Reproduce the command the instructor used to create the first branch in the demo repository.

A: git switch -c dan-b1. (00:21:31)

Q: What does the instructor start his branch names with in shared repositories?

A: His own name, so others know whom to talk to if something looks weird. (00:20:31)

Q: What changed in the git status output right after git switch -c dan-b1?

A: Only the branch line: it said On branch dan-b1 instead of On branch main. (00:21:03)

Q: Quote the definition of switch -c that the instructor added to README.md on dan-b1.

A: `switch -c <name>`: create and move HEAD to the branch <name>. (00:21:56)

Q: What was the commit message for the first commit on dan-b1, as typed?

A: define swtich -c, with “switch” misspelled. (00:22:31)

Q: Where in VS Code or Positron can you see the same branch picture as the terminal log?

A: In the graph view of the Git tab. (00:24:09)

Q: Which command moved HEAD from dan-b1 back to main?

A: git switch main. (00:25:12)

Q: Which flag must you add to git log --oneline to see your other branch names?

A: --all, as in git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all. (00:25:38)




7. git checkout and git branch versus git switch (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:26:40–00:28:26

Q: Will students be tested on using git checkout rather than git switch?

A: No. The instructor said checkout is fine and he is not going to test you on it. (00:26:42)

Q: Name the older command that did what git switch does, and roughly when the change happened.

A: git checkout; switch came in around 2019. (00:26:59)

Q: Which command does the instructor use day to day, and when does he use switch?

A: He uses git checkout, and only uses switch when teaching. (00:26:59)

Q: Besides moving HEAD, what else did git checkout do that newer commands were split out from?

A: Much of what revert and restore do. Those behaviours still exist in checkout. (00:27:09)

Q: What did the instructor say to do if Copilot or ChatGPT tells you to run checkout and you don’t know what the command does?

A: Prompt it to do the same thing with switch instead. (00:27:44)

Q: State the checkout equivalent of git switch -c <name>.

A: git checkout -b <name>. (00:28:10)

Q: What does git branch <name> do, and what does it not do?

A: It creates the branch but does not move you to it, so you still have to checkout or switch afterwards. (00:28:13)




8. Pushing a branch and viewing it on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: Name the two terms for the review process used to get a branch into main.

A: A pull request, also called a merge request. (00:28:58)

Q: What did a bare git push print when run on main while the new commit was on dan-b1?

A: Everything up-to-date. It did not push dan-b1. (00:29:34)

Q: Reproduce the command the instructor used to send the dan-b1 branch to GitHub.

A: git push origin dan-b1, run while on dan-b1. (00:30:36)

Q: What did the output of the first git push origin dan-b1 print, besides the transfer details?

A: A link to create a pull request for dan-b1: https://github.com/chendaniely/2026-11-17-git/pull/new/dan-b1, and * [new branch] dan-b1 -> dan-b1. (00:30:36)

Q: After pushing dan-b1, which new reference appeared in the Git log, and which one did not move?

A: origin/dan-b1 appeared next to dan-b1, while origin/main and main stayed where they were. (00:31:19)

Q: Where on a GitHub repository page do you switch to view another branch, such as dan-b1?

A: The dropdown in the top left-hand corner that says main. (00:32:21)

Q: Where on GitHub can you see the list of all a repository’s branches?

A: The branch button next to the branch dropdown. (00:33:16)




9. Opening a pull request (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:41:16

Q: What does the button GitHub shows after you push a branch say?

A: “Compare and Pull Request” (Compare & pull request). (00:34:25)

Q: How long did the instructor say the “Compare & pull request” pop-up lasts, and how do you reach the same page once it’s gone?

A: About a day. Go to the branches tab, find your branch, open its expansion menu and choose “New pull request”. (00:35:00)

Q: In which later course did the instructor say the merge target will not always be main?

A: DSCI 524. (00:36:14)

Q: What title did the instructor give pull request #1 in 2026-11-17-git?

A: “Learning about branches and PRs”. (00:37:15)

Q: What description did the instructor write for pull request #1?

A: “We are learning about Git switch and creating PRs.” (00:37:21)

Q: Name the junk files the instructor listed as ones that should not appear in a pull request’s changed files.

A: .ipynb_checkpoints from Jupyter, .DS_Store on a Mac, and hidden backup files from Microsoft Word. Your .gitignore is still really important. (00:39:23)

Q: What did the instructor warn happens if files that don’t belong appear in your repository?

A: Points are taken off, even if the instructions don’t explicitly say so. (00:38:44)

Q: What did the instructor call reviewing the changed-files list on GitHub, after reviewing on your own computer?

A: The second line of defence. (00:39:42)

Q: Which green button finally creates the pull request?

A: “Create Pull Request”. (00:39:56)

Q: Where can you find a pull request again after leaving its page?

A: The Pull Request tab at the top of the repository. (00:40:15)

Q: Which comment on a pull request should you edit as the work grows, rather than adding new comments?

A: The very first comment, because that is what people read. (00:40:55)




10. Code review and updating a pull request (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:41:16–00:45:41

Q: Name the pull request tab where code review happens.

A: Files Changed. (00:41:16)

Q: What does the Files Changed tab show you?

A: The diff between the original file and the new file. (00:41:22)

Q: How do you leave a comment on a specific line in the Files Changed tab?

A: Hover over the line and click the little plus button. (00:41:34)

Q: Recall the example review comment the instructor left on pull request #1.

A: Asking why switch is used and not checkout. (00:41:34)

Q: Whose job is it to fix the code in a pull request after review?

A: The author’s: the reviewer says what to rewrite, and it is your job, as the person who opened the pull request, to fix it. (00:42:17)

Q: How do you update an open pull request with new changes?

A: Go back to the same branch on your computer, then add, commit and push. You don’t close the pull request and create a new one. (00:43:15)

Q: Which command did the instructor add to README.md on dan-b1 to update pull request #1?

A: git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all. (00:43:36)

Q: What was the commit message of the second commit on dan-b1?

A: show you the long git log command. (00:44:12)

Q: What does GitHub do to a review comment on a line you later change?

A: It may auto-collapse it and mark it as outdated. (00:45:02)




11. AI reviewers and draft pull requests (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:55:41

Q: Name the AI tool GitHub lets you request a review from.

A: Copilot. (00:52:30)

Q: List the three things you can do with an LLM reviewer’s comment.

A: Push back on it, reject it, or accept it. You don’t have to keep every comment. (00:53:01)

Q: Which button turns an open pull request into a draft, and where is it?

A: “Convert to Draft”, in the top right corner. (00:53:52)

Q: What colour bar does a draft pull request show instead of green?

A: Gray. (00:54:04)

Q: What happens to the merge button on a draft pull request?

A: It is grayed out, so no one can accidentally merge it. (00:54:30)

Q: How long has the instructor kept draft pull requests open?

A: Three or four months. (00:55:00)

Q: What did the instructor believe a draft pull request also stops an AI agent from doing?

A: Merging everything that’s green. (00:55:03)

Q: Which button turns a draft back into an open pull request, and where is it?

A: “Ready for review”, at the bottom of the pull request where it says it is a work in progress. (00:55:28)

title: Git branches, pull requests, and conflict resolution: review questions, tier 2 — Understand
text:
Date: 2026-11-17

Generated by qwen3.6-35b-a3b, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 2 of 5: Understand. Explain each answer in your own words before you read it; tier 1 (Remember) covers the facts, tiers 3 to 5 put them to use.

1. The problem with parallel work on main (8 Git branches)
00:04:04–00:09:43

Q: Why does the instructor recommend creating branches instead of having all group members push directly to main at the same time?

A: Pushing directly to main causes constant pull-before-push friction and merge conflicts when multiple people work simultaneously. Branches isolate each person’s work into parallel streams, allowing individuals to commit and push without interfering with teammates until the work is ready for review and merging. (00:08:07)

Q: What is the difference between the main branch and a feature branch in terms of the code they contain?

A: The main branch is treated as the stable, working production state where everything should be finished and functional. Feature branches are used for exploratory work, testing, or developing new features that are not yet ready to be combined with the stable codebase. (00:15:10)

Q: Why does the instructor advise syncing your local repository with git pull origin main before creating a new branch?

A: Syncing ensures your local repository is up to date with what your teammates have already pushed. Starting a branch from an outdated local state means you might redo work that was already completed elsewhere, wasting time and creating unnecessary coordination overhead. (00:18:09)




2. Creating and managing branches locally (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:09:43–00:25:12

Q: How does the git switch -c command change the state of the Git repository compared to the standard commit workflow?

A: The -c flag creates a new branch and immediately moves the HEAD pointer to it, so all subsequent commits increment that new branch name instead of main. This keeps the main branch stationary while your experimental work develops independently in its own timeline. (00:20:18)

Q: What is the purpose of the git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all command during branch development?

A: This command visualizes the commit history and clearly shows where the HEAD pointer is attached to a specific branch. It helps you see that while your new branch advances with each commit, the origin/main reference remains static until you sync or push. (00:21:15)

Q: Why does the instructor prefer using git switch over the older git checkout command for branch management?

A: git checkout historically performed multiple functions, including branch switching, file restoration, and commit history modification. git switch was introduced to specialize specifically in moving the HEAD pointer, making it safer to use and reducing the risk of accidentally overwriting local work. (00:26:59)




3. Pushing branches and initiating Pull Requests (9 Pull requests)
00:25:12–00:46:00

Q: What is the function of a Draft Pull Request in a collaborative workflow?

A: A Draft Pull Request signals to the team that the work is still in progress and not yet ready for review or merging. It grays out the merge button to prevent accidental integration and allows the author to continue pushing commits and updating the PR before marking it as ready. (00:53:52)

Q: How does the GitHub interface communicate that a Pull Request has been updated after the author pushes new commits?

A: The Pull Request page is tied directly to the branch, so pushing additional commits to the same branch automatically updates the PR’s commit history and file diffs. GitHub refreshes the view to reflect the new state without requiring a new PR to be created. (00:43:56)

Q: What should you look for when reviewing the “Files Changed” tab of a Pull Request?

A: You should verify that all intended code changes are present in the diff and check for stray temporary files like .DS_Store or .ipynb_checkpoints that shouldn’t be in the repository. This second line of defense ensures the .gitignore is working and the PR contains only relevant work. (00:38:26)




4. Merging, cleanup, and local synchronization (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:52:17–01:03:51

Q: Why does the instructor recommend deleting branches on GitHub after they have been merged?

A: Over the lifetime of a project, repositories can accumulate a long list of inactive branches that clutter the interface. Deleting merged branches cleans up the repository, though it does not remove the commits from history since they are now part of main. (00:56:08)

Q: What does the git fetch --prune command accomplish on your local machine?

A: This command synchronizes your local repository with the remote and actively removes local tracking references for branches that were deleted on GitHub. It prevents your local branch list from becoming outdated or cluttered with ghost references. (01:01:30)

Q: Why does the lowercase -d flag in git branch -d refuse to delete a branch that hasn’t been merged, while uppercase -D does not?

A: The lowercase -d flag is a safety mechanism that prevents accidental deletion of unmerged work, which could result in lost commits. The uppercase -D bypasses this check for forced deletion, which carries a high risk of permanently destroying work and should be used very carefully. (01:02:46)




5. Resolving merge conflicts via rebase (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:03:51–01:21:43

Q: Why does a merge conflict typically appear only after the first Pull Request has already been merged into main?

A: When the first PR merges, main advances and incorporates new commits. When the second PR attempts to merge, Git rechecks its diff against the updated main. If both branches edited the same lines independently, Git detects the overlapping changes and flags a conflict to prevent overwriting one team member’s work. (01:10:08)

Q: How does git rebase main change the local commit history to help resolve a conflict?

A: The command replays your branch’s commits sequentially on top of the updated main branch locally. This triggers the conflict resolution process on your machine before you push, allowing you to edit the conflict markers and fix the code in a controlled environment. (01:14:16)

Q: Why is git push --force-with-lease required after resolving a merge conflict via rebase?

A: Rebasing rewrites the commit history of the branch, changing its SHA hashes. A standard push will be rejected because the remote history no longer matches your local history. Force-pushing updates the remote branch to match your rewritten history, and the --lease flag adds a safety check to prevent overwriting teammates’ new commits. (01:19:34)

title: Git branches, pull requests and rebasing to fix conflicts: review questions, tier 3 — Apply
text:
Date: 2026-11-17
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 3 of 5: Apply. Work each situation through before you read the answer; tiers 1 (Remember) and 2 (Understand) cover the facts and reasons it relies on.

1. Git recap: setting up the demo repository
00:04:07–00:06:49

Q: You have just cloned 2026-11-17-git and edited README.md on main. In order, what do you run to check the change, record it and send it to GitHub?

A: Run git status to confirm README.md is modified and git diff to read the change. Then run git add README.md, git commit -m "intro and review" and git push origin main. This is the same add–commit–push cycle from DSCI 521. (00:06:32)

Q: You want to see exactly which lines of README.md you changed before you stage it. Which command do you run, and what will it show?

A: Run git diff. It shows the old lines prefixed with - and the new lines prefixed with +, for example the added line linking the Git branches chapter. Run it before git add, while the change is still unstaged. (00:06:13)

Q: You have just run git push origin main after committing “intro and review”. Predict where HEAD, main and origin/main sit in git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all.

A: All three sit on the same commit: 145ff16 (HEAD -> main, origin/main, origin/HEAD) intro and review. You committed on main and then pushed, so your computer’s record of GitHub’s main caught up with your local main. (00:06:38)




2. Why branches: escaping the 521 push/pull friction (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: You and a teammate both commit to main on the group project. You try to push and are refused, even though you edited different files. What happened, and how do you avoid this happening all week?

A: Your teammate pushed first, so you have to pull before you can push again, even without a conflict. To avoid this, each person works on their own branch. You can then push and pull your branch freely without depending on what others are doing. (00:07:06)

Q: Your group is in the first week of the project, and nothing exists yet except the plan. Can all four of you start separate branches of independent work straight away?

A: Usually not. Early in a project, everyone is blocked on one or two people getting the basics in place, so some of the old push/pull friction is unavoidable. Move to parallel branches once each person owns a self-contained part. (00:07:50)

Q: You own a self-contained part of the project and plan to work on it from Tuesday to Friday. How do you work during the week, and when does your work meet your teammates’ work?

A: Work on your own branch, pushing as often as you like without caring what others are doing. On Friday the group reviews everyone’s branches and merges the work together. (00:09:19)




3. Review: the local–remote picture
00:09:46–00:11:47

Q: Your analysis is committed on your laptop, but you never pushed it before the milestone deadline. Will it be graded?

A: No. GitHub is what gets graded and published. Work that exists only on your computer “effectively doesn’t really exist” for grading or project purposes, so you must push it. (00:10:53)

Q: You already cloned the group repository last week. Today a teammate pushes a new commit. Do you run git clone again to get it?

A: No. clone is a one-time command. To bring down commits your teammates pushed, run pull. (00:11:47)

Q: You and three teammates each have the project on your own laptop. Choose the place everyone’s work must end up in, and the command that sends your commits there.

A: The GitHub remote is the place that matters; every teammate’s computer coordinates with it. You send your commits there with push, and teammates’ commits come down with pull. (00:11:33)




4. What a branch is: main, HEAD and origin/main (8 Git branches)
00:12:03–00:17:54

Q: You make two commits on main and do not push. Predict where main and origin/main sit in git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all.

A: main (with HEAD attached) is two commits ahead of origin/main. origin/main is only what your computer thinks GitHub’s main is, and it does not move until you sync with GitHub. (00:13:44)

Q: You are on a branch named b1 and run git add and git commit. Which branch name moves forward, and which stays where it was?

A: b1 moves forward to the new commit, and main stays put. The git add/git commit workflow is unchanged; the only difference is that your commits drag along your branch name instead of main. (00:14:25)

Q: You are doing exploratory data analysis for the group project, and your plots are still rough. The cleaned dataset is finished. What goes on main, and where does the EDA live?

A: main holds the cleaned dataset, which everyone builds on. Treat main as the stable version, where at least the code works. Your EDA stays on your own branch until it is ready to be reviewed and merged. (00:15:49)

Q: You spend an afternoon on a branch trying a new approach, and none of it works. How do you get back to your starting point?

A: Switch back to main and either delete the branch or start a new one. This is much easier than untangling a single commit that did twenty things on main. git reset/git revert would also work, but branches make it simpler. (00:17:22)

Q: You are the only person working in a repository, but others read it while you edit, as with a textbook being taught from that day. Should you still use branches?

A: Yes. Make your edits on branches so the published version does not shift around mid-use. Merge only after you have reviewed and tested everything. Branches section off work even when you work alone. (00:16:51)




5. Creating and switching branches (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:26:29

Q: You are about to start a new task in your group project that builds on what your teammates have pushed. In order, what do you run before your first commit?

A: Run git status to confirm you are On branch main. Run git pull origin main to sync with everything your team has pushed. Then run git switch -c <name> to create your branch and move to it. Skipping the pull can mean you redo work that already exists elsewhere. (00:18:39)

Q: On main at commit 145ff16, you run git switch -c dan-b1 and nothing else. Predict the output of git status and of git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all.

A: git status says On branch dan-b1 with a clean working tree. The log shows 145ff16 (HEAD -> dan-b1, origin/main, origin/HEAD, main). No new commit is made: you only created a branch and attached HEAD to it. (00:21:15)

Q: On dan-b1 you commit a new README line (“define swtich -c”). Predict where dan-b1, main and origin/main sit in the log.

A: dan-b1 (with HEAD) is on the new commit 4a14a64, one commit ahead. main and origin/main both stay on 145ff16. You have not pushed, so GitHub knows nothing about the branch yet. (00:23:21)

Q: You committed a new line to README.md on dan-b1, then ran git switch main. You open README.md. Is the new line there, and where did dan-b1 go?

A: The line is gone, because the files on disk now show main’s version. dan-b1 has not moved. Switch back with git switch dan-b1 and the line returns. (00:25:46)

Q: You run git log --oneline --graph --decorate, but your other branches do not appear. What do you add?

A: Add the --all flag: git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all. Without it, you may not see the other branch names. (00:25:38)

Q: You are creating a branch in a shared group repository. How can you name it so teammates know whom to ask if something on it looks odd?

A: Start the branch name with your own name, as in dan-b1. Teammates then know who is responsible for that work. (00:20:31)




6. git checkout and git branch versus git switch (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:26:40–00:28:26

Q: ChatGPT tells you to run git checkout -b my-feature. What is the git switch command that does the same thing?

A: git switch -c my-feature. Both create the branch and move HEAD to it; checkout -b is the older form. (00:28:10)

Q: You run git branch my-idea and then immediately commit a change. Which branch does the commit land on?

A: It lands on the branch you were already on, not my-idea. git branch only creates the branch and does not move you to it. You still need git switch my-idea (or checkout) before committing. (00:28:13)

Q: An AI assistant hands you a git checkout command you don’t fully understand, in a codebase where you are worried about losing work. What do you do?

A: Don’t run it blindly; ask for the switch version instead. checkout does more than move HEAD: it also does much of what restore and revert do. You should know what a command will do before running it on work you care about. (00:27:44)




7. Pushing a branch and viewing it on GitHub (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: Your new commit is on dan-b1, but you are on main. You run git push, and it prints Everything up-to-date, but the commit isn’t on GitHub. What went wrong, and what fixes it?

A: The bare git push from main had nothing new to send, because the commit is on dan-b1. Run git switch dan-b1, then git push origin dan-b1. The last word of the push names the branch you are pushing, not main. (00:30:36)

Q: You have just run git push origin dan-b1 for the first time. Predict what changes in git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all.

A: origin/dan-b1 now appears on the same commit as dan-b1. origin/main has not moved, because you pushed the branch, not main. (00:31:27)

Q: You pushed dan-b1 and refresh the repository’s main page on GitHub, but your change isn’t in the README. Where do you look to confirm it reached GitHub?

A: Use the branch dropdown at the top left, which says main, and choose dan-b1. The main page only shows main’s content until the branch is merged. The branch button next to the dropdown lists all branches. (00:32:29)

Q: A teammate made a figure you want to learn from, but their work is not merged and you don’t want to run it. How do you read their code?

A: Ask them to push their branch. Then pick that branch in the branch dropdown on GitHub and browse its files, even though it isn’t in main yet. (00:32:36)

Q: Your work on dan-b1 is finished, and you want it in main. Choose between merging it locally and another route.

A: Push the branch and merge it through a pull request on GitHub rather than on your computer. The review process happens there. (00:28:58)




8. Opening a pull request (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:41:16

Q: You pushed a branch two days ago, and the “Compare & pull request” pop-up on GitHub is gone. How do you open the pull request now?

A: Go to the Branches tab, find your branch, open its expansion menu and choose “New pull request”. You land on the same page the pop-up would have taken you to. (00:35:00)

Q: You are starting a task that will take a few days. When do you open its pull request so you don’t lose the easy route to it?

A: Open it right away. Make a small change, push the branch and start the pull request even though the work isn’t done. Then keep pushing to the branch, and the pull request updates as you go. (00:35:15)

Q: On the “Open a pull request” page, what do you check in the line at the top before writing anything?

A: Check that it shows the branch you are working on and the branch you are merging into, which is main in this course. In other settings the target isn’t always main, and with forks you must make sure the code is going to the right repository. (00:36:55)

Q: Scrolling the changed files at the bottom of your new pull request, you see .ipynb_checkpoints and a .DS_Store. What do you do before creating it?

A: Remove them and add them to your .gitignore. Files that don’t belong in the repository lose points even if the instructions don’t explicitly mention them. This file list is your second line of defence for catching them. (00:39:23)

Q: A script you know you wrote is missing from your pull request’s list of changed files. What probably went wrong?

A: You probably forgot to add, commit or push it, or you typed something wrong. Run git add, git commit and git push origin <branch> from the same branch, and the file will appear. (00:39:37)

Q: Your pull request has grown to cover more work than its original description. How do you update what reviewers read?

A: Edit the first comment (the description) so it explains all the changes. Don’t keep adding “now I’m also doing…” comments. People read the first comment. (00:41:03)




9. Code review and updating a pull request (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:41:16–00:45:41

Q: You are reviewing a teammate’s pull request and want to ask why a particular line uses switch and not checkout. Where do you leave the comment?

A: Open the Files changed tab, hover over that line in the diff, click the + and write the comment. It is also tracked in the main Conversation tab. (00:41:34)

Q: You review a teammate’s pull request and find a line that looks wrong. Do you fix it yourself?

A: No. As the reviewer, your job is to point it out (“rewrite this”, “this doesn’t look right”). The author of the pull request is responsible for fixing it. (00:42:17)

Q: A reviewer asks you to change your open pull request from dan-b1. Do you close it and open a new one? What do you run?

A: Don’t close it. Go back to the same branch locally (git switch dan-b1), make the change, then run git add README.md, git commit -m "..." and git push origin dan-b1. The pull request is tied to the branch, so it updates with the new commit. (00:43:15)

Q: You pushed a new commit to your pull request’s branch, but the commit doesn’t show on the pull request page yet. What do you try first?

A: Refresh the page. The pull request tracks every commit you push to the branch, but sometimes you need a refresh to see it. (00:45:00)

Q: You change a line that a reviewer had commented on, then push. Predict what happens to their comment.

A: It doesn’t disappear, but GitHub may collapse it and mark it as outdated, because the line it refers to has changed. (00:45:02)




10. AI reviewers and draft pull requests (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:55:41

Q: You request a Copilot review on your pull request, and it leaves several comments. Must you act on all of them?

A: No. You can accept some, push back on others or reject them. More eyes on your work is never really a bad idea, but an LLM’s comments are not orders. (00:53:01)

Q: You opened a pull request early and will keep pushing to it for several days. A teammate, or an agent, might merge it because everything looks green. What do you do?

A: Click “Convert to draft” at the top right. The pull request shows a grey bar instead of green, and the merge button is greyed out, so nobody can merge it by accident. Agents are also less likely to merge it just because it is green. (00:54:30)

Q: Your draft pull request is now finished. How do you make it mergeable again?

A: Scroll to the bottom, where it says the pull request is still a work in progress, and click “Ready for review”. It becomes an open pull request with green merge buttons again. (00:55:28)




11. Merging and deleting the branch on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:55:41–00:59:07

Q: Your pull request from dan-b1 has just been merged. What do you do on GitHub so the branch dropdown doesn’t turn into a giant list over the project?

A: Click “Delete branch” on the merged pull request. The branch count drops (from two to one in the demo), and only live branches stay in the list. (00:57:42)

Q: You hesitate to delete dan-b1 on GitHub because you fear losing its commits. Predict what main’s commit history shows afterwards.

A: The branch’s two commits are still there, plus a merge commit, “Merge pull request #1 from chendaniely/dan-b1”. Deleting the branch only removes the label, not the work. (00:58:19)

Q: A merged feature later turns out to be a mistake, and its branch was deleted long ago. Where do you go to undo it?

A: Look in main’s history for the commits related to that pull request and its merge commit, and undo from there. Nothing is really lost in this workflow. (00:58:38)

Q: Your workplace has legal or compliance rules about keeping records. Do you still delete merged branches?

A: No. If compliance requires it, don’t delete them, even though the branch list gets long. Otherwise follow your team’s workflow, and at least clean up your own branches. (00:57:00)




12. Syncing and cleaning up locally after a merge (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:59:07–01:03:51

Q: Your pull request was merged on GitHub. You run git switch main locally, but README.md doesn’t have the merged lines. What do you run?

A: Run git pull origin main. Local main doesn’t update itself. The pull brings the merge down (in the demo it fast-forwarded and added 6 lines to README.md). (01:00:27)

Q: You deleted dan-b1 on GitHub, but git branch -a still lists remotes/origin/dan-b1. What removes it?

A: Run git fetch --prune. It syncs history with origin and removes local references to branches that were deleted on GitHub. The output shows [deleted] (none) -> origin/dan-b1. (01:01:30)

Q: You want to bring your local record of GitHub’s history up to date without any of your working files changing. Choose between git pull and git fetch.

A: Use git fetch. git pull runs a fetch and then a merge, which changes your files. fetch alone only coordinates the history. (01:02:07)

Q: You run git branch -d my-experiment on an experiment branch that was never merged, and Git refuses. What is going on, and what is the risky alternative?

A: Lowercase -d only deletes merged branches, so Git is protecting work you would otherwise lose. Capital git branch -D force-deletes it anyway. It is a one-character difference, so be very careful when an AI hands you -D: you could delete commits you are still working on. (01:03:21)

Q: Your pull request from dan-b1 has been merged and the branch deleted on GitHub. In order, what do you run locally to finish cleaning up?

A: Run git switch main, then git pull origin main, then git fetch --prune, then git branch -d dan-b1. Pulling first makes dan-b1 count as merged, so the lowercase -d succeeds. (01:03:21)




13. Setting up two conflicting pull requests (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:04:00–01:10:00

Q: You want to practise a merge conflict on your own in your demo repository. How do you set it up?

A: Create two branches from main (such as dan-fetch and dan-delete) that each change the same line of the same file. Push both and open two pull requests. Don’t merge the first one straight away: a conflict comes from the same change to the same line of the same file. (01:06:07)

Q: You run git pull main to sync before branching, and get fatal: 'main' does not appear to be a git repository. What fixes it?

A: Run git pull origin main. The first argument has to be the remote (origin) and the second the branch. Git read main as the name of a repository. (01:04:28)

Q: You commit a “fetch –prune” line on dan-fetch, then run git switch main and git switch -c dan-delete. Is the fetch line in README.md?

A: No. dan-delete was created from main, which doesn’t contain the dan-fetch commit, so that line isn’t in this version of the file. (01:07:20)

Q: You type git switch -b dan-delete and get error: unknown switch `b'. What do you run instead?

A: Run git switch -c dan-delete. The -b flag belongs to git checkout -b; switch uses -c to create a branch. (01:06:43)

Q: Both dan-fetch and dan-delete are pushed, each with its own commit. Predict the shape of git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate.

A: Two lines leave the same main commit (3851b00): one to 157c3cd on dan-fetch and one to cb810d5 on dan-delete. Those are two parallel pieces of work. (01:08:19)

Q: You open both pull requests, #2 and #3, side by side on GitHub. Each says it can be merged into main. Will GitHub warn you that they edit the same line?

A: No. Nothing on either pull request tells you a conflict is coming; each is only checked against the current main. You only find out when one of them is merged. (01:09:53)




14. When a merge creates the conflict: resolving on GitHub (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:10:00–01:12:44

Q: Pull requests #2 and #3 both look green. You merge #2. Predict what happens to #3.

A: Merging #2 changes main, and GitHub rechecks every pull request that merges into main. #3 now shows a merge conflict, because both edited the same line. (01:10:19)

Q: The conflict on your pull request is a small one in README.md. How do you resolve it without leaving GitHub?

A: Open the web editor from the conflict page and find the conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>). Edit the section into its final form and remove the markers. (01:10:59)

Q: You resolve a conflict on line 13 of a script by renaming a variable, and the markers are gone. The old name is still used on line 50. Are you done?

A: No. Fixing a conflict means the code works from top to bottom again, not just that the markers are gone. Update line 50 and run the code; any knock-on breakage from your fix is still your problem. (01:11:39)

Q: The conflict is in your group’s report prose rather than code. What must be true when you have resolved it?

A: The text that remains must be English that makes sense, not just text with the markers deleted. (01:11:09)




15. Resolving the conflict locally with rebase (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:12:44–01:20:42

Q: #2 was merged, and your pull request from dan-delete now conflicts. In order, what do you run to fix it on your own computer with rebase?

A: Run git switch main and git pull origin main to get the merged commit. Then run git switch dan-delete and git rebase main, fix the markers in README.md, git add README.md and git rebase --continue. Finally, run git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete. The rebase replays your commit on top of the updated main, so the conflict appears locally where you can fix it. (01:17:08)

Q: git rebase main stops with CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in README.md. What do you do next, and how do you know?

A: Fix the conflict markers in README.md in your editor. git status then tells you to run git add README.md to mark the conflict resolved. After that, it tells you to run git rebase --continue, which asks you to confirm the commit message. (01:18:44)

Q: You are midway through a rebase, the conflict looks like a mess, and you are afraid you’ve broken something. How do you get back to where you started?

A: Run git rebase --abort. It returns your branch to its state before git rebase main, and git status lists it as an option. (01:18:20)

Q: After git rebase --continue on dan-delete, predict where dan-delete and origin/dan-delete sit in git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate.

A: dan-delete is a new commit, 0e16503, sitting directly on top of main (3167d10), with the conflict fixed. origin/dan-delete still points at the old commit, cb810d5, on the old base. The rebase rewrote your local branch but not GitHub’s copy. (01:19:14)

Q: After the rebase, you plan to run git push origin dan-delete. Will it work? What do you run instead?

A: A plain push will be rejected, because the rebased commit has a new parent and the branch’s history has changed. You have to force-push with git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete. GitHub then records that a force push happened, which is why you rebase only your own branch. (01:19:47)

Q: You type git push --force-with-leasse origin dan-delete and get error: unknown option `force-with-leasse'. What fixes it?

A: It’s a typo in the flag. Re-run it as git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete, and the output shows (forced update). (01:19:47)

Q: Your force push succeeded, and the pull request from dan-delete shows a green merge button again. What remains to be done?

A: Merge the pull request and delete the branch on GitHub. Then clean up locally: git switch main, git pull origin main, git fetch --prune and git branch -d dan-delete. (01:20:35)
