text:
Date: 2026-11-17

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 3 of 5: Apply. Work each situation through before you read the answer; tiers 1 (Remember) and 2 (Understand) cover the facts and reasons it relies on.

1. Review Git basics in the demo repository (8 Git branches)
00:04:07–00:06:49

Q: You are in the 2026-11-17-git demo repository, on main, and you have edited README.md. In order, what do you run to inspect, stage, commit, and publish that change to origin?

A: Run git status and git diff to inspect the change, then git add README.md, git commit -m "intro and review", and git push origin main. The commit only updates local main; git push origin main is the step that updates the remote branch. (00:06:38)

Q: You commit your README.md change to local main, but a teammate’s clone does not show it. What step did you skip, and what command fixes it?

A: You skipped pushing the local commit to the remote; run git push origin main. Work that exists only on your computer is not the shared repository state that the remote project uses. (00:11:03)

Q: You have just committed and pushed to main. What does git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all show that tells you local main and origin/main are synchronized?

A: It shows HEAD -> main and origin/main on the same commit. That decoration means your local branch and your local record of the remote branch point to the same place. (00:06:38)




2. Branches, local state, and remote origin (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:16:05

Q: Your teammate is still updating shared setup files, but you have a self-contained analysis task. What Git workflow do you use to avoid having to pull before every push?

A: Create your own branch for that task and commit there until it is ready for review. A branch gives a separate stream of work that does not move main or block on other people’s pushes. (00:08:41)

Q: You are on dan-b1 and make a commit. What happens to main and origin/main in the Git graph?

A: They stay where they were; only HEAD -> dan-b1 moves forward. A branch commit increments the branch name you are on, not the default branch or the remote-tracking branch. (00:14:15)

Q: You are making exploratory plots and tests that are not ready for teammates to rely on. Where should that work live while main remains stable?

A: It should live on a branch, not on main. main is treated as the stable place, while unfinished or exploratory work can be tested on a branch until it is reviewed and merged. (00:15:10)




3. Creating and switching branches (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:28:26

Q: You are on main and are about to start work that builds on teammates’ coordinated changes. What do you check before creating the new branch?

A: Run git status to confirm you are on main, then synchronize with the remote using git pull origin main. Starting from an outdated local main can cause you to redo work that already exists on the remote. (00:18:39)

Q: You are on main and want to start a new branch named feature-cleanup. What single command creates the branch and moves HEAD to it?

A: Run git switch -c feature-cleanup. The -c flag creates the branch and switches to it in one step, so subsequent commits move that branch instead of main. (00:20:09)

Q: You have an existing local branch named dan-fetch and want to move your working tree to that branch without creating a new branch. What command do you run?

A: Run git switch dan-fetch. Omit -c because you are not creating a branch; this moves HEAD to the existing branch and shows that branch’s file state. (00:25:12)

Q: A helper suggests git checkout -b dan-b1 for creating and switching to a new branch. If you prefer the modern command shown in the session, what do you use instead?

A: Use git switch -c dan-b1. git checkout is the older equivalent, and using switch makes the intent clearer when you are only moving or creating branches. (00:26:59)

Q: You need a local branch to exist but do not want to move to it immediately. What command creates it, and what command later moves to it?

A: Run git branch <branch> to create it without moving HEAD, then later run git switch <branch> to move to it. This two-step workflow differs from git switch -c, which creates and switches in one command. (00:28:10)




4. Pushing a branch and opening a pull request (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:28:31–00:39:56

Q: You are on main and run plain git push; it says Everything up-to-date. You still need to publish the commit you made on dan-b1. What sequence publishes that branch?

A: Run git switch dan-b1, then git push origin dan-b1. The remote branch name must match the local branch you want to push; git push from main does not push dan-b1. (00:30:05)

Q: After git push origin dan-b1, what does git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all show that proves your local computer now knows GitHub has that branch?

A: It shows origin/dan-b1 on the pushed commit. That reference is the local record of the remote branch; it appears after the push even before the branch is merged into main. (00:31:19)

Q: You pushed a new branch but the GitHub “Compare and pull request” popup is gone a day later. How do you start the same pull-request process?

A: Go to the repository’s branches view, find the branch, and use its menu to start a new pull request. This reaches the same compare-and-pull-request page that the temporary popup used to provide. (00:34:32)

Q: You are preparing the pull request for dan-b1 to main. Before clicking Create pull request, what two things should you verify in the changed files?

A: Check that every file you intended to work on is present, and that files that do not belong in the repository are absent, such as .ipynb_checkpoints or .DS_Store. Missing files usually mean you did not git add, commit, and push; extra junk files can lose points. (00:39:16)




5. Reviewing and updating a pull request (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:39:56–00:45:41

Q: You want to add a line-specific review comment in the Files changed tab of a pull request. What UI action starts the inline comment?

A: Hover over the diff line and click the + button. The comment is tracked in the pull request conversation while the code review happens on the diff. (00:41:32)

Q: The review comment says your code is wrong. Whose job is it to change the code, and what do you do without closing the pull request?

A: It is your job as the pull-request author to fix it; go back to the branch, make the change, git add the file, commit, and push to the same branch. The open pull request updates automatically with the new commit, after refreshing if needed. (00:43:15)

Q: You add a second commit to dan-b1 and push it with git push origin dan-b1. What happens to pull request #1?

A: Pull request #1 remains open and now includes the new commit because it is tied to the dan-b1 branch. You do not need to close and recreate the pull request to add more work. (00:44:43)

Q: You edit a line that has an existing inline comment, and the comment looks like it disappears from the review. What is likely happening?

A: GitHub may collapse the comment as outdated because the code line it referred to was changed. The review conversation still exists; the collapse is a signal that the original comment may no longer apply to the new line. (00:45:10)

Q: You write the first pull-request comment, then make more changes. What should you do to the description?

A: Edit the original first comment so it explains the full set of changes, rather than only appending notes. Readers use the first comment as the main description of the pull request. (00:40:55)




6. Draft pull requests, merging, and remote cleanup (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:58:51

Q: Your pull request will take several days. What GitHub control do you use to tell teammates not to merge it yet?

A: Use “Convert to Draft” on the open pull request. The pull request then shows a gray visual cue and the merge control is disabled so it is not accidentally merged. (00:54:04)

Q: Your draft pull request is now ready for review. What control turns it back into a mergeable open pull request?

A: Click “Ready for review” in the pull request conversation or merge area. It turns the draft back into an open pull request, restoring the green merge controls. (00:55:28)

Q: After pull request #1 is merged into main, what cleanup do you perform on the dan-b1 branch on GitHub?

A: Delete the remote branch from GitHub after merging so the branch dropdown does not accumulate finished branches. The commits are still in main history, including the merge commit, even though the branch marker is removed. (00:58:10)

Q: You merge a pull request and then look at main on GitHub. What do you expect to see in the commit history?

A: You see the branch’s commits and a separate merge commit describing that the pull request was merged. Deleting the branch later does not remove those commits from history. (00:58:10)




7. Cleaning local branches after a merge (8 Git branches)
00:58:53–01:03:51

Q: Pull request #1 has been merged on GitHub, but your local main is still behind. What two commands bring local main up to date?

A: Run git switch main if you are not already there, then git pull origin main. Local main does not update automatically when a remote pull request is merged. (01:00:27)

Q: You run git branch -a after merging dan-b1. What does the star next to main mean?

A: It means main is the branch your HEAD is currently on. The other listed branches are local branches and remote-tracking branches that your local repository knows about. (01:01:11)

Q: You deleted the dan-b1 remote branch on GitHub, but origin/dan-b1 still appears in local logs. What command removes that stale remote-tracking reference?

A: Run git fetch --prune. It updates your remote-tracking references and removes local references to branches that no longer exist on GitHub. (01:01:30)

Q: Your local dan-b1 branch has been merged into main. What command deletes it safely, and what happens if you try the same command on an unmerged branch?

A: Use git branch -d dan-b1 with lowercase -d; Git allows deletion only if the branch is merged. For an unmerged branch, lowercase -d refuses, protecting commits that are not yet in another branch. (01:02:54)

Q: You are trying to discard an unmerged local branch that contains no work you need. A helper suggests git branch -D branch-name. What is the risk?

A: Capital -D force-deletes the branch even if it has unmerged commits, so you can permanently lose work. Use lowercase -d for normal cleanup and only force-delete when you are sure the work is unnecessary. (01:03:21)

Q: You type git pull main after merging a pull request and get fatal: 'main' does not appear to be a git repository. What command retrieves the updated main from GitHub?

A: Run git pull origin main. Git needs both the remote name, origin, and the branch, main; main alone is not a remote repository. (01:00:34)




8. Creating a two-branch conflict scenario (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:03:51–01:10:51

Q: You are creating dan-delete from main and type git switch -b dan-delete, then get error: unknown switch 'b'. What command fixes the creation step?

A: Run git switch -c dan-delete. git switch uses -c for create-and-switch; -b is the flag for the older git checkout create workflow. (01:06:40)

Q: You have created the first branch and opened its pull request, but you still want to practice a conflict with a second branch. What key step must you avoid?

A: Do not immediately merge the first pull request. Leave it open so you can create a second branch with overlapping changes and see how the second pull request becomes conflicted after the first merge. (01:06:07)

Q: You create dan-fetch and dan-delete from the same main state, and both edit the same region of README.md. Why can this produce a conflict?

A: Both branches contain changes to the same region while main has not moved between their creation. If one branch is merged first, main changes and the other branch’s same-line edit can no longer apply cleanly. (01:08:02)

Q: You open pull requests #2 and #3 side by side before merging either one. What might the pages not tell you?

A: They may not make it obvious that the two branches will conflict, because each pull request is evaluated against main before the other is merged. The conflict can only appear after one merge changes main and GitHub rechecks the other pull request. (01:09:53)

Q: Pull request #2 from dan-fetch is merged. What does GitHub do to open pull request #3 from dan-delete?

A: It rechecks whether #3 can still be merged into the updated main. If the same lines changed in both branches, GitHub reports a merge conflict instead of allowing a clean merge. (01:10:19)




9. Resolving a conflict with git rebase and force pushing (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:10:51–01:20:42

Q: Pull request #2 has been merged, but your local main is still behind before resolving conflict on dan-delete. What two commands synchronize local main?

A: Run git switch main and then git pull origin main. This brings the merged dan-fetch commit into your local main so you can rebase against the current default branch. (01:16:25)

Q: You are on dan-delete, and its commit was based on the old main. What command replays that commit on top of the updated main?

A: Run git rebase main. Git attempts to apply the branch’s commit onto the new main and stops with a conflict when the same lines were changed in both branches. (01:17:14)

Q: git rebase main stops with CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in README.md. What local steps complete the rebase?

A: Edit README.md to remove the conflict markers and make the file correct, run git add README.md, then run git rebase --continue. If you are scared of the state, git rebase --abort returns you to the pre-rebase state. (01:18:32)

Q: After resolving and continuing the rebase, why can you not use a plain git push origin dan-delete?

A: The rebase rewrote the commit that was already pushed to origin/dan-delete, so the local branch history no longer matches the remote branch. You must force-update the branch with git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete. (01:19:47)

Q: You type git push --force-with-leasse origin dan-delete and get error: unknown option 'force-with-leasse'. What is the correct command?

A: Use git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete. The option name is --force-with-lease; the typo makes Git treat it as an unknown flag. (01:19:23)

Q: You remove the conflict markers in README.md, but later find a variable name used later in the file now causes the analysis to fail. What does “fix the conflict” require?

A: It requires making the whole file or report work from top to bottom, not only deleting the markers. A conflict on one line can affect code elsewhere, and you are responsible for the final working state. (01:11:21)

title: Git branches, pull requests, and conflict resolution: review questions, tier 4 — Analyze
text:
Date: 2026-11-17

Generated by qwen3.6-35b-a3b, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 4 of 5: Analyze. Take each one apart yourself before you read the answer; tiers 1 to 3 cover the facts, reasons and steps it relies on.

1. The problem with parallel work on main (8 Git branches)
00:04:04–00:09:43

Q: Trace the workflow of two collaborators working directly on main versus using separate branches: which pointers (HEAD, main, origin/main) advance in each scenario, and how does branching prevent the pull-before-push friction the class experienced in 521?

A: When two people work directly on main, both local HEAD and remote origin/main compete on a single line of history, forcing one person to constantly pull before pushing and causing merge conflicts. With branches, HEAD detaches and advances independently on a parallel line, allowing commits to accumulate without interfering with the stable main branch. This separation transforms a single shared line into parallel streams where teammates can work freely until they coordinate through a Pull Request. (00:08:19)




2. Creating and managing branches locally (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:09:43–00:25:12

Q: Examine the output of git log --oneline --graph --decorate --all after running git switch -c dan-b1 and making a commit: which pointer moves forward, which pointer remains static, and what does this graph tell you about where your new changes are safely stored?

A: The HEAD pointer moves forward to point at your new commit on dan-b1, while origin/main and origin/HEAD remain static at the last shared commit. The graph visually separates your branch as a new line branching off the main line, proving that your commits are isolated and do not affect the repository’s main history. This structure confirms that your experimental work is safely stored on a parallel track, ready to be integrated later without disrupting the stable codebase. (00:14:34)




3. Pushing branches and initiating Pull Requests (9 Pull requests)
00:25:12–00:46:00

Q: Follow a new branch from your local terminal to the GitHub interface: which command links your local work to the remote, what visual cue does GitHub provide to start a review, and how does converting the request to a draft alter the interface to prevent accidental integration?

A: Running git push origin dan-b1 uploads the new branch to GitHub, which immediately triggers a banner prompting you to click “Compare & pull request” to initiate a review. The Pull Request page presents a “Files Changed” tab where teammates can inspect the diff and leave comments on the proposed code. Converting the request to a draft grays out the merge button and displays a gray progress bar, explicitly signaling that the work is incomplete and protecting main from being accidentally merged. (00:30:44)




4. Merging, cleanup, and local synchronization (8.1.2 Getting remote branches you did not create locally)
00:52:17–01:03:51

Q: Break down the cleanup workflow after a Pull Request is merged on GitHub: how do git pull origin main, git fetch --prune, and git branch -d each address a different part of the synchronization process between your local machine and the remote repository?

A: After merging on GitHub, git pull origin main fast-forwards your local main branch to include the newly integrated commits. git fetch --prune communicates with the remote to remove local tracking references for branches that were deleted on GitHub. Finally, git branch -d dan-b1 safely removes the local branch itself, ensuring your local repository no longer tracks stale or redundant lines of development. (01:00:34)




5. Resolving merge conflicts via rebase (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:03:51–01:21:43

Q: Compare the local commit history before and after running git rebase main on a branch that falls behind an updated main: how does rebasing restructure the history, what specific markers appear in the file to signal the conflict, and why is a force push required afterward?

A: Rebasing replays your branch’s commits sequentially on top of the updated main branch, rewriting the history so your work appears as if it was started from the latest commit rather than an older one. When Git encounters the same modified lines, it halts and inserts conflict markers (<<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>>) into the file for you to manually resolve. Because rebasing creates new commit hashes, a standard push will be rejected, so you must use git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete to safely update the remote branch with the rewritten history. (01:19:22)

title: Git branches, pull requests and rebasing to fix conflicts: review questions, tier 5 — Evaluate
text:
Date: 2026-11-17
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 5 of 5: Evaluate. Decide and justify your verdict before you read the answer; the criteria are the ones given in class.

1. Course logistics: lab groups, attendance and interview week
00:00:01–00:04:04

Q: A group member lets an AI agent write their part of the group project and plans to skip reading it, because the seven-minute interview-week conversation does not affect their grade. Judge whether that plan is sound.

A: It is not sound. The interview covers your group’s actual code base, and anything in it is fair game, “especially in the world of AI.” The instructor’s standard is that you should know the code base you are working in, as you would at work, whatever the grading. (00:03:15)




2. Why branches: escaping the 521 push/pull friction
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: Once each group member owns a self-contained part of the project, the group proposes that everyone keep committing and pushing directly to main, as in the DSCI 521 shared slide-deck exercise. Assess this plan.

A: It is a poor plan for that phase of the project. When several people push to the same branch, you keep hitting the friction of having to pull before you can push, whether or not there is a conflict. The class’s goal was parallel streams on branches, where each person can push and pull freely until their work is ready for review. (00:08:41)




3. Review: the local–remote picture
00:09:46–00:11:47

Q: Before a milestone deadline, a teammate says their analysis is “done” because it is committed on their laptop, and they will push it next week. Judge whether their part of the milestone is complete.

A: It is not complete. The GitHub remote is the thing that matters: it is what gets graded and published. Work that exists only on your local computer “effectively doesn’t really exist” for grading or project purposes, like a product that was never shipped. (00:10:53)




4. What a branch is: main, HEAD and origin/main (8 Git branches)
00:12:03–00:17:54

Q: A teammate is still exploring the dataset and wants to commit their half-finished EDA plots straight to main so everyone can see them. Critique this plan.

A: The work belongs on a branch, not on main. In class, main was described as the production version: the stable branch where at least the code works. Exploratory work that isn’t ready stays on the author’s branch, while main holds the shared, cleaned dataset that everyone builds on. (00:15:24)

Q: A student working alone argues that branches are pointless without collaborators and commits every experiment directly to main. Argue for or against this approach.

A: Argue against it. The instructor uses branches even when he is the only contributor, because they section off work and keep main from changing until he has reviewed it. A failed idea on a branch is easy to discard by switching back to main. By contrast, undoing part of a commit that “did twenty different things” means digging through history. (00:17:22)




5. Creating and switching branches (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)

Q: A group member who hasn’t touched the project in a few days runs git switch -c straight away to start a new feature that builds on the team’s shared work. Judge this sequence.

A: It skips a step. If your work builds on coordinated work, you should first sync your starting point with git pull origin main, so that you branch from everything the team has already pushed. Otherwise you risk redoing work. The instructor described wasting time this way after forgetting that half the work was already done on another laptop. (00:18:39)


00:17:54–00:26:29


6. git checkout and git branch versus git switch (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:26:40–00:28:26

Q: ChatGPT gives you a git checkout command that you don’t fully understand, to run in your group project’s repository. Decide whether to run it as given.

A: Don’t run it blindly. checkout does far more than move HEAD: it also does much of what restore and revert do. If you don’t know what a command does, the instructor’s advice was to ask for the switch version instead, and to think carefully about what you type, especially when you’re worried about losing work. (00:27:44)




7. Pushing a branch and viewing it on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: A teammate finishes their work on branch dan-b1 and plans to merge it into main on their own laptop, then push main. Recommend whether the group should accept this workflow.

A: Don’t accept it. The class’s recommended route is not to merge on your local computer, but to push the branch with git push origin dan-b1 and merge it through a pull request. That way the work goes through a review process before it reaches main. (00:28:58)




8. Opening a pull request (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:41:16

Q: On the “Compare & pull request” page, the file list shows your notebook, an .ipynb_checkpoints folder and a .DS_Store file. The assignment doesn’t mention these files. Decide whether to click “Create pull request” as it is.

A: No. Files that don’t belong in the repository, such as checkpoint folders, .DS_Store and hidden backup files, lose points even when the instructions don’t mention them. Reviewing this file list is your second line of defence. Remove the files and fix your .gitignore before you create the pull request. (00:39:16)

Q: As a pull request grows, its author adds a new comment each time (“now I’m also doing…”) and leaves the original description unchanged. Assess this habit.

A: It is a poor habit. The very first message is what people read, so all of the changes should be defined and explained there. Edit the opening comment instead of piling on follow-ups. (00:41:03)

Q: A student plans to wait until a branch is completely finished before opening its pull request. Judge this plan against the instructor’s practice.

A: It is risky. The “Compare & pull request” pop-up disappears after about a day, so the instructor opens a pull request right away, even after a tiny commit, and keeps pushing to it. You can still recover the page from the Branches tab with “New pull request”, but opening the pull request early avoids the problem entirely. (00:35:15)




9. Code review and updating a pull request (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:41:16–00:45:41

Q: While reviewing a teammate’s pull request, you spot a bug, so you plan to rewrite their code yourself in the “Files changed” tab. Judge this as a reviewer’s approach.

A: It goes against the rule of thumb from class. If it’s your pull request, it is your job to fix it. The reviewer’s job is to point out problems (“rewrite this”, “this doesn’t look right”) in a comment, not to fix the author’s code. (00:42:17)

Q: After getting review comments on pull request #1, the author plans to close it and open a fresh pull request containing the fixes. Recommend whether to do this.

A: Don’t do it. There’s no need to close the pull request. Go back to the branch it was made from (dan-b1), then add, commit and push to that same branch, and the pull request updates itself, as the second commit did in class. (00:43:15)




10. AI reviewers and draft pull requests (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:55:41

Q: A group decides that every comment from a Copilot review must be applied before merging. Assess this rule.

A: The rule goes too far. Asking Copilot for a review is fine, since more eyes are never really a bad idea. But not every comment an LLM makes is one you have to keep. You can push back, reject it or accept it. (00:53:01)

Q: You open a pull request early for work that will take several days, and keep pushing to it. A teammate who sees green buttons might merge it. Justify converting it to a draft.

A: Converting it is the right call. A draft shows a grey bar that signals “not ready yet”, and it greys out the merge button, so nobody can merge it by accident. The instructor believes a draft also stops an agent from merging everything that’s green. Click “Ready for review” when the work is done. (00:54:30)




11. Merging and deleting the branch on GitHub (8.2 Useful things you can do with branches on GitHub)
00:55:41–00:59:07

Q: After pull request #1 is merged, a teammate refuses to click “Delete branch” on dan-b1, worried that it will erase the branch’s commits. Assess their concern.

A: The concern is unfounded. Deleting the branch marker doesn’t delete the commits: main’s history still shows the branch’s two commits plus the “Merge pull request #1” commit, so you can still find and undo the feature. Deleting merged branches keeps the branch list from growing into a giant list, so at least clean up your own. The exception is a workplace with compliance rules that forbid deleting. (00:58:19)




12. Syncing and cleaning up locally after a merge (8.1.3 Useful command line Git branching commands)
00:59:07–01:03:51

Q: To clean up local branches, ChatGPT suggests git branch -D on every branch, including one with an experiment you never merged. Would you run it?

A: No: use lowercase git branch -d. It deletes a branch only if it has been merged, because Git deliberately makes it harder to lose work. Capital -D force-deletes even unmerged branches, and the instructor warned to be very careful copying this one-character difference from ChatGPT, since it can delete commits you’re still working on. (01:03:21)




13. Setting up two conflicting pull requests (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:04:00–01:10:00

Q: To practise merge conflicts alone, a student pushes dan-fetch, opens its pull request and merges it immediately. Only then do they create dan-delete from main and edit the same line. Critique this setup.

A: It won’t produce the conflict. The key is not to merge the first pull request right away, but to keep it open while you create the second branch from the same main. That mimics two people with pull requests that change the same line. (01:06:07)




14. When a merge creates the conflict: resolving on GitHub
01:10:00–01:12:44

Q: Pull requests #2 and #3 both show green buttons, so a teammate plans to open both tabs and click merge on each without coordinating. Judge this plan.

A: It is unsafe. Each pull request on its own gives no sign of a coming conflict. But once one is merged, main changes and GitHub rechecks every other pull request that targets main, which is how #3 ended up in conflict. Green buttons aren’t a guarantee when people aren’t paying attention and coordinating their work. (01:10:31)

Q: A teammate resolves a conflict on line 13 of a script in GitHub’s web editor by deleting the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers, but their choice renamed a variable that line 50 still uses. Is the conflict resolved?

A: No. In this class, fixing a conflict in code means the code works from top to bottom again, not just that the markers are gone. A change at the conflicting line can break code elsewhere, and that is still your problem to deal with. (01:11:39)




15. Resolving the conflict locally with rebase (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:12:44–01:20:42

Q: After git rebase main and git rebase --continue on dan-delete, a student says a plain git push origin dan-delete should be enough, and that force-pushing is always wrong. Assess this claim.

A: The claim is wrong here. The rebase changed the branch’s history: its commit now sits on a different parent. A simple push can’t update it, so you can’t get around force-pushing, as in class with git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete. The instructor noted that this does “mangle history”, and GitHub records that a force push happened, which matters in compliance settings. (01:19:47)

Q: Midway through git rebase main, a student panics at the conflict and plans to delete the repository and re-clone. Recommend a better course.

A: Re-cloning is unnecessary. Let git status guide you: it tells you to git add the fixed file and then run git rebase --continue. If you’re scared that something got messed up, git rebase --abort gets you back to the state before the rebase. (01:18:20)

title: Git branches, pull requests, and merge conflicts: review questions, tier 5 — Evaluate
text:
Date: 2026-11-17

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 5 of 5: Evaluate. Decide and justify your verdict before you read the answer; the criteria are the ones given in class.

1. Course logistics
00:00:01–00:04:04

Q: A group decides that interview week is not graded, so they do not need to be able to explain their group codebase and Git workflow in the seven-minute conversation. Judge the plan.

A: Reject it. The class framed the interview as a technical-interview-style check on what you know about your actual group codebase, even though it will not affect your grade. The instructor said that, as in work, you should know what you are doing and all fair game is the codebase you are working in. (00:03:15)




2. Why branches exist (8 Git branches)
00:06:49–00:09:43

Q: Your group has reached a phase where each student owns a self-contained part, but a teammate proposes that everyone keep committing directly to main and just pull before pushing. Is that acceptable for the project?

A: No, not the workflow the class set up. The instructor wants parallel streams so each person can work in their own branch, push and pull until the work is ready, and then wait for team review. This avoids the DSCI 521 friction of constantly needing to pull because someone else pushed. (00:08:46)




3. Local repository versus remote origin
00:09:46–00:11:11

Q: A student says their milestone is complete on their laptop, but they have not pushed to GitHub, and the group assumes the local repository can be used for submission. Would you approve that?

A: No. The instructor said the remote is the thing that matters, is graded, and gets published. If your work exists only on your local computer, it effectively does not exist for grading or project purposes. (00:10:53)




4. main, origin/main, HEAD, and what a branch is (8 Git branches)
00:11:11–00:16:05

Q: A teammate wants to merge exploratory plots and unfinished analysis into main because the work is still their assigned responsibility. Would you approve the merge?

A: No. The class treated main as the stable, working, production-like branch where code should be in working order or finished. Exploratory, unfinished work should stay on a branch until it is ready to be incorporated. (00:15:10)




5. Branches are useful even when working alone (8 Git branches)
00:16:05–00:17:54

Q: A solo student argues that branches are unnecessary for them and plans to commit many experimental changes directly to main, then undo with git reset if things go wrong. Assess that plan.

A: It is a weaker plan than the branch approach the instructor described. Branches let you section off work and keep main from changing until you have reviewed and tested it. If the branch was a bad idea, it is much easier to abandon or delete the branch than to untangle commits on main. (00:17:22)




6. Creating a branch with git switch -c (8.1 Creating a branch using the command line)
00:17:54–00:23:46

Q: Before starting coordinated work for the group project, a student runs git switch -c from their current local state without first checking their branch and synchronizing with the remote. Judge that approach.

A: It is risky and not the practice the instructor recommended. He said to run git status to confirm where you are and, when building on coordinated project work, synchronize with the remote first so your starting point is up to date. Otherwise you may start from an old state and duplicate work. (00:18:09)




7. Switching between branches (8.1.1 Switching to branches that already exist)
00:23:46–00:28:26

Q: A student is not comfortable with git checkout, but a tool suggests using it to switch or create branches. Should they follow that suggestion?

A: No, they should ask the tool to use git switch instead. The instructor said he uses switch when teaching and advised that if you do not know your way around checkout, you should prompt for switch. checkout is an older command that did more than moving HEAD. (00:27:44)




8. Pushing a branch to origin (8 Git branches)
00:28:31–00:33:40

Q: A student wants to make their branch visible on GitHub so a teammate can inspect it, but only runs git push while still on main. Is that sufficient?

A: No. The instructor said to check which branch you are on and push the branch with git push origin <branch>, not rely on a plain git push from main. In the demo, the branch was made visible with git push origin dan-b1, after which origin/dan-b1 appeared. (00:30:44)




9. Opening a pull request and reviewing the changed files (9.1 Creating a pull request)
00:33:40–00:39:56

Q: A pull request updates README.md but also adds .ipynb_checkpoints and .DS_Store files. Would you approve it as is?

A: No. The class standard is to review the changed files and make sure files that do not belong in the repository are not included, such as checkpoint files and hidden backup files. The instructor warned that, in this course, visible unwanted files in a repository can cost points. (00:39:23)




10. Pull request conversation, code review, and updating the same branch (10 Code review on GitHub)
00:39:56–00:45:41

Q: A reviewer changes the author’s code directly, then merges the pull request without asking the author to address the review comments. Judge that workflow.

A: It does not match the class rule of thumb. The instructor said that if it is your pull request, it is your job to fix the issues; the reviewer’s job is to point out what is wrong or needs rewriting. The author should make the changes, commit, and push to the same branch. (00:42:17)

Q: A teammate closes a pull request and opens a new one to add a small review fix instead of committing to the branch that the original pull request was using. Is that required?

A: No. The instructor said you do not need to undo or close the pull request to make a change. Go back to the branch the pull request was working from, add, commit, and push to the same branch, and the pull request updates. (00:43:15)




11. Draft pull requests, merging, and deleting the remote branch (9.2 Draft pull requests)
00:52:11–00:58:51

Q: A pull request is still being worked on, but the team leaves it open with the normal green merge button available. Would you recommend converting it to a draft?

A: Yes. The instructor said a draft pull request signals that the work is not ready, shows a gray bar instead of a green one, and disables the merge button so nobody accidentally merges something explicitly not ready. When the work is ready, it can be marked ready for review. (00:54:12)

Q: After merging pull request #1, a teammate proposes keeping the remote dan-b1 branch permanently because the commits are still in history. Judge that cleanup decision for this course.

A: For this class, it is better to delete the merged remote branch after the pull request is merged. The instructor recommended deleting it so the branch dropdown does not become a long list, while noting that the commits remain in history and there are compliance cases where you must not delete things. (00:56:08)




12. Local cleanup after a merge (8 Git branches)
00:58:53–01:03:51

Q: A tool suggests running git branch -D dan-b1 after the branch has been merged. Would you use that command as the cleanup step?

A: No; use lowercase git branch -d dan-b1 for normal local cleanup. The instructor said lowercase -d allows deletion only when the branch has been merged and protects you from deleting unmerged work. He specifically warned that a capital -D force-delete, especially from copied AI advice, can delete commits you were still working on. (01:03:21)




13. Creating a merge-conflict scenario with two branches (8.3 What happens when my feature branch falls behind main?)
01:03:51–01:10:51

Q: Two open pull requests each look green when viewed side by side, so a student concludes that both can be merged in any order without checking for conflicts. Judge that conclusion.

A: It is not a safe conclusion. The instructor explained that after one pull request is merged into main, GitHub rechecks the other open pull requests against the changed main. A pull request that looked mergeable can become conflicted after the first merge. (01:10:19)




14. Resolving the conflict locally with git rebase main and git push --force-with-lease (8.3.2 Using rebase)
01:10:51–01:20:42

Q: After git rebase main stops on a conflict in README.md, a student removes the conflict markers and considers the work fixed. Is that enough?

A: No. The class standard is that the result must work from top to bottom again, not just have the conflict markers removed. A conflict on one line can affect later code, so the student is still responsible for making the whole report or script work. (01:11:39)

Q: After rebase rewrites the commit on dan-delete, a student tries to update the branch with a normal git push origin dan-delete. Would you approve that?

A: No, because rebase changed the history of a branch that was already pushed. The session showed that the update requires a force push, specifically git push --force-with-lease origin dan-delete, after which GitHub shows the forced update and the pull request can proceed. (01:19:47)

title: Docker Containers and Workflow Practices
text:
1. Git Workflow and Project Management

GitHub Issues: Used for tracking tasks, meeting notes, and ideas. Issues and pull requests share a single sequential numbering system.
Auto-closing with Keywords: Writing fixes #N or closes #N in a pull request description automatically closes the corresponding issue when the PR is merged into the target branch.
Branch Cleanup: After merging a pull request, the branch should be deleted on GitHub. Locally, run git fetch --prune to remove stale remote-tracking references, then git branch -d <branch> to delete the local branch.
Keep Analysis Simple: The course prioritizes reproducible workflows over complex statistical modeling. A technically correct, simple analysis is preferred over an over-engineered one that complicates the pipeline.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Docker Containers and Workflow Practices
text:
2. Containerization Fundamentals

What is a Container?: A lightweight, isolated computing environment that virtualizes the operating system user space. Unlike virtual machines, containers share the host OS kernel, lack a graphical interface, and are significantly smaller and faster to start.
Solving “Works on My Machine”: Containers guarantee that everyone uses the exact same versions of programming languages, packages, and system-level dependencies. This eliminates compatibility issues across different host operating systems (macOS, Windows, Linux) and architectures.
Ephemeral State: By default, interactive containers discard all changes upon exit. To persist an environment or installed software, it must be baked into a new container image.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Docker Containers and Workflow Practices
text:
3. Running Containers with Docker

docker run: Launches a container instance from an image.
--rm: Automatically removes the container instance when it stops, preventing stopped containers from piling up and consuming disk space.
-it: Two combined flags. -i keeps standard input open (interactive), and -t allocates a pseudo-TTY terminal.
Port Mapping (-p): Routes network traffic from the host to the container. Format is -p <host_port>:<container_port>. Essential for running web-based IDEs like RStudio or Jupyter inside containers.
Environment Variables (-e): Pass configuration into the container at runtime using -e KEY="VALUE". Commonly used to set passwords or toggle features.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Docker Containers and Workflow Practices
text:
4. Building Custom Images with Dockerfiles

Dockerfile: A plain-text configuration file that instructs Docker on how to build a container image. It builds in layers, starting from a base image.
Key Instructions:

FROM: Specifies the base image to build upon (e.g., rocker/r-ver:4.6.2).
RUN: Executes shell commands during the image build process (e.g., installing packages).
CMD: Sets the default command that runs when a container is launched from the new image.

Building and Caching: Use docker build --tag <name> . to build an image from the Dockerfile in the current directory. Docker caches each layer; if a RUN command hasn’t changed, Docker reuses the cached layer, making rebuilds extremely fast.

Git branch, PR, and cleanup workflow
git switch -c today                       # Create and switch to a new feature branch

git commit -m "today we are talking about containers" # Commit changes

git switch main                           # Switch back to the main branch

section: Pulling and running base R containers
text:
Pulling and running base R containers
docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2            # Download a specific version of the base R image
docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2    # Run interactively; --rm cleans up after exit
The container runs a fresh Linux environment with R 4.3.2 installed. Any R packages installed during this session are lost when you exit because the container instance is ephemeral.

section: Running web apps (RStudio) with port mapping
text:
Running web apps (RStudio) with port mapping
docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2
docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 -e PASSWORD="apassword" rocker/rstudio:4.4.2
The -p 8787:8787 flag maps port 8787 on your computer to port 8787 inside the container, allowing you to access the RStudio web interface via http://localhost:8787. The -e flag overrides the container’s default randomly generated login password.

title: Docker Containers and Workflow Practices
text:
Building a custom image
# Test the installation command inside an interactive bash shell
Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"

# Build the image using the Dockerfile in the current directory
docker build --tag hello-cowsay .

# Run the custom image; it executes the CMD instruction automatically
docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay
The Dockerfile instructed Docker to FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2, RUN the installation command, and CMD to print a message using cowsay. The build output shows CACHED [2/2] RUN ..., demonstrating how Docker skips rebuilding layers that haven’t changed.

text:
27.7 Image vs container?
Analogy: The program Chrome is like a Docker image, whereas a Chrome window is like a Docker container.

You can list the container images on your computer that you pulled using Docker via docker images. After pulling the images for this chapter, the list includes these three, and any other images you have:
Terminal
docker images
Output
IMAGE                                             ID             DISK USAGE   CONTENT SIZE   EXTRA
quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14   bf25d19758c0       9.06GB         2.17GB        
rocker/r-ver:4.3.2                                4e32addfc4da       1.11GB          313MB        
rocker/rstudio:4.4.2                              6bfc87fb66d0       3.16GB          734MB        
DISK USAGE is how much space an image takes on your computer, and CONTENT SIZE is about how much was downloaded.
You can list the states of containers that have been started by Docker on your computer (and not yet removed) via docker ps -a. Here, the R container from the first exercise and the RStudio container from the second are both running:
Terminal
docker ps -a
Output
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE                  COMMAND   CREATED        STATUS                  PORTS                                         NAMES
adf3ea77f63f   rocker/rstudio:4.4.2   "/init"   1 second ago   Up Less than a second   0.0.0.0:8787->8787/tcp, [::]:8787->8787/tcp   objective_hoover

text:
27.8 What is a container registry?
A container registry is a remote repository, or collection of repositories, used to share container images. This is similar to remote version control repositories for sharing code. Instead of code, however, it is container images that are pushed and pulled to/from there. For this course we will focus on the widely used Docker Hub container registry: https://hub.docker.com/.
However, there are many container registries that can be used, including:

https://github.com/
https://quay.io/
https://aws.amazon.com/ecr/

In the examples above, we have used the rocker/rstudio container, which comes from Docker Hub, and the Jupyter server comes from quay.io.
Exercise
Exploring container registries
Let’s visit the repositories for the two container images that we used in the exercise earlier in class:

rocker/rstudio
quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook

Question: you pulled these images with docker pull before you started. What would docker run ... have done if you had not?
Answer: docker run ... will first look for images you have locally, and run those if they exist. If they do not exist, it then attempts to pull the image from the registry named in the image (Docker Hub, if the image name does not name a registry).

28.1.2 Mounting volumes to containers
Oftentimes, we want to use the software made available to us in containers on files on our computers. To do this, we need to explicitly tell Docker to mount a volume to the container. We can do this via: -v <path_to_local_computer_directory>:<absolute_path_to_container_directory>.
Often, we want to mount the volume from our current directory (where we are working), and we can do that with $(pwd), which prints the current directory, in place of the path to our computer’s directory. This is a useful shorthand command when you work with multiple people, so the same command will work on different computers since you are not hard-coding the local computer path.
To mount our current directory at /workspace in a container from the ubuntu:24.04 image, we type the following on our laptop:

macOS and Linux
Windows (Git Bash)
Windows (PowerShell)

Terminal
docker run --rm -it -v "$(pwd):/workspace" ubuntu:24.04
Terminal
docker run --rm -it -v "/$(pwd):/workspace" ubuntu:24.04
docker run --rm -it -v "${PWD}:/workspace" ubuntu:24.04
Then, at the container’s prompt, go to the directory where you mounted your files and list them:
Terminal
cd /workspace
ls
Output
hello.R
Here, the current directory on the laptop held one file, hello.R.
Why /$(pwd) in Git Bash?
Git Bash turns command-line arguments that start with / into Windows paths, so /workspace could reach Docker as C:/Program Files/Git/workspace. Doubling the first slash stops that (see “Known issues” in the Git for Windows release notes). /$(pwd) does it for the mount, and a path inside the container, such as /workspace/hello.R below, is written //workspace/hello.R in Git Bash.
Note
If you are mounting volumes to a container from a Docker image that runs a web app, be sure to read the documentation to see where you should mount that volume. Usually, the web apps are only exposed to certain directories, and you will only be able to access the files in the mounted volume if you mount them to the correct place. For example, in the rocker/rstudio image that we loaded earlier, volumes need to be mounted within /home/rstudio/ to be able to access them via the RStudio Server web app.

Windows notes for mounting volumes

Windows machines need to explicitly share drives with Docker. This should be part of your computer setup!
On Windows, the laptop path depends on what shell you are using. Here are some details:

If you are going to run it in Windows terminal, then the command to share the current directory should be:

Terminal
docker run --rm -it -v /$(pwd):<PATH_ON_CONTAINER> <IMAGE_NAME>

If you are going to run it in PowerShell, then the command should be:

Terminal
docker run --rm -it -v <ABSOLUTE_PATH_ON_YOUR_COMPUTER>:<PATH_ON_CONTAINER> <IMAGE_NAME>
(pwd and variants do not seem to work). And the path must be formatted like: C:\Users\tiffany.timbers\Documents\project\:/home/project




28.1.5 Use a container to execute a script
What if, instead of running the container interactively, we wanted to run a script? Let’s take this R script, named hello.R, shown below, which prints the version of R that runs it, and a summary of a column of R’s built-in mtcars data:
# hello.R
cat("Hello from", R.version.string, "\n")
summary(mtcars$mpg)
Assuming that script is in our current working directory, we can mount the directory and then run the script with Rscript in a container from the rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 image:

macOS and Linux
Windows (Git Bash)
Windows (PowerShell)

Terminal
docker run --rm -v "$(pwd):/workspace" rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 Rscript /workspace/hello.R
Terminal
docker run --rm -v "/$(pwd):/workspace" rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 Rscript //workspace/hello.R
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/workspace" rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 Rscript /workspace/hello.R
This should result in:
Output
Hello from R version 4.3.2 (2023-10-31) 
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  10.40   15.43   19.20   20.09   22.80   33.90 
The script ran with R 4.3.2, the version in the image, whatever version of R your computer has.
Now, that was a small example, but the same docker run command can run a whole analysis non-interactively. Python and R in one image uses it to render a project’s reports in Python and R.

28.2 Docker command-line commands
The table below summarizes the Docker commands we have learned so far and can serve as a useful reference when we are using Docker:

28.2.1 Docker commands







command/flag
What it does




pull
Downloads a Docker image from Docker Hub


images
Tells you what container images are installed on your machine


rmi
Deletes a specified container image from your machine


ps -a
Tells you what containers are on your machine, including stopped ones


stop
Stops a specified running container


rm
Removes a specified stopped container


run
Launches a container from an image


exit
Exits a Docker container





28.2.2 Docker run commands







command/flag
What it does




-it
Tells Docker to run the container interactively


--rm
Makes a container ephemeral (deletes it upon exit)


-v
Mounts a volume of your computer to the Docker container


-p
Specifies the ports to map a web app to


-e
Sets environment variables in the container (e.g., PASSWORD=“apassword”)





29.1.3 Layer caching
Docker saves each step’s result as a layer, and reuses a layer when nothing in its step, or in the steps above it, has changed. To see this, change only the message on the CMD line of the Dockerfile:
CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Moo! Only my message changed.')"]
Then build again:
Terminal
docker build --tag hello-cowsay .
Output
[+] Building 0.2s (6/6) FINISHED                                               docker:desktop-linux
 => [internal] load build definition from Dockerfile                                           0.0s
 => => transferring dockerfile: 179B                                                           0.0s
 => [internal] load metadata for docker.io/rocker/r-ver:4.6.2                                  0.0s
 => [internal] load .dockerignore                                                              0.0s
 => => transferring context: 2B                                                                0.0s
 => [1/2] FROM docker.io/rocker/r-ver:4.6.2@sha256:8739c76d2d9316698a7145b032601f1e82249fdee3  0.0s
 => => resolve docker.io/rocker/r-ver:4.6.2@sha256:8739c76d2d9316698a7145b032601f1e82249fdee3  0.0s
 => CACHED [2/2] RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"                                   0.0s
 => exporting to image                                                                         0.1s
 => => exporting layers                                                                        0.0s
 => => exporting manifest sha256:f2d1c5ab15c8048a1863f62aa572f3bc2c971015fe8a2c04c5a4f1123137  0.0s
 => => exporting config sha256:0146dc6311dfcf1595b66373383e7f7bc1b4f0deae336219d9487b03da6d38  0.0s
 => => exporting attestation manifest sha256:bc8aca2ce37900fcdcd01fda5fed9286c997df019e23c971  0.0s
 => => exporting manifest list sha256:168f3c35f574628804baaf63e71be4164a7d1534ca35229a6827c7c  0.0s
 => => naming to docker.io/library/hello-cowsay:latest                                         0.0s
 => => unpacking to docker.io/library/hello-cowsay:latest                                      0.0s
The RUN step says CACHED. Docker reused the layer with cowsay installed and only changed the default command:
Terminal
docker run --rm hello-cowsay
Output
 _______________________________ 
< Moo! Only my message changed. >
 ------------------------------- 
      \
       \

        ^__^ 
        (oo)\ ________ 
        (__)\         )\ /\ 
             ||------w|
             ||      ||
Installing one package took a few seconds, but installing many packages, or packages that R compiles from source, can take many minutes, and the cache skips all of it. This is why a Dockerfile puts the steps that change least often, such as installing software, near the top, and the steps that change most often near the bottom. A change to one step rebuilds that step and every step below it.
docker image ls lists the image, and docker history lists its layers, newest first (head -5 keeps the first five lines):
Terminal
docker image ls hello-cowsay
Output
IMAGE                 ID             DISK USAGE   CONTENT SIZE   EXTRA
hello-cowsay:latest   168f3c35f574       1.45GB          390MB        
Terminal
docker history hello-cowsay | head -5
Output
IMAGE          CREATED          CREATED BY                                      SIZE      COMMENT
168f3c35f574   17 seconds ago   CMD ["Rscript" "-e" "cowsay::say('Moo! Only …   0B        buildkit.dockerfile.v0
<missing>      17 seconds ago   RUN /bin/sh -c Rscript -e "install.packages(…   4.17MB    buildkit.dockerfile.v0
<missing>      11 days ago      COPY scripts /rocker_scripts # buildkit         168kB     buildkit.dockerfile.v0
<missing>      11 days ago      CMD ["R"]                                       0B        buildkit.dockerfile.v0
The top two rows are the layers our Dockerfile added. The RUN layer holds the 4.17MB of R packages, and it shows that Docker ran the command with /bin/sh -c. The CMD layer adds no files, only the default command, so its size is 0B. The rows below come from rocker/r-ver:4.6.2, including its CMD ["R"], which our CMD replaces.
More information
Docker runs RUN commands with the shell /bin/sh, not Bash, unless the Dockerfile picks another shell with the SHELL instruction (see Docker’s Dockerfile reference). For commands like these, the two shells behave the same.


29.1.4 Guidelines for RUN commands
Each RUN command creates a new layer in the Docker image. Each layer in a Docker image takes more disk space. As a consequence, we want to minimize the number of layers where reasonably possible. How can we do this?
Install everything that can be installed by a tool (e.g., apt-get, or install.packages() in R) at once (i.e., when installing 5 programs via apt-get, do not call apt-get five times; instead do: apt-get install tool1 tool2 tool3 tool4 tool5, and in R, install.packages(c("pkg1", "pkg2"))). However, doing this can lead to long lines. In response, we can break a single command across lines in the shell by using the \ character. For example, to reduce the long line below, which uses apt-get to install the programs Git, Tiny Nano, Less, and wget:
Terminal
apt-get install --yes git nano-tiny less wget
We can use \ after each program to break the long command across lines and make the command more readable (especially if there were even more programs to install). Similarly, we indent the lines after \ to increase readability:
Terminal
apt-get install --yes \
    git \
    nano-tiny \
    less \
    wget
We can also group together related commands that depend upon each other. When doing this, we need to be careful, though, as sometimes we don’t want to run a command if the command that was run immediately before it failed. We can specify this in the shell using &&. For example, if we want to not run apt-get installation commands if apt-get update failed, we can write:
Terminal
apt-get update && \
    apt-get install --yes git


29.2.1 CMD or ENTRYPOINT?
Both set what a container runs when it starts. They differ in what docker run can replace. A command after the image name in docker run replaces CMD. For example, this runs R --version in the hello-cowsay image in place of its cowsay message (head -1 keeps the first line):
Terminal
docker run --rm hello-cowsay R --version | head -1
Output
R version 4.6.2 (2026-10-29) -- "Diversified Portfolio"
ENTRYPOINT is not replaced this way. Anything after the image name is passed to it as arguments, and replaces only CMD. With both, ENTRYPOINT holds the part that always runs, and CMD holds the default arguments. For example, this Dockerfile, in a folder of its own, always runs Rscript -e, with cowsay R code as the default:
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"

ENTRYPOINT ["Rscript", "-e"]
CMD ["cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"]
Terminal
docker build --tag cowsay-entrypoint .
docker run --rm cowsay-entrypoint
Output
 ____________________________ 
< Hello from my first image! >
 ---------------------------- 
      \
       \

        ^__^ 
        (oo)\ ________ 
        (__)\         )\ /\ 
             ||------w|
             ||      ||
Passing different R code replaces the default, but still runs it with Rscript -e:
Terminal
docker run --rm cowsay-entrypoint "cowsay::say('Only the R code changed.')"
Output
 __________________________ 
< Only the R code changed. >
 -------------------------- 
      \
       \

        ^__^ 
        (oo)\ ________ 
        (__)\         )\ /\ 
             ||------w|
             ||      ||
The images in this book, rocker/r-ver among them, set only CMD, so that a command such as bash after the image name replaces it, as in step 3 of the workflow.

29.3.1 Good base images to work from for R or Python projects!



Image
Software installed




rocker/r-ver
Ubuntu Linux and R; the base of this book’s R examples


rocker/rstudio
R, RStudio


rocker/tidyverse
R, R packages (including the tidyverse), RStudio, Make; ARM-based computers need tag 4.5.1 or later


ubuntu
Ubuntu Linux only; add uv to install Python and its packages


python
Debian Linux and Python; the -slim tags leave out software most projects do not need

Use rocker/tidyverse:4.5.1 or later
rocker/tidyverse images before 4.5.1 were built only for Intel and AMD computers (amd64). From 4.5.1 on, they are also built for ARM computers (arm64), such as Macs with Apple silicon. On an ARM computer, pulling an older tag fails:
Terminal
docker pull rocker/tidyverse:4.5.0
Output
Error response from daemon: no matching manifest for linux/arm64/v8 in the manifest list entries: no match for platform in manifest: not found
So use 4.5.1 as the minimum version. The rocker/tidyverse tags page lists each tag with the platforms it was built for (linux/amd64, linux/arm64), so you can check a tag before you use it.

text:
33.1 Docker Compose to launch containers
It can be fiddly and error-prone to type long commands into the terminal, or a GUI every time you want to launch a container. Even if you are copying and pasting commands, it can be difficult to make changes to long commands because you cannot click to a location to make edits.
A better approach is to use Docker Compose to specify how you want to launch the container. This way, all the parts of your command are saved in a file. This helps document how to run the Docker image, and it can be version controlled as part of a project.
Docker Compose uses a YAML file, specifically named docker-compose.yml, to record how the container should be launched. This file can include details such as:

the Docker image and version to use, or how to build it
how to mount volumes
what ports to map
what environment variables to set

docker run commands are interchangeable with the parameters specified in docker-compose.yml; the compose file makes it easier to manage all the docker run parameters. See this resource that can convert a run command to a compose file: https://www.composerize.com/
Here is the docker-compose.yml file of docker-uv-renv, the project from Python and R in one image:
services:
  analysis-env:
    build: .
    image: docker-uv-renv
    ports:
      # 2222 on your computer, 22 in the container.
      # "127.0.0.1:2222:22" stops others on the same Wi-Fi from reaching it.
      - "2222:22"
    volumes:
      - .:/workspace
      # ro: read-only
      - ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub:/root/.ssh/authorized_keys:ro
Without Docker Compose, building the image and starting the container takes these two commands, from the project folder:
Terminal
docker build --tag docker-uv-renv .
docker run --detach -p 2222:22 -v "$(pwd):/workspace" -v ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub:/root/.ssh/authorized_keys:ro docker-uv-renv
Each part of the docker run command is a line of the file:

services: lists the containers the project runs. This project has one, which it calls analysis-env.
build: . builds the image from the Dockerfile in this folder, like docker build ..
image: docker-uv-renv names the image, like --tag docker-uv-renv.
ports: maps port 2222 on your computer to port 22 in the container, like -p 2222:22. Port 22 is where the container’s ssh server listens. The file uses 2222 on your computer, because your computer may already use 22.
volumes: mounts two things, like the two -v options. .:/workspace mounts the project folder at /workspace. The second line mounts your ssh public key as the list of keys that may log in to the container as root, and ro makes it read-only inside the container. The key is the one from SSH for authentication.

No ssh key yet?
To check that you have the key, list it:
Terminal
ls ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
If ls says No such file or directory, make a key as in SSH for authentication:
Terminal
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
Press Enter to save it in the default place, ~/.ssh/id_ed25519. Make the key before you start the container. If the key is missing when the container starts, Docker makes a folder at ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub instead, and you cannot log in to the container.
Docker Compose reads the paths in the file itself, so the same file works on macOS, Linux and Windows, without the Git Bash /$(pwd) change from the earlier chapters.

section: 2. Project advice: keep the analysis simple
text:
2. Project advice: keep the analysis simple
00:01:41–00:05:57

The biggest tip: do not make your analysis difficult. If a straight line fits, fit the straight line model. Don’t treat the project as your “time to shine” with a neural net.
This is not a modelling course: the course is about workflows, and there is almost no machine learning code in the lectures. The report is not the point of the class.
What the project still needs: code that downloads the data, possibly cleaning code, EDA code, modelling code, and figures and tables. All of it should stay very simple.
Correctness still counts: model performance doesn’t matter (60% accuracy is fine), but the techniques must be correct data science. Fitting logistic regression to predict a numeric outcome, for example, is simply wrong.
Portfolio ambitions: if you want a portfolio piece, build it separately and in parallel, not in this assignment.
Schedule: this week’s work is getting everything onto Git, and next week is containers. It is the same project, built up over three or four weeks.


[!WARNING]
Don’t pick a complicated model for the group project: “You’re going to have a very bad time in about two weeks if you do that.” Simple models are not penalised, but incorrect techniques are.

3. Git review: working on a branch
00:06:16–00:09:50

Setup: the instructor cloned the demo repository 2026-11-19-docker and added the line “today we will talk about containers” to README.md.
Caught on main: git status showed he was still on branch main. He had not committed yet, so he could create the branch now with git switch -c today. Uncommitted edits travel with you to the new branch.
If you already committed on main: there is a cheat sheet in the textbook with commands to move those commits onto a branch.
Branch habit: in a branch workflow, which the course assumes from now on, look at which branch you’re on right before git add, and definitely before git commit.
Stay up to date: when actively collaborating, pull main first so you aren’t making changes to something out of date.
The sequence: git diff to review the change, git add README.md, git commit -m "today we are talking about containers", then git push origin today.


[!WARNING]
With several people working on several branches, committing on the wrong branch, or on top of a stale main, is the common mistake. Check git status before you add and commit, and pull main before you start.

section: 4. GitHub issues as a project board
text:
4. GitHub issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

What issues are for: tracking what is happening in a project, as a simple project board. The course practises them now, and DSCI 524 covers them further.
Who does what: document who is responsible for what as issues.

The MDS team uses an internal repository’s issues for meeting notes.
Action items from a meeting become separate issues spawned from the notes issue.

Demo issues:

Issue #1 what are we doing today? asked “what is today’s topic?”.
Issue #2 edit the readme with today’s topic referred back with “meeting from #1”.

Shared numbering: issues and pull requests use one counter. After two issues, the next pull request is number 3.
Two-way references: typing #1 in an issue or pull request links to item 1, and item 1 automatically shows a link back. This automatic linking is a big part of why GitHub became popular, beyond Git itself.
Idea dump: issues are a fine place for stray ideas such as “maybe a neural net later” or stretch goals.

The instructor sometimes asks a coding agent to file an issue for a passing thought, so he doesn’t have to switch to a browser and lose focus.

Assignees and reviewers: you can assign people to issues and to pull requests.

You normally assign yourself to your own pull request, which claims it as your responsibility.
Teammates go in the separate reviewer section. Some projects block merging until someone has reviewed.
In the demo the instructor added Copilot as a reviewer.

One pull request, many issues: it doesn’t have to be one issue, one branch, one pull request. The lab asks for three issues, and one pull request may deal with all three.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 5. Pull request descriptions, checkboxes and closing keywords
text:
5. Pull request descriptions, checkboxes and closing keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Keep the first comment current: edit the opening comment as decisions are made. Readers want to know “why does this exist?” from the top, not by reading the whole conversation. Project owners can usually edit others’ comments too.
Markdown checkboxes: - [ ] item lists track what is still to do. They show teammates the work isn’t finished, as an alternative or complement to marking the pull request as a draft.
Closing keywords: a sentence with closes #1 or fixes #2 in a pull request makes merging that pull request auto-close those issues. This is a GitHub feature, not a Git feature.
The demo pull request: #3 today we are talking about containers had this description:
this is the fix for #2

- [x] item 1
- [ ] item 2

closes #1 fixes #2
Did closes work? In class the instructor wasn’t sure closes had taken effect. He usually uses fixes. The demo repository shows both #1 and #2 closed by #3.
Commit messages work too: keywords also work in commit messages, but they are harder to see there.
The payoff: the issues tab shrinks as work merges. The instructor’s textbook workflow is to file an issue, work, write “fixes #N” in the pull request, then pick the next issue from the list.

One textbook refactor of the containers and virtual environments chapters fixed several issues in a single pull request.

Grading: you won’t be graded on closing all your issues. Open stretch-goal issues are fine.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
text:
6. Cleaning up after a merge
00:22:18–00:25:19

Update local main: git switch main, then git pull origin main, which fast-forwarded to the merge commit.
Delete the remote branch: after merging, click the delete-branch button on the pull request. Alternatively, go to the branches view, find the merged branch (it shows pull request #3, merged) and click the trash can.
Optional in this course: you don’t have to delete branches, and you may keep them as a record. Teams and companies differ a lot in how they use Git; this is one way, and others are variations on it.
Remove stale references locally:

git fetch --prune drops the origin/today reference to the branch deleted on GitHub.
git branch -d today deletes the local branch.

The history stays: the merge commit and its parent are still in the graph. You only lose the shortcut name. That is why some people keep branches: git switch today is easier than switching to 3c6d82a.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 7. Why data science workflows need stable environments (27.1 Documenting and loading dependencies)
text:
7. Why data science workflows need stable environments (27.1 Documenting and loading dependencies)
00:25:29–00:30:13

What changes now: until now, assignments came with a ready-made package list. Projects last longer than a homework assignment and involve other people.
Each project differs: groups choose their own language and libraries, such as Python or R, and Altair, Plotly or Matplotlib. You adapt the environment to the project, as you would at a company.
Bare-minimum package lists: don’t install everything.

It wastes disk space.
Packages update on different cycles, so a big environment can become impossible to install all at once.

Two stability goals:

Keep your own environment stable over days, weeks, months or years.
Make it reproducible on a teammate’s machine that may run a different OS, or even a different chip. Macs and Windows machines differ, and Windows itself now ships on both ARM and Intel.

“It works on my machine” isn’t enough: the course’s tooling is about stable computing environments and modular pipelines that others can run.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 8. What a container is (27.2 What is a container?)
text:
8. What a container is (27.2 What is a container?)
00:30:13–00:34:28

Where uv/renv stop: DSCI 521 covered uv and renv, which keep package versions consistent. A uv.lock file lets someone install your Python packages, but they still need uv installed and a similarly set-up computer.
The container idea: “here’s my computer”. You build a virtual computer from scratch, give it to everyone, and everyone runs their code on it, even on different physical machines. See 27.4 Contrasting common computational environment virtualization strategies and 27.5 Virtualization strategy advantages and disadvantages for reproducibility.
Prototype locally, run big: the same environment can run on your laptop and on a larger machine that holds all the data.
Cost: there is a performance hit from the extra layer.
Sandboxing: remote machines’ admins may not let you install software directly, but they can hand you a container to play in. If you break it, you restart it and get a fresh sandbox. It is the safe place to muck around with an operating system.
Tools: the course uses Docker. LXC, LXD and Podman are alternatives, and cloud providers have their own.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 9. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
text:
9. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
00:34:31–00:36:40

Virtual machine: a full-blown operating system, such as all of Windows, with its graphical interface and buttons.
Container: a stripped-down version with typically no graphical interface. It holds only the bare minimum you install. This is why DSCI 521 pushed typing commands, since sometimes the terminal is the only interface you get.
Size and performance: a Windows VM can take 50–80 GB. The containers used in class are a couple of GB or less yet run a full computational stack. They are lighter on disk, memory and compute.
VMs still have uses: the instructor uses one to test the MDS install instructions as if on Windows.
