title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 10. Pulling and running a container: R 4.3.2 beside local R (28.1.1 Launch and run containers)
text:
10. Pulling and running a container: R 4.3.2 beside local R (28.1.1 Launch and run containers)
00:36:40–00:45:01

docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2: downloads an image. The name looks like a GitHub user/repo because it works similarly. rocker is the organisation, and these images have only R installed. The tag 4.3.2 picks the R version. If the image is already present, the output says “Image is up to date” and shows a digest hash.
Two R versions at once: R --version on the laptop shows R 4.6.2, and the container gives R 4.3.2.
Real-world case: in pharmaceutical work, clinical trials research runs for years while R updates every six months. Regulators can ask for your code and the full compute environment, so you hand over the container that ran the analysis.
Beyond lock files: lock files pin packages; containers pin the tools themselves, such as R or Git. A container with an old Git could even prevent anyone from using git switch.
Similar names across tools: docker pull echoes git pull because tools borrow each other’s vocabulary.
docker run flags:

--rm: a double dash marks a multi-letter flag. When the container stops, it is deleted automatically; otherwise you delete it by hand.
-it: single-letter flags can be chained, as in ls -alh. -i is interactive and -t allocates a terminal (TTY). You’ll see -it everywhere.
The image name comes last. docker run also downloads the image if it isn’t present.

Isolation shown: in the container, library(tidyverse) fails because the image has only R. In a local terminal, tidyverse loads fine. Two terminals on one laptop behave like two different machines.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 11. Know which machine you are typing on
text:
11. Know which machine you are typing on
00:45:01–00:46:44

Read your prompt: after quitting the container, the laptop’s own prompt returns. The prompt is often your only visual cue.
Same idea remotely: the instructor opened a terminal on a machine in his closet at home. The only clue was the hostname he’d given it.
Why whoami exists: it reports the username on that computer, which is another way to confirm you’re on the machine you think you are.
Applies everywhere: the same habit matters in containers and on remote cloud systems.


[!WARNING]
With containers and remote machines you are sometimes given nothing but a blinking cursor. Check your prompt (or whoami) before running commands, so you don’t run something on the wrong machine.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 12. Why so many data science tools run in a browser
text:
12. Why so many data science tools run in a browser
00:46:44–00:49:11

Applications as browsers: many desktop apps are built on Electron, which is essentially a browser packaged as an app.
Why: a browser-first application can run inside a container or on a remote machine while you view it in your local browser.
Jupyter Lab: you open it at a localhost address because it was designed to run on remote machines with more cores and memory but the same interface.
VS Code: it is effectively a big browser app. GitHub’s Codespaces button gives you VS Code in a browser, running on a machine whose whole compute environment someone has set up.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 13. Running RStudio in a container and mapping ports (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
text:
13. Running RStudio in a container and mapping ports (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:54:10–00:58:59

Jupyter users too: projects are written in Quarto, but the same setup applies if you prefer a Jupyter interface.
Keep --rm: each running container uses RAM. Without it you can end up with “five computers” running and a laptop that grinds to a halt.
Ports: like Jupyter Lab on 8888, RStudio Server listens on 8787 inside the container. The numbers are arbitrary choices by the tool’s developers.
-p host:container: the left number is the port on your machine and the right is the port in the container. -p 8787:8787 puts the container’s 8787 on the laptop’s 8787. To run RStudio twice, map the second container to a different host port.
Open it: go to localhost:8787 in the browser. The username is rstudio, and the start-up output prints a generated password.
Different machines again: this RStudio runs R 4.4.2 in the container. The desktop RStudio runs the laptop’s R 4.6.2, and the earlier r-ver container ran R 4.3.2.


[!WARNING]
Running containers without --rm, or leaving several running, keeps using your computer’s RAM. Use --rm so a container is cleaned up when you exit.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 14. Passing environment variables into a container
text:
14. Passing environment variables into a container
00:59:20–01:02:53

-e NAME=value: passes an environment variable into the container. rocker/rstudio reads PASSWORD, so -e PASSWORD="apassword" replaces the hard-to-remember generated password (see the RStudio exercise in 27.2 What is a container?).
Container-specific: not every container supports the same variables. It depends on how the image was built, so check its documentation.
Showing the password is fine here: the port is only reachable from the instructor’s own machine. If you can’t log into his laptop, his 8787 isn’t available to you.
Looking ahead to DSCI 532: a dashboard runs in a browser. Put the dashboard code in a container and anyone with Docker can docker run it and visit the port. They skip the whole install process (renv, snapshots and so on) because you’ve given them a computer you built from scratch.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 15. Starting from a base image and working inside it (29.1.1 Workflow for building a Dockerfile)
text:
15. Starting from a base image and working inside it (29.1.1 Workflow for building a Dockerfile)
01:03:00–01:08:19

Start from someone else’s machine: when building your own container you still pick a starting machine. rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 already has R plus the system pieces R needs, the equivalent of the compiler tools students installed on their laptops. That saves steps.
Override the default command: docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash gives a shell instead of R. The prompt changes to the container’s (root@<id>:/#), and you can still type R to start R (see 28.1.4 Changing the containers default command).
Try first, then document: test install steps interactively, and once they work, write them down as the build instructions.
Demo: install.packages("cowsay") in the container’s R, then cowsay::say('hello') drew an ASCII cow. The instructor used cowsay instead of tidyverse because tidyverse takes far too long to install.
No saved state: after exiting and starting the container again, library(cowsay) failed with “there is no package called ‘cowsay’”. A container resets to how its image was built every time.
A good place to experiment: even destructive commands from DSCI 521 are safe in a container, because restarting gives a clean machine.
The problem this creates: making users follow README install steps inside a container every time is painful, for example a 15-minute tidyverse install for a 30-second analysis.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 16. Running R from the command line with Rscript -e (29.1.2 Build your first image)
text:
16. Running R from the command line with Rscript -e (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:08:19–01:10:18

The key question: do you know the terminal command that makes the install happen? Build steps have to be shell commands.
Rscript: runs R code from the shell. -e means “here is an R expression”.
The command: Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')". Note the quoting: double quotes outside and single quotes inside.
Confirmed, then lost: R in that container could library(cowsay) afterwards. Exiting and re-entering lost it again, so the information has to be saved somewhere.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 17. The Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, CMD (29.2 Dockerfile command summary)
text:
17. The Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, CMD (29.2 Dockerfile command summary)
01:10:18–01:15:01

Dockerfile: a special file named with a capital D. It holds the instructions for installing and setting up the computer. The rocker images have their own Dockerfiles, which is how RStudio comes installed with its port open. See also 27.6 Container usage workflow.
FROM (all caps): normally the first line. It names the starting machine, here rocker/r-ver:4.6.2.

You could start from a bare-minimum Linux and install everything yourself. That is a good learning project for a break.
Disk space is relatively cheap, so a beefier base image is acceptable.

RUN: the shell commands the image runs during the build, here the same Rscript -e line tested by hand.
CMD: what a container from the image runs by default.

It is written as a list instead of space-separated words.
It runs only if you don’t give another command such as bash, which overrides it.
ENTRYPOINT also exists, but the instructor called it rare.

The class’s file (Dockerfile):
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"

CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"]
For a Python project: the RUN section would install uv, COPY in the lock files and run uv sync. Next week, project containers also install the language and Quarto.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 18. Building and running your own image (29.1 Building container images from Dockerfile’s)
text:
18. Building and running your own image (29.1 Building container images from Dockerfile’s)
01:15:01–01:18:44

docker build --tag hello-cowsay .: --tag names the image.

The . is the directory to build from, the current one. It may be the first time a lone . is something you must type.
Docker looks for a file named exactly Dockerfile there.

Run from the project root: you can point docker build at another path. Milestone instructions assume every command runs from the repository root, so commands can be copy-pasted without changing directories (see 29.4 Dockerfile FAQ).
docker images: lists every image on your machine, including the new hello-cowsay.
Run it: docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay prints the cow message from CMD.
Shell access: docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash gives a shell inside the image, which is useful when something “works on my machine but not in the container”. There, library(cowsay) now loads, because the build installed it.
Typical shape: one FROM, a middle section of many RUN and COPY lines (and port instructions where relevant), and a CMD. Writing it all depends on knowing shell commands.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers
section: 19. Pinning versions, and what comes next
text:
19. Pinning versions, and what comes next
01:18:44–01:20:39

Next week: this week’s lab doesn’t need any of this. Next week’s work does.
Pin the language: the FROM line pins the R version. A placeholder section would then hold the renv or uv setup that installs the packages.
Pin the tools: you can choose a specific, even older, Quarto version. A year later you are still on the same versions, as long as you don’t touch that install line.
A real failure: in another class a few weeks earlier, the instructor restarted a container without hard-pinned versions. Something had updated the day before, and nothing worked. Hours of fixing an update instead of doing the real work is why you control what updates and when.
Coming up: more on building containers, and stringing several containers together.


[!WARNING]
If you don’t pin versions in your container, an upstream update can break everything overnight, as it did in the instructor’s other class. Install explicit versions and change them only when you mean to.

section: 1. Class setup: Docker Desktop and the pre-lecture docker pull commands (27 Introduction to containerization)
text:
1. Class setup: Docker Desktop and the pre-lecture docker pull commands (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:00:14–00:01:41

Docker Desktop must be running: on macOS and Windows, open Docker Desktop before running any docker command; if you get an error like “can’t find Docker”, install Docker (the application called Docker) and start it, or the commands will tell you to turn it on.
Pre-lecture pulls: run the three docker pull commands posted in Slack before class so the images are downloaded by the time the session begins — pulling takes a while.

The three images: rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, rocker/rstudio:4.4.2, and quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14 (the Jupyter image is the largest, around 9 GB).

The exercise for the day: practice making a branch, creating a pull request, and merging it, plus working with pull requests and issues.
Why it matters: this is the same workflow you will reuse for every assignment moving forward.

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 2. Project advice: keep the analysis simple and correct
text:
2. Project advice: keep the analysis simple and correct
00:01:41–00:06:05

Do not make the analysis difficult: the single biggest tip — if your model is a straight line, fit a straight line; resist the urge to add a neural network “to make it your time to shine.”
This course is not model fitting: DSCI 522 is about workflows, so almost no machine-learning code appears in the lectures.
The report is not the point: there is a lot more to do than write a report; keep the analysis short, but still include data-download code, some cleaning, EDA, modelling code, and figures and tables.
Accuracy does not matter, correctness does: a 60%-accurate model is fine, but the data science and ML techniques must be technically correct — for example, do not fit logistic regression to a numeric outcome.
Portfolio projects later: if you want a portfolio piece, build it in parallel, not inside this assignment.
Timeline: it is the same project you build on for three or four weeks; you need a machine-learning project to start with even though no ML code is shown in class; this week’s individual focus is getting everything on Git, next week’s is containers.


[!WARNING]
Over-scoping the project is the common mistake that backfires: the instructor warned that if you turn a simple task into a complicated model now, “you’re going to have a very bad time in about two weeks.” Keep it simple and correct.

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 3. Git review: branch, commit, and push for the pull-request task
text:
3. Git review: branch, commit, and push for the pull-request task
00:06:05–00:09:50

The task: create a repository, bring it onto your local machine (git clone the demo repository), then create a pull request.
Check your branch before committing: in a branch workflow, run git status right before git add and definitely before git commit to confirm which branch you are on; a cheat sheet in the textbook lists commands for moving commits if you accidentally commit on main.
Pull main before you start: in an actively collaborating environment, make sure main is up to date so you are not changing something stale.
The live sequence: edit README.md, git switch -c today to create the branch, git status to confirm you are on today, git diff to show the added line, git add README.md, git commit -m "today we are talking about containers", then git push origin today.
Why this is new since 521: what was single-user in DSCI 521 now matters with multiple people actively working on multiple branches.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
text:
4. Issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Issues track what is happening: a simple view of who is responsible for what; the issue board can even double as meeting notes (MDS keeps meeting notes in the issue board of an internal repository).
Action items spawn issues: write a meeting note, then create separate issues for each to-do and assign them.
Shared numbering: issues and pull requests share one counter (issue #2, then PR #3), so you can reference any item with a hash number, e.g. #1.
Two-way references: referencing #1 from another item creates a back-link automatically; this cross-linking is a big reason GitHub (as a service) became popular.
Ideas and agents: use issues as a dump for random ideas or stretch goals; when working with an agent, you can ask it to file an issue so you do not lose track.
One pull request can close several issues: the class requires three issues, but one pull request is allowed to deal with all three.
Assignment and review: you can assign people to issues and to pull requests; the assign section claims responsibility, while the reviewer section requests a look-over (larger projects can block a merge until a reviewer approves).
Demo repository items: issue #1 what are we doing today? and issue #2 edit the readme with today’s topic.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 5. Pull-request descriptions, checkboxes, and auto-close keywords
text:
5. Pull-request descriptions, checkboxes, and auto-close keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Keep the first comment current: the first comment on an issue or pull request should hold all the context, because people read that and not the later conversation; project owners can edit others’ comments to keep it up to date.
Markdown checkboxes: use - [x] item 1 and - [ ] item 2 in a pull request to track what is done; with the draft button, teammates can see status at a glance.
closes and fixes keywords: a sentence ending in closes #1 or fixes #2 references those issues; when the pull request merges, GitHub auto-closes the referenced issues.
GitHub, not Git: this auto-close is a GitHub service feature, not part of the Git version-control system; you can reference multiple issues or the same one multiple times.
Strategic messages: write the description so that merging the pull request closes all the issues at once instead of clicking close several times; the instructor’s own textbook workflow does this (“fixes #N” in the message closes the issue on merge).
Stretch goals as issues: you can create issues for future ideas; the class does not grade on all issues being closed.
The demo pull request is #3 today we are talking about containers, whose description uses closes #1 fixes #2.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 6. Merging the pull request and cleaning up branches
text:
6. Merging the pull request and cleaning up branches
00:22:18–00:25:29

Finish on main: after the pull request merges, git switch main and git pull origin main to bring the merge down locally.
Delete the remote branch: on GitHub, after merging there is a “delete branch” button; or use the branches view and click the trash can. This is not required in the class — you may keep branches as a record.
Teams differ: the way shown here is one valid way to work with Git; other teams and companies do it differently.
Clean up local references: git log --oneline --graph --all still shows the branch tip; run git fetch --prune to drop the remote-tracking reference, then git branch -d today to delete the local branch.
Why keep or delete: deleting loses the quick git switch today shortcut, but the merge commit still records that it happened; some keep branches so they do not lose the reference.

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 7. Why containers: a stable, shareable compute environment (27 Introduction to containerization)
text:
7. Why containers: a stable, shareable compute environment (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:25:29–00:33:21

From homework to projects: 522 moves from short, instructor-supplied package files to data-science projects that can last days to years and are often team-based.
Different package needs: each project (R or Python; Altair, Plotly, or Matplotlib) has its own package requirements; you now manage your own list instead of the instructor’s, and keep it to the bare minimum.
Stable for you and others: uv and renv (from 521) keep packages consistent on one machine; Docker goes further so a teammate on a different operating system or CPU architecture (Intel vs ARM, Mac vs Windows) can run the same environment.
“Works on my machine” fails: the goal of the course is a compute environment you can share and run all of your code through, not a private one.
A virtual computer: instead of handing over your machine, build a virtual one (a container) and give everyone that; you can prototype locally and then run the identical environment on a bigger machine.
Sandbox and performance: there is a performance hit from the extra layer; if you break the sandbox you just restart it; it is a safe place to learn to muck around an operating system.
Instances and other tools: cloud “instances” are often containers; besides Docker there are LXC, LXD, Podman, and cloud-specific variants.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 8. Containers versus virtual machines (27 Introduction to containerization)
text:
8. Containers versus virtual machines (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:33:21–00:36:47

Virtual machine: a full operating system (for example, a complete Windows install with a graphical interface) that you log into; the instructor still uses VMs, e.g. to test the MDS install while pretending to be on Windows.
Container: a stripped-down environment containing only what you install plus a terminal; it has no graphical interface, which fits the 521 habit of working at the command line.
Size difference: a virtual machine can take 50–80 GB; the containers used in class are under about 1–2 GB and still run a full computational stack.
Performance: containers are lighter in disk, memory, and compute because there is less to run; think of a container as a virtual machine with the full operating system and visual bits removed.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 9. Running the R container: docker pull and docker run (27 Introduction to containerization)
text:
9. Running the R container: docker pull and docker run (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:36:47–00:45:01

docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2: the name looks like user/repo:tag; rocker is an organization that builds R-only images, and the tag picks R 4.3.2. Pulling downloads the image, or reports it is up to date and shows a content hash.
Two versions of R: the host has R 4.6.2 (check with R --version), while the container runs R 4.3.2. A real case is a pharmaceutical or clinical-trial analysis where the R version must stay fixed for years, and a drug submission requires the code plus the exact compute environment.
Lock files vs system tools: uv/renv lock files pin package versions but not the tooling itself (for example, the installed version of git); a container pins the system tools too.
docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2: docker run starts a container, pulling the image first if needed; --rm deletes the container when it stops so stopped containers do not pile up; -i keeps input open (interactive) and -t attaches a TTY so R runs interactively; single-letter flags can be chained (-it).
Proof it is a different machine: the container opens R 4.3.2 while the host has 4.6.2; library(tidyverse) fails in the bare container (there is no package called 'tidyverse') but works on the host — two terminals on one computer doing different things.
Know where you are typing: the only cue is the prompt (the container’s prompt looks different from the host’s); this mirrors working on a remote or cloud machine, and is why 521 taught whoami-style checks.

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 10. Web-app containers: RStudio and browser-first tools (28 Using and running containers)
text:
10. Web-app containers: RStudio and browser-first tools (28 Using and running containers)
00:45:01–00:54:10

Browser-first applications: many data-science tools — JupyterLab at localhost:8888, VS Code, GitHub Codespaces — are built as browser apps (often via Electron) so the same interface can run on a remote machine or in a container.
RStudio as a web app: the rocker/rstudio image runs RStudio Server, which you reach from a browser; it is an easier one to teach than a plain terminal.
Why it matters for 532: a dashboard is a browser app; you can containerize it so an end user only needs Docker to run it.
Same interface, different machine: connecting to the container’s web app is the same idea as connecting to cloud compute.
The class took a five-minute break at this point before continuing with the RStudio container.

section: 11. Port mapping the RStudio container (28 Using and running containers)
text:
11. Port mapping the RStudio container (28 Using and running containers)
00:54:10–00:59:14

docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2: the RStudio image listens on port 8787; -p host:container maps a local port to the container’s port.
Running it more than once: the container side is fixed at 8787, but you can map it to a different local port (up to roughly 60,000 ports) so multiple RStudio containers run at the same time.
Open it in the browser: go to http://localhost:8787; sign in with username rstudio and the password printed in the terminal (a generated one on the first run).
Confirm it is the container, not the host: local RStudio runs the host’s R (4.6.2), while the containerized RStudio runs a different version (the rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 image) — two independent machines.
Resources: each running container uses RAM; leaving several open can make the machine sluggish, which is why --rm is used.

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 12. Environment variables and running dashboards in containers (28 Using and running containers)
text:
12. Environment variables and running dashboards in containers (28 Using and running containers)
00:59:20–01:03:00

-e PASSWORD="apassword": pass environment variables at run time; the rocker/rstudio image reads PASSWORD to set the login password instead of generating a random one.
Not every container exposes the same variables: behavior depends on how the image was built; more is covered when building containers.
Is the port reachable by others?: the instructor checked that localhost:8787 is only reachable by someone who can log into the host machine — a good habit for verifying what a port mapping actually exposes.
Dashboards in 532: put dashboard code in a container; the end user installs nothing but Docker and runs docker run with the right flags, so all the heavy installation (environment, Quarto, etc.) is already done inside.

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 13. Building interactively: base image and the cowsay package (29 Customizing and building containers)
text:
13. Building interactively: base image and the cowsay package (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:03:00–01:08:46

Start from a base image: even when customizing, pick a starting point; here rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 already has R and the tooling a fresh install would otherwise need (like the compiler setup that Windows and Mac users had to do by hand).
Get a shell, not R: docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash starts bash instead of the image’s default R, so you can run the install commands you plan to document.
Try before you write: run the steps interactively first (install cowsay with install.packages("cowsay"), then cowsay::say('hello')), and only document what actually works.
No persistence: exit the container and any package you installed is gone the next time you start it — a container has no save state and resets to the image; that is also a safe place to run destructive commands or experiment with new packages without harming the real machine.

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 14. Writing the Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, and CMD (29 Customizing and building containers)
text:
14. Writing the Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, and CMD (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:08:46–01:15:01

The Dockerfile: a plain-text file (capital D, no extension) holding the instructions to build the machine; it is version-controlled like a pyproject.toml or lock file (see the Dockerfile the class committed).
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2: the first line sets the base image; you can choose an even smaller, near-bare Linux image and install everything by hand.
RUN: bash commands to run during the build, e.g. RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"; mind the quoting (double quotes on the outside, single quotes on the inside), because Rscript -e runs an R expression from the command line.
CMD: the default command when the container starts; here CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"] so the image prints the message; ENTRYPOINT is the rarer alternative for fixed commands.
COPY + uv sync: for a Python image you would COPY in your lock files and run uv sync so the packages are installed at build time; next week you will install the language, Quarto, and packages the same way.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 15. Building and running the hello-cowsay image (29 Customizing and building containers)
text:
15. Building and running the hello-cowsay image (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:15:01–01:18:44

docker build --tag hello-cowsay .: --tag (or -t) names the image; the . is the build context / current directory where Docker looks for the Dockerfile.
Run from the repository root: the . convention assumes you run commands from the directory root — the same assumption used in the milestone-one instructions.
Check it built: docker images lists local images, including hello-cowsay:latest and its disk size (about 1.45 GB).
Run it: docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay executes the CMD (the cowsay message); docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash drops you into a shell where library(cowsay) now works, proving the RUN step baked the package into the image.
crumbs: Nov 19 · Git issues and pull requests, then an introduction to Docker containers

title: Containers: Running and Building a Shareable Compute Environment
section: 16. Version pinning and wrap-up (29 Customizing and building containers)
text:
16. Version pinning and wrap-up (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:18:44–01:20:39

Pin your tooling: add a placeholder for the uv/renv setup and pin the Quarto version (or any tool version, e.g. an older Quarto) so the image installs exactly those versions.
Control what updates: as long as you do not change the install line, a year from now you are still on the same tool versions.
The Dockerfile as the control point: you say “here is the version I want; it will not change until I update that line.”
Next time: this was an introduction to containers (using and building them); the next class builds on it, including stringing multiple containers together and the sections listed as not reached.


[!WARNING]
Do not let tool versions float. The instructor recounted restarting a container without hard-version-pinning its tools, where an overnight update broke everything and hours were spent fixing the update instead of doing the work. Pin the versions in the Dockerfile so an unexpected update cannot silently break a validated build.

title: Git issues and pull requests, then Docker containers: review questions, tier 1 — Remember
text:
Date: 2026-11-19
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 1 of 5: Remember. Answer each question before you read its answer; tiers 2 to 5 build on these.

1. Opening: pull the Docker images and start the branch exercise (Download the images before you start)
00:00:14–00:01:41

Q: How many Docker commands were posted in Slack for students to run at the start of class, and roughly how long did the instructor say they would take?

A: Three Docker commands, which should be done in about ten minutes. (00:00:18)

Q: Name the three images the start-of-class docker pull commands download.

A: rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 and quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14. (00:00:18)

Q: What application must be open before you run the class’s Docker commands?

A: Docker Desktop. If it is off, the commands tell you to turn it on. If you get an error that Docker can’t be found, you still need to install Docker. (00:00:33)

Q: List the three steps of the warm-up Git exercise at the start of class.

A: Make a branch, create a pull request, and merge it. (00:00:43)

Q: State which courses the instructor said will use pull requests and issues from now on.

A: All of your project-based courses moving forward. (00:00:57)




2. Project advice: keep the analysis simple
00:01:41–00:05:57

Q: What did the instructor call his biggest tip for the group project?

A: Do not make your analysis difficult. If a straight-line model fits, fit the straight-line model. (00:01:56)

Q: Quote the instructor’s warning about choosing an ambitious model, such as a neural net, for the project.

A: “You’re going to have a very bad time in about two weeks if you do that.” (00:02:16)

Q: How much machine learning code did the instructor say students will see in the lectures?

A: Almost none. The course is not a model-fitting course. (00:02:28)

Q: List the kinds of code the instructor said the project still needs, even when kept simple.

A: Code that downloads the data, possibly cleaning code, EDA code, modelling code, and figures and tables. (00:02:41)

Q: State what the instructor said about model accuracy versus correctness.

A: It doesn’t matter if the model is 60% accurate, but it has to be technically correct, using correct data science and machine learning techniques. (00:03:08)

Q: What did the instructor say to do if you want the project to become a portfolio piece?

A: Don’t do it in this assignment. Do it in parallel if you really want to. (00:03:27)

Q: Name the example of an incorrect technique the instructor gave.

A: Fitting logistic regression when you’re trying to predict a numeric outcome: “That’s just wrong.” (00:05:24)

Q: State the topic of this week’s project work and the topic of next week’s.

A: This week is getting everything on Git, and next week is containers. (00:04:49)

Q: How long do students build on the same project?

A: Three or four weeks. (00:05:37)




3. Git review: working on a branch
00:06:16–00:09:50

Q: Name the demo repository the instructor cloned for this class.

A: 2026-11-19-docker. (00:06:20)

Q: What line did the instructor add to the demo repository’s README.md?

A: “today we will talk about containers”. (00:07:39)

Q: Which branch did git status show the instructor was on after he edited README.md in the demo repository?

A: main, which is not where he meant to work. (00:07:44)

Q: Where did the instructor say to find commands for fixing commits you accidentally made on main?

A: In a cheat sheet in the textbook. (00:07:44)

Q: When did the instructor say to check which branch you are on in a branch workflow?

A: Right before you run git add, and definitely before you run git commit. Getting this wrong becomes a common problem once you work with several people on several branches. (00:08:08)

Q: What did the instructor say to do with main before making changes in an active collaborating environment?

A: Pull main so everything is up to date, so you aren’t making changes to something out of date. (00:08:27)

Q: What command created and switched to the today branch in the demo repository?

A: git switch -c today. (00:08:57)

Q: What command did the instructor run to see his changes to README.md before staging them?

A: git diff. (00:09:25)

Q: What commit message did the instructor use for the README.md change on the today branch?

A: "today we are talking about containers". (00:09:25)

Q: What command pushed the today branch to GitHub?

A: git push origin today. (00:09:44)




4. GitHub issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: What did the instructor say issues are a good way to do?

A: To track what is happening in your project. He described them as a very simple view of a project board. (00:10:08)

Q: Which later MDS course did the instructor say will cover issues in more depth?

A: DSCI 524. (00:10:08)

Q: What did the instructor say you should document as an issue?

A: Who is responsible for what. (00:10:28)

Q: State one way the instructor said MDS uses the issue board of an internal repository.

A: To keep meeting notes. Action items from the meeting can then be spun out into separate issues. (00:10:49)

Q: Name the two issues in the 2026-11-19-docker demo repository.

A: Issue #1 “what are we doing today?” and issue #2 “edit the readme with today’s topic”. (00:11:37)

Q: State how GitHub numbers issues and pull requests in the same repository.

A: They share one numbering sequence. If you create an issue and then a pull request right after, the pull request is number two. (00:12:07)

Q: What text did issue #2 in the demo repository use to refer to issue #1?

A: “meeting from #1”. (00:12:30)

Q: What happens to the referenced item when you write a # number in an issue or pull request?

A: It becomes a two-way reference: the referenced item automatically shows a link back. (00:13:34)

Q: What did the instructor say he sometimes asks a coding agent to do when he has a random thought?

A: File an issue for it, so he doesn’t tab over to a browser and lose track. (00:13:24)

Q: According to the instructor, what made GitHub super popular, beyond Git itself?

A: Issues and pull requests, and tracking everything as a project management system. (00:13:47)

Q: How many issues does this course ask you to have, and must each get its own pull request?

A: Three issues. It’s okay if one pull request deals with all three. (00:14:23)

Q: Who did the instructor assign as a reviewer on the demo pull request?

A: Copilot. (00:15:14)

Q: Name the two roles you can give people on a pull request.

A: Assignee, which claims it as your responsibility, and reviewer, for a teammate who looks over your work. (00:14:47)




5. Pull request descriptions, checkboxes and closing keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: Which comment in an issue or pull request did the instructor say to keep up to date?

A: The first comment, so readers can see what is happening and why the thing exists without reading the whole conversation. (00:16:56)

Q: Whose comments can a project owner typically edit?

A: Other people’s comments. (00:16:51)

Q: What Markdown feature did the instructor use in the pull request description to track remaining work?

A: Checkboxes, such as - [ ] item. (00:17:49)

Q: Name the pull request button the instructor mentioned as another way to show that work isn’t done yet.

A: The draft button. (00:17:49)

Q: Name the two pull request keywords the instructor gave for linking issues.

A: closes and fixes. (00:18:33)

Q: Is auto-closing issues with keywords a Git feature or a GitHub feature?

A: A GitHub feature, not a feature of the Git version control system. (00:18:54)

Q: What happens to issues named after fixes or closes in a pull request description when that pull request is merged?

A: The issues are closed automatically. (00:19:30)

Q: Which closing keyword does the instructor almost always use?

A: fixes. (00:19:55)

Q: Besides a pull request description, where else did the instructor say you can write a closing keyword?

A: In a commit message, but it’s harder to see there. (00:19:55)

Q: Reproduce the closing line of pull request #3’s description in the demo repository.

A: closes #1 fixes #2. The description also opened with “this is the fix for #2”. (00:14:14)

Q: What example did the instructor give of one pull request fixing several issues in his own work?

A: A refactor of the containers and virtual environments chapters in the textbook. Moving the old material and writing the new material were separate issues, all fixed by one pull request. (00:21:17)

Q: State whether students are graded on closing all their issues by the end of the course.

A: No. Stretch-goal and longer-term issues can stay open. (00:21:50)




6. Cleaning up after a merge
00:22:18–00:25:19

Q: After the demo pull request was merged, what two commands brought local main up to date?

A: git switch main, then git pull origin main. (00:22:25)

Q: Name the two places on GitHub where you can delete a merged branch.

A: The delete-branch button on the pull request after merging, or the trash can icon in the branches view. (00:22:53)

Q: Which pull request number did GitHub’s branches view show for the today branch?

A: Pull request number three, marked as merged. (00:22:53)

Q: Are students required to delete their branches in this course?

A: No. You can keep them as a record if you want. (00:23:16)

Q: What command did the instructor use to view the branch history as a graph?

A: git log --oneline --graph --all. (00:23:56)

Q: What was the merge commit’s message in the demo repository’s log?

A: “Merge pull request #3 from chendaniely/today”. (00:23:56)

Q: What command removed the local reference to the branch that had been deleted on GitHub?

A: git fetch --prune, which dropped origin/today. (00:24:30)

Q: What command deleted the local today branch?

A: git branch -d today. (00:24:30)

Q: What hash would you have to type with git switch once the today name is gone?

A: 3c6d82a, which is why some people keep the branch name. (00:25:05)




7. Why data science workflows need stable environments (27.1 Documenting and loading dependencies)
00:25:29–00:30:13

Q: What is DSCI 522 called?

A: Data Science Workflows. (00:25:48)

Q: Name the Python plotting libraries the instructor mentioned as different project choices.

A: Altair, Plotly and Matplotlib. (00:27:06)

Q: State the two problems the instructor gave with installing every package instead of a bare-minimum list.

A: It wastes disk space. Also, packages update on different cycles, so you can end up unable to install everything together. (00:28:04)

Q: Name the two kinds of Windows chips the instructor mentioned.

A: ARM Windows chips and Intel Windows chips. (00:28:53)

Q: Quote the phrase the instructor said doesn’t really work when teammates can’t run your code.

A: “This works on my machine.” (00:29:39)

Q: Name the two goals the instructor gave for the course’s tooling.

A: Creating a stable computing environment, and building modular data science pipelines. (00:29:55)




8. What a container is (27.2 What is a container?)
00:30:13–00:34:28

Q: Which tools did the instructor say handled keeping package versions consistent in DSCI 521?

A: uv and renv. (00:30:13)

Q: How did the instructor define a container?

A: A virtual computer built from scratch that you give to others, so everyone does their work on the same computer even on different physical machines. (00:31:49)

Q: What cost of containers did the instructor name?

A: A performance hit, because there is an extra layer on top. (00:32:34)

Q: What happens if you mess up a container sandbox?

A: You restart it and get a new sandbox. (00:33:05)

Q: Besides Docker, name the container tools the instructor listed.

A: LXC, LXD and Podman. He added that Amazon probably has its own. (00:34:03)

Q: Asked what an “instance” is, what did the instructor say cloud providers such as Google give you?

A: A container on one of their servers, not an actual machine. Pretty much all cloud compute runs on some version of containers. (00:33:30)




9. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
00:34:31–00:36:40

Q: How did the instructor define a virtual machine?

A: A full-blown operating system, such as all of Windows, with the graphical interface and all its buttons. (00:34:48)

Q: What does a container typically leave out compared with a virtual machine?

A: The graphical interface. It holds only the bare minimum you install. (00:35:00)

Q: State the size the instructor gave for a Windows virtual machine and for the containers used in class.

A: A Windows install is about 50 to 80 GB. The containers used in class are under two gigabytes, or even under one. (00:36:16)

Q: For what does the instructor still use virtual machines?

A: Testing the MDS install instructions, because he has to pretend he is on a Windows machine. (00:36:01)




10. Pulling and running a container: R 4.3.2 beside local R (28.1.1 Launch and run containers)
00:36:40–00:45:01

Q: What command downloads the R 4.3.2 image used in class?

A: docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2. (00:37:02)

Q: In rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, what is rocker, and what do its r-ver machines contain?

A: rocker is the organisation, and these machines have only R installed. (00:37:22)

Q: What version of R did R --version report on the instructor’s laptop?

A: R 4.6.2. (00:37:32)

Q: How often did the instructor say R updates?

A: Every six months. (00:38:10)

Q: In the pharmaceutical example, what do regulators want with a drug submission besides your code?

A: The whole compute environment, so they can reproduce your work. (00:38:23)

Q: What did the instructor say he could do to stop everyone from using git switch?

A: Give them a container with an old version of Git that predates git switch. (00:39:02)

Q: What status did docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 print when the image was already downloaded?

A: Status: Image is up to date for rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, along with a digest hash. (00:39:47)

Q: Which Git command did the instructor say docker pull sounds like?

A: git pull, because both pull something onto your computer. (00:40:33)

Q: What does the --rm flag of docker run do?

A: It deletes the container automatically when it is turned off. Otherwise you have to delete it by hand. (00:40:55)

Q: What do the -i and -t in docker run -it stand for?

A: -i is interactive, and -t is TTY, which gives you a terminal you can interact with. (00:41:48)

Q: Which ls command did the instructor use to show that single-letter flags can be chained?

A: ls -alh: all, list, and human-readable sizes. (00:41:20)

Q: What does docker run do if the image is not on your computer yet?

A: It downloads the image first. (00:42:16)

Q: What command ran R 4.3.2 interactively in a container?

A: docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2. (00:42:38)

Q: How do you start R in a terminal?

A: Type capital R. (00:42:38)

Q: What error did library(tidyverse) give inside the rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 container?

A: there is no package called 'tidyverse', because the container has only R in it. (00:43:49)




11. Know which machine you are typing on
00:45:01–00:46:44

Q: What did the instructor say is often your only visual cue for which machine you are typing on?

A: The terminal prompt. Sometimes you are given nothing but a blinking cursor, so know where you’re typing. (00:45:04)

Q: Where was the remote computer the instructor connected to from his terminal?

A: In his closet at home. (00:45:45)

text:
Date: 2026-11-19

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 1 of 5: Remember. Answer each question before you read its answer; tiers 2 to 5 build on these.

1. Class setup: Docker Desktop and pre-lecture pulls
00:00:14–00:01:41

Q: What application must be open before you run docker commands on macOS or Windows?

A: Docker Desktop. (00:00:33)

Q: How many docker pull commands were posted in Slack for students to run before the session?

A: Three. (00:00:18)

Q: What is the exercise for the day, as stated at the start of the session?

A: Practice making a branch, creating a pull request, and merging it. (00:00:43)




2. Project advice: keep the analysis simple and correct
00:01:41–00:06:05

Q: What is the “biggest tip” the instructor gives for the group project?

A: “Do not make your analysis difficult.” (00:01:56)

Q: What does the instructor warn will happen if you turn a simple task into a complicated model now?

A: “You’re going to have a very bad time in about two weeks.” (00:02:16)

Q: According to the instructor, what must be true about the model even if its accuracy is low?

A: It must be technically correct; the instructor says they “don’t care if your model is sixty percent accurate, but it does have to be technically correct.” (00:03:04)

Q: What specific modelling mistake does the instructor cite as “just wrong” when the outcome is numeric?

A: Fitting logistic regression when you’re trying to predict a numeric outcome. (00:05:24)

Q: What is this week’s individual assignment focus, and what is next week’s?

A: This week is getting everything on Git; next week is containers. (00:04:49)

Q: Over how many weeks is the group project built?

A: Three or four weeks. (00:05:37)




3. Git review: branch, commit, and push for the pull-request task
00:06:05–00:09:50

Q: What command did the instructor use to create and switch to the new branch called today?

A: git switch -c today. (00:09:17)

Q: What commit message was used on the today branch?

A: “today we are talking about containers”. (00:09:25)

Q: Which file was modified, staged, and committed in the Git workflow demo?

A: README.md. (00:09:25)

Q: What command was used to push the today branch to GitHub?

A: git push origin today. (00:09:44)

Q: What habit does the instructor recommend immediately before running git add and git commit?

A: Check the branch you are on (e.g., with git status) to confirm you are on the correct branch. (00:08:08)




4. Issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: What is the title of issue #1 in the demo repository chendaniely/2026-11-19-docker?

A: “what are we doing today?” (00:10:49)

Q: What is the title of issue #2 in the demo repository?

A: “edit the readme with today’s topic”. (00:11:37)

Q: How are issues and pull requests numbered on GitHub, according to the instructor?

A: They share the same numbering counter; an issue and a pull request are not separate counting sequences. (00:11:54)

Q: Besides tracking tasks, what else can the issue board be used for, per the instructor’s MDS example?

A: Keeping meeting notes. (00:10:49)

Q: How many issues does the class require students to create for the project?

A: Three. (00:14:23)

Q: Can a single pull request close more than one issue, and does the instructor allow this?

A: Yes; the instructor says it is okay if one pull request deals with all three issues. (00:14:23)




5. Pull-request descriptions, checkboxes, and auto-close keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: What are the two keywords that trigger auto-closing of issues when a pull request is merged?

A: closes and fixes. (00:18:33)

Q: What happens to a referenced issue when a pull request whose message contains “fixes #2” is merged?

A: The issue is automatically closed. (00:19:30)

Q: Is the auto-close keyword behaviour a feature of Git or of the GitHub service?

A: It is a GitHub service feature, not the version-control Git feature. (00:18:54)

Q: Which of the two auto-close keywords does the instructor say he “almost always use[s] all the time”?

A: fixes. (00:19:55)

Q: What Markdown notation can be used inside issues and pull requests to track individual tasks?

A: Checkboxes, e.g. - [x] item 1 and - [ ] item 2. (00:17:49)

Q: What does the instructor say about the first comment on an issue or pull request?

A: It should contain all the references and context you need, because people read the first comment rather than the later conversation. (00:16:24)




6. Merging the pull request and cleaning up branches
00:22:18–00:25:29

Q: What is the pull request number for the today branch in the demo repository?

A: #3. (00:22:53)

Q: After the pull request is merged, what two commands does the instructor run to bring the merge down to local main?

A: git switch main and git pull origin main. (00:22:25)

Q: What command drops the remote-tracking branch reference after the GitHub branch has been deleted?

A: git fetch --prune. (00:24:30)

Q: What command deletes the local branch today?

A: git branch -d today. (00:24:30)

Q: What button appears on GitHub after merging a pull request that allows you to delete the branch?

A: A “delete branch” button. (00:22:49)

Q: Is deleting the branch after a merge required in this class?

A: No; the instructor says you can keep branches as a record if you want. (00:23:16)




7. Why containers: a stable, shareable compute environment (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:25:29–00:33:21

Q: What is the stated goal of DSCI 522 regarding compute environments?

A: To create a compute environment that you can share with other people and run all of your code through, rather than relying on “this works on my machine.” (00:29:32)

Q: How does the instructor describe what a container does in one sentence?

A: “Here is a computer that I’m going to build from scratch… I’m going to give you this computer, and now you do all of your code on that computer instead of locally on your actual computer.” (00:31:49)

Q: What performance tradeoff does the instructor mention about containers?

A: There is a performance hit because there is an extra layer on top. (00:32:34)

Q: What other container tools besides Docker did the instructor name?

A: LXC, LXD, and Podman. (00:33:30)

Q: What does the instructor say you can do if you mess up inside a container?

A: Restart it; you get a new sandbox. (00:33:05)




8. Containers versus virtual machines (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:33:21–00:36:47

Q: How does the instructor describe a virtual machine?

A: A full-blown operating system install (e.g., Windows) with all the buttons and a graphical interface you log into. (00:34:48)

Q: How does the instructor describe a container relative to a virtual machine?

A: A container is a virtual machine with all the visual bits and the full operating system removed; it is the bare minimum set of things you install. (00:35:33)

Q: What approximate sizes did the instructor give for a virtual machine versus the containers used in class?

A: A virtual machine takes about 50–80 GB; the containers used in class are less than 2 GB or less than 1 GB. (00:36:16)

Q: In terms of resources, what advantage do containers have over virtual machines according to the instructor?

A: They use less disk space, memory, and compute because there is less stuff in them. (00:36:32)




9. Running the R container: docker pull and docker run (28 Using and running containers)
00:36:47–00:45:01

Q: What does docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 download?

A: An image (a pre-built “computer”) that has R version 4.3.2 installed. (00:37:05)

Q: What R version does the tag 4.3.2 in rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 select?

A: R version 4.3.2. (00:37:26)

Q: What version of R is installed on the instructor’s host machine, as shown by R --version?

A: R 4.6.2. (00:37:32)

Q: What does the --rm flag do in a docker run command?

A: When you turn off (stop) the container, it automatically deletes the container so stopped containers do not pile up. (00:40:55)

Q: What do the single-letter flags -i and -t each stand for in docker run -it?

A: -i is for interactive (gives you a terminal to type in) and -t is for TTY (connects you to a terminal you can interact with). (00:41:48)

Q: What error message does library(tidyverse) produce inside the bare rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 container?

A: “there is no package called ‘tidyverse’”. (00:43:54)

Q: What do uv or renv lock files track that a container additionally pins?

A: Lock files track package versions; a container additionally pins the system tools themselves (e.g., the version of Git installed on the machine). (00:38:46)

Q: What real-world use case does the instructor give for needing a fixed R version over multiple years?

A: Pharmaceutical clinical-trial analysis, where the analysis must remain stable for years and a drug submission requires the code plus the exact compute environment. (00:37:58)




10. Web-app containers and browser-first tools (28 Using and running containers)
00:45:01–00:54:10

Q: What technology does the instructor name as the reason many applications run in a browser?

A: Electron. (00:47:39)

Q: What URL pattern does the instructor mention for Jupyter Lab?

A: localhost:8888. (00:48:04)

Q: How does the instructor describe VS Code in relation to browsers?

A: VS Code is “really like a giant browser application that’s running.” (00:48:33)

Q: What does clicking the “Code Space” button in GitHub give you?

A: VS Code in a browser. (00:48:49)




11. Port mapping the RStudio container (28 Using and running containers)
00:54:10–00:59:14

Q: What port does the rocker/rstudio image use internally?

A: 8787. (00:55:56)

Q: What does the flag -p 8787:8787 do in the docker run command?

A: It maps port 8787 on your local computer to port 8787 inside the container, so you can reach the web app at localhost:8787. (00:56:38)

Q: What username does the instructor say to use when signing in to the containerized RStudio?

A: rstudio. (00:58:29)

Q: What does the instructor say about running multiple RStudio containers at the same time?

A: The container side is fixed at 8787, but you can redirect it to a different local port so multiple instances run simultaneously. (00:56:38)

Q: What approximate upper limit on port numbers did the instructor mention?

A: Sixty thousand. (00:57:29)




12. Environment variables and dashboard containers (28 Using and running containers)
00:59:20–01:03:00

Q: What flag is used to pass an environment variable into a running container?

A: -e. (00:59:34)

Q: What is the name of the environment variable that sets the RStudio login password?

A: PASSWORD. (00:59:34)

Q: What does the instructor say about who can access localhost:8787 when the container is running on his machine?

A: Only someone who can log into his physical machine can reach port 8787; it is not available to others. (01:00:28)

Q: What does the instructor say about containerizing a dashboard for DSCI 532?

A: The end user only needs Docker installed; they run docker run with the right flags and the application is running, without going through the entire installation process. (01:02:20)




13. Building interactively: base image and the cowsay package (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:03:00–01:08:46

Q: What command did the instructor use to start a rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 container with a bash shell instead of the default R prompt?

A: docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash. (01:04:44)

Q: Which R package did the instructor install inside the container for the demo?

A: cowsay. (01:06:08)

Q: What happens to the cowsay package when the instructor exits the container and starts it again?

A: It is gone; the container has no save state and resets to the image. (01:07:10)

Q: What does the instructor say about using a container as a safe place to try destructive commands or new packages?

A: It is a good place because it will delete the computer (the container), but it is in a container, so you just turn it off and back on and it resets. (01:07:25)




14. Writing the Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, and CMD (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:08:46–01:15:01

Q: What is the name of the file that holds the instructions for building a container, and how is it capitalised?

A: Dockerfile, with a capital D. (01:10:22)

Q: What is the first line of the Dockerfile the class wrote, and what does FROM specify?

A: FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2; FROM states the base image (starting-point machine) the new image is built on. (01:11:30)

Q: What does the RUN instruction in a Dockerfile do?

A: It specifies bash commands to run during the image build process. (01:12:44)

Q: What command does the class use inside RUN to install the cowsay package from the command line?

A: Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')". (01:12:52)

Q: What does the -e flag in Rscript -e mean?

A: It means “expression”; you give it an R expression to run from the command line. (01:09:38)

Q: What does the CMD instruction set in a Dockerfile?

A: The default command the container runs when it starts; in this class’s Dockerfile it runs cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!'). (01:13:52)

Q: What is the other Dockerfile command the instructor mentions alongside CMD, and how does he characterise its commonness?

A: ENTRYPOINT; he says it is “pretty rare.” (01:13:36)

Q: For a Python container, what two-step process does the instructor mention for installing packages at build time?

A: Use a COPY command to copy in your lock files, then run uv sync. (01:14:15)




15. Building and running the hello-cowsay image (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:15:01–01:18:44

Q: What is the full command used to build the hello-cowsay image?

A: docker build --tag hello-cowsay . (01:15:06)

Q: What does the --tag (or -t) flag do in docker build?

A: It gives the image a name (tag). (01:15:11)

Q: What does the . at the end of docker build --tag hello-cowsay . signify?

A: It tells Docker to look for the Dockerfile in the current directory (the build context). (01:15:38)

Q: What file does docker build look for by default?

A: A file called Dockerfile with a capital D. (01:15:57)

Q: What command lists all local Docker images?

A: docker images. (01:17:01)

Q: What does running docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay (without appending bash) execute?

A: The CMD from the Dockerfile, which prints the cowsay message “Hello from my first image!”. (01:17:14)

Q: What working-directory assumption does the instructor state for these build commands, in relation to milestone one?

A: Assume all commands are run from the root of the directory. (01:16:29)




16. Version pinning and wrap-up (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:18:44–01:20:39

Q: What does the instructor say about controlling tool versions in the Dockerfile?

A: You specify the version explicitly: “here’s the version I want you to install, and you’re not going to change until I tell you until I update that line.” (01:20:27)

Q: What happened to the instructor when he restarted a container without hard-version-pinning its tool versions?

A: Something updated the day before and nothing worked; he spent hours fixing the update instead of doing the actual work. (01:19:50)

Q: What does the instructor say is the next class’s topic after this introduction to containers?

A: More about containers, including how to string up multiple containers together. (01:20:39)

Q: What does the instructor say about the Dockerfile build relative to this week’s lab assignment?

A: You do not need it for this week’s lab; it is all you need for next week. (01:18:48)

text:
Date: 2026-11-19

Generated by qwen3.6-35b-a3b, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 2 of 5: Understand. Explain each answer in your own words before you read it; tier 1 (Remember) covers the facts, tiers 3 to 5 put them to use.

1. Project Advice and Course Logistics
00:00:14–00:05:43

Q: Why does the instructor advise keeping the group project’s data analysis simple and technically correct, rather than trying to build a complex or highly accurate model?

A: Because the course focuses on teaching reproducible data science workflows, not on model fitting or high accuracy. Attempting a complex model would complicate the workflow and make it difficult to manage the new tooling being introduced in the class at the same time. (00:02:03)

Q: Why shouldn’t a student use this specific course assignment as an opportunity to build a complex portfolio project?

A: There is already a significant amount of new tooling and workflow concepts being introduced in the class, and adding the burden of developing a complicated report or model simultaneously would be overwhelming and counterproductive to learning the core concepts. (00:03:27)

Q: Why is the written report considered secondary to the code and data downloading, cleaning, and EDA in this class?

A: The main point of the class is to establish a correct, reproducible data science pipeline, which encompasses all the code and data handling steps. The report is just the final output of this larger workflow, so mastering the underlying code and data processes is what truly matters for the course objectives. (00:02:41)




2. Git Branching and Pull Requests
00:06:05–00:25:29

Q: Why is it important to check which branch you are on before running git add or git commit?

A: Working in a branch workflow means that commits will only be recorded on the currently active branch. If you accidentally commit on main instead of your feature branch, you disrupt the isolation of your changes and complicate the pull request process. (00:08:08)

Q: Why do GitHub issues and pull requests share a single, unified numbering sequence instead of having separate counters?

A: Sharing a single numbering sequence makes it easy to cross-reference different items. You can use #<number> to link an issue to a pull request or another issue, creating automatic two-way references that help track how different tasks and discussions relate to each other. (00:12:07)

Q: Why should the first comment in a pull request or issue be kept up to date with all necessary references and summaries?

A: Teammates and reviewers primarily look at the first comment to understand the purpose and status of the request. The subsequent conversation is secondary, so keeping the initial description current ensures that anyone reviewing the work immediately understands the context and required actions. (00:16:40)

Q: Why is it recommended to run git fetch --prune after a pull request has been merged and the remote branch deleted?

A: Running git fetch --prune removes the tracking references to the deleted remote branch from your local repository. This cleans up your local view, preventing confusion when running commands like git log and keeping your repository references accurate. (00:24:30)




3. Introduction to Containers and Docker (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:25:33–00:46:44

Q: How do containers solve the “it works on my machine” problem that persists even when using virtual environments like uv or renv?

A: Virtual environments only manage programming language packages, but they do not control the underlying operating system or system dependencies. Containers isolate the entire operating system user space, ensuring that the exact same environment runs regardless of the host machine’s operating system or installed software. (00:29:32)

Q: Why are containers significantly more performant and smaller in size compared to virtual machines?

A: Containers are stripped-down environments that only contain the bare minimum set of software and dependencies needed for the application. Unlike virtual machines, which emulate full hardware and install a complete graphical operating system, containers share the host OS and lack visual interfaces, consuming far fewer resources. (00:35:23)

Q: Why might a remote computing platform prefer to give users a container (a sandbox) instead of direct access to install software on the host machine?

A: Remote platforms often restrict direct installation for security, stability, or to prevent users from interfering with other processes on the shared machine. Providing a container gives users a safe, isolated sandbox where they can freely experiment without risking the host system, and the container can simply be restarted if it is broken. (00:32:34)




4. Running Web Applications in Containers (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:46:47–01:03:00

Q: Why are tools like JupyterLab and RStudio Server specifically designed to run as browser-based applications inside containers?

A: Running as web apps allows these tools to be accessed from any browser while executing the actual computational heavy lifting inside a powerful remote container. This architecture separates the lightweight user interface from the compute environment, enabling seamless access to more cores and memory than a local laptop provides. (00:48:04)

Q: How can you run multiple instances of the same container application (like RStudio) on your local machine at the same time?

A: You use the -p flag in the docker run command to map different host ports to the same container port. For example, you can map your local port 8788 to the container’s internal port 8787, allowing you to open separate browser tabs for each instance without port conflicts. (00:56:38)

Q: Why and how do you use the -e flag when starting a container that has a default, auto-generated password?

A: You use the -e flag followed by the environment variable name and your desired value (e.g., -e PASSWORD="mysecurepassword") to manually set configuration parameters for the container. This is useful to avoid remembering or copying a randomly generated password, provided the container’s setup script supports that specific environment variable. (01:00:05)




5. Building Custom Containers with Dockerfile (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:03:00–01:20:39

Q: Why are changes made interactively inside a running container (like installing a package) lost when the container is stopped and restarted?

A: Containers are ephemeral and do not save their state between runs. When you stop a container, it reverts to its initial, base configuration. Any packages or modifications made during an interactive session are only temporary and are discarded once the container exits. (01:06:58)

Q: What is the purpose of the FROM instruction at the beginning of a Dockerfile, and why might you choose a larger base image?

A: The FROM instruction specifies the base image that serves as the starting point for your custom container. Choosing a larger, more established base image (like one with R pre-installed) saves time because it already includes essential compilers and system dependencies, avoiding the need to build the environment from a bare-bones Linux skeleton. (01:11:44)

Q: How does the RUN instruction in a Dockerfile differ from running the same command interactively in a terminal?

A: Commands prefixed with RUN are executed during the image building process (docker build). This permanently bakes the results of the command—such as installed packages—into the image’s layers, ensuring they are available every time a container is launched from that image, rather than just existing for a single session. (01:12:48)

Q: What is the function of the CMD instruction, and how does it interact with the docker run command?

A: The CMD instruction sets the default command that a container automatically runs when it starts. If you append a different command to the end of the docker run command (like bash), it overrides the CMD, allowing you to interact with the container directly instead of executing the predefined startup action. (01:13:52)
