title: Git pull requests and an introduction to Docker containers: review questions, tier 3 — Apply
text:
Date: 2026-11-19
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 3 of 5: Apply. Work each situation through before you read the answer; tiers 1 (Remember) and 2 (Understand) cover the facts and reasons it relies on.

1. Opening: pull the Docker images and start the branch exercise
00:00:14–00:01:41

Q: You paste a docker pull command into your terminal and get an error saying Docker can’t be found. What do you check, and in what order?

A: First check that the Docker Desktop application is open, because the Docker commands won’t work while it is off. If there is no Docker application to open, you need to install Docker. (00:00:33)

Q: You need the three course images, rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 and quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14, for an exercise later in the session. When should you start the docker pull commands, and why?

A: Start them right at the beginning, before the exercises. The downloads take around ten minutes, so pulling early means the images are ready when you need them. (00:00:18)

Q: You are doing the warm-up exercise in a fresh repository. Put these steps in order: merge the pull request, make a branch, clone the repository, open a pull request, create the repository.

A: Create the repository, clone it to your computer, make a branch, open a pull request, then merge it. This branch-and-pull-request cycle is the workflow that project-based courses use from now on. (00:00:43)




2. Project advice: keep the analysis simple
00:01:41–00:05:57

Q: Your group’s data looks roughly linear, but a teammate wants to use the project to build a neural network. What do you choose, and why?

A: Fit the simple straight-line model. This is a workflows course, not a modelling course, and an ambitious model means “you’re going to have a very bad time in about two weeks.” Simple models are not penalised. (00:02:03)

Q: Your group’s outcome variable is numeric, and a teammate proposes logistic regression because it is simple. Is that acceptable for the project?

A: No. Simplicity is fine, but the technique must be correct, and fitting logistic regression to predict a numeric outcome is just wrong. Choose a model that suits a numeric outcome, such as linear regression. (00:05:24)

Q: Your model reaches only about 60% accuracy, and you want to keep improving it so the project can go in your portfolio. What should you do?

A: Leave the course project as it is, because the results of the model don’t matter as long as the methods are technically correct. If you want a portfolio piece, build it separately, in parallel, and not in this assignment. (00:03:08)




3. Git review: working on a branch
00:06:16–00:09:50

Q: In the demo repository 2026-11-19-docker, you add a line to README.md and then git status says On branch main. You have not committed anything yet. What do you run to put this work on a branch called today?

A: Run git switch -c today. Because nothing has been committed, the uncommitted edit comes with you, and git status then reports On branch today with README.md modified. (00:08:57)

Q: You have an edited README.md on a new branch called today. In order, what do you run to review the change, commit it and send it to GitHub?

A: Run git diff to review the added line, then git add README.md, then git commit -m "today we are talking about containers", then git push origin today. GitHub then offers a pull request for the today branch. (00:09:25)

Q: Your group is actively working on several branches at once, and you are about to start a new piece of work. What do you do first, and what do you check before you git add and git commit?

A: Pull the main branch first (git pull origin main), so you aren’t changing something that is out of date. Then, right before git add, and definitely before git commit, check which branch you are on with git status. Committing on the wrong branch, or on a stale main, is the common mistake. (00:08:27)

Q: You realise you have already made commits on main that should have gone on a branch. Where do you look for a fix?

A: Use the cheat sheet in the textbook, which gives a set of commands for moving those commits around. Switching with git switch -c alone only carries work you have not committed yet. (00:07:44)




4. GitHub issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: Your repository has two issues, #1 and #2, and nothing else. You now open a pull request. What number will it get?

A: It will be #3. Issues and pull requests share one counter on GitHub, so the pull request takes the next number after the issues. (00:12:07)

Q: You write “meeting from #1” in the body of issue #2. What will someone see when they open issue #1?

A: Issue #1 shows a link back to #2. A # number creates a two-way reference, so the two items link to each other automatically. (00:13:34)

Q: Your group keeps its meeting notes in one issue, and the meeting produces action items for different people. How do you track them?

A: Write the action items in the notes issue, then create a separate issue for each one, spawned from that note. Assign each issue to the person responsible, so the board shows who is responsible for what. (00:11:08)

Q: You open a pull request in your group project and want a teammate to check your work before it goes in. How do you set the pull request up?

A: Assign yourself, because it is your pull request and that claims it as your responsibility. Add your teammate in the separate reviewer section. Some projects block changes until someone has reviewed them. (00:14:47)

Q: Your lab asks for three issues, and one branch ends up resolving all three. Do you need three separate branches and pull requests?

A: No. It does not have to be one issue, one branch, one pull request; one pull request may deal with all three issues. What matters is getting experience with the issue system. (00:14:23)

Q: While coding, you think of a stretch idea for the project (“maybe a neural net later”) that nobody will work on now. Where do you record it?

A: File it as an issue. Issues are a fine place to dump ideas and stretch goals so they aren’t lost, even if they are never acted on. (00:12:37)




5. Pull request descriptions, checkboxes and closing keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: Pull request #3 in the demo repository resolves issue #2. What do you write in the pull request’s description so that #2 closes without any extra clicks, and when does it close?

A: Write a closing keyword with the issue number, such as fixes #2. When the pull request is merged, GitHub closes the issue automatically. This is a GitHub feature, not a Git feature. (00:19:30)

Q: One pull request in your project resolves issues #4, #5 and #6. How do you avoid closing each issue by hand after the merge?

A: Write the description strategically, with a keyword for each issue, for example fixes #4, fixes #5 and fixes #6. Merging then closes all three, so you don’t go back and click close three times. (00:21:02)

Q: You could put fixes #2 in a commit message or in the pull request description. Which do you choose, and why?

A: Both work, but put it in the pull request description. A keyword in a commit message is harder to see, while one in the description is visible to everyone reading the pull request. (00:19:55)

Q: Your pull request is open but two tasks are still unfinished, and you want teammates to see that at a glance. What can you add?

A: Either mark the pull request as a draft, or add Markdown checkboxes to its description, such as - [x] item 1 and - [ ] item 2. Unchecked boxes show the work isn’t done yet. (00:17:49)

Q: Partway through a long pull request conversation, your team makes a major decision. Where do you record it?

A: Edit the first comment of the pull request so it describes the decision. Readers want to know why the pull request exists without reading the whole conversation, and project owners can usually edit other people’s comments too. (00:16:56)

Q: Your group finishes the project with some stretch-goal issues still open. Will this cost you marks?

A: No. You are not graded on having every issue closed by the end, so leaving issues open for longer-term ideas is fine. (00:21:50)




6. Cleaning up after a merge
00:22:18–00:25:19

Q: Your pull request from the today branch has just been merged on GitHub, and you are still on today locally. What do you run to get the merged work into your local main?

A: Run git switch main, then git pull origin main. The pull fast-forwards your main to the merge commit from the pull request. (00:22:25)

Q: After a merge, you want to delete the today branch on GitHub, but you have navigated away from the pull request page. Where do you go?

A: Open the branches view, find the today branch (it shows pull request #3, merged) and click the trash can. On the pull request page itself, a delete-branch button appears after merging. (00:22:53)

Q: You deleted today on GitHub, but git log --oneline --graph --all still shows (origin/today, today) next to commit 3c6d82a. What do you run to remove both labels, and what remains afterwards?

A: Run git fetch --prune to drop the stale origin/today reference, then git branch -d today to delete the local branch. The commit and the merge are still in the history; you only lose the shortcut names. (00:24:30)

Q: You expect to return to the work on a merged branch later. Why might you keep the branch instead of deleting it?

A: Keeping it means you can run git switch today instead of switching to a commit hash like 3c6d82a. Deleting branches is optional in this course, and teams differ in how they handle it. (00:25:05)




7. Why data science workflows need stable environments (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:25:29–00:30:13

Q: To avoid missing-package errors, a teammate proposes installing every package you might possibly use. What problems do you predict?

A: It wastes disk space on packages you mostly never use. Worse, packages update on different cycles, so updating everything at once can leave you with packages that are incompatible and an environment you cannot install at all. Keep the package list to the bare minimum. (00:28:04)

Q: Your code runs on your Mac, and a teammate on an ARM Windows laptop needs to run it. Is “it works on my machine” good enough, and what do you need?

A: No. Different operating systems and chips install things differently, so you need a computing environment you can share and that runs the same on their machine. That is what the course’s tooling, ending with containers, is for. (00:28:53)

Q: Your project will run for several months. Besides your teammates’ machines, which environment do you also need to keep stable?

A: Your own, over time. You need packages and tools not to upgrade underneath you during the project, as well as making the environment reproducible for other people. (00:28:26)




8. What a container is (27.2 What is a container?)
00:30:13–00:34:28

Q: You send a collaborator your uv.lock file, but they don’t use uv and worry that installing it will disturb their setup. What can you give them instead?

A: A container: a virtual computer you build from scratch with everything installed, so they run your code on it instead of on their own setup. A lock file only pins the packages and still assumes the receiving computer is set up like yours. (00:31:17)

Q: You prototype on your laptop, but the full analysis must run on a larger machine that holds all the data. How do you make sure both machines have the same compute environment?

A: Run the analysis in the same container on both machines. The container carries the whole environment, so it is identical wherever it runs. Expect a small performance cost from the extra layer. (00:32:15)

Q: You want to experiment with risky operating-system commands without damaging your laptop. Where do you run them, and what happens if you break things?

A: Run them in a container. If you blow it up, you just restart it and get a fresh sandbox. (00:33:13)

Q: The administrators of a shared remote server won’t let you install Python directly on it. How can you still get your environment there?

A: Ask for a container on the server. It gives you a sandbox to install and play in without touching the machine itself, and if you mess it up, it can be restarted fresh. (00:32:34)




9. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
00:34:31–00:36:40

Q: You need to share a full computational stack for an analysis, and you are worried about disk space and memory. Which do you choose, a container or a virtual machine, and roughly how big will it be?

A: A container. A Windows virtual machine can take 50–80 GB, while the containers used here are under two gigabytes yet still run a full stack. Containers are also lighter on memory and compute. (00:36:16)

Q: You need to test install instructions exactly as a Windows user would see them, clicking through the Windows interface. Which do you choose, a container or a virtual machine?

A: A virtual machine. It installs a full operating system with its graphical interface, which is why one is still used to test the MDS install instructions as if on Windows. A container typically has no graphical interface. (00:36:01)

Q: You start a container and expect to double-click through folders. What will you actually get, and what skill does it rely on?

A: You will get only a terminal, because containers usually have no graphical interface. You have to type commands, such as cd, to move around, which is why typing shell commands matters so much. (00:35:00)




10. Pulling and running a container: R 4.3.2 beside local R (28.1.1 Launch and run containers)
00:36:40–00:45:01

Q: You already pulled rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 before class, and you run docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 again. What do you expect to see?

A: A short output with a Digest: sha256:... hash and Status: Image is up to date for rocker/r-ver:4.3.2. Nothing is downloaded again unless a newer version of the image has been published. (00:39:51)

Q: R --version on your laptop reports R 4.6.2. You run docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2. Which R version starts, and why?

A: R 4.3.2 starts, because the container has its own R installed, separate from your laptop’s. This is how you can have two versions of R on one computer. (00:42:38)

Q: Inside docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 you type library(tidyverse), and it works fine in R on your laptop. What happens in the container, and why?

A: It fails with there is no package called 'tidyverse'. The image contains only R, and the container behaves like a separate machine that doesn’t see your laptop’s packages. (00:43:54)

Q: You leave --rm out of docker run -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2. What happens to the container when you quit?

A: It is not deleted automatically, so you have to delete it by hand later. With --rm, the container is removed as soon as it stops. (00:40:55)

Q: Your docker run command needs both interactive input and a terminal. How do you write those two single-letter flags, and what does each do?

A: Write them chained together as -it, the same way ls -alh chains flags. -i makes the session interactive, so what you type reaches the program, and -t gives you a terminal (TTY) to interact with. (00:41:48)

Q: You run docker run --rm -it with an image you never pulled. What will Docker do?

A: It downloads the image first and then runs it. docker run pulls an image that isn’t already on your machine; pulling ahead of time just saves waiting. (00:42:16)

Q: Your clinical-trials analysis must stay reproducible for years, R releases a new version about every six months, and a regulator will ask for your full compute environment. What do you hand over?

A: The container that ran the analysis. It pins the version of R itself, not just the packages that a uv or renv lock file tracks, so the analysis can be reproduced without your laptop. (00:38:46)

Q: You want everyone on a project to use a specific system tool version, for example an older Git that lacks git switch. Can a lock file enforce that? What can?

A: No: lock files only track packages, not tools installed on the system. A container can, because it ships with the tool installed. A container with a 2019 Git would mean nobody could run git switch. (00:39:02)




11. Know which machine you are typing on
00:45:01–00:46:44

Q: You quit R with q() in docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2. How do you confirm you’re back on your own computer before running the next command?

A: Look at the prompt. Your laptop’s usual prompt, such as dan@Heartsbane ..., returns once you’ve left the container. When working with containers or remote systems, the prompt is often your only visual cue. (00:45:04)

Q: You connect to a remote machine and get only a blinking cursor. How can you check you are on the machine you think you are?

A: Check the hostname in the prompt, and run whoami, which reports the username on that computer. Both tell you whose machine your commands are running on. (00:46:08)




12. Running RStudio in a container and mapping ports (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:54:10–00:58:59

Q: You want to use RStudio Server from rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 in your browser at localhost:8787. What docker run command do you use?

A: Run docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2, then open localhost:8787 in your browser. In -p host:container, the left number is the port on your computer and the right is the port inside the container, where RStudio listens on 8787. (00:57:05)

Q: You already have one RStudio container on localhost:8787 and want to run a second at the same time. How do you change the -p flag?

A: Keep the container side at 8787 and map it to a different port on your computer, for example -p 8788:8787, then browse to that port. Several things can run at once as long as each uses a different host port. (00:56:38)

Q: You open localhost:8787 and RStudio asks you to sign in, but you never set a password. Where do you find the login details?

A: The username is rstudio, and the password is printed in the container’s start-up output, as The password is set to .... (00:58:29)

Q: Your laptop has slowed to a crawl after an afternoon of starting containers without --rm. What is the likely cause, and how do you prevent it?

A: Each container uses RAM, so you probably have several machines still running. Add --rm so each container shuts down and is cleaned up when you exit it. (00:55:24)

Q: You run RStudio from rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 while your desktop RStudio uses your laptop’s R 4.6.2. Which R version does the browser RStudio show?

A: It shows the R installed in the container, 4.4.2, not your laptop’s 4.6.2. The container is effectively a separate machine with its own R. (00:58:51)




13. Passing environment variables into a container (27.2 What is a container?)
00:59:20–01:02:53

Q: The generated RStudio password is too hard to remember. How do you modify docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 so you can log in with apassword?

A: Add an environment variable with -e: docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 -e PASSWORD="apassword" rocker/rstudio:4.4.2. The image reads PASSWORD, sees that you set one, and uses it for the login. (01:00:05)

Q: You try -e PASSWORD=... with a different image, and nothing changes. What is the likely reason?

A: Not every container uses the same variables; it depends on how whoever built the image set it up. PASSWORD works for rocker/rstudio because that image reads it. Check the image’s documentation for the variables it supports. (00:59:45)

Q: You typed your RStudio container password in plain view on your own laptop. Can someone else use it to reach your RStudio?

A: Not in this setup. Port 8787 is only available on your own machine, so someone would first need access to your physical computer. (01:00:28)

Q: You build a dashboard and want a user to run it without installing your language, packages or renv snapshot. What do you give them, and what must they have?

A: Give them a container with the dashboard and everything it needs installed. They only need Docker: they docker run it with the right flags and visit the port in their browser. (01:02:20)




14. Starting from a base image and working inside it (28.1.4 Changing the containers default command)
01:03:00–01:08:19

Q: rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 opens R by default, but you want a shell inside it to try install commands. What do you run, and how do you know it worked?

A: Run docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash. Adding bash replaces the default command, and the prompt changes to the container’s, such as root@95765251a970:/#. You can still type R there to start R. (01:04:53)

Q: Inside docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash you run install.packages("cowsay") in R, and cowsay::say('hello') works. You exit, run the same command again and type library(cowsay). What happens, and why?

A: It fails with there is no package called 'cowsay'. A container has no saved state: each time it starts, it resets to how its image was built, so anything installed by hand is gone. (01:07:10)

Q: You need a custom R machine. Why choose rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 as the starting point instead of a bare Linux image?

A: The image builders have already installed R and the system pieces R needs, the equivalent of the compiler tools you installed on your laptop. Starting from it skips those steps. (01:04:00)

Q: You are designing a container and are not sure which install commands will work. How do you proceed?

A: Start a shell in the base image, go through the install steps interactively, and once they work, write them down as the instructions for building the machine. (01:05:48)




15. Running R from the command line with Rscript -e
01:08:19–01:10:18

Q: At a container’s Bash prompt you want to install cowsay without opening R, in a form you can later put in a build file. What do you type?

A: Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')". Rscript runs R from the shell, and -e means “here is an R expression”. Build steps have to be terminal commands, so this is the form you need. (01:09:27)

Q: You write Rscript -e "install.packages("cowsay")" and it breaks. What do you fix?

A: Fix the quoting: the inner quotes must differ from the outer ones. Use double quotes outside and single quotes inside: Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')". (01:09:41)

Q: You install cowsay with Rscript -e at a container’s prompt, and library(cowsay) now works there. You exit and start the container again. Will cowsay still be there?

A: No. Exiting and re-entering loses it again, because installs made in a running container are not saved. The working command has to be recorded somewhere the image is built from. (01:10:01)




16. The Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, CMD (29.2 Dockerfile command summary)
01:10:18–01:15:01

Q: You want an image based on R 4.6.2 with cowsay installed, which by default prints a cow saying “Hello from my first image!”. Write the three-line Dockerfile.

A: FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2, then RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')", then CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"]. FROM picks the starting machine, RUN runs the shell command during the build, and CMD sets the default command. (01:13:52)

Q: You are writing a Dockerfile from scratch. What do you name the file, and what goes on its first line?

A: Name it Dockerfile with a capital D, which is the convention Docker looks for. Make the first line FROM (in caps), followed by the base image. Only metadata such as a maintainer or name comes before it. (01:11:10)

Q: Your image ends with CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"], but you start it with bash after the image name. Which runs, the cow or a shell?

A: A shell. CMD is only the default command, and giving another command such as bash overrides it. (01:13:52)

Q: Your project is in Python, not R. What goes in the middle section of its Dockerfile so the container has your packages?

A: RUN commands that install uv, a COPY command that copies in your lock files, and a RUN uv sync. The packages are then installed in the image, so the machine has your compute environment ready. (01:14:15)




17. Building and running your own image (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:15:01–01:18:44

Q: Your Dockerfile is in the root of your project, and you are in that folder. What do you run to build an image named hello-cowsay?

A: docker build --tag hello-cowsay .. --tag names the image, and the . tells Docker to look in the current directory, where it expects a file named exactly Dockerfile. (01:15:38)

Q: You write build instructions in your project README. Which directory should every command assume, and why?

A: The root of the repository. Then docker build --tag ... . and the other commands can be copy-pasted without anyone changing directories in the middle. You could give the full path to a Dockerfile instead, but the root convention is what you’ll see everywhere. (01:16:11)

Q: You just ran docker build --tag hello-cowsay .. How do you confirm the image exists, and what do you run to see its default behaviour?

A: Run docker images, which lists every image on your machine, including hello-cowsay:latest. Then run docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay, which runs the CMD and prints the cow saying “Hello from my first image!”. (01:17:01)

Q: Your code works on your laptop but not in your container. How do you get inside the hello-cowsay image to investigate, and what should library(cowsay) do there?

A: Run docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash to get a shell inside the container, then start R. library(cowsay) loads, because the RUN line installed it when the image was built. (01:17:30)

Q: Put these steps in order to get a package permanently into a container: build the image, write the working command as a RUN line, test the install interactively in the base image, run the new image.

A: Test the install interactively in the base image, write the working command as a RUN line, build with docker build, then run the new image. Only after the build does every container from the image start with the package installed. (01:17:52)




18. Pinning versions, and what comes next
01:18:44–01:20:39

Q: You restart a project container that installs its tools without pinned versions, and today nothing works, though it did yesterday. What most likely happened, and how do you prevent it?

A: Something updated upstream the day before, and your container picked up the new version. Pin explicit versions in the Dockerfile, so tools change only when you edit that line. Otherwise you can spend hours fixing an update instead of doing the actual work. (01:19:55)

Q: Your project uses Quarto, and you want a year from now to get exactly the same Quarto version. What do you do in your Dockerfile?

A: Install a specific Quarto version, even an older one such as 1.10, in its install command. As long as you don’t change that line, rebuilding gives the same version. (01:19:25)

Q: Which line of your project Dockerfile keeps the R version stable, and what goes after it to keep the packages stable?

A: The FROM line pins the R version, for example FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2. After it, a section holds your renv or uv setup, which installs the locked package versions. (01:19:02)

title: Running and building containers: review questions, tier 3 — Apply
text:
Date: 2026-11-19

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 3 of 5: Apply. Work each situation through before you read the answer; tiers 1 (Remember) and 2 (Understand) cover the facts and reasons it relies on.

1. Class setup: Docker Desktop and the pre-lecture docker pull commands (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:00:14–00:01:41

Q: You are on macOS and a teammate says docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 returned an error suggesting Docker cannot be found. What do you check before retrying, and what is the fix?

A: Check that Docker Desktop is running; start it if it is not. If Docker itself is not installed, install the Docker application, then open Docker Desktop and retry the pull. The commands need the Docker app to be on before they can talk to Docker. (00:00:33)

Q: You have not run any of the three pre-lecture image downloads. Complete the setup order for getting rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, rocker/rstudio:4.4.2, and quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14 onto your computer without starting them.

A: Start Docker Desktop, then run docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2, docker pull rocker/rstudio:4.4.2, and docker pull quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook:2025-03-14. docker pull downloads the images from a registry without running them, so doing this before class avoids waiting for downloads later. (00:00:18)

Q: You run docker pull rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 and see Status: Image is up to date for rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 followed by a digest. What does that tell you, and what should you not keep doing if your goal was only to have the image available?

A: It tells you the image is already local and the digest identifies that image content, so no new download is needed. You can move on to using the image later; you do not need to keep re-running docker pull just to have it available. (00:39:51)




2. Project advice: keep the analysis simple and correct
00:01:41–00:06:05

Q: You plan to predict a continuous numeric outcome, but your draft uses a logistic regression model. What must you fix before the milestone?

A: Use a model appropriate to a numeric outcome, such as a linear regression model, instead of logistic regression. Logistic regression is wrong for predicting a numeric outcome, even if the pipeline still runs. Keep the analysis simple but technically correct. (00:05:24)

Q: Your analysis is currently a single straight-line model, and a teammate wants to add a neural network before the next milestone. What should you choose, and what risk does the other choice create?

A: Keep the analysis at the simple level needed for the workflow assignment; if the current model is a straight line, fit the straight line. Adding a complicated model now risks a very bad time in a couple of weeks because the assignment is about reproducible workflows, not model sophistication. (00:02:03)

Q: You want the project to become a portfolio piece, but you still need to complete the current workflows project. What do you do with the portfolio work?

A: Do not fold the portfolio complexity into this assignment; build the portfolio project in parallel if you really want it. The goal here is a short, correct analysis with data download, cleaning, EDA, modelling, and figures or tables. (00:03:27)




3. Git review: branch, commit, and push for the pull-request task
00:06:05–00:09:50

Q: You cloned the demo repository, edited README.md, and git status still says On branch main with no commits yet. What command moves your uncommitted work onto a new branch named today?

A: Run git switch -c today. It creates the branch and switches to it while leaving the working-tree change to README.md uncommitted so you can add it on today. After that, git status should show On branch today. (00:08:57)

Q: You are about to git add README.md in an actively collaborated repository but have not checked where you are. What two checks should you complete immediately before adding or committing, and what do they prevent?

A: Run git status to confirm you are on the intended branch, and make sure main is up to date, for example with git pull origin main before starting branch work. This prevents committing to the wrong branch and building changes on an old version of the repository. (00:08:27)

Q: Put in order the commands used to finish the README.md change after the branch today already exists.

A: Run git diff, then git add README.md, then git commit -m "today we are talking about containers", then git push origin today. The push creates the remote today branch and prints the URL for opening the pull request. (00:09:25)




4. Issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: You just finished a planning meeting with issue #1 containing the meeting note. Three action items come out of that meeting. Complete the issue-board setup.

A: Create separate issues for the action items that spawn out of the meeting note, and assign the responsible person in each issue. The meeting issue records the discussion while the separate issues track each to-do. (00:11:08)

Q: You write in issue #2: meeting from #1. What happens to that reference, and why is it useful?

A: GitHub creates a two-way link between issue #2 and issue #1, so you can move from one item to the other. It makes the project board cross-reference related items without keeping a separate document. (00:13:34)

Q: You need to record that a teammate is responsible for an issue and that another teammate must review the pull request before merging. Where do you set each?

A: Use the assign section to assign the responsible teammate to the issue or pull request, claiming responsibility. Use the reviewer section on the pull request to request the review; larger projects can block merging until a reviewer approves. (00:14:47)




5. Pull-request descriptions, checkboxes, and auto-close keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: Your pull request will fix issue #2 and close issue #1 when merged. What should you include in the pull request description to make that automatic?

A: Include a sentence ending with closes #1 and fixes #2, for example closes #1 fixes #2. When the pull request merges, GitHub auto-closes the referenced issues. This auto-close behavior is a GitHub service feature, not part of Git itself. (00:18:33)

Q: Your pull request description has a Markdown task list. How do you show that item 1 is done and item 2 is still open?

A: Write - [x] item 1 and - [ ] item 2. Teammates can see the status at a glance, especially if the pull request is not marked as a draft. (00:17:37)

Q: A teammate’s pull request later contains an important decision, but the first comment still describes the original scope. What should you do, and why?

A: Edit the first comment to include the decision and current references, because readers mainly look at the first comment to understand why the pull request exists. Project owners can edit comments to keep the primary description current. (00:16:56)




6. Merging the pull request and cleaning up branches
00:22:18–00:25:29

Q: Pull request #3 from today has merged into main, but your local main does not have the merged README.md line. What commands bring it down?

A: Run git switch main, then git pull origin main. This updates local main with the merge commit and the README change from the merged pull request. (00:22:25)

Q: After deleting the today branch on GitHub, git log --oneline --graph --all still shows a today reference. What two commands remove the remaining references, and what does each remove?

A: Run git fetch --prune to remove the remote-tracking reference origin/today, then git branch -d today to delete the local branch. The merge commit still remains in main; you are only deleting the quick branch reference. (00:24:30)

Q: You do not want to lose the shortcut git switch today, but you have already merged the pull request. What is the safe choice?

A: Keep the local today branch instead of deleting it, or use the commit hash if you need the exact commit. The merge is still recorded in main, but deleting the branch removes the convenient name for the branch tip. (00:25:05)




7. Why containers: a stable, shareable compute environment (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:25:29–00:33:21

Q: Your teammate will run the project on an ARM Windows machine while your environment is a Mac. What do you need beyond a uv or renv lock file, and why?

A: Use a container that includes the language, packages, and system tools as a shareable virtual computer. Lock files pin package versions but not the underlying tools or OS dependencies, so a different CPU architecture or operating system can still fail. (00:28:53)

Q: You prototype on your laptop and later need to run the same code on a bigger machine with access to data. What do you compare to ensure the environments match?

A: Use the same container image on both machines, so the code runs through the same virtual computer. This addresses “works on my machine” by sharing the compute environment rather than asking the other machine to install everything locally. (00:32:15)

Q: You accidentally break the container while learning Linux commands. What do you do, and why is this safer than breaking the host machine?

A: Restart the container to get a fresh sandbox. If the container gets messed up, you can discard it and start again without damaging the physical machine. (00:33:05)




8. Containers versus virtual machines (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:33:21–00:36:47

Q: You need to test an MDS installation by pretending to use a full Windows desktop with a graphical interface. Which environment do you choose, and why?

A: Choose a virtual machine. A VM installs a full operating system with the visual interface you can log into, whereas a container is a stripped-down environment without a graphical interface. (00:34:48)

Q: You need to share a lightweight analysis environment that includes R, packages, and required system tools but does not need a desktop. Which do you choose, and what size contrast supports that choice?

A: Choose a container. Containers can be under about 1–2 GB and still run the computational stack, while a virtual machine can be a 50–80 GB full operating system install. (00:36:16)

Q: Your laptop has limited RAM and you need several isolated analysis environments. What feature of containers helps compared with several full virtual machines?

A: Containers are lighter in disk, memory, and compute because they contain only the bare minimum software you install. A virtual machine includes a full operating system and graphical layer, which consumes more resources. (00:36:01)




9. Running the R container: docker pull and docker run (28 Using and running containers)
00:36:47–00:45:01

Q: You have already downloaded rocker/r-ver:4.3.2. What command starts an interactive container where R opens, and what do the flags do?

A: Run docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2. --rm removes the container when it stops; -it chains -i interactive and -t TTY so R runs as an interactive terminal. (00:40:55)

Q: Inside that container, library(tidyverse) returns an error. What does that prove, and how would you test the host version?

A: It proves the container is a separate machine whose R does not have tidyverse installed, even if your host has it. Open another terminal on the host and run library(tidyverse) or start host R to compare the two environments. (00:43:54)

Q: Your host R --version says 4.6.2, but the container starts R 4.3.2. What is the advantage of being able to run both at once?

A: You can use an older R version for a stable project without changing the host R. This supports reproducible analyses that require a fixed tool version, not just fixed package versions. (00:37:43)

Q: You type docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 but the image is not local. What happens?

A: Docker downloads the image first, then runs the container. docker run can pull the image if it does not already exist locally. (00:42:16)




10. Web-app containers: RStudio and browser-first tools (28 Using and running containers)
00:45:01–00:54:10

Q: You need to give a teammate the same RStudio interface without installing RStudio on their machine. What do you run, and where do they access it?

A: Run the rocker/rstudio image with port mapping, for example docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2, and open http://localhost:8787 in a browser. The container runs RStudio Server as a web app. (00:58:19)

Q: You see JupyterLab open at localhost:8888 in a browser. What does that interface imply about where the compute is running?

A: It implies Jupyter is running as a web app on another machine or container, with the browser as the interface. The same idea applies to containerized or remote compute: you connect to a browser interface rather than double-clicking a local desktop application. (00:48:04)

Q: You click the Codespaces button in GitHub and see VS Code open in a browser. What does that tell you about using the same interface on a different machine?

A: It shows that a browser-first application can run on a different machine or in a container while giving the same interface. The browser connection is the way to reach the compute environment you are working on. (00:48:49)




11. Port mapping the RStudio container (28 Using and running containers)
00:54:10–00:59:14

Q: You run docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 rocker/rstudio:4.4.2. What does -p 8787:8787 mean, and what URL do you open?

A: It maps port 8787 on your local computer to port 8787 inside the container, where RStudio Server listens. Open http://localhost:8787 to reach the container’s RStudio. (00:56:57)

Q: You already have one RStudio container mapped to local port 8787 and want a second one at the same time. How do you choose the second command?

A: Keep the container port 8787 on the right side, but choose a different host port on the left, such as -p 8788:8787, then open http://localhost:8788. The container port is fixed by the application; the host port is the local connection point. (00:56:38)

Q: You open localhost:8787 but see the local RStudio desktop instead of the container. What should you check?

A: Confirm the container is running with the -p 8787:8787 mapping and that the browser is pointing to the host port mapped to the container. Compare R versions: local RStudio uses the host R, while containerized RStudio uses the R version inside the image. (00:58:41)




12. Environment variables and running dashboards in containers (28 Using and running containers)
00:59:20–01:03:00

Q: Your first docker run of rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 prints a random password such as The password is set to .... How do you rerun it with a known password?

A: Add -e PASSWORD="apassword" to the same docker run command, for example docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 -e PASSWORD="apassword" rocker/rstudio:4.4.2. The image uses the PASSWORD environment variable to set the login password. (01:00:05)

Q: You set PASSWORD="apassword" and map -p 8787:8787. Is the port automatically reachable by anyone on the network? What did the session check?

A: No; the check was that localhost:8787 is only reachable by someone who can log into the host machine. Port mapping connects to the local machine, so access to the host is still required. (01:00:28)

Q: You are containerizing a dashboard for an end user who only has Docker. What advantage does the container give the end user?

A: The end user only needs Docker and the right docker run flags; all packages and environment setup are already inside the container. They avoid installing the environment, Quarto, and other dependencies manually. (01:02:20)




13. Building interactively: base image and the cowsay package (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:03:00–01:08:46

Q: You want to test install commands for an R image before writing a Dockerfile. What command starts the base image with a shell instead of starting R?

A: Run docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash. The trailing bash replaces the image’s default R command, giving you the container’s terminal prompt. (01:04:44)

Q: Inside that shell, you run Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" and then exit. You start the same image again and run R. Why is cowsay missing?

A: The container has no save state; exiting and restarting returns to the original image. Packages installed interactively are not persisted unless you record the install command in a Dockerfile and build a new image. (01:07:10)

Q: You are deciding whether to run a risky rm command on your laptop or in a container. Where do you run it, and why?

A: Run it in a container because the sandbox can be discarded and restarted without damaging the host machine. If the container gets messed up, turning it back on resets it to the built image. (01:07:37)




14. Writing the Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, and CMD (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:08:46–01:15:01

Q: You have tested Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" inside rocker/r-ver:4.6.2. What two lines do you write in the Dockerfile to start from that image and install the package at build time?

A: Write FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 and RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" . FROM sets the base image, and RUN executes the shell command during the image build. Use double quotes on the outside and single quotes inside for the R expression. (01:12:44)

Q: You want the new image to print a cow message by default when someone runs it. What Dockerfile line do you add?

A: Add CMD ["Rscript", "-e", "cowsay::say('Hello from my first image!')"]. CMD sets the default command a container runs when it starts, replacing the base image’s default R command. (01:13:52)

Q: Your Python project already has uv.lock. How did the session say to install the Python packages inside a container image?

A: Use COPY to bring the lock files into the image, then run uv sync with a RUN line so packages are installed during the build. That bakes the compute environment into the image instead of installing it on each host. (01:14:15)




15. Building and running the hello-cowsay image (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:15:01–01:18:44

Q: You are in the project root where Dockerfile lives. What command builds and names the image hello-cowsay, and what does . mean?

A: Run docker build --tag hello-cowsay .. The . is the current directory, or build context, where Docker looks for the Dockerfile; --tag names the image. (01:15:38)

Q: After building, how do you confirm the image exists locally?

A: Run docker images and look for hello-cowsay:latest in the image list. It shows the local image ID and disk usage. (01:17:01)

Q: You run docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay and see the cow message without entering R. Why?

A: The Dockerfile’s CMD runs Rscript -e ... and prints the message, so the container starts, runs that command, and exits. To inspect the environment instead, run docker run --rm -it hello-cowsay bash and then test library(cowsay). (01:17:52)




16. Version pinning and wrap-up (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:18:44–01:20:39

Q: Your Dockerfile installs Quarto but leaves the version unpinned. A year later, a new Quarto release appears. What likely happens if the install command is pinned and you do not edit it?

A: If the install command is pinned to a version, it continues installing that same version until you explicitly update the line. Pinning prevents an unexpected tool update from silently changing a validated environment. (01:19:35)

Q: You remember an environment broke because a tool updated while the Dockerfile did not hard-pin versions. What change prevents that?

A: Pin the tool versions explicitly in the Dockerfile, for example by installing a specific Quarto or other tool version. The Dockerfile becomes the control point: the version does not change until you edit that install command. (01:20:27)

Q: You need to support an older Quarto 1.10 in a project while the latest version is 1.11. How do you choose the image behavior?

A: Write the install command in the Dockerfile to use Quarto 1.10, not the floating latest version. This lets you build and share the same older tool version for the project. (01:19:14)

title: Git Workflows and Containerization: review questions, tier 4 — Analyze
text:
Date: 2026-11-19

Generated by qwen3.6-35b-a3b, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 4 of 5: Analyze. Take each one apart yourself before you read the answer; tiers 1 to 3 cover the facts, reasons and steps it relies on.

1. Git Branching and Pull Requests Workflow
00:06:05–00:25:29

Q: Break down the lifecycle of the today branch in the demo repository: trace the sequence of Git commands used to isolate the change, push it, and then clean up both the remote and local tracking references after the pull request was merged. How do the outputs of git log --oneline --graph --all differ before and after running git fetch --prune followed by git branch -d today?

A: The workflow starts by switching to a new branch (git switch -c today) to isolate the edit, then staging and committing it before pushing to the remote. After the pull request is merged into main, the remote branch is deleted on GitHub, and running git fetch --prune removes the origin/today remote tracking reference from the local repository. Finally, git branch -d today deletes the local branch reference. Before pruning, git log shows the origin/today pointer still attached to the commit, but after running both cleanup commands, only the merged commit history on main remains visible with the remote branch pointer gone. (00:22:41)

Q: Examine the relationship between GitHub Issues and pull requests as demonstrated in class: how do the shared numbering system, the cross-reference syntax, and the closing keywords work together to transform a Git repository into a project management system?

A: GitHub assigns a single sequential number to both issues and pull requests, allowing them to reference each other directly using #<number>. When a pull request description includes fixes #<number> or closes #<number>, GitHub creates a two-way link between the PR and the issue, so viewing one shows the other. Upon merging that pull request, the keyword triggers an automatic state change that closes the linked issue. This integration replaces external tracking documents by keeping task assignments, status updates, and solution records in a single, interconnected version-controlled workspace. (00:12:07)




2. Introduction to Containers and Docker (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:25:33–00:46:44

Q: Differentiate between virtual environments, virtual machines, and Docker containers based on their level of isolation and resource consumption as explained in class. How does this distinction solve the problem of running different versions of the same software on one machine?

A: Virtual environments isolate only programming language packages on the host OS, making them extremely lightweight but porous to host-level dependencies. Virtual machines emulate entire hardware and operating systems, providing maximum isolation but consuming gigabytes of disk space and memory. Containers sit in the middle by virtualizing the OS user space, sharing the host kernel while keeping the filesystem and installed software completely separate. This structure allows a container to run a specific software version (like R 4.3.2) alongside the host version (R 4.6.2) without conflicts, ensuring reproducible environments regardless of the physical machine’s configuration. (00:28:50)




3. Running Web Applications in Containers (28 Using and running containers)
00:46:47–01:03:00

Q: Trace how the docker run command translates configuration flags into accessible application behavior when launching RStudio Server inside a container. How do the -p and -e flags modify the container’s network and authentication state compared to its default settings?

A: By default, the RStudio container image exposes port 8787 internally but requires a randomly generated password for security. The -p 8787:8787 flag maps the container’s internal port to the host machine’s localhost, routing browser traffic from the user directly to the application. The -e PASSWORD="value" flag intercepts the container’s startup environment variables to override the default credentials with a user-defined password. Together, these flags transform an isolated, terminal-based container into a locally accessible, password-protected web application without exposing it to the wider network. (00:55:41)




4. Building Custom Containers with Dockerfile (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:03:00–01:20:39

Q: Break down the workflow for persisting software installations into a Docker image. How do the Dockerfile instructions FROM, RUN, and CMD each contribute to transforming a temporary container session into a permanent, reproducible computational environment?

A: The FROM instruction establishes the base image, providing the starting OS and pre-installed tools like R. The RUN instruction executes shell commands during the image build phase, permanently baking software installations into the new image’s layers so they survive container restarts. Finally, CMD defines the default command that executes automatically when a container from this image starts, replacing the base image’s original startup behavior. This sequence replaces manual, ephemeral terminal sessions with a version-controlled blueprint that guarantees identical environments across any machine. (01:08:46)

title: Git issues and pull requests, and an introduction to Docker containers: review questions, tier 5 — Evaluate
text:
Date: 2026-11-19
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 5 of 5: Evaluate. Decide and justify your verdict before you read the answer; the criteria are the ones given in class.

1. Project advice: keep the analysis simple
00:01:41–00:05:57

Q: A teammate says the group project is their “time to shine” and proposes a neural net when a straight-line model fits the question. Judge the proposal.

A: Reject it and fit the straight-line model. This is a workflows course, not a model-fitting course, and the instructor warned “you’re going to have a very bad time in about two weeks if you do that.” The report is not the point of the class, and the workflow work still has to get done. (00:02:16)

Q: A group’s model reaches only 60% accuracy. The model itself is logistic regression, and it predicts a numeric outcome. Assess whether the submission meets the course’s standard.

A: It does not, but the accuracy is not the reason. Model results do not matter, but the techniques must be correct data science. Using logistic regression to predict a numeric outcome is “just wrong.” (00:05:24)

Q: A student wants to turn the group project into a polished portfolio piece with a more elaborate report. Recommend whether to do that in this assignment.

A: Don’t do it in this assignment. If you want a portfolio project, build it in parallel. A lot is happening in this class, and you don’t want to be dealing with a complicated report at the same time. (00:03:27)




2. Git review: working on a branch
00:06:16–00:09:50

Q: In the 2026-11-19-docker repository, the instructor edited README.md while still on main and had not committed. A student says the edit is now stuck on main. Assess running git switch -c today at that point.

A: It is fine. Nothing had been committed yet, so the uncommitted edit moved to the new today branch, and git status then showed On branch today with README.md modified. Only commits already made on main need the textbook’s cheat sheet of commands to move them. (00:08:57)

Q: A teammate in an active group project starts editing and committing straight away, without checking which branch they are on or pulling main. Critique this habit.

A: It is risky in a branch workflow with several people and several branches. Look at your branch right before git add, and definitely before git commit, so commits don’t land on the wrong branch. Pull main first, so you aren’t making changes to something that is out of date. (00:08:27)




3. GitHub issues as a project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: The lab asks for three issues, and a group resolves all three with a single pull request instead of one branch and one pull request per issue. Is that acceptable?

A: Yes. “One issue, one branch, one pull request” is only one extreme and isn’t always the case. The class said explicitly that one pull request may deal with all three issues. The aim is experience with the project-board system. (00:14:23)

Q: A group keeps its meeting notes and the to-do list it assigns from them in a shared Google Doc instead of GitHub issues. Recommend whether to switch.

A: Switch to issues. They record who is responsible for what, and action items can become separate issues spawned from the meeting-notes issue. Because # references link both ways automatically, everything stays connected to the pull requests that do the work, “and you’re not relying on a Google Doc of notes.” (00:15:48)




4. Pull request descriptions, checkboxes and closing keywords
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: Halfway through a pull request’s discussion, the team makes a major decision and records it only in a later comment. Judge whether that is enough.

A: It is not enough. Update the first comment so it describes the decision. Readers want to know “why does this thing exist?” from the top, and “no one’s really going to care about the conversation.” The first comment is editable precisely because a pull request evolves. (00:16:56)

Q: Pull request #3 in 2026-11-19-docker resolves issues #1 and #2. A teammate plans to merge it and then close both issues by hand, instead of writing closes #1 fixes #2 in the description. Which approach is better?

A: Write the keywords in the pull request description. Merging the pull request then closes the issues automatically, so you don’t have to go back and close each one, and the issues tab shrinks as work merges. A commit message also works, but keywords there are harder to see. (00:21:02)

Q: A group decides it must close every issue, including stretch-goal ideas, before submitting the milestone. Assess that plan.

A: It is unnecessary. The course does not grade on whether all issues are closed by the end of class. Issues for longer-term ideas and stretch goals are fine to leave open, and the point is to practise with the system. (00:21:50)




5. Cleaning up after a merge
00:22:18–00:25:19

Q: After pull request #3 is merged, a teammate wants to keep the today branch on GitHub as a record. Another insists that branches must always be deleted. Decide between them.

A: Both are acceptable in this course. You are not required to delete branches, and keeping them as a record is allowed. Teams and companies handle Git differently, and the class’s way is only one way. (00:23:16)

Q: A student refuses to run git fetch --prune and git branch -d today because they fear it will erase the merged work from history. Is the fear justified?

A: No. The git log --oneline --graph --all output still shows commit 3c6d82a and the merge commit. You lose only the shortcut name, so you would switch by hash instead of git switch today. Cleaning up is worth it when too many references make the Git state hard to read. (00:24:30)




6. Why data science workflows need stable environments (27.1 Documenting and loading dependencies)
00:25:29–00:30:13

Q: To avoid “missing package” errors, a teammate proposes installing every data science package they might ever need into the project environment. Critique the proposal.

A: Reject it and keep the package list to the bare minimum. Installing packages you don’t use wastes disk space. Packages also update on different cycles, so a big environment can end up impossible to install all at once. (00:28:04)

Q: A teammate defends their code with “it works on my machine,” even though a groupmate on a Windows ARM laptop can’t run it. Is that defence acceptable?

A: No. The goal of the class is a compute environment you can share, so that others can run the same analysis. “It works on my machine” doesn’t work when a teammate can’t run your code, and teammates may have a different operating system or even a different chip architecture. (00:29:43)




7. What a container is (27.2 What is a container?)
00:30:13–00:34:28

Q: You send a collaborator your uv.lock file, but they don’t use uv and don’t want to install it. Assess whether the lock file alone is enough to share your environment.

A: It is not enough. A lock file only lets someone with the right tools install your packages. Installing uv might mess up other things on their machine, and their computer may be set up differently. A container gives everyone the same virtual computer, so all of you work on the same machine despite different hardware. (00:31:17)

Q: A student wants to learn Linux by experimenting with system commands, but is worried about breaking their laptop. Recommend where they should do it.

A: Do it in a container. A container is a sandbox: if you mess it up, you restart it and get a fresh one. The cost is a performance hit from the extra layer, which is acceptable for experimenting. (00:33:13)




8. Containers versus virtual machines (27.3 Contrasting containers with virtual machines)
00:34:31–00:36:40

Q: A group plans to share its analysis environment as a full Windows virtual machine instead of a container. Judge the plan.

A: A container is the better choice. A Windows VM can take 50–80 GB because it carries the full operating system and graphical interface. The containers used in class are a couple of gigabytes or less and still run a full computational stack, so they use less disk, memory and compute. VMs still have uses, such as testing the MDS install on Windows. (00:36:16)




9. Pulling and running a container: R 4.3.2 beside local R (28.1.1 Launch and run containers)
00:36:40–00:45:01

Q: A pharmaceutical team running a multi-year clinical trial analysis plans to rely on renv.lock alone for its regulatory submission. Assess the plan.

A: It is insufficient. R updates every six months, and the regulator needs to reproduce the full compute environment, not only the package versions. Lock files track packages but not the tool itself, such as the version of R. Handing over the container that ran the analysis pins R and the other system tools too. (00:38:46)




10. Know which machine you are typing on
00:45:01–00:46:44

Q: After working in a container and on a remote machine, a student is faced with a bare blinking cursor and runs a destructive command without checking anything. Critique this.

A: It is dangerous. With containers and remote systems, your prompt is sometimes the only cue to where you are typing. Check the prompt, or run whoami to see the username, before running anything, so the command doesn’t run on the wrong machine. (00:46:08)




11. Running RStudio in a container and mapping ports (28.1.3 Mapping ports to containers with web apps)
00:54:10–00:58:59

Q: While practising, a student leaves --rm off their docker run commands and starts several containers through the day. Judge this practice.

A: It is a mistake. Each running container takes up RAM, so you end up with “five computers” running and a laptop that stops working well. --rm shuts down and deletes the machine when you exit. (00:55:24)

Q: A student wants two RStudio containers at once and gives both -p 8787:8787. Assess the plan.

A: It won’t work as written. Inside each container RStudio runs on 8787, but each must be mapped to a different port on your machine, with the host port on the left of the :. Multiple things can run at the same time only because they use different host ports. (00:56:38)




12. Passing environment variables into a container (27.2 What is a container?)
00:59:20–01:02:53

Q: The instructor ran docker run --rm -p 8787:8787 -e PASSWORD="apassword" rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 with the password visible on screen. Was that acceptable?

A: Yes, in that context. The container’s port 8787 is only reachable from the instructor’s physical machine, so someone who can’t log into that machine can’t reach the RStudio login. (01:00:16)

Q: For a dashboard project, a group debates two options: shipping install instructions (install renv, restore the snapshot, and so on) or shipping a container that users start with docker run. Recommend one.

A: Ship the container. You have done all the installation already, so the end user only needs Docker and a docker run command with some flags, then visits the port. In effect you give them a computer you built from scratch, although the instructor acknowledged that installing Docker is itself a pretty big lift. (01:02:20)




13. Starting from a base image and working inside it (28.1.4 Changing the containers default command)
01:03:00–01:08:19

Q: A group’s README tells users to start rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 and install the needed packages by hand each time before running the analysis. Judge the approach.

A: It is a poor approach. A container has no saved state: cowsay, installed by hand, was gone after a restart. Making users repeat installs every time is painful, for example a 15-minute tidyverse install to run a 30-second analysis. The steps belong in the image’s build instructions. (01:08:19)

Q: A student writes a whole Dockerfile from memory without testing any command first. Another opens docker run --rm -it rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash, tries each install, and writes it down only once it works. Which workflow is better?

A: The second is better. Going through the steps interactively first, then documenting those that work, gives you instructions for building the machine from scratch that you know succeed. The bash at the end of the command gives a shell instead of the default R prompt, so you can do exactly this. (01:05:48)




14. The Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, CMD (29.1 Building container images from Dockerfile’s)
01:10:18–01:15:01

Q: One teammate wants the Dockerfile to start FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2. Another insists on a bare-minimum Linux base with every tool installed by hand, for performance. Decide.

A: rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 is a reasonable choice. It already has R and the system pieces R needs, which saves steps. Disk space is relatively cheap, so a beefier base image is acceptable. Building from bare Linux is possible and teaches you a lot, but the instructor suggested it as a learning project for a break, not as a project requirement. (01:12:15)




15. Building and running your own image (29.1.2 Build your first image)
01:15:01–01:18:44

Q: A group’s milestone instructions say “cd docker/ and then run docker build --tag hello-cowsay .”, with other commands run from other folders. Critique the instructions.

A: They fall short of the class’s convention. Commands are assumed to run from the root of the repository, which is why docker build --tag hello-cowsay . uses . to mean “the Dockerfile right here”. Instructions should be copy-pasteable without changing directories partway through. (01:16:29)




16. Pinning versions, and what comes next (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:18:44–01:20:39

Q: A pull request adds a Quarto install to the project Dockerfile without specifying a version, “so we always get the latest.” Would you approve it?

A: No. Ask for an explicit version. The instructor restarted a container without hard-pinned versions, something had updated the day before, and nothing worked, so hours went into fixing the update instead of the real work. With a pinned install line, you stay on the same versions a year from now and change them only when you decide to. (01:19:55)

text:
Date: 2026-11-19

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 5 of 5: Evaluate. Decide and justify your verdict before you read the answer; the criteria are the ones given in class.

1. Pre-lecture Docker setup (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:00:14–00:01:41

Q: Judge whether a teammate can run the three pre-lecture docker pull commands with Docker Desktop closed, because the command will download the needed image automatically.

A: Do not approve it. The instructor said to make sure Docker Desktop is open before running these commands; otherwise Docker cannot be found or the commands will tell you to turn it on. The pre-lecture pulls assume Docker is already running. (00:00:33)




2. Project scope and correctness
00:01:41–00:06:05

Q: A group proposes replacing a simple straight-line model with a neural network because they want the DSCI 522 project to be a portfolio piece. Assess whether that plan is acceptable.

A: Reject the plan for this course project. The instructor’s main tip is not to make the analysis difficult and not to turn the assignment into a portfolio project; DSCI 522 is about workflows, not model fitting. The model can be simple, but the data science and machine-learning techniques must still be technically correct. (00:03:27)

Q: A teammate’s plan keeps the analysis short but fits logistic regression to predict a numeric outcome. Decide whether you would accept that analysis.

A: No, accept it only if that mistake is fixed. The class criterion is that model results do not have to be impressive, but techniques must be technically correct; fitting logistic regression to a numeric outcome is called out as wrong. Simplicity is allowed, correctness is not optional. (00:05:24)




3. Branch workflow before committing
00:06:05–00:09:50

Q: A teammate plans to git add and git commit on a branch without first checking git status, because they believe they are still on today. Judge that plan for the group project.

A: The plan is unsafe and should not be accepted. In a branch workflow, the instructor said to check the branch you are on right before git add and definitely before git commit. This habit prevents committing the README.md change to the wrong branch, such as main. (00:08:08)

Q: A plan skips pulling main before creating a feature branch because the teammate has already cloned the repository. Assess that plan in an active team environment.

A: It is not acceptable in an active team environment. The instructor said to pull main so everything is up to date before making changes; otherwise you may be working from an outdated branch. This is a new concern once multiple people are working in multiple branches. (00:08:27)




4. Using GitHub issues as the project board
00:09:50–00:16:17

Q: A team proposes to keep the meeting plan and responsible parties in a shared Google Doc instead of creating GitHub issues. Judge that approach.

A: Do not recommend it for this course’s Git workflow. Issues are the lightweight project board for tracking what is happening and who is responsible, and the instructor explicitly contrasted this with relying on a Google Doc of notes. Issues also create shared numbers that can cross-reference pull requests. (00:15:48)

Q: A teammate argues that pull request #3 should be rejected because it is associated with both issue #1 and issue #2. Decide whether that objection is correct.

A: The objection is not correct under the class criterion. One pull request does not have to fix exactly one issue; the instructor said it is okay for one pull request to deal with all three required issues. The issues and pull requests are on the same numbering system precisely so they can be cross-referenced. (00:14:23)




5. Pull-request description and auto-close
00:16:17–00:22:18

Q: A pull request’s first comment says only “see conversation below” and leaves out the issue numbers, while the later comments explain what the PR changes. Judge whether that description meets the class standard.

A: It does not meet the standard. The instructor said the first comment should contain all the references and context because readers focus on what is happening and why the item exists, not on the later conversation. If a decision changes later, update the first comment rather than relying on the thread. (00:16:40)

Q: A team plans to merge the pull request and then manually close issue #1 and issue #2 one by one. Assess that plan when the pull request message can say closes #1 fixes #2.

A: The manual-closing plan is unnecessary and less aligned with the class workflow. The instructor explained that when a sentence in the pull request ends with closes or fixes and an issue number, GitHub auto-closes that issue when the pull request merges. Writing the message strategically avoids going back and closing each issue. (00:19:30)




6. Merging and branch cleanup
00:22:18–00:25:29

Q: A teammate claims that after pull request #3 is merged, the team must delete the today branch on GitHub and locally, or the merge is not complete. Judge that claim.

A: The claim is too strong. The instructor said the class is not saying you have to delete branches; you may keep them as a record. Cleanup such as deleting the branch and removing references is a way to avoid confusing Git states, but it is not the only valid way teams work. (00:23:16)




7. Choosing a shareable compute environment (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:25:29–00:33:21

Q: A teammate proposes installing every package the team might use, even unused ones, to avoid having to adjust the package list later. Judge that approach for the group project.

A: Do not approve it. The instructor said the package list should be the bare minimum of what the project needs, because installing unused packages wastes disk space and can create update-compatibility problems later. The goal is a stable, shareable environment, not a maximal one. (00:27:38)




8. Container versus virtual machine (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:33:21–00:36:47

Q: Assess whether a full Windows virtual machine with a graphical desktop is a better shared environment than a container for a data-science project that must be shared with teammates.

A: A container is the better fit for this course’s goal. The instructor contrasted a virtual machine as a full operating system with visual components, which can be 50–80 GB, with a container as a stripped-down, lighter environment that still runs the computational stack. Containers are preferred when the criterion is a shareable, lower-resource compute environment. (00:36:32)




9. Running the R container (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:36:47–00:45:01

Q: A teammate runs docker run -it rocker/r-ver:4.3.2 without --rm, leaving stopped R containers on the machine. Assess whether that command matches the class workflow.

A: It does not match the demonstrated workflow. The class command includes --rm so Docker deletes the container when it stops; otherwise you have to manually delete stopped containers. This keeps repeated practice from piling up container instances. (00:40:55)




10. Port mapping for RStudio (28 Using and running containers)
00:54:10–00:59:14

Q: A plan tries to run two rocker/rstudio:4.4.2 containers at the same time using -p 8787:8787 for both. Judge whether that plan will let both be used in a browser.

A: It is not a good plan. The container side is fixed at 8787, but the local host port can be redirected to a different number so multiple containers can run at the same time. One host port cannot serve both, so the second container should use a different host port mapping. (00:57:05)




11. Environment variables and dashboard sharing (28 Using and running containers)
00:59:20–01:03:00

Q: A 532 dashboard plan asks end users to install the environment, Quarto, and packages on their own machines. Judge that plan when the class says the dashboard can be put into a container.

A: The plan is not the recommended one. The instructor said a dashboard can be containerized so the end user only needs Docker and can run docker run with the right flags; the heavy installation is already done inside the container. That makes the shared compute environment easier to reproduce. (01:02:20)




12. Testing commands before writing the Dockerfile (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:03:00–01:08:46

Q: A teammate writes RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" into the Dockerfile before ever running the command inside the container. Assess that workflow.

A: It is not the workflow the class used. The instructor’s method is to start the base image with bash, try the install commands interactively, and only after they work document them in the Dockerfile with RUN. That reduces troubleshooting by recording commands that are known to work. (01:06:01)




13. Writing the Dockerfile: FROM, RUN, and CMD (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:08:46–01:15:01

Q: A proposed Dockerfile for the hello-cowsay image has FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 and a CMD that calls cowsay::say(...), but no RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')" line. Judge whether it will satisfy the class goal.

A: It does not satisfy the goal. The RUN line is what installs cowsay into the image during the build; without it, the container is just the base rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 image. A CMD can set the default command, but it does not install the package. (01:12:44)




14. Building and running the hello-cowsay image (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:15:01–01:18:44

Q: A teammate runs docker build --tag hello-cowsay . from a subfolder that does not contain the project’s Dockerfile, expecting Docker to find the Dockerfile at the repository root. Judge that plan.

A: It is not acceptable as stated. The . in docker build is the current directory / build context, so Docker looks for the Dockerfile there. The class convention is to assume commands are run from the root of the directory, as in the milestone-one instructions. (01:16:29)




15. Version pinning in the Dockerfile (29 Customizing and building containers)
01:18:44–01:20:39

Q: A proposed Dockerfile installs Quarto and other tools without version numbers, so the next build can pick up newly released versions automatically. Judge whether that meets the class standard.

A: It does not meet the standard. The instructor warned that unpinned tool versions can update without you saying so and can break a previously working build; he gave an example where a restart without hard version pinning met an overnight update. Pin the version in the install line so the environment remains stable until you deliberately change it. (01:19:55)
