title: Building Reproducible Compute Environments with Docker and uv
text:
1. Dockerfile Layer Caching and Structure

Layer caching: Every instruction in a Dockerfile creates a new image layer. Docker reuses cached layers if their inputs haven’t changed. To optimize builds, place heavy, infrequently changing steps (e.g., installing system packages or running uv sync) at the top, and place frequently changing steps (e.g., COPYing project code) at the bottom. Changing a middle step forces a rebuild of all subsequent layers, which can be slow for large dependencies.
WORKDIR: Sets the container’s working directory. Using WORKDIR /workspace ensures that subsequent COPY, RUN, and CMD commands execute relative to that path, and it becomes the default directory when the container starts.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building Reproducible Compute Environments with Docker and uv
text:
2. Pinning Dependencies with uv

pyproject.toml declarations: This file declares dependencies. By default, uv add writes lower bounds (e.g., pandas>=3.1.1). Lower bounds are flexible but risky for long-running analyses because a future uv lock --upgrade could pull in a breaking major version.
Exact pins (==): Data analysis projects should use exact pins (e.g., cowsay==6.1) to guarantee reproducibility. Configure uv to write exact pins automatically by adding [tool.uv] add-bounds = "exact" to pyproject.toml.
uv.lock vs pyproject.toml: uv.lock always records exact versions and is used for actual installations. However, external tools (like pip or CI systems) and humans reading the code reference pyproject.toml. Exact pins in pyproject.toml ensure the declared versions match the locked versions, making the analysis transparent to reviewers.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building Reproducible Compute Environments with Docker and uv
text:
3. Cross-Platform Virtual Environments in Containers

The mounting conflict: When running docker run -v "$(pwd):/workspace", the host’s .venv folder is mounted into the container, hiding the container’s own .venv. If uv sync runs inside the container, it will recreate the environment for the host’s OS/architecture, breaking cross-platform compatibility.
Fix with ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT: Add ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv to the Dockerfile before running uv sync. This forces uv to install packages in /opt/venv (outside the mounted directory), preserving the Linux-compiled packages and ignoring the host’s .venv.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building Reproducible Compute Environments with Docker and uv
text:
4. Volume Mounting for Live Development

-v "$(pwd):/workspace": Mounts the host’s current directory into the container at /workspace. This creates a live sync, meaning edits to code on the host are immediately visible inside the container without rebuilding the image.
Separation of concerns: Instead of COPYing entire projects into the image (which requires constant rebuilds and snapshots), volume mounting separates the static compute environment (built in the image) from the dynamic source code (mounted at runtime). This mirrors how you would work on your local machine while keeping dependencies isolated.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building Reproducible Compute Environments with Docker and uv
text:
5. Docker Compose for Reproducible Commands

docker-compose.yml: A YAML file that replaces long, error-prone docker run command-line flags. It stores parameters like build, image, volumes, and ports in a version-controlled file, making workflows easier to document, share, and reproduce.
Usage: Run docker compose build to build images and docker compose up to start containers. Compose reads paths natively across OSes, avoiding shell-specific syntax issues like /$(pwd) in Git Bash.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building Reproducible Compute Environments with Docker and uv
section: Setting up the local uv project
text:
Setting up the local uv project
uv init --bare          # Initialize an empty Python project
uv add cowsay           # Add a dependency; with `add-bounds = "exact"`, writes `==`
uv sync                 # Install dependencies into .venv
uv run hello.py         # Execute a Python script using the project's environment
These commands set up the local development environment that will later be replicated inside the container.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building Reproducible Compute Environments with Docker and uv
text:
Building the Docker image
docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker .   # Build image from Dockerfile in current directory
docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker    # Launch container interactively; defaults to CMD ["R"]
docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker bash  # Overwrite CMD to get a bash shell
The . at the end specifies the build context (current directory). --tag names the image. --rm removes the container after exit. Overwriting the default command with bash is necessary when the image lacks a default shell or when you want direct terminal access.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building Reproducible Compute Environments with Docker and uv
text:
Running with volume mounts
docker run --rm -it -v "$(pwd):/workspace" 2026-11-24-docker bash
Mounts the host’s current directory to /workspace inside the container. Enables live code editing and running uv run against local files without rebuilding the image.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Building Reproducible Compute Environments with Docker and uv
text:
Managing with Docker Compose
docker compose build   # Builds using docker-compose.yml
docker compose up      # Starts the container(s) defined in the compose file
docker compose ps      # Lists running containers for the project
Consolidates build and run flags into a single YAML configuration. docker compose up reads all volume and port mappings defined in the compose file.

title: Building Reproducible Compute Environments with Docker and uv
text:
What went wrong live

Missing text editors: Tried to edit files inside the container using nano and vi, but the base ubuntu:24.04 image lacks these tools. Terminal returned bash: nano: command not found and bash: vi: command not found.
Typo in detach flag: Ran docker compose up --detatch. Docker rejected it with unknown flag: --detatch. The correct flag is --detach (with one t).
Container exited immediately: After docker compose up, the container created but exited with code 0 immediately. This happened because the container image lacked a foreground process (like an SSH server or a long-running script) to keep it alive. The instructor noted this would be addressed in the next class by adding an appropriate entrypoint.
.venv conflict warning: When first mounting the volume, uv run warned warning: Ignoring existing virtual environment linked to non-existent Python interpreter... Removed virtual environment at: .venv. This occurred because the host’s .venv was mounted into the container, confusing uv about which environment to use. Resolved by updating the Dockerfile to use ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv, moving the container’s packages outside the mounted directory.

section: 22.1 What uv add writes by default
text:
22.1 What uv add writes by default
In uv: projects, uv add wrote a lower bound for each package. Here is a fresh project after uv add pandas:
Terminal
uv add pandas
Output
Using CPython 3.14.3
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Resolved 5 packages in 19ms
Installed 4 packages in 65ms
 + numpy==2.5.5
 + pandas==3.1.1
 + python-dateutil==4.0.0
 + tzdata==2026.6
pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "pins-demo"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "pandas>=3.1.1",
]
pandas>=3.1.1 declares “pandas 3.1.1 or anything newer”. The exact version you got is still written down, but only in uv.lock:
uv.lock
[[package]]
name = "pandas"
version = "3.1.1"
So the project declares a range and locks one version. As long as everyone runs uv sync against that uv.lock, everyone gets pandas 3.1.1.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Course materials: 2026-11-24 lecture
section: 22.2 Why an analysis project declares exact versions
text:
22.2 Why an analysis project declares exact versions
The range in pyproject.toml matters whenever the lockfile is not the thing being read.

The lockfile gets regenerated. uv lock --upgrade, a deleted uv.lock, or a merge conflict resolved by re-locking lets every package move anywhere inside its range, and nothing in pyproject.toml records that the analysis was run with 3.1.1.
People read pyproject.toml, not uv.lock. It is short enough to read in a code review or a README. pandas==3.1.1 says what the analysis was run with, and pandas>=3.1.1 does not.
Other tools read pyproject.toml too. pip install --only-deps . installs from it, and it ignores uv.lock.

With an exact pin in pyproject.toml, the declared version and the locked version are the same, and a version only changes when someone changes the pin. That change shows up in the diff of pyproject.toml, where reviewers will see it.
A package, the kind of project you will build in the packaging chapters, is the opposite case. A package gets installed into other people’s environments, next to whatever versions of pandas their projects already use. Exact pins there would make your package impossible to install alongside theirs, so packages declare ranges and leave the exact choice to the project that installs them.








Kind of project
Declares
Why




Data analysis (an application)
exact versions, pandas==3.1.1
The result depends on the exact versions, and nobody installs it into another environment


Package (a library)
ranges, pandas>=3.0
It has to fit into other people’s environments

title: Course materials: 2026-11-24 lecture
section: 22.3 Making uv add write exact versions
text:
22.3 Making uv add write exact versions
uv has a setting for this. Add a [tool.uv] table to pyproject.toml:
pyproject.toml
[tool.uv]
# `uv add` writes an exact version (==)
add-bounds = "exact"
That table and comment are taken from the docker-uv-renv example project (MIT license), which the container chapters build on.
From then on, uv add writes ==. Here is the same project after removing pandas and adding it again:
Terminal
uv remove pandas
uv add pandas
Output
Resolved 1 package in 5ms
Uninstalled 4 packages in 200ms
 - numpy==2.5.5
 - pandas==3.1.1
 - python-dateutil==4.0.0
 - tzdata==2026.6
Resolved 5 packages in 7ms
Installed 4 packages in 29ms
 + numpy==2.5.5
 + pandas==3.1.1
 + python-dateutil==4.0.0
 + tzdata==2026.6
pyproject.toml
[project]
name = "pins-demo"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "pandas==3.1.1",
]

[tool.uv]
add-bounds = "exact"
The setting lives in pyproject.toml, so everyone on the project gets the same behavior from uv add.
For a single command, uv add --bounds exact pandas does the same thing without the setting. --bounds also accepts lower (the default), major, and minor, which write wider ranges.
Existing lower bounds do not change
The setting only changes what uv add writes from now on. Running uv add pandas again in a project that already has pandas>=3.1.1 leaves that line as it is.
To convert a package you already have, look up the version you are using and add it again with that version:
Terminal
uv tree --depth 1
Output
Resolved 6 packages in 13ms
penguin-analysis v0.1.0
├── palmerpenguins v0.1.6
└── pandas v3.1.1
Terminal
uv add "pandas==3.1.1" "palmerpenguins==0.1.6"

title: Course materials: 2026-11-24 lecture
text:
22.4 Changing a pinned version
With an exact pin, uv lock --upgrade-package pandas cannot move pandas, because pyproject.toml only allows one version. To move it, change the pin:
Terminal
uv add "pandas==3.0.5"
Output
Resolved 5 packages in 118ms
Downloading pandas (9.5MiB)
 Downloaded pandas
Prepared 1 package in 1.16s
Uninstalled 1 package in 100ms
Installed 1 package in 14ms
 - pandas==3.1.1
 + pandas==3.0.5
One command updates pyproject.toml, uv.lock, and .venv/ together, and the commit that changes the pin is the record of when and why it moved.
The packages you did not name, such as numpy and python-dateutil here, are still pinned exactly, but only in uv.lock. uv lock --upgrade-package numpy moves one of them, as in uv: sharing and managing an environment.

text:
22.5 The same idea in R
R projects declare their packages in a DESCRIPTION file, and this book pins those exactly too:
DESCRIPTION
Depends:
    dplyr (== 1.2.1)
DESCRIPTION with == plays the part of pyproject.toml with add-bounds = "exact", and renv.lock plays the part of uv.lock. renv: declaring packages in DESCRIPTION shows how.

text:
27.8 What is a container registry?
A container registry is a remote repository, or collection of repositories, used to share container images. This is similar to remote version control repositories for sharing code. Instead of code, however, it is container images that are pushed and pulled to/from there. For this course we will focus on the widely used Docker Hub container registry: https://hub.docker.com/.
However, there are many container registries that can be used, including:

https://github.com/
https://quay.io/
https://aws.amazon.com/ecr/

In the examples above, we have used the rocker/rstudio container, which comes from Docker Hub, and the Jupyter server comes from quay.io.
Exercise
Exploring container registries
Let’s visit the repositories for the two container images that we used in the exercise earlier in class:

rocker/rstudio
quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook

Question: you pulled these images with docker pull before you started. What would docker run ... have done if you had not?
Answer: docker run ... will first look for images you have locally, and run those if they exist. If they do not exist, it then attempts to pull the image from the registry named in the image (Docker Hub, if the image name does not name a registry).

29.3 Choosing a base image for your Dockerfile

Source: https://themuslimtimes.info/2018/10/25/if-i-have-seen-further-it-is-by-standing-on-the-shoulders-of-giants/

29.3.1 Good base images to work from for R or Python projects!



Image
Software installed




rocker/r-ver
Ubuntu Linux and R; the base of this book’s R examples


rocker/rstudio
R, RStudio


rocker/tidyverse
R, R packages (including the tidyverse), RStudio, Make; ARM-based computers need tag 4.5.1 or later


ubuntu
Ubuntu Linux only; add uv to install Python and its packages


python
Debian Linux and Python; the -slim tags leave out software most projects do not need


quay.io/jupyter/datascience-notebook
JupyterLab, with libraries for data analysis from the Python, R and Julia communities



Use rocker/tidyverse:4.5.1 or later
rocker/tidyverse images before 4.5.1 were built only for Intel and AMD computers (amd64). From 4.5.1 on, they are also built for ARM computers (arm64), such as Macs with Apple silicon. On an ARM computer, pulling an older tag fails:
Terminal
docker pull rocker/tidyverse:4.5.0
Output
Error response from daemon: no matching manifest for linux/arm64/v8 in the manifest list entries: no match for platform in manifest: not found
So use 4.5.1 as the minimum version. The rocker/tidyverse tags page lists each tag with the platforms it was built for (linux/amd64, linux/arm64), so you can check a tag before you use it.

30.1 The project
This chapter puts the Python packages of a small uv project into a Docker image. It is a uv project like the ones in Virtual environments: Python (uv), and its files are in the book repository’s demos/docker-uv/end folder. hello.py prints a message with the cowsay package:
import cowsay

cowsay.cow("Hello from Python in my image!")
pyproject.toml lists the package with an exact version, and add-bounds = "exact" makes uv add write exact versions too (see uv: pinning exact versions):
[project]
name = "docker-uv"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "cowsay==6.1",
]

[tool.uv]
# `uv add` writes an exact version (==)
add-bounds = "exact"
.python-version holds 3.14, and uv.lock locks cowsay and everything it needs. On your computer, uv run creates the project’s .venv folder and runs the script:
Terminal
uv run hello.py
Output
Using CPython 3.14.3
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Installed 1 package in 9ms

| Hello from Python in my image! |
  ==============================

                                     ||     ||

title: Course materials: 2026-11-24 lecture
section: 30.2 A Dockerfile for a uv project
text:
30.2 A Dockerfile for a uv project
Here is the project’s Dockerfile. Its uv lines are the same as in docker-uv-renv, the example project that Docker Compose uses:
# Ubuntu Linux, with no Python: uv installs Python itself
FROM ubuntu:24.04

# install python uv
# https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/integration/docker/#installing-uv
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

# The project is mounted over /workspace, so the packages go in /opt
WORKDIR /workspace

# python packages in /opt/venv
ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./
# --locked: stop if uv.lock doesn't match pyproject.toml
RUN uv sync --locked

FROM ubuntu:24.04 starts from Ubuntu Linux, which has no Python. uv installs the Python version that .python-version asks for.
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 copies the uv and uvx programs out of the image that uv publishes, as uv’s Docker guide shows. The tag pins uv’s version, the same way a lockfile pins a package’s.
WORKDIR /workspace makes /workspace the working directory, for the rest of the build and for containers that run from the image. You will mount your project folder there.
ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv tells uv to put the project’s virtual environment in /opt/venv, instead of in .venv inside the project folder (see uv’s environment variables). The section after next shows why.
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./ copies only the files that list the packages, not the code. Editing hello.py then never reinstalls the packages, because the COPY and RUN steps above it have not changed (see Building images).
RUN uv sync --locked installs Python and the packages listed in uv.lock. --locked stops the build if uv.lock does not match pyproject.toml.

30.4 Run the project in a container
The image has the packages but not the code. Mount the project folder at /workspace, and run the script with uv run in place of the image’s default command (see Running containers):

macOS and Linux
Windows (Git Bash)
Windows (PowerShell)

Terminal
docker run --rm -v "$(pwd):/workspace" docker-uv uv run hello.py
Terminal
docker run --rm -v "/$(pwd):/workspace" docker-uv uv run hello.py
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/workspace" docker-uv uv run hello.py
Output
  ______________________________
| Hello from Python in my image! |

                                 (__)\       )\/\

Why /$(pwd) in Git Bash?
Git Bash turns command-line arguments that start with / into Windows paths, so /workspace could reach Docker as C:/Program Files/Git/workspace. Doubling the first slash, which /$(pwd) does, stops that (see “Known issues” in the Git for Windows release notes).

text:
30.5 Why the packages go in /opt/venv
Without a mount, /workspace holds the three files the Dockerfile copied:
Terminal
docker run --rm docker-uv ls -a
Output
.
..
.python-version
pyproject.toml
uv.lock
With the project folder mounted, /workspace shows your computer’s folder instead, including the .venv folder that uv run created on your computer:

macOS and Linux
Windows (Git Bash)
Windows (PowerShell)

Terminal
docker run --rm -v "$(pwd):/workspace" docker-uv ls -a
Terminal
docker run --rm -v "/$(pwd):/workspace" docker-uv ls -a
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/workspace" docker-uv ls -a
Output
.
..
.gitignore
.python-version
.venv
Dockerfile
hello.py
pyproject.toml
uv.lock
A mount hides whatever the image had at that path. If the image kept its packages in /workspace/.venv, the mount would hide them. Worse, uv in the container would find your computer’s .venv instead, which holds a program for your computer’s operating system, not for Linux. On a Mac:
Terminal
file .venv/bin/python3
Output
.venv/bin/python3: Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64
With the ENV line left out of the Dockerfile, running uv run hello.py with the mount printed these lines, among others:
Output
Removed virtual environment at: .venv
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
uv deleted your computer’s .venv and made a Linux one in its place, which no longer works on your computer. With UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv, the container leaves .venv alone and uses the environment that the image built:

macOS and Linux
Windows (Git Bash)
Windows (PowerShell)

Terminal
docker run --rm -v "$(pwd):/workspace" docker-uv uv run python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"
Terminal
docker run --rm -v "/$(pwd):/workspace" docker-uv uv run python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/workspace" docker-uv uv run python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"

/opt/venv

30.6 Add a package

Installed 4 packages in 100ms

Because of add-bounds = "exact", uv add wrote pandas into pyproject.toml with its exact version:
dependencies = [
    "cowsay==6.1",
    "pandas==3.1.1",
]
It also updated uv.lock with pandas and the packages pandas needs. Build the image again:
Terminal
docker build --tag docker-uv .
Here are the steps from the output:
Output
[+] Building 16.5s (12/12) FINISHED                                            docker:desktop-linux

30.7 When uv.lock does not match pyproject.toml

text:
32.1 The example project
Many data analyses use Python and R together, for example a Python script that cleans the data and an R script that fits a model. This chapter builds one image with both, from docker-uv-renv, the example project that the rest of this part of the book uses. Get a copy of it with Git:
Terminal
git clone https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv.git
cd docker-uv-renv
Its Python packages are listed in pyproject.toml and locked in uv.lock, as in the uv chapter:
[project]
name = "docker-uv-renv"
version = "2026.11.13"
requires-python = ">=3.14"
dependencies = [
    "altair==6.3.0",
    "pandas==3.1.1",
    # Altair charts as images, for PDFs
    "vl-convert-python==1.9.0.post1",
    # Quarto needs these to run Python code
    "ipykernel==7.4.0",
    "nbclient==0.11.0",
    "pyyaml==6.0.3",
]

[tool.uv]
# `uv add` writes an exact version (==)
add-bounds = "exact"
Its R packages are listed in DESCRIPTION and locked in renv.lock, as in the renv chapter:
Type: project
Version: 2026.11.13
Description: The R packages this project uses. renv.lock locks them.
Depends:
    dplyr (== 1.2.1),
    ggplot2 (== 4.0.3),
    knitr (== 1.52),
    rmarkdown (== 2.32)
Its reports/ folder has two Quarto reports that make the same table and chart, report-python.qmd with pandas and Altair, and report-r.qmd with dplyr and ggplot2.

title: Course materials: 2026-11-24 lecture
text:
32.2 The Dockerfile
Here is the project’s whole Dockerfile:
# Ubuntu with R. Other versions:
# https://rocker-project.org/images/versioned/r-ver.html
FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2

# libuv1-dev: the fs R package needs it (see renv::sysreqs())
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install --yes \
    curl \
    git \
    less \
    libuv1-dev \
    make \
    nano \
    openssh-server

# install quarto
# quarto comes with Typst for PDFs, so no LaTeX.
# dpkg --print-architecture: amd64 or arm64, to match your computer.
RUN curl --location --output quarto.deb \
    https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/releases/download/v1.11.9/quarto-1.11.9-linux-$(dpkg --print-architecture).deb \
  && apt-get install --yes ./quarto.deb \
  && rm quarto.deb

# install python uv
# https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/integration/docker/#installing-uv
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/

# The project is mounted over /workspace, so the packages go in /opt
WORKDIR /workspace

# python packages in /opt/venv
ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv
# ssh logins don't see ENV, only /etc/environment
RUN echo "UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=$UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT" >> /etc/environment
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./
# --locked: stop if uv.lock doesn't match pyproject.toml
RUN uv sync --locked

# R packages in /opt/renv/library
RUN echo "RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY=/opt/renv/library" >> /usr/local/lib/R/etc/Renviron.site
COPY renv.lock .Rprofile ./
COPY renv/activate.R renv/
RUN Rscript -e "renv::restore()"

# For linux laptops:
# StrictModes no: sshd wants root to own the key file,
# but on Linux the mounted one is yours
# RUN echo "StrictModes no" > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/container.conf

# -D: stay in the foreground, so the container keeps running
CMD ["/usr/sbin/sshd", "-D"]
Most of it comes from the two previous chapters. It starts from the R image, because rocker/r-ver has no Python:
Terminal
docker run --rm rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 bash -c 'command -v python3 || echo "no python3"'
Output
no python3
That does not matter, because uv installs the Python version in .python-version, as it did on top of Ubuntu. So the uv lines can be added to the R image unchanged:

FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2, the RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY line, the two COPY lines for renv and renv::restore() are the lines from R packages with renv in an image.
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7, ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv, the COPY line for uv and uv sync --locked are the lines from Python packages with uv in an image.
WORKDIR /workspace is in both.

The rest is new:

The apt-get line installs curl and libuv1-dev, as in the renv chapter. This project needs libuv1-dev because rmarkdown needs fs, through the packages bslib and sass. git, less and nano let you use Git, read files and edit files inside the container, make runs a Makefile (see Data analysis pipelines with GNU Make), and openssh-server lets you log in to the container over ssh.
The Quarto RUN line downloads Quarto 1.11.9 for your computer’s processor, installs it, and deletes the download. $(dpkg --print-architecture) runs dpkg --print-architecture and puts what it prints, amd64 or arm64, into the download address. Deleting the download in the same RUN line keeps it out of the image’s layers (see Building images). Quarto makes PDFs with Typst, which comes with it, so the image does not need LaTeX.
The line that adds UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT to /etc/environment is for ssh. ENV applies to the commands Docker starts in a container, but a session that logs in over ssh reads /etc/environment instead.
CMD ["/usr/sbin/sshd", "-D"] makes a container run an ssh server when it starts, and -D keeps the server in the foreground, so the container keeps running. As in the earlier chapters, a command after the image name in docker run replaces it. Docker Compose starts this server, and a later chapter logs in to it.
The commented-out StrictModes no line is for Linux computers, where the ssh server refuses a key file that the mount makes yours, not root’s.

The order follows Building images. The steps that rarely change, such as installing software, come first, and the files that list packages are copied last, so that adding a package rebuilds only the steps after its COPY.
Exercise
Demonstration of container images being built from layers
Let’s follow the images that the docker-uv-renv image is built on:

docker-uv-renv’s Dockerfile
rocker/r-ver:4.6.2’s Dockerfile
The Ubuntu image on Docker Hub

Questions:

What image does it build off?
What image does that build off?
And then the next one?

title: Course materials: 2026-11-24 lecture
text:
33.1 Docker Compose to launch containers
It can be fiddly and error-prone to type long commands into the terminal, or a GUI every time you want to launch a container. Even if you are copying and pasting commands, it can be difficult to make changes to long commands because you cannot click to a location to make edits.
A better approach is to use Docker Compose to specify how you want to launch the container. This way, all the parts of your command are saved in a file. This helps document how to run the Docker image, and it can be version controlled as part of a project.
Docker Compose uses a YAML file, specifically named docker-compose.yml, to record how the container should be launched. This file can include details such as:

the Docker image and version to use, or how to build it
how to mount volumes
what ports to map
what environment variables to set

docker run commands are interchangeable with the parameters specified in docker-compose.yml; the compose file makes it easier to manage all the docker run parameters. See this resource that can convert a run command to a compose file: https://www.composerize.com/
Here is the docker-compose.yml file of docker-uv-renv, the project from Python and R in one image:
services:
  analysis-env:
    build: .
    image: docker-uv-renv
    ports:
      # 2222 on your computer, 22 in the container.
      # "127.0.0.1:2222:22" stops others on the same Wi-Fi from reaching it.
      - "2222:22"
    volumes:
      - .:/workspace
      # ro: read-only
      - ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub:/root/.ssh/authorized_keys:ro
Without Docker Compose, building the image and starting the container takes these two commands, from the project folder:
Terminal
docker build --tag docker-uv-renv .
docker run --detach -p 2222:22 -v "$(pwd):/workspace" -v ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub:/root/.ssh/authorized_keys:ro docker-uv-renv
Each part of the docker run command is a line of the file:

services: lists the containers the project runs. This project has one, which it calls analysis-env.
build: . builds the image from the Dockerfile in this folder, like docker build ..
image: docker-uv-renv names the image, like --tag docker-uv-renv.
ports: maps port 2222 on your computer to port 22 in the container, like -p 2222:22. Port 22 is where the container’s ssh server listens. The file uses 2222 on your computer, because your computer may already use 22.
volumes: mounts two things, like the two -v options. .:/workspace mounts the project folder at /workspace. The second line mounts your ssh public key as the list of keys that may log in to the container as root, and ro makes it read-only inside the container. The key is the one from SSH for authentication.

No ssh key yet?
To check that you have the key, list it:
Terminal
ls ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
If ls says No such file or directory, make a key as in SSH for authentication:
Terminal
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
Press Enter to save it in the default place, ~/.ssh/id_ed25519. Make the key before you start the container. If the key is missing when the container starts, Docker makes a folder at ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub instead, and you cannot log in to the container.
Docker Compose reads the paths in the file itself, so the same file works on macOS, Linux and Windows, without the Git Bash /$(pwd) change from the earlier chapters.

Learning Objectives

Explain how Positron works inside a running container over ssh

title: Course materials: 2026-11-24 lecture
text:
34.1 How it works
With the docker-uv-renv container running, you can work inside it from Positron, as if it were a remote Linux computer. Positron’s Remote SSH documentation has the steps. Here is how the pieces from the earlier chapters fit together:

The image runs an ssh server when a container starts, because of its CMD ["/usr/sbin/sshd", "-D"] (see Python and R in one image).
docker compose up --detach starts the container in the background. Docker Compose maps port 2222 on your computer to the container’s port 22, and mounts your ssh public key as the key that may log in as root (see Docker Compose, including how to make a key).
In Positron, run “Remote SSH: Show Remote Menu” from the Command Palette, pick “Connect to Host”, and type root@localhost:2222. The first time, Positron installs its server inside the container, which takes a minute.
Open the folder /workspace, which is your project folder. Positron’s terminals, and its Python and R sessions, now run in the container.
For Python, pick the interpreter /opt/venv/bin/python, the environment the image built from uv.lock. R uses the packages in /opt/renv/library without any setup, because of the RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY line in R’s Renviron.site.
An ssh login does not see the image’s ENV settings, only the ones in /etc/environment. That is why the Dockerfile also writes UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT there, so that uv in a Positron terminal uses /opt/venv too.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Course materials: 2026-11-24 lecture
text:
34.2 When it does not connect
These are the problems the docker-uv-renv README lists, and their fixes:

~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub is a folder. Docker made it because the key did not exist when the container started. Run docker compose down, delete the folder, make the key, and run docker compose up --detach again.
Your key has a different name. Change the key’s path in docker-compose.yml.
Positron or ssh says the remote host identification has changed. The container’s ssh server has its own keys, which the image made when apt-get installed openssh-server. Rebuilding that step makes new ones, so your computer no longer recognizes the container. Forget the old key, then connect again:
Terminal
ssh-keygen -R "[localhost]:2222"
On a Linux computer, the ssh server refuses the mounted key, because the file belongs to you, not to root. Uncomment the StrictModes no line in the Dockerfile and run docker compose build.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Course materials: 2026-11-24 lecture
text:
34.3 An optional ssh shortcut
To type ssh docker-uv-renv instead of ssh -p 2222 root@localhost, and to pick docker-uv-renv from a list in Positron, add this to ~/.ssh/config on your computer:
Host docker-uv-renv
  HostName localhost
  Port 2222
  User root
  StrictHostKeyChecking no
  UserKnownHostsFile /dev/null
The last two lines skip the host key check, so that a rebuilt image does not cause the host key error above.

section: 35.1 One image, one kind of processor
text:
35.1 One image, one kind of processor
An image holds programs compiled for one kind of processor. Macs with Apple silicon, and some Windows laptops, have ARM processors (arm64). Most other laptops, and GitHub’s usual Linux computers, have Intel or AMD processors (amd64). docker build builds for the computer it runs on, so the hello-cowsay image from Building images, built on a Mac with Apple silicon, is for arm64 only:
Terminal
docker image inspect hello-cowsay --format '{{.Os}}/{{.Architecture}}'
Output
linux/arm64
A classmate with an Intel laptop could not use it as it is, just as an ARM computer cannot pull the older rocker/tidyverse images (see the warning in Building images).
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

section: 35.2 Build for both kinds on your computer
text:
35.2 Build for both kinds on your computer
--platform builds the image for each platform you list. Here are the steps of building hello-cowsay for both:
Terminal
docker build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --tag hello-cowsay .
Output
[+] Building 65.7s (9/9) FINISHED                                              docker:desktop-linux
 => [linux/arm64 internal] load metadata for docker.io/rocker/r-ver:4.6.2                      0.1s
 => [linux/amd64 internal] load metadata for docker.io/rocker/r-ver:4.6.2                      1.4s

 => [linux/arm64 1/2] FROM docker.io/rocker/r-ver:4.6.2@sha256:8739c76d2d9316698a7145b032601f  0.0s
 => CACHED [linux/arm64 2/2] RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"                       0.0s
 => [linux/amd64 2/2] RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"                             12.7s
The arm64 steps were already cached. For amd64, Docker downloaded the amd64 version of rocker/r-ver:4.6.2, and ran the RUN step by emulating an Intel processor, which is slower than running it on one. docker image ls --tree shows that the one tag now has both:
Terminal
docker image ls --tree hello-cowsay
Output
IMAGE                 ID             DISK USAGE   CONTENT SIZE   EXTRA
hello-cowsay:latest   fcb420e64e33       1.86GB          800MB        
├─ linux/amd64        7f260b562e1c        410MB          410MB        
└─ linux/arm64        f2d1c5ab15c8       1.45GB          390MB        
--platform on docker run picks which one to run, and uname -m prints the processor the container sees:
Terminal
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 hello-cowsay uname -m
docker run --rm --platform linux/arm64 hello-cowsay uname -m
Output
x86_64
aarch64
Docker’s guide to multi-platform builds has the details, including what your Docker needs to build them.

title: Course materials: 2026-11-24 lecture
text:
35.3 Push both to Docker Hub
To share the image, push it to a container registry such as Docker Hub, where you need a free account. The image’s name must start with your Docker Hub username, so replace USERNAME below with yours:
Terminal
docker login
docker tag hello-cowsay USERNAME/hello-cowsay:0.1
docker push USERNAME/hello-cowsay:0.1

docker login signs you in to Docker Hub.
docker tag gives the image a second name, with your username and a version, 0.1.
docker push uploads it. Because the image has both platforms, it uploads both, under the one tag.

Anyone can then run docker pull USERNAME/hello-cowsay:0.1, and Docker downloads the version for their computer. To list the platforms an image in a registry has:
Terminal
docker buildx imagetools inspect USERNAME/hello-cowsay:0.1

title: Course materials: 2026-11-24 lecture
text:
35.4 On GitHub Actions
A project can also build its image on GitHub’s computers, every time you push. docker-uv-renv does this with build-and-render.yml:
name: Build image and render reports

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  build-and-render:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Build the image
        run: docker build --tag docker-uv-renv .

      # not `make render`: CI has no ssh key to mount
      - name: Render the reports
        run: docker run --rm --volume "$PWD:/workspace" docker-uv-renv uv run quarto render

      # download them from the run's Summary page
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: reports
          path: |
            reports/*.html
            reports/*.pdf
On every push to main and every pull request, a fresh Linux computer (ubuntu-latest, an amd64 computer) builds the image from the Dockerfile in the repository, renders the reports in a container, and keeps them for you to download from the run’s page, as in this run. Because the build starts from nothing, it shows that the Dockerfile and lockfiles work on a computer other than yours. GitHub also has ARM computers (ubuntu-24.04-arm), and the project’s check-platforms.yml builds the image on both. GitHub Actions explains how workflow files work.

section: 1. Docker and AI-Assisted Setup Review (28 Using and running containers)
text:
1. Docker and AI-Assisted Setup Review (28 Using and running containers)
00:00:00–00:13:56

AI-assisted scaffolding: The instructor used Claude Code to generate a new GitHub repository containing a Dockerfile, Makefile, and README.md. The agent correctly inferred the need for a Docker-based setup and initialized it with the rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 image.
Reviewing local images: The docker images command lists all container images pulled or built on the machine. It displays the image name, ID, disk usage, and content size, which helps manage local storage.
Building the image: docker build --tag <name> . reads the Dockerfile in the current directory (.) and compiles the layers into a named image. The . argument is required because Docker needs a context to look for the default Dockerfile and build instructions.
Running containers interactively: docker run --rm -it <image> launches the container. The --rm flag ensures the container is automatically deleted when it exits, preventing orphaned processes. The -it flags allocate a terminal and capture input/output.
Overriding default commands: The initial Dockerfile contained CMD ["R"], which automatically starts the R interpreter. Appending bash to the docker run command overrides this default, providing a standard shell prompt for exploration.
Docker Desktop requirement: Students must ensure Docker Desktop is actively running before executing any Docker commands. If it is not, commands will silently fail or return unhelpful errors.


[!WARNING]
Always keep Docker Desktop running. If it is closed, the terminal will return vague errors when you attempt to pull, build, or run containers.

title: Docker Workflows with uv and Docker Compose
section: 2. Building a Python Container with uv (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
text:
2. Building a Python Container with uv (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:13:56–00:33:35

Choosing a base image: The instructor switched from an R-specific image to ubuntu:24.04 to create a leaner, more generic Linux environment. Ubuntu is a standard starting point that balances size with package availability.
Installing uv inside the image: Rather than installing uv via system package managers, the Dockerfile uses a multi-stage copy: COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/. This pulls the exact uv binaries from Astral’s official registry and places them in the container’s PATH.
Setting the working directory: WORKDIR /workspace sets the default directory for all subsequent commands and interactive sessions. Starting inside a dedicated project folder avoids navigating the system root and keeps the environment organized.
Pinning dependencies: In pyproject.toml, the [tool.uv] table includes add-bounds = "exact". This configuration forces uv add to write strict version pins (e.g., "cowsay==6.1") rather than lower bounds (>=), ensuring long-term reproducibility for the analysis.
Lockfile verification: The Dockerfile includes RUN uv sync --locked. The --locked flag instructs uv to strictly compare the lockfile against pyproject.toml. If they are out of sync, the build halts with an error, preventing the image from being built with mismatched dependencies.
Verifying the environment: After building, running uv run hello.py inside the container confirms that uv successfully resolved the environment and executed the script using the image’s Python interpreter.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Docker Workflows with uv and Docker Compose
section: 3. Layer Caching and Dockerfile Optimization (29.1.3 Layer caching)
text:
3. Layer Caching and Dockerfile Optimization (29.1.3 Layer caching)
00:33:35–00:51:21

How Docker layers work: Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a new read-only layer. Docker caches these layers and reuses them if the instruction and its inputs have not changed since the last build.
The cost of rebuilding: If you modify a RUN command or add a COPY instruction early in the file, Docker must discard the cached layer and rebuild every subsequent layer. This can add significant time to the build process.
Optimizing instruction order: To minimize rebuild times, place long-running, static setup steps (installing system packages, running uv sync) at the top of the Dockerfile. Place frequently changing instructions (copying application code, hello.py) at the bottom.
The snapshot problem: Copying your code directly into the image during the build process snapshots a static version of your files. When you edit a script on your host machine, the container still contains the old version unless you rebuild the entire image. This defeats the purpose of rapid iteration during exploratory data analysis.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Docker Workflows with uv and Docker Compose
section: 4. Volume Mounting and Cross-Platform Environments (30.5 Why the packages go in /opt/venv)
text:
4. Volume Mounting and Cross-Platform Environments (30.5 Why the packages go in /opt/venv)
00:51:21–01:06:55

Mounting local volumes: Instead of copying code into the image, use the -v flag during docker run: docker run -v "$(pwd):/workspace" <image>. This mounts your local project directory directly into the container’s filesystem, creating a live, bidirectional sync.
Live code editing: Changes made to files on your host machine appear instantly inside the container. You can edit scripts, run tests, and debug without ever rebuilding the image.
Cross-platform binary incompatibility: By default, uv stores the virtual environment in a local .venv folder. When this folder is mounted into the container, it overwrites the container’s built-in packages. The Linux container then attempts to execute macOS-compiled binaries, leading to crashes and errors.
Isolating the container environment: To solve this, the Dockerfile sets ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv. This forces uv to install packages in a completely separate directory outside the mounted workspace. The container ignores your local .venv and uses only the Linux-compiled packages it built during the image creation.
Verifying the fix: Running uv run which python inside the mounted container returns /opt/venv/bin/python, confirming that the environment variable successfully redirected uv to the correct, isolated virtual environment.


[!WARNING]
Never allow a mounted local .venv to overwrite the container’s environment. The container will attempt to run host-machine binaries (e.g., macOS/Windows) on Linux, causing silent failures or crashes. Always redirect the virtual environment to an unmounted path like /opt/venv.
crumbs: Nov 24 · Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose

title: Docker Workflows with uv and Docker Compose
section: 5. Docker Compose and Milestone Assignment (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
text:
5. Docker Compose and Milestone Assignment (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
01:06:55–01:20:07

Managing long commands: Typing out full docker run commands with multiple volume mounts, port forwards, and environment variables is error-prone and difficult to maintain. docker-compose.yml consolidates these parameters into a readable YAML file.
Compose file structure: The file begins with services:, under which each container is defined. Properties like build: . point to the Dockerfile, volumes: maps the local directory, and ports: handles network routing.
Essential Compose commands:

docker compose build: Reads the compose file and builds the image.
docker compose up: Starts the container according to the defined parameters.
docker compose exec <service> bash: Opens an interactive shell inside a running container without leaving the compose context.

Industry applications: Docker Compose is standard practice outside academia for deploying complex applications. It is used to spin up databases, web servers, and automation tools (like personal finance or media servers) with a single, version-controlled configuration file.
Milestone requirements: Students must create a Dockerfile that replicates their project’s compute environment. The container must use volume mounting for the code and successfully execute uv run quarto render to generate the final report. TAs will grade submissions by pulling the repository, building the image, and running the analysis inside the container.

title: Course materials and Docker setup
text:
A classroom lecture by instructor Daniel Chen with student questions covered Docker builds, Python environments, and running analysis inside containers. The central goal is a reproducible compute environment that can be shared without requiring everyone to set it up by hand.

Course materials and Docker setup
The exercise began with a review: create a GitHub repository containing a Dockerfile that uses the specified image. Daniel also planned to try a similar task with a Cloud Agent. He showed updates to the course website and reviewed Docker startup requirements.

Course materials: The website now includes material from Sky’s class, including her slide decks and summary notes. Transcripts and links remain on the private side; students no longer need the GitHub UBC student repository to find the summaries.
Optional notes: The notes include comparisons between language models and lecture questions organized at different levels of Bloom’s taxonomy, from factual recall to questions that require understanding how things work. Daniel offered them as a possible template for other classes, but said students were not required to read them. The command-history page may be enough for some.
Docker Desktop: Students should make sure Docker Desktop is running before using Docker commands. Without it, commands may fail and prompt them to start Docker.
Starting point: Daniel created a new repository for the class exercise and used Claude to create a Dockerfile. He stressed that effective prompts rely on knowing terms such as “Dockerfile” and naming the intended image; vague instructions like “make a thing” give an agent less to work with.



Docker image build and run — reviewing the R container
The first build showed how an agent creates an image and how Docker commands work. The generated files and commands were useful to inspect, but Daniel noted that Claude started in a different folder and created the repository in a temporary location rather than the intended one.

Generated files: Claude created a Dockerfile, a README, and a Makefile. Daniel said only the Dockerfile was needed for the exercise, though the other files reflected his usual requests.
Agent activity: The terminal history showed commands such as ls, mkdir, and Docker and GitHub CLI checks. Claude built the image and ran a script in the container. The demo cost fifty cents.
Default command: The Dockerfile’s CMD makes R start when the container runs without another command. Users can supply another command to override that default.
Build command: docker build uses -t or --tag to name the image. The name can be chosen by the user. The dot at the end gives Docker the current directory as its build context; Docker looks there for a file named Dockerfile by default.
Build steps: Docker runs the instructions in the Dockerfile to make the image. The base image used the R version from the previous class. If that image is not already downloaded, retrieving it can take seconds or minutes, depending on internet speed.
Run command: docker run --rm -it starts a container and gives the user terminal access. --rm removes the container when it exits. With the default CMD, R starts; supplying bash instead opens a shell.
Container filesystem: The shell starts at the root of the container, where system files are visible. The class container has no user assigned in the home directory. Daniel described its setup as a shared analysis environment, not a public-facing service.
Temporary changes: Once a container started with --rm exits, its changes are discarded. Daniel compared this to a disposable environment for testing software such as PyTorch: if a test goes wrong, users can restart the container.



Python environment — packages, versions, and project files
The class will focus on Python because students are working on Python projects. Daniel used Ubuntu 24.04 as the base rather than the R image, which carries extra R software. He also noted that a single project can use more than one language; the textbook example supports both R and Python.

Base image: Ubuntu is a common Linux starting point for containers. Alpine is smaller, but may require installing more software. Daniel urged students to keep images small to limit disk use.
Installing UV: The Dockerfile uses COPY to take UV and UVX from an existing image and place them in the container’s /usr/local/bin directory. Installing UV in the container helps make the environment reproducible for someone who has not configured Python or UV on their own computer.
Working directory: WORKDIR sets the container’s starting directory. The example uses /workspace, so users do not start at the root of the filesystem. Daniel connected this to the working-directory concept students have used in Python and R.
Project files: The setup uses pyproject.toml, uv.lock, and .python-version. The first holds project metadata and package requirements; the lock file records resolved package versions; .python-version specifies the Python version to install.
Adding a package: The example initializes a project with uv init --bare, then adds a package either by editing pyproject.toml or running uv add. The transcript’s package name is unclear, but the example showed it at version 6.1.
Version constraints: A >= 6.1 requirement could admit version 7.0 after a rebuild. Daniel said a change in the first version number typically signals a backward-incompatible change, which could break a long-running project. For packages that must remain consistent, he recommended pinning an exact version, such as == 6.1.
Locking and dependencies: uv.lock pins resolved versions, but it is generated from pyproject.toml. The project file should specify versions that matter; the dependency resolver can select compatible versions for the rest. A downstream dependency may still change and cause a problem, so some projects also pin those dependencies.
Python version choice: The Python version can affect which package versions are available. Daniel cited PyTorch as an example that is often not compatible with the newest Python release. Pinning Python can help avoid that issue.
Testing new Python releases: Package authors can use .python-version to test release candidates or upcoming Python versions. Daniel said supporting those versions is part of ensuring a package works for its users as Python changes.
Example program: Daniel showed a short Python file that imports the example package and prints an ASCII cow greeting. On a local computer, uv sync sets up the environment, and uv run runs the file in it.



Building the Python image — syncing dependencies and using the cache
The Dockerfile needs the project files and installation steps that reproduce the local environment. Daniel showed that Docker can reuse unchanged build layers, which affects how files and commands should be ordered.

Copying setup files: The Dockerfile copies the project files into /workspace. The build then runs uv sync with a lock-checking option. Daniel said it errors if the project file and lock file are out of sync, rather than silently building from inconsistent inputs.
Build result: The build copied the files, set the working directory, and ran the sync step. When Daniel entered the resulting container, it opened in /workspace and showed the copied files and the Python environment.
Layers and cache: Docker caches build layers. Unchanged steps can use their cached versions; a change to one layer requires rebuilding the steps after it. Fewer layers can save disk space, but having more Dockerfile lines is fine, especially when they make the environment and code easier to distinguish.
Order of operations: Daniel recommended placing slow, relatively stable installation steps before files that change often. Then a small code edit need not rerun a long dependency installation.
Code change test: After Daniel copied the example Python file later in the Dockerfile, rebuilding was quick because Docker did not rerun uv sync. The file was available in the container, where he ran it with UV.
Sharing the setup: Students can build an image from the Dockerfile. Daniel said a later class would cover publishing an image so others can use docker pull rather than build it themselves.



Live code in a container — mounting the project folder
Copying code into an image snapshots it at build time. Daniel presented a volume mount as a way to keep the software environment in the image while using the current project files from the host computer.
Copying the full project into the image would make active development cumbersome: users would need to track which version was copied, commit and push changes, then rebuild to update the container. Installing Git inside the container is possible, and Daniel has used that approach when he wanted to reproduce a student’s terminal experience. For this class’s purpose, he recommended separating installed software from source code.

Volume mount: The -v option mounts a host folder into the running container. Daniel’s example maps the current working directory to /workspace.
Live changes: The container and host then use the same files. A change made in one is visible in the other without rebuilding the image. Daniel said this is a shared folder, not a cloud-sync copy.
Using Git on the host: The mount avoids having to set up Git credentials inside a disposable container. Daniel noted that container-based Git use can require SSH keys or access tokens, and that rebuilding containers can make key management cumbersome.
Editor refresh: Positron may not notice that a file changed on disk, so users may need to refresh it. The files themselves remain shared.
Testing: Students can run their analysis locally and in the container. The mounted code lets them test the container setup against current changes without rebuilding it each time.
Required build files: The project and lock files still need to be copied into the image because the image build uses them to install the environment. The source code itself can be mounted at run time.



Cross-platform dependencies — keep the container’s environment separate
A mounted virtual environment can overwrite the one created in the Linux image. That can cause problems when the host and container use different operating systems or processor architectures.

Platform differences: Daniel described AMD64 and ARM64 as different processor architectures, and Windows and Mac as different operating systems. He counted four combinations across those systems, or six if Linux is included.
Lock-file scope: A UV lock file can contain package information for other systems, but a local uv sync installs for the current system. A build inside the container resolves and installs for Linux.
Risk from mounting .venv: Mounting the project folder can place the host’s .venv over the image’s environment. A virtual environment built for one operating system or architecture may not work on another. Daniel said simple packages may not expose the problem, but packages such as pandas or software that uses compiled code are more likely to.
Separate environment path: The Dockerfile sets UV’s project-environment variable before running uv sync, directing the installed environment to /opt/venv instead of the project’s .venv folder. UV then uses that location, even when the host folder is mounted over /workspace.
Rebuild after the change: Moving the setting earlier in the build means Docker must rerun the steps below it. The rebuilt container uses its Linux environment rather than the mounted host environment, making it portable across the systems Daniel described.



Docker Compose — save run settings in a file
The Docker run command grows as users add mounts and other settings, such as port forwarding for JupyterLab or RStudio. Daniel introduced a Compose YAML file as a version-controlled place to store those settings.

Service definition: The file begins with services and defines a container, with a name chosen by the user. It can describe more than one container.
Settings: The class example specifies the build, image, and volume. A service may also specify ports; the example left out extra mounts that the class would cover later.
Multiple services: Compose is useful when an application has separate parts, such as a dashboard and a database, that need to run together but should not be combined into one container.
Commands: docker compose build builds from the file. docker compose up starts the service, and docker compose up -d runs it in the background.
Demo status: The live Compose demo did not work as intended. Daniel said he would fix it for the next class. He explained that Compose was meant to apply the settings that would otherwise go into the Docker run command. 



This week’s analysis container — required work and grading
The main assignment is to create a Dockerfile for the analysis environment. The teaching assistants will build the image from each repository and try to run the analysis inside it.

Required result: The container should reproduce the analysis’s compute environment. Students should mount the necessary folders and run uv run quarto render on their report.
Starting materials: The analysis should already run locally, and the project should already have a pyproject.toml. The task is to make that project run in the container.
Optional additions: Students may install other tools, such as a text editor, if they need them inside the container. Some package stacks may also need system tools from Ubuntu; Daniel gave geospatial analysis as an example.
Scope: The Dockerfile is the main goal for this class. Compose is not required for the assignment; Daniel said he would return to it after fixing the demo.



Docker Compose beyond class — examples of ready-to-run software
Daniel connected Compose to software people can run outside the course. Many open-source applications provide Compose files that specify how to start their containers.

Personal finance: Actual Budget and Firefly III are personal-finance applications. Daniel showed a Compose file for Actual Budget with a service image, ports, environment variables, volumes, and a health check.
Starting an application: Running docker compose up -d can download the image and start the application, which users can then access through its port.
Where to run it: The application could run on a personal computer, an old laptop, or a computer kept at home; users could also pay for a cloud machine.
Other examples: Daniel named Jellyfin for serving movies and other media, n8n for AI automation, and a recipe app that can store recipes from Instagram collections. These applications run in a browser through a port.
Broader use: Compose files are useful beyond the class’s analysis environment. Users who know Docker can often start an application from its Compose file with a simple command.



Action Items
@students (students)

Create a Dockerfile that reproduces the analysis environment, mount the required folders, and render the report inside the container 

@Daniel Chen (instructor)

Fix the Docker Compose demo for the next class
