title: Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose: review questions, tier 2 — Understand
text:
Date: 2026-11-24
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 2 of 5: Understand. Explain each answer in your own words before you read it; tier 1 (Remember) covers the facts, tiers 3 to 5 put them to use.

1. Letting Claude Code build the repository
00:07:21–00:11:24

Q: Why did the instructor say that knowing Docker vocabulary still matters when a coding agent writes the Dockerfile for you?

A: The prompt has to contain the right words, such as “Dockerfile”, “image” and the exact image name. Those words steer the agent toward the correct answer. Someone who had never heard of Docker would not know which words to use, and would struggle to get a useful result. (00:08:06)

Q: Explain why Claude Code created a README.md and a Makefile in 2026-11-24-docker when the prompt never asked for them.

A: The instructor had set up his computer so that the agent uses his usual defaults, and he normally asks for those files. He pointed out that this is a benefit of coding agents: once you have templates you like, the agent can apply them for you. (00:11:24)

Q: Summarize what the shell commands visible in the agent’s run show it was doing before and after it wrote the Dockerfile.

A: First it explored the machine. It ran ls, checked that docker and gh exist, and ran a Docker command to learn what kind of computer it was on. Then it ran mkdir to make the folder and wrote a Dockerfile starting from Rocker. Finally it built the image and ran a script in the container to test it. (00:09:26)

Q: Why did the agent put the repository under ~/temp instead of the instructor’s usual Git folder?

A: The instructor had started Claude in a different folder. His guess was that the agent therefore treated the project as temporary. For a class demo the location did not matter. (00:10:11)




2. The default command: CMD ["R"] (29.2.1 CMD or ENTRYPOINT?)
00:11:24–00:12:41

Q: The exercise only needed FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2. Why did Claude Code also add CMD ["R"]?

A: Claude reasoned that someone who picks an R container probably wants to do R things with it. So it made R the program that starts by default. (00:11:44)

Q: What is the difference between the FROM line and the CMD ["R"] line in the warm-up Dockerfile?

A: FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 names the image you build on, and it was all the task required. CMD ["R"] only says what runs when you start the container without giving it any other input. It is a default, and you can always pass other parameters to start something that is not R. (00:12:01)

Q: Explain the instructor’s double-click analogy for CMD.

A: If the image were a file and you double-clicked it, CMD decides what opens. In this image, R opens by default. (00:12:28)




3. Listing and building images (27.7 Image vs container?)
00:12:42–00:16:40

Q: Why does docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker . need the trailing ., and why is forgetting it a common mistake?

A: By default, docker build looks for a file named Dockerfile, but you still have to tell it where to look. The . means “where I currently am”. It works like a function argument with no default: you can’t leave it empty. The . is easy to miss because it looks like a full stop, but it is a location. (00:14:57)

Q: What is the --tag value in docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker . for, and what happens when you reuse an existing image’s name?

A: The tag is the name you give the image, and it can be anything you like, even pizza. The instructor reused the name Claude had already built, 2026-11-24-docker, so the build rebuilt and replaced that image. The latest that docker images shows is simply the tag Docker uses by default. (00:14:03)

Q: Why did the rebuild of the R image finish almost instantly, and when would its FROM step take much longer?

A: The rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 image had already been downloaded in the previous class, so nothing new had to happen. If you change to an R version you haven’t downloaded yet, the FROM step has to pull that image first. That can take seconds or minutes, depending on your internet speed. (00:16:15)




4. Running a container, overriding CMD, and throwaway containers (28.2.2 Docker run commands)
00:16:40–00:20:07

Q: Explain what --rm and -it each do in docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker.

A: --rm deletes the container when you exit, so it isn’t left running on your computer. -it gives you terminal access and passes what you type through to the container. The image name at the end says which machine to start. (00:16:53)

Q: How does docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker bash differ from running the same command without bash?

A: Without bash, the container runs its default CMD, so R starts. Adding bash overrides that default and gives you a normal terminal, like Git Bash or the macOS terminal, with that kind of access to the Linux machine. (00:17:45)

Q: Interpret what you saw after starting the container with bash: pwd printed / and /home was empty. Why didn’t the instructor treat this as a problem for the course?

A: The container starts you at the root of the file system, so you see the system-level folders. There is no user set up in /home. In this course everyone uses the container as the same analysis setup, not as a service for the general public, so ownership of the container doesn’t really matter. (00:18:45)

Q: Why does --rm make a container a safe place to try something risky, such as installing PyTorch?

A: Once the container is closed, any changes you made inside it are gone, and the next start is clean again. The instructor compared it to a version of Git that automatically resets all your changes. If the experiment goes wrong, you restart the container and nothing bad has happened. (00:19:58)




5. Choosing a base image for a Python project (29.3 Choosing a base image for your Dockerfile)
00:20:07–00:24:22

Q: Why build the project’s packages into the image instead of having each person install them?

A: The goal is that you can tell someone to pull the container, and once they run it they don’t have to set anything up. Everything is already installed, apart from the bigger download. This works even for someone who has never used Python, or who sets things up differently. (00:21:33)

Q: Why are you working in Linux inside a container, even on a Mac or Windows laptop?

A: Docker containers generally run on top of some version of Linux. So once you are inside a container you are in the Linux world, most likely some version of Ubuntu, whatever your own computer runs. (00:23:33)

Q: Why did the new Dockerfile start FROM ubuntu:24.04 rather than keep the R image?

A: The R image has a lot of R software installed that a Python project doesn’t need, and the instructor wanted something smaller. He asked students to be respectful of other people’s disk space, which has become expensive because of the AI boom. (00:23:55)

Q: Compare Ubuntu with a smaller base image such as Alpine, as the instructor described them.

A: Alpine is even smaller than Ubuntu, but starting there may mean installing more yourself, depending on what you need. Ubuntu is a pretty good starting point for a lot of that software. (00:24:13)

Q: Why does the textbook’s example container hold both R and Python, when the class demo used only Python?

A: One project mixing several languages is common and valid. For example, the instructor likes ggplot2 and R’s table tools. The class demo used only Python because every group is working on a Python project. (00:22:42)




6. Installing uv with COPY --from, and setting WORKDIR (30.2 A Dockerfile for a uv project)
00:24:22–00:27:42

Q: Interpret COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/.

A: COPY can copy from one image into another. Read the image name like a GitHub path: who published it, the repository, then the version number. The line takes the uv and uvx programs out of that image and puts them in the container’s /usr/local/bin/ folder, which is how uv’s own documentation installs uv. (00:25:14)

Q: Why does the image need to install uv at all?

A: You are building a machine from scratch, as a virtual copy of your own machine. Everyone installed uv at orientation. So if you want to hand someone a reproducible environment, that machine needs uv too. (00:25:46)

Q: Why add WORKDIR /workspace to the Dockerfile?

A: Without it, the container starts at the root of the file system, among operating-system files. If you moved a folder or messed something up there, everything could stop working. WORKDIR changes the working directory, so you start in a folder just for the project, and Docker creates the folder if it doesn’t exist. (00:26:27)

Q: Explain the instructor’s point that the working-directory idea “will never go away”.

A: Every command needs to know its starting point in some way. You met that idea in 521 and in reading files in your R and Python classes. Tools call it different things, such as pwd, cd or WORKDIR, but the idea of where you start stays. (00:26:42)




7. Setting up the uv project locally (22.1 What uv add writes by default)
00:27:42–00:29:58

Q: Explain how pyproject.toml, uv sync and uv.lock work together to install a package such as cowsay.

A: pyproject.toml lists the project and its dependencies. Running uv sync creates the uv.lock file from it. The lockfile is then what’s used to install the packages. (00:28:03)

Q: Why does the uv setup still have to work on your own computer before it goes into the image?

A: The image is built from files copied over from your computer. At this point the image only has uv installed, and what remains is getting the project’s packages into the container. So the project files have to exist and work locally first, and the container then repeats the same process. (00:28:18)

Q: Compare the two ways shown for adding cowsay as a dependency.

A: You can type it into the dependencies list of pyproject.toml by hand. Or, if you want to do everything with commands, you can run uv add cowsay. In class, uv add cowsay installed cowsay==6.1 and wrote a >= bound for 6.1 into pyproject.toml. (00:29:51)




8. Pinning exact versions in pyproject.toml (22.2 Why an analysis project declares exact versions)
00:29:58–00:33:35

Q: Why is a >= bound such as cowsay>=6.1 risky in a project that runs for a long time?

A: It allows any newer version. If cowsay 7.0 comes out next week and you rebuild the container next week, you actually get 7.0. If your analysis relies on behaviour from 6.x, it can break without you changing anything. (00:31:06)

Q: What does a change in the first number of a version, such as 6.x to 7.x, usually signal?

A: It typically means a change that breaks backwards compatibility. Some things that worked in the 6.x version no longer work in 7.x. (00:30:37)

Q: Explain how the [tool.uv] table with add-bounds = "exact" fits into pyproject.toml.

A: pyproject.toml is a general Python metadata file that other tools also know how to read. The [tool.uv] table holds the settings that control how uv itself behaves. Setting add-bounds = "exact" there makes future uv add commands write == instead of >=. (00:31:49)

Q: Compare the version information in uv.lock with the pins you write in pyproject.toml.

A: uv.lock always pins one specific version, but it is generated from the TOML file. pyproject.toml holds the explicit versions you care about. You pin those with == and let the resolver choose compatible versions for everything else. (00:33:16)

Q: Why might you sometimes pin a package you never use directly?

A: A downstream dependency can still update on its own. The instructor has pinned pandas and still had something far downstream update and break pandas. In that case you add the downstream package to pyproject.toml and pin it as well. (00:32:47)




9. Copying the environment files and uv sync --locked (30.7 When uv.lock does not match pyproject.toml)
00:35:01–00:39:25

Q: Why does COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./ put the files in /workspace?

A: ./ means the current directory. The earlier WORKDIR /workspace line has already changed that directory to /workspace, so that is where the files land. (00:35:09)

Q: Why does the project need a .python-version file when uv.lock already exists?

A: uv.lock only locks the packages and their dependencies. .python-version says which version of Python to install if the environment is built again, because you don’t always want the latest one. The Python version also decides which package versions can be installed, since not every package is compatible with the newest Python. (00:37:05)

Q: Give the instructor’s example of why pinning the Python version matters.

A: PyTorch is almost never compatible with the latest version of Python. So to get the whole neural-network stack installed, you almost always have to pin an older Python version. (00:35:59)

Q: Why is .python-version also useful to package authors?

A: A package author can point it at an upcoming Python release candidate. That creates an environment for checking that the package still works when Python actually updates. The instructor described this as part of an author’s responsibility to the people who use the package. (00:37:22)

Q: Summarize the role of each of the three files the Dockerfile copies.

A: .python-version says which version of Python to use. uv.lock says which packages to install and at which versions. pyproject.toml is the human-readable file that controls all of that. (00:37:44)

Q: Why use uv sync --locked in the Dockerfile instead of plain uv sync?

A: --locked requires pyproject.toml and uv.lock to be in sync. If one of them is out of date, the build throws an error. That is what you want: the build happens the way you expect, or it fails loudly at that point. (00:39:14)




10. Building the image and layer caching (29.1.3 Layer caching)
00:39:25–00:44:33

Q: Why did the build of the Python image pause at the RUN uv sync --locked step?

A: That step really was running uv sync --locked inside the image. It is the same command you run on your own computer when you get a new project or a new homework assignment. Installing Python and the packages takes time. (00:40:07)

Q: Why did the instructor use ls -a rather than ls to check /workspace in the new container?

A: Some of the files are hidden, such as .python-version and the .venv environment. Plain ls showed only pyproject.toml and uv.lock, while ls -a showed the copied files and the virtual environment too. (00:41:03)

Q: Why do many Dockerfiles squeeze their work into as few instructions as possible, and does a beginner need to?

A: Each instruction is cached as its own layer, and combining steps saves a little disk space. It is about efficiency and doesn’t really affect the outcome. So there is nothing wrong with having more lines while you are starting out, for example to keep environment steps separate from code steps. (00:41:59)

Q: Explain why slow, rarely changing steps belong near the top of a Dockerfile and frequently changing files near the bottom.

A: When you change a layer, Docker has to rerun everything below it. If your code were copied before a slow install, fixing a typo in a script could make you wait for a reinstall such as a fifteen-minute tidyverse install. Putting the slow installs first and your code last avoids that. (00:43:10)

Q: Interpret why the rebuild after adding COPY hello.py ./ as the last line was so fast.

A: The new line came after everything else, so the earlier layers were reused from the cache and uv sync didn’t have to run again. Only the new copy step ran, and copying a file is very fast. (00:43:54)

Q: Compare handing someone your Dockerfile with publishing your image.

A: With the Dockerfile, they build the image themselves and end up with exactly your setup. With a published image, they just run docker pull, the way they would get any other image. They don’t have to deal with the Dockerfile or with docker build at all. (00:44:16)




11. Why not bake your code into the image (30.4 Run the project in a container)
00:49:36–00:53:26

Q: Why is copying your project code into the image a poor fit for work that is still changing, such as milestone EDA?

A: All the code is snapshotted into the image at build time. Anyone who opens the container then has to wonder when the code was copied, and which teammate copied it. (00:50:27)

Q: Explain why the instructor called “copy everything in and rebuild” not scalable.

A: Every change would mean committing and pushing as usual, and also remembering to rebuild the image. Only then would the image hold the right version of each file. (00:50:47)

Q: When did the instructor consider installing Git in the image and cloning the repository inside the container acceptable?

A: With only what students knew before this class, it is a valid approach, and he has used it himself. He has done it to build a container that mimics a student’s terminal, where he really does want to clone something. He added that better ways exist for an analysis environment. (00:51:51)

Q: What does “separate compute from source code” mean for the project’s image?

A: The image only holds the installed software and packages, and the code stays outside it. That is why the COPY hello.py ./ line was removed. (00:52:21)

Q: Why do pyproject.toml, uv.lock and .python-version still have to be copied into the image, even though the code no longer is?

A: Those files are what actually build the environment. Without them, the image couldn’t be built. (00:52:30)

Q: Why did removing the COPY hello.py ./ line still require rebuilding the image?

A: Deleting something from the Dockerfile is also a change to the image. You have to rebuild so that the step no longer runs and the file is no longer in the image. (00:53:16)

Q: Why did the instructor stress paying attention to the terminal prompt during this part of the demo?

A: He was jumping between his laptop and the container. The prompt is how you know which machine you are typing commands into. (00:52:59)




12. Mounting the project folder with -v (28.1.2 Mounting volumes to containers)
00:53:26–00:59:33

Q: Explain what -v (--volume) does when you run a container.

A: It mounts a volume: a folder on your computer appears inside the container. It works like a shared drive, so changes made inside the container are also on your computer. It isn’t a Google Drive-style sync. You are literally working on the same file, so you can’t clobber your own work. (00:55:34)

Q: Interpret -v "$(pwd):/workspace" in docker run --rm -it -v "$(pwd):/workspace" 2026-11-24-docker bash.

A: In Bash, the dollar sign pulls in a special variable or command, here pwd, so $(pwd) is your current working directory. The flag takes that folder and places it at /workspace in the container. On Windows you may need an extra slash, which the textbook shows. (00:57:13)

Q: Why did the my_secrets.txt demo need a second step to show that a mount differs from copying?

A: At first the file simply appeared in the container, which looked as if the instructor had copied everything in. Then he added a line (“i eat baby food.”) on his laptop, and cat in the container showed the new line straight away. That proved the container was live-updating from the shared folder. (00:58:53)

Q: Why is mounting the folder better than installing Git inside the container?

A: Git in a container needs its own SSH key or personal access token to push and pull. Every time the container is built, you would create a new key and have to register it again. Mounting avoids all of that, because Git keeps running on your laptop, where 521 already solved the problem. (00:55:24)

Q: Why is the folder mounted at docker run rather than set up during docker build?

A: During the build, all you can do is copy. Only when the container runs can you say “take this folder and sync it in this other location”. (00:56:13)

Q: With the project mounted, why is it still worth running uv run hello.py (for your milestone, uv run quarto render) inside the container?

A: Your changes still show up inside the container, so you can check that the code runs the way the container is set up. That gives you tests that your work runs on your local machine and in the container. (00:59:06)

Q: Why might Positron show an old version of a file that was changed through the mount?

A: Positron sometimes doesn’t notice that a file was updated on disk, so you have to refresh it. That is an editor problem, separate from the mount itself, which is a live sync. (00:55:59)




13. Keeping the image’s environment in /opt/venv (30.5 Why the packages go in /opt/venv)
00:59:33–01:06:53

Q: Explain what the .venv folder holds, and why python gave command not found in the container while uv run worked.

A: .venv holds the actual Python binary and the packages for the project. Plain python doesn’t exist on the container’s system. uv knows to look in the project’s environment folder, so Python is reached through uv run. (01:00:15)

Q: Why does a mounted .venv become a problem when you work in a group?

A: Teammates can be on different operating systems (Windows, macOS, Linux) and different CPU architectures (AMD64 and ARM64), which gives up to six different kinds of computer. The image was built under Linux, but the mount covered /workspace with your laptop’s .venv. The instructor compared it to copying a program from your Mac onto Windows and hoping it works. (01:02:40)

Q: If uv.lock records packages for every operating system, why doesn’t your laptop’s .venv work everywhere?

A: The lockfile has the information for all the other operating systems, but uv sync only installs for the system it is running on. A Mac has no reason to install the Windows versions, and sometimes they aren’t even compatible. (01:01:42)

Q: Which kinds of packages are most likely to break when an environment moves between systems?

A: Anything that “runs fast” in Python, or that is compiled or has some C code. pandas is likely to be a problem, while cowsay is too simple to show it. (01:02:33)

Q: Interpret the output of uv run hello.py in the mounted container before the ENV line was added: “Ignoring existing virtual environment linked to non-existent Python interpreter” and then “Removed virtual environment at: .venv”.

A: uv found the Mac’s .venv through the mount and saw that it pointed to a macOS Python that doesn’t exist in the container. It then deleted that .venv and created a new Linux one. Treat this as a warning: the mount is the same folder as on your laptop, so the container replaced your own computer’s environment. (00:59:06)

Q: How does ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv fix the mounted-.venv problem?

A: It tells uv where to save the environment and where to look for it. The environment then lives in /opt/venv instead of .venv, so uv ignores the mounted local .venv. The packages in /opt/venv were installed with the Linux dependencies at build time, so the image works whichever computer the project folder comes from. (01:04:46)

Q: Why must the ENV line come before RUN uv sync --locked, and why did the next build rerun uv sync?

A: The variable has to be set when uv sync runs, so that the environment is created in /opt/venv. Apart from that, its position doesn’t matter. Adding the line was a change higher up in the Dockerfile, so every step below it, including uv sync --locked, had to run again. (01:05:33)

Q: What does uv run which python printing /opt/venv/bin/python in the mounted container show?

A: It shows that uv now uses the image’s own environment in /opt/venv and no longer looks in .venv. The Linux container runs its Linux stack, your laptop keeps its own environment, and the container stays portable across operating systems. (01:06:37)




14. Docker Compose (33.1 Docker Compose to launch containers)
01:06:53–01:14:06

Q: Why did the instructor bring in a docker-compose.yml file?

A: The docker run command keeps getting longer: --rm, -it, -v, and a -p port for tools like JupyterLab or RStudio. A pasted command is hard to edit because you can’t click into it and have to arrow across. A file can be version controlled, its changes are tracked, and you run short commands instead of copying and pasting. (01:11:46)

Q: What is Docker Compose mainly designed for, and why is it still useful with one container?

A: It runs several containers at the same time. For example, a dashboard and the database it reads from are kept separate, because some people only care about the database. With one container it is a little overkill, but it still records all the run settings in a file. (01:09:04)

Q: Interpret each line of the class’s docker-compose.yml: services:, analysis-env:, build: ., image: 2026-11-24-docker and volumes: - .:/workspace.

A: services: lists the containers, and analysis-env is just the name of this one (it could be pizza). build: . builds from the Dockerfile in the current folder, and image: names the resulting image. volumes: mounts the current folder at /workspace, like -v. (01:10:25)

Q: How does docker compose build differ from the docker build and docker run commands used earlier in the session?

A: Before, you typed docker build and then a long docker run with all its flags. docker compose build reads the compose file and builds whatever it specifies. The file acts as all the flags of the docker run command. (01:11:09)

Q: What does --detach (-d) do in docker compose up --detach?

A: It turns the container on and runs it in the background, so the container keeps running while you get your terminal back. The instructor noted it isn’t very useful for this particular container. (01:12:14)

Q: What was the live docker compose up demo meant to show, and what happened instead?

A: Compose should have read the file as the flags of the earlier docker run command and started that container. Instead the terminal showed analysis-env-1 exited with code 0, and docker compose ps listed nothing running. The instructor did not resolve this in class and said he would fix the demo for next class. (01:13:50)




15. This week’s milestone: a Dockerfile for your analysis
01:14:06–01:17:04

Q: Explain how the TAs will check your milestone Dockerfile, and what that check proves.

A: The TAs take your repository, build a container from it, and try to run the analysis in that container, for example uv run quarto render on your report. That checks the goal of the course: a reproducible compute environment, where a file or image holds everything that needs to be installed. (01:15:09)

Q: Why might you add extra RUN lines for a text editor to your image?

A: The image from class had no text editor, which is why the instructor couldn’t edit a file inside the container. An editor lets you quickly change or look at files in the container. It is optional, and you should know why you add each extra line. (01:15:41)

Q: Give the instructor’s example of why some projects need system tools installed from Ubuntu.

A: Some Python packages need system tools underneath them. Geospatial analysis is the example: its packages are built on system libraries that you may have to install in the image. What you need depends on the tool stack your project uses. (01:16:16)




16. Docker Compose outside the course
01:17:04–01:20:07

Q: Why does knowing Docker Compose help you use open-source tools outside MDS?

A: Many open-source tools already ship a Compose file. Someone else has set up the machine and the software, so you don’t have to work out how to install it. If you know your way around Docker, you run docker compose up and the tool runs. (01:19:44)

Q: Interpret the parts of the Actual Budget Compose file shown in class.

A: Under services there is one container, called actual server. It comes from a published image and has ports, environment variables, volumes, and a health check that keeps the server alive. docker compose up -d downloads the image and runs the software, and you then connect to that port to use your own personal finance app. (01:18:29)

Q: How do tools such as Jellyfin, n8n or a recipe manager run once you start them with Compose, and where can they run?

A: They are web applications that run on a port and are used in a browser, just like RStudio. They can run on any machine you choose, from an old laptop in a closet to a cloud machine you pay for monthly. This is why containers are a useful skill beyond compute environments. (01:19:34)

title: Building a reproducible Docker + uv compute environment: review questions, tier 2 — Understand
text:
Date: 2026-11-24

Generated by qwen3.8-27b-sglang, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 2 of 5: Understand. Explain each answer in your own words before you read it; tier 1 (Remember) covers the facts, tiers 3 to 5 put them to use.

1. Warm-up exercise and course logistics
00:00:00–00:07:15

Q: Why did the course website’s colours and layout change?

A: Because the other instructor had the materials from her own class folded into the student repository. She teaches out of slide decks rather than summary notes, so the site now hosts her slide decks and the summary notes directly, meaning you no longer have to look in the UBC student repository for the notes. (00:04:44)

Q: Why are the per-lecture review notes written at different levels of Bloom’s taxonomy?

A: To test different levels of understanding. Some questions are basic factual ones, while others are more complicated and require you to actually know what is going on under the hood, so a lecture can be broken down into question-and-answer topics at each level. (00:05:48)

Q: Why does the instructor stress that everyone make sure Docker Desktop is actually running before running Docker commands?

A: Because if it is not running, any docker command will not reach the daemon — Docker usually prompts “do you mean to turn on Docker?” but you should not rely on that prompt and instead start it deliberately. It is flagged especially because one student in the class is on a Linux machine (which does not use Docker Desktop) while the rest are on Windows or Mac. (00:07:04)




2. Creating the repository with a coding agent
00:07:15–00:11:00

Q: Why did specifying the exact image name and the word Dockerfile in the prompt matter for the coding agent?

A: Because the information you feed into the prompt is what steers the result toward the correct answer; the instructor contrasted this with a vague “go make a thing” prompt from someone who has never heard of Docker, which would fail. Knowing the tooling vocabulary lets you point the agent at the right image and file. (00:08:38)

Q: What shell commands did the coding agent run before writing the files, and why?

A: It ran ordinary shell commands — ls, mkdir, and docker — to check its environment: whether docker and the gh command exist, and what type of computer it was on. This is the kind of setup an agent performs before writing the Dockerfile. (00:09:20)

Q: Why did the agent create a Makefile and a README.md even though the warm-up only asked for a Dockerfile?

A: Because those are things the instructor typically asks for, and his machine is set up with defaults learned in DSCI 522, so the agent reproduces those defaults; a student with their own templates can do the same. (00:11:24)




3. Reviewing the Dockerfile: the CMD command (29.2.1 CMD or ENTRYPOINT?)
00:11:00–00:12:45

Q: In the instructor’s “double-click a file” analogy, what does the CMD ["R"] line answer?

A: It answers “what opens by default” when you start the container with no other input; here, R opens. CMD is the line that sets that default command for the container. (00:12:28)

Q: Why did the warm-up Dockerfile need only the FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 line to meet the requirement, yet Claude still added CMD ["R"]?

A: The base-image line was enough to fulfill the task, but Claude recognized the base was an R container and inferred you would want to do R things with it, so it set R as the default command. (00:11:44)

Q: If the container’s CMD is ["R"], why is CMD a default rather than a hard requirement?

A: Because you can always give the container other parameters or commands when you run it to start something that is not R; CMD only controls what happens when you provide no other input. (00:12:19)




4. Building the image: docker build and the . (29 Customizing and building containers)
00:12:45–00:16:40

Q: Why does docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker . end with a dot .?

A: The dot comes from DSCI 521 week 1, where . meant “your current location.” docker build looks for a file called Dockerfile (capital D) by default and must be given a location to look; the dot says that default file is where you currently are. It is like a function that needs an input, so you cannot leave it empty. (00:14:46)

Q: Why did rebuilding the R image build so quickly this time?

A: Because the base rocker/r-ver:4.6.2 image was already available locally, so the build just ran through the steps fast. Had you pointed at an R version you had not downloaded, the pull step would have taken a couple of seconds to minutes depending on your internet speed. (00:15:45)

Q: What does the --tag (or -t) flag do, and why can the tag be anything?

A: It names the image you are building. The tag can be any name you choose — the instructor joked you could call it “pizza” — it simply labels the image locally. (00:14:13)




5. Running the image: docker run, --rm, -it (28 Using and running containers)
00:16:40–00:20:05

Q: What do the --rm and -it flags each do in docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker?

A: --rm makes the container ephemeral: when you exit (or Ctrl-C), it is deleted and any changes inside are undone. -it gives you an interactive terminal, meaning Docker captures what you type and passes it along to the container. (00:16:53)

Q: Why is a container run with --rm a good place to try a risky install such as PyTorch?

A: Because exiting deletes the container and undoes all of your changes — the instructor compared it to “another version of Git that automatically resets all of your changes.” If the install goes wrong, you just restart it and nothing bad has happened. (00:19:50)

Q: Why do you start at the root of the filesystem inside the container, and why is there no dedicated user?

A: Because a lot of Docker containers are set up with stuff just thrown in, so you end up seeing the operating-system files from the system level. For this class the container is a self-contained analysis setup, not a public service, so ownership is not a concern and commands start at the root. (00:18:24)

Q: Why does adding bash after the image name in docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker bash give you a normal shell instead of starting R?

A: Because a command after the image name overwrites the container’s default CMD of R; you then have normal terminal access, just like Git Bash on Windows or your terminal on a Mac, with the same type of access to that machine. (00:17:26)




6. Choosing a base image and installing uv (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:20:05–00:27:40

Q: Why did the class choose ubuntu:24.04 as the base image instead of keeping the R image?

A: Because the R image has a lot of R-specific stuff installed, and the instructor wanted something smaller to be respectful of other people’s disk space — he noted disk is “very expensive now because of the AI boom.” Alpine is even smaller but may need more manual installs, so Ubuntu is a good general starting point. (00:23:55)

Q: What is the COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/ line doing, and why copy from that registry image?

A: It copies the uv and uvx programs out of the image that uv publishes — “copy from one image to another image” — into the new container’s /usr/local/bin. The ghcr.io/... name is a registry path (a username, a repository, a version), and the version is pinned by tag the way a lockfile pins a package; this line comes straight from uv’s Docker guide. (00:25:14)

Q: What does WORKDIR /workspace do, and why set it?

A: It changes the working directory of the container (creating the folder if it does not exist), so when you start the container you land in /workspace instead of the root. The working-directory idea comes from DSCI 521 and from R/Python, where commands always need a starting point. (00:26:42)

Q: If most of the class is on Windows or Mac, why does a container run on Linux?

A: Because Docker containers work on top of some version of Linux; as soon as you are inside a container you are in the Linux world, most likely some version of Ubuntu. (00:23:33)




7. Pinning exact versions with pyproject.toml (22 uv: pinning exact versions)
00:27:40–00:34:45

Q: Why pin cowsay==6.1 with == rather than the cowsay>=6.1 that uv add writes by default?

A: Because a lower bound is a liability for a long-running project: if cowsay released 7.0 and you rebuilt the container, you would pull it, and when a package’s first number changes it is typically a backwards-compatibility-breaking change that can break the analysis. Pinning with == keeps the declared and locked versions identical, so a version only moves when someone edits the pin. (00:30:51)

Q: What does add-bounds = "exact" in the [tool.uv] table of pyproject.toml change?

A: It makes every future uv add write an exact version (==) instead of a lower bound (>=). Because the setting lives in pyproject.toml, everyone on the project gets the same behaviour from uv add. (00:31:06)

Q: What is the difference between pyproject.toml and uv.lock?

A: pyproject.toml is a general Python metadata file that holds the explicit versions you care about, while uv.lock pins the whole set (including downstream dependencies) to specific versions and is generated from the toml. You specify what matters in the toml and let the resolver handle the rest, though you may pin extra downstream packages if one updates and breaks things. (00:33:35)




8. The uv Dockerfile: three files and uv sync --locked (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:35:00–00:39:25

Q: What is the .python-version file for, and how does it differ from uv.lock?

A: It tells uv what version of Python to install; it is a separate file that says, if you were to install again, which Python version to use, because you do not always want the latest. uv.lock, by contrast, only locks the packages and their dependencies, not the Python version. (00:36:38)

Q: Why does the class pin the Python version at all?

A: Because the version of Python determines which dependency versions of a package are installable — not everything is compatible with the latest Python. His biggest example is PyTorch, which is almost never compatible with the latest Python, so you often have to pin a version; it also lets a package author test against an upcoming Python release. (00:35:59)

Q: What does RUN uv sync --locked do at build time, and what does the --locked flag add?

A: It installs the Python and the packages at build time, exactly as you would run uv sync on your machine. The --locked flag makes the step error out if uv.lock and pyproject.toml are out of sync — the instructor called these “little placeholders” so the build fails when you want it to, instead of quietly updating the lockfile inside the image. (00:39:14)




9. Layer caching and ordering (29.1.3 Layer caching)
00:39:25–00:44:30

Q: How does Docker’s layer caching work, and what does it mean for rebuild speed?

A: Docker saves each step’s result as a layer, and reuses a layer when that step and the steps above it have not changed; if a layer is unchanged it just uses the cached version. That is why a build can finish very quickly. (00:41:35)

Q: Why put the slow, rarely-changing steps near the top of the Dockerfile and the frequently-changing steps near the bottom?

A: Because any change to a layer forces Docker to rerun that layer and everything below it. If uv sync takes a long time and you copied your code before it, a typo in a script would make you wait through the slow install again — his example was that the tidyverse can take around fifteen minutes — so copying code last avoids that. (00:42:40)

Q: Why did copying hello.py at the end make the next rebuild fast?

A: Because copying a file is super fast, and the earlier uv sync layer was already cached, so only the copy step had to run. (00:43:54)

Q: What are the two ways to hand someone a working copy of your analysis once the image is built?

A: You can give them the Dockerfile and have them build it, or you can publish the image to a registry and have them docker pull it so the image is already there and they skip the build entirely. (00:44:16)




10. Separating compute from source code (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:49:36–00:52:15

Q: Why is copying all of your code into the image and rebuilding a poor way to work on an actively developed project?

A: Because it snapshots the code at one moment, so you then have to worry about who copied what and when, and remember to commit/push and re-copy and rebuild so the image matches. The instructor called this not a very scalable way to deal with work that is actively being developed. (00:50:27)

Q: Why is installing Git inside the container and cloning the repository a valid but inferior alternative?

A: Because the goal is to separate compute (the installed software/packages) from source code; installing Git just re-introduces the code into the container. The instructor said it is totally valid and he has done it (for example, to mimic a student’s terminal), but there is always a better way. (00:51:40)

Q: Why remove the COPY hello.py line from the Dockerfile while keeping the pyproject.toml, uv.lock, and .python-version copies?

A: Because the three package-listing files are required for the build — without them the container could not build — whereas the actual code is brought in another way (mounted) so the container holds only the installed software. (00:52:30)




11. Mounting volumes with -v (28.1.2 Mounting volumes to containers)
00:52:15–00:59:35

Q: What does the -v flag in docker run --rm -it -v "$(pwd):/workspace" 2026-11-24-docker bash do?

A: It “mounts” a volume: it takes a folder from your computer and makes it available in the container when it runs, so the container sees your live files. It is like a shared drive — changes you make on your computer appear in the container and vice-versa, because it is the same folder, not a synced copy. (00:54:30)

Q: Why use $(pwd) in the -v flag instead of a hard-coded path?

A: The $ in $(pwd) is a Bash way to pull in a command’s output, and pwd prints your current working directory, so the flag takes your current directory as the folder to share. That keeps you from hard-coding a local path. (00:56:59)

Q: Why is the mounting done in the docker run process rather than the docker build process?

A: Because at build time Docker can only COPY a snapshot of the files, but at run time it can mount a live folder and keep it in sync at that location. (00:56:06)

Q: Why don’t you need to install Git (with SSH keys or a personal access token) inside the container when you use the mount?

A: Because the shared drive means you are not doing git push/pull in the container; otherwise every rebuild would create a new SSH key you would have to re-register, which makes Git a big problem. You are just working by yourself on the same file, so there is no risk of clobbering a teammate’s work. (00:54:52)

Q: Why did the instructor warn to pay attention to the terminal prompt?

A: Because he was jumping between his local machine and the container, and mixing them up means you might edit or run commands in the wrong environment. (00:52:53)




12. Keeping the environment in /opt/venv (30.5 Why the packages go in /opt/venv)
00:59:35–01:07:00

Q: Why is a local .venv folder not portable across a team’s different machines?

A: Because the .venv holds the actual Python binary and the installed packages, all built for your machine’s operating system and CPU architecture. A team spans Windows/Mac/Linux and two CPU architectures (amd64 and arm64), so a .venv built on a Mac will not run on Windows — like you cannot double-click a Mac Excel file on Windows and expect it to work. (01:00:45)

Q: What went wrong when the project folder (with its local .venv) was mounted over /workspace?

A: The mount overwrote the image’s Linux-built .venv; running uv run in the container then found your local .venv, warned that it was “linked to non-existent Python interpreter,” removed it, and created a Linux one in its place. The result is that your Mac .venv is gone and the new one does not work on your machine. (01:02:40)

Q: Why set ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv in the Dockerfile?

A: It tells uv to put the project’s virtual environment in /opt/venv instead of .venv inside the mounted project folder, and it must be set before uv sync runs. Then the container ignores the mounted local .venv and uses the Linux environment the image built, which makes the image portable across the team’s machines. (01:04:35)

Q: Why does uv.lock already contain the package information for other operating systems even though uv sync only installed your local one?

A: Because the lock file records the hashes, locations, and dependencies for all the other operating systems; uv sync simply did not install them locally because you do not need them on your machine. When the container builds on Linux, it is those Linux entries in the lock file that are used. (01:01:22)

Q: How did the instructor verify that the container now uses /opt/venv?

A: By running uv run which python inside the container, which returned /opt/venv/bin/python, confirming uv was no longer looking in .venv. (01:06:27)




13. Docker Compose (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
01:07:00–01:14:05

Q: Why use a docker-compose.yml file instead of a long docker run command?

A: Because as the docker run command accumulates flags (-v, and -p for ports when using JupyterLab or RStudio on port 8787) it becomes long and painful to edit — you cannot click into the middle of a pasted command to fix it. A file is nicer because it can be version controlled and tracked, and you rely on simple commands to run. (01:11:28)

Q: What are the parts of the docker-compose.yml the class wrote for the analysis-env service?

A: It is a YAML file that, under services:, lists one container: build: . (build the image from the current Dockerfile), image: 2026-11-24-docker (the tag to build into), volumes: with .:/workspace (mount the current directory at /workspace), and optionally ports:. (01:10:34)

Q: Why is Docker Compose useful beyond a single container?

A: Because it is really for running several containers at once — for example a dashboard plus its database in a microservices setup, where some people only care about the database and you want separation between the pieces. One service is a bit overkill here but still useful. (01:08:53)

Q: What does docker compose up --detach do compared with docker compose up?

A: --detach (or up -d) starts the container in the background so the prompt returns, whereas a plain up attaches. In this session up created the container but it exited with code 0 immediately, and the instructor said he would fix the demo next class. (01:12:14)




14. The homework: a Dockerfile as compute environment (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
01:14:05–01:17:00

Q: Why might the Dockerfile need extra system tools beyond the Python packages installed by uv?

A: Because some packages need system tools to actually function — the instructor’s example was geospatial analysis, which needs many system tools and the underlying libraries those Python packages are built on. The requirement is that you understand why you are installing each thing. (01:16:16)

Q: How is this week’s Dockerfile milestone graded, and what does that grading check?

A: The TA takes your repository, builds a container from it, and runs the analysis inside that container. It checks that you have a reproducible compute environment — hand someone the Dockerfile or an image and the analysis is fully contained. (01:15:09)

Q: Why must the container mount your project folder and render with uv run quarto render?

A: Because the homework requires that you mount the folders that need to be mounted and that uv run quarto render renders your report inside the container, so the analysis is verified to run in the container and not just on your machine. (01:14:44)




15. Docker Compose outside the class (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
01:17:00–01:20:10

Q: Why can you stand up whole applications with just docker compose up if you know your way around Docker?

A: Because many open-source tools ship a docker-compose.yml that defines the service(s), image, ports, and environment variables; docker compose up then downloads the image, runs the software, and exposes the port, so you do not have to learn each tool’s install steps. (01:19:44)

Q: What did the Actual Budget compose file define, and what does docker compose up -d do for it?

A: It defines one service (actual-server) with an image, some ports, the environment variables it needs, some volumes, and a health check. docker compose up -d downloads the image, runs the software, and exposes the port, giving you your own personal-finance app in a browser. (01:18:19)

Q: Why do tools like Jellyfin, N8N, and the recipe app “run like RStudio”?

A: Because they all run on a port in a browser; the only thing you have to arrange is a machine to run them on, whether an old laptop or a machine you pay for in the cloud. (01:19:21)

Q: Explain how the compose-file skill used for the class’s compute environment applies to deploying these open-source apps.

A: It is the same skill: read the docker-compose.yml and run docker compose up, so Docker is not only for reproducible analysis — the same mechanism stands up whole applications. (01:19:56)

title: Docker Workflows with uv and Docker Compose: review questions, tier 3 — Apply
text:
Date: 2026-11-24

Generated by qwen3.6-35b-a3b, a local model, from the class recording, logs and readings. It can be wrong, or say things the class didn’t cover.

Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 3 of 5: Apply. Work each situation through before you read the answer; tiers 1 (Remember) and 2 (Understand) cover the facts and reasons it relies on.

1. Docker and AI-Assisted Setup Review (27 Introduction to containerization)
00:00:00–00:13:56

Q: A teammate clones your project and tries to run docker run but gets a vague error about not being able to connect to the Docker daemon. What did they likely forget to launch on their computer, and what happens if they run a Docker command while it’s off?

A: They forgot to launch Docker Desktop. When Docker Desktop is not running, any Docker command will fail with vague or unhelpful errors because the Docker daemon is unavailable. (00:07:00)

Q: You build an image from a Dockerfile that contains CMD ["R"]. You want to inspect the file system inside the container interactively instead of starting R immediately. How do you modify the docker run command to override the default command and get a shell prompt?

A: Append bash to the end of the docker run command (e.g., docker run --rm -it <image> bash). This overrides the CMD instruction, giving you standard terminal access to explore the container’s file system. (00:17:45)

Q: After running a container, you want to ensure that any files or changes made inside it are discarded and the container is automatically removed when you exit. Which flag must you include in your docker run command to achieve this?

A: Include the --rm flag in your docker run command. This flag ensures the container is ephemeral and automatically deleted upon exit, preventing orphaned containers from lingering on your machine. (00:16:53)




2. Building a Python Container with uv (30 Python packages with uv in an image)
00:13:56–00:33:35

Q: You are writing a Dockerfile to set up a Python project. Instead of relying on system package managers to install uv, you want to pull the exact binaries directly from Astral’s registry. How do you write a COPY instruction to install uv and uvx into the container’s PATH?

A: Use COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/. This multi-stage copy pulls the specific uv binaries from Astral’s official registry and places them directly into the container’s executable PATH. (00:24:53)

Q: You add a new dependency to your project locally using uv add pandas. When you rebuild the Docker image, you want to guarantee that the build stops immediately if your local uv.lock file does not match pyproject.toml. Which flag must you append to your uv sync command in the Dockerfile?

A: Append --locked to the uv sync command (e.g., RUN uv sync --locked). This flag forces uv to strictly verify that the lockfile matches the project metadata, halting the build with an error if they are out of sync. (00:38:26)

Q: You want to ensure that every package added to your project via uv add is pinned to an exact version (e.g., ==6.1) rather than a lower bound (e.g., >=6.1). What configuration must you add to the [tool.uv] section of your pyproject.toml file?

A: Add add-bounds = "exact" inside the [tool.uv] table in pyproject.toml. This setting forces uv add to write strict exact version pins instead of the default lower bounds, ensuring long-term reproducibility. (00:31:31)




3. Layer Caching and Dockerfile Optimization (29.1.3 Layer caching)
00:33:35–00:51:21

Q: Your Dockerfile takes a long time to build because it runs uv sync early on. You recently changed a single line of Python code in hello.py. If hello.py is copied into the image before the RUN uv sync step, how does Docker’s layer caching affect your rebuild time?

A: Docker will discard the cached uv sync layer and rebuild it entirely because a preceding COPY step changed. Since uv sync is computationally expensive, this forces a full reinstall of dependencies every time you edit your code. (00:41:53)

Q: You want to minimize rebuild times for a project where configuration and dependency installation rarely change, but application code changes frequently. In what order should you arrange the COPY and RUN instructions in your Dockerfile to leverage Docker’s caching effectively?

A: Place the static setup steps (like COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock and RUN uv sync) at the top of the file, and place the COPY instructions for your application code at the bottom. This way, changes to your code only invalidate the final layers, leaving the expensive dependency installation cached. (00:42:40)

Q: You decide to snapshot your entire project folder into the image by adding COPY . /workspace to your Dockerfile. Why is this approach problematic for active exploratory data analysis, and what workflow burden does it create when you edit a script?

A: This approach snapshots a static version of your files, so any edits you make on your host machine will not reflect inside the container until you rebuild the entire image. This defeats rapid iteration during analysis and forces you to commit and rebuild every time you tweak a script. (00:50:14)




4. Volume Mounting and Cross-Platform Environments (28.1.2 Mounting volumes to containers)
00:51:21–01:06:55

Q: You are actively developing a Python project and want to edit scripts on your host machine while testing them inside a Linux container. Which docker run flag and syntax should you use to mount your current directory into the container at /workspace?

A: Use the -v flag with the syntax -v "$(pwd):/workspace". This mounts the current working directory from your host machine directly into the container’s /workspace path, creating a live, bidirectional sync. (00:54:18)

Q: After mounting your local project directory into a container, you run uv run hello.py and receive an error about binary incompatibility. You realize the container is trying to execute a .venv folder that was copied from your macOS machine. How do you prevent uv from using the mounted local virtual environment?

A: Add ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv to your Dockerfile before running uv sync. This environment variable forces uv to install and look for packages in /opt/venv inside the container, completely ignoring the mounted local .venv folder. (00:53:59)

Q: You have set up UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv in your Dockerfile. You run a container with a mounted volume and want to verify that uv is correctly ignoring your host’s .venv and using the container’s isolated Linux environment. Which command should you run inside the container to check the Python executable’s path?

A: Run uv run which python inside the container. The command will output /opt/venv/bin/python, confirming that uv is ignoring the mounted local virtual environment and using the isolated, Linux-compiled packages. (01:06:12)




5. Docker Compose and Milestone Assignment (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
01:06:55–01:20:07

Q: Your docker run commands are becoming unwieldy with multiple volume mounts, port forwards, and environment variables. You decide to switch to Docker Compose to manage these parameters declaratively. What is the exact filename Docker Compose expects, and which top-level key defines the individual containers your project will run?

A: The file must be named docker-compose.yml. Inside the file, the services: top-level key lists the individual containers (e.g., analysis-env:) and their configurations. (01:07:43)

Q: You have a docker-compose.yml file that builds your image and mounts your local directory. You want to build the image exactly as specified in the compose file without typing out the full docker build command. Which command should you run from your project folder?

A: Run docker compose build. This command reads the docker-compose.yml file, locates the build: . instruction, and compiles the image using your Dockerfile. (01:11:28)

Q: You are submitting your milestone project and need to ensure the container runs your analysis automatically. The teaching assistants will grade your submission by pulling your repository, building the image, and executing your report. What specific command must your container successfully run to generate the final Quarto report?

A: The container must successfully run uv run quarto render. This command uses the container’s installed Python environment to render your Quarto reports, ensuring the final output is generated reproducibly inside the Docker environment. (01:14:44)

title: Building a Python analysis image with uv, volume mounts and Docker Compose: review questions, tier 4 — Analyze
text:
Date: 2026-11-24
Instructor: Daniel Chen
Tier 4 of 5: Analyze. Take each one apart yourself before you read the answer; tiers 1 to 3 cover the facts, reasons and steps it relies on.

1. Letting Claude Code build the repository
00:07:21–00:11:24

Q: Break down what Claude Code did when asked to create the 2026-11-24-docker repository with a Dockerfile. Which commands were checks, which built the project, and which results were the agent’s own choices rather than the prompt’s?

A: The checks came first. It ran ls, checked that docker and the gh command exist, and ran a Docker command to find out what kind of computer it was on. Then it built the project: it ran mkdir to make the folder, wrote a Dockerfile starting from Rocker, built the image, and ran a script in the container to test it. Its own choices were to put the folder in the temp folder instead of the Git folder, to add a README.md and a Makefile (the instructor usually asks for these, so they had become defaults), and to add CMD ["R"]. The instructor said the precise words in the prompt, such as Dockerfile and the image name, are what steered it to the right answer. (00:10:37)




2. Listing and building images (29 Customizing and building containers)
00:12:42–00:16:40

Q: Break down docker build --tag 2026-11-24-docker . into its parts. Then examine why the rebuild of the R image finished in 0.2 s with CACHED [1/1] FROM docker.io/rocker/r-ver:4.6.2.

A: docker build looks for a file named Dockerfile (capital D) by default. --tag (-t) gives the image a name, which can be anything, even pizza, and reusing an existing name rebuilds that image. The trailing . is not a full stop. It means “here”: the location to look in, a required input with no default, like a function argument. The Dockerfile had only one build step, FROM rocker/r-ver:4.6.2, and that image was already downloaded from last class, so the step was cached. A base image you don’t have yet would make that step take seconds or minutes, depending on your internet speed. (00:15:45)




3. Running a container, overriding CMD, and throwaway containers (28 Using and running containers)
00:16:40–00:20:07

Q: Separate the parts of docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker bash and relate each part to what happened in class. Why did this command give a shell at / when docker run --rm -it 2026-11-24-docker had started R?

A: --rm deletes the container when you exit. -it gives you terminal access and passes what you type through to the container. 2026-11-24-docker picks the image to start. Without anything after the image name, the image’s CMD ["R"] ran, so R started. Adding bash replaced that default, so you got a normal terminal instead. The Dockerfile set no working directory, so pwd printed / and the system folders were visible, and /home was empty because the image has no user. (00:17:45)

Q: Distinguish what survives and what is thrown away when you exit a container started with --rm. How does that split make a container a safe place to experiment?

A: The image survives. The container, with every change you made inside it, is removed when you exit. Starting again builds a fresh container from the unchanged image, so your earlier changes are gone. The instructor compared this to a version of Git that automatically resets all your changes. That is why something risky, such as installing PyTorch, belongs in a container: if it goes wrong, you restart and nothing bad has happened. (00:19:29)




4. Choosing a base image for a Python project (29.3 Choosing a base image for your Dockerfile)
00:20:07–00:24:22

Q: Set rocker/r-ver, ubuntu:24.04 and Alpine side by side, as the class discussed them. For each, what comes installed, how big it is, and how much you have to add yourself?

A: All three are Linux. Inside any container you are in the Linux world, most likely some version of Ubuntu, even on a Mac or Windows laptop. rocker/r-ver has a lot of R software installed, which a Python project doesn’t need, so it is the largest. ubuntu:24.04 is smaller, though still a fairly big image, and it is a good starting point: the class added uv to it. Alpine is even smaller, but you may have to install more yourself, depending on what you need. Smaller images matter because disk space has become expensive, and you should be respectful of other people’s disk space. (00:23:46)




5. Installing uv with COPY --from, and setting WORKDIR (30.2 A Dockerfile for a uv project)
00:24:22–00:27:42

Q: Break down COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/ into its source, what it copies, and its destination. Then relate the destination to what which uv printed later in the mounted container.

A: --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 names another image. Read it like a GitHub path: the owner, then the repository, then the version tag. /uv and /uvx are the programs copied out of that image. /usr/local/bin/ is where they land in the new image. This installs uv in a machine built from scratch, just as everyone installed uv at orientation. Later, which uv inside the container printed /usr/local/bin/uv, the destination from this line. (00:24:53)

Q: Examine WORKDIR /workspace in the Ubuntu image’s Dockerfile. What does it change for the build steps after it, and for a container started from the image, as the R image’s pwd and the Python image’s pwd showed?

A: WORKDIR /workspace makes /workspace the current directory and creates the folder if it doesn’t exist. For the steps after it, COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./ copies to ./, which is /workspace. For a running container, pwd printed /workspace straight away, while the R image without a WORKDIR had printed /. Landing in a project folder keeps you away from the system files at the root, where moving the wrong folder could break everything. (00:40:54)




6. Setting up the uv project locally (22.1 What uv add writes by default)
00:27:42–00:29:58

Q: Follow cowsay into the 2026-11-24-docker project, from uv init --bare to uv add cowsay. What does each step create or change, and what did uv add record in pyproject.toml compared with what it installed?

A: uv init --bare created pyproject.toml, with a name, a version and requires-python set to 3.14 or newer. uv add cowsay added cowsay to the dependencies list, which you could also type in by hand. It also printed Creating virtual environment at: .venv and installed cowsay==6.1. The project folder then held a uv.lock next to pyproject.toml. uv add installed exactly 6.1, but by default it wrote the lower bound cowsay>=6.1 into pyproject.toml. (00:29:38)




7. Pinning exact versions in pyproject.toml (22 uv: pinning exact versions)
00:29:58–00:33:35

Q: Trace how the line cowsay>=6.1 could break a long-running analysis. Which outside event and which rebuild cause it, and which two changes to pyproject.toml close that path?

A: >= allows any newer version. Suppose cowsay 7.0 comes out next week. Rebuilding the container next week then installs 7.0, and the package updates without anyone asking for it. A change in the first number usually means a backwards-incompatible change, so behaviour your code relies on in 6.x may not work in 7.x, and the analysis breaks. The fix is to write cowsay==6.1, and to add a [tool.uv] table with add-bounds = "exact" so that uv add always writes == from then on. The instructor warned that >= in a long project carries a real chance of this break. (00:31:06)

Q: Distinguish what pyproject.toml and uv.lock each record about versions. Which packages are left to the resolver, and what did the instructor do when one of them broke pandas?

A: uv.lock always pins one exact version of every package, but it is generated from pyproject.toml. pyproject.toml holds the versions you care about, pinned with ==, and the resolver picks compatible versions for everything else. That means downstream dependencies can still update on their own. The instructor once had pandas pinned when something far downstream updated and broke pandas. The fix was to add that downstream package to pyproject.toml and pin it too. (00:33:16)




8. Copying the environment files and uv sync --locked (30.2 A Dockerfile for a uv project)
00:35:01–00:39:25

Q: Separate the three files in COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./ by what each one controls. Then point out what RUN uv sync --locked checks between two of them.

A: .python-version (here 3.14) says which version of Python to install. uv.lock only locks the packages and their dependencies. pyproject.toml is the human-readable file that controls the rest. The Python version matters for the packages too: it decides which package versions can be installed, and PyTorch, for example, is almost never compatible with the newest Python. --locked requires pyproject.toml and uv.lock to be in sync, and the build errors if one is out of date, so it fails when you want it to fail. (00:37:44)




9. Building the image and layer caching (29.1.3 Layer caching)
00:39:25–00:44:33

Q: Examine the build output after COPY hello.py ./ was added as the last line of the Dockerfile. Which steps say CACHED, which step ran, and how does that relate to where the new line sits?

A: Steps 2/6 to 5/6 (COPY --from for uv, WORKDIR /workspace, copying the three environment files, and RUN uv sync --locked) all say CACHED. Only [stage-0 6/6] COPY hello.py ./ ran, and the whole build took under a second. In the first Ubuntu build, by contrast, RUN uv sync --locked was the step that stalled while it installed Python and cowsay. Docker reruns a changed step and everything below it, so a new line at the bottom reruns only itself. Copying a file is fast, so the rebuild was fast. (00:43:49)

Q: Distinguish the two habits for writing a Dockerfile that the instructor described: using as few instructions as possible, and ordering steps by how often they change. What does each one save, and does either change the resulting image?

A: Each instruction becomes a cached layer. Squeezing work into few instructions saves disk space. It doesn’t affect the outcome, and having more lines is fine when you are starting out. Ordering matters for rebuild time: a change to a layer reruns everything after it. So slow, rarely changing installs go at the top and fast-changing files, such as your code, go at the bottom. Otherwise fixing a typo in a script could make you wait something like 15 minutes for tidyverse to reinstall. (00:42:40)




10. Why not bake your code into the image (30.4 Run the project in a container)
00:49:36–00:53:26

Q: Break down what happens on every code change when a group’s code is copied into the image with COPY. What questions does someone opening the container have to ask, and which COPY lines stay in the Dockerfile once the code is taken out?

A: Every change means you git commit and push, and you also have to remember to copy everything in and rebuild, so the image holds the right version of each file. The code in the image is a snapshot. Anyone opening the container has to ask when the code was copied and which teammate copied it. That does not scale for work that is changing quickly, such as EDA during the milestones. The goal is to separate compute from source code. COPY hello.py ./ was removed, and removing a line is also a change that needs a rebuild. pyproject.toml, uv.lock and .python-version are still copied, because the image can’t be built without them. (00:50:47)




11. Mounting the project folder with -v (28.1.2 Mounting volumes to containers)
00:53:26–00:59:33

Q: Trace the my_secrets.txt demo step by step. At which step did the mount still look like a plain copy, and which step showed that it is a shared folder?

A: The file was created on the laptop with “i’m afraid of the dark.” Running docker run --rm -it -v "$(pwd):/workspace" 2026-11-24-docker bash and then ls showed it in /workspace. At that point it looked as if every file had simply been copied in. nano and vi gave command not found in the container, so the instructor added “i eat baby food.” on the laptop. Running cat my_secrets.txt again in the container showed the new line straight away. That proves the container and the laptop share the same folder. (00:58:53)

Q: Break down -v "$(pwd):/workspace" into its parts. Then deduce why this is a docker run option and not something written in the Dockerfile at build time.

A: -v (--volume) mounts a volume. In Bash, $(pwd) runs pwd and substitutes your current working directory. That folder appears at /workspace in the container. On Windows a leading slash may be needed, and the textbook shows each shell. A build can only copy files into the image. Only at run time can Docker take a folder from your computer and keep it in sync at another location. (00:56:06)

Q: Set two ways of getting a group’s code into a running container side by side: installing Git in the image and cloning the repository, and mounting the folder with -v. Compare what each needs for authentication and what happens each time the container is rebuilt.

A: Cloning is valid, and the instructor has done it to mimic a student’s terminal. But Git in the container needs its own SSH key or personal access token to push and pull. Every rebuilt container would make a new key, which you would have to register again each time, so Git becomes a big problem there. Mounting uses the folder on your laptop, where 521 already set up authentication. Inside the container, you are working on the same files as on your laptop. (00:54:52)




12. Keeping the image’s environment in /opt/venv (30.5 Why the packages go in /opt/venv)
00:59:33–01:06:53

Q: Examine what uv run hello.py printed in the mounted container before the ENV line was added. What does each line reveal, and what did it do to a folder your own computer uses?

A: The warning said the existing .venv/bin/python pointed to /Users/dan/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.14-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.14. That is the Mac’s Python, which doesn’t exist inside the Linux container. Using CPython 3.14.10 shows uv fetching a Linux Python instead. Removed virtual environment at: .venv and Creating virtual environment at: .venv show uv deleting the mounted .venv and rebuilding it. Because /workspace is the laptop’s own folder, the laptop’s .venv was overwritten. The instructor warned that this is like copying your Mac files to Windows and hoping they run. (01:02:40)

Q: Break down why a .venv that works on one teammate’s laptop can’t be trusted in the container. Name the two ways computers differ, what uv sync installs compared with what uv.lock records, and which packages are most likely to break.

A: Computers differ in operating system (Windows, Mac, Linux) and in CPU architecture (AMD64 or ARM64), which gives up to six combinations in one group. uv sync installs only for the system it runs on. uv.lock records the packages for every other system too, but they don’t get installed. The image is built under Linux, so a Mac .venv mounted over it is for the wrong system. Pure-Python packages like cowsay get away with it. Packages with compiled C code, such as pandas, anything that “runs fast” in Python, are where it breaks. (01:01:22)

Q: Trace the fix from ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv to the check inside the container. Where must the line go, what reruns when you rebuild, and what showed that the mounted .venv is now ignored?

A: The variable tells uv where to save and look for the project environment, so it must come before RUN uv sync --locked. Its exact position otherwise doesn’t matter. Adding it is a change to the image, so the rebuild ran uv sync --locked again, and this time the environment went into /opt/venv under Linux. In the mounted container, uv run which python printed /opt/venv/bin/python. uv now ignores the laptop’s .venv, so the image works whoever’s laptop the project folder comes from. (01:06:20)




13. Docker Compose (33.1 Docker Compose to launch containers)
01:06:53–01:14:06

Q: Relate each line of the class’s docker-compose.yml (services:, analysis-env:, build: ., image: 2026-11-24-docker, volumes: - .:/workspace) to the docker build or docker run option it stands in for. Which option did the class leave out?

A: services: lists the containers, here one named analysis-env, a name you choose (it could be pizza). build: . builds from the Dockerfile in the current folder, like docker build .. image: 2026-11-24-docker names the image, like --tag. volumes: - .:/workspace mounts the current folder at /workspace, like -v "$(pwd):/workspace". A ports: entry would replace -p for a tool like RStudio, but the class left it out. With the file in place, docker compose build reads it and builds, and the settings are version controlled instead of living in a pasted command. (01:11:09)

Q: Examine the terminal output from the class’s Compose attempt. Separate the commands that worked from the ones that didn’t, and point out the typo among the failures.

A: docker compose build worked. Every step was CACHED, and it ended with Image 2026-11-24-docker Built. docker compose up created the network 2026-11-24-docker_default and the container 2026-11-24-docker-analysis-env-1, then printed analysis-env-1 exited with code 0, so no container stayed running. docker compose up --detatch failed with unknown flag: --detatch, a misspelling of --detach. Then docker compose ps listed nothing, and docker compose exec analysis-env bash reported the service was not running. The instructor left this unresolved and will fix the demo next class. (01:12:32)




14. This week’s milestone: a Dockerfile for your analysis
01:14:06–01:17:04

Q: Break down how the TAs check this week’s milestone into its steps. What in the group’s repository does each step depend on?

A: First, the TAs build an image from the repository’s Dockerfile. That build needs the pyproject.toml and lockfile the analysis already uses, copied in so that the packages get installed. Next, they go into the container and mount the folders that need to be mounted, which brings the analysis code in. Finally, they run uv run quarto render on the report, and it should render inside the container. Extra RUN lines, such as a text editor or Ubuntu system libraries for geospatial work, are optional, as long as you know why you added each one. (01:15:01)




15. Docker Compose outside the course (33 Containers: Docker Compose)
01:17:04–01:20:07

Q: Break down the Actual Budget Compose file shown in class into its parts. Then relate what docker compose up -d does with it to what a user has to do.

A: It has services with one container, named actual server, which comes from a ready-made image rather than being built from a local Dockerfile. It also sets ports, environment variables the software needs to run, volumes, and a health check that keeps the server alive. docker compose up -d downloads the image, runs the software, and you connect to that port in your browser. The user doesn’t need to know how to install the software, just how to run Docker. The machine can be an old laptop in a closet or a paid cloud machine. (01:18:10)

text:
Date: 2026-11-24
